The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code read with section 34 for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars, from the evidence of an accomplice, that he had a liaison with his wife, and that the knife was used by him as a wrestler and that he was responsible for the murder. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was unsustainable. The evidence of the approver was sufficient to convict the appellant. The statement of the co accused was no corroboration of the accomplice 's story because the knife had been got prepared by accused No. 1 and the appellant had a torch and two others who were unarmed. The appellant had no motive for committing the murder, as he had no direct or direct relationship with his deceased wife. The conviction of an accused on the testimony of an approver was unsustainable, the law being that there should be corroboration of his story because of the fact that the accomplice made a confessional statement to his brother. Bhuboni Sahu vs King (A.I.R. , re Rajagopal, A.I.,R. and Bhubani Sahu vs The King, , referred to. In re Rajagopal (A I.R, and re Rajagopal , approved. The combined effect of sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Evidence Act is that there must be corroboration in the evidence Of an accomplice. It cannot be doubted that under section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure a conviction based merely on the uncorroborated testimony of the witness may not be illegal, but the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence on the sole ground that it is within their legal province to convict upon such unconfirmed evidence. Bhurboni Sahu v The King (I.L.R., and Bhurba Sahu vs State of Orissa, , approved, referred to, In re: Rajagopal, I.L., and B.S.K.B.658, distinguished. Held further, that in the present case there was no independent corroboration of an offence and the conviction was unsustainable on this ground. The fact that a conviction could not be said to be illegal merely because it proceeds upon the uncoroborated evidence of a witness without corroboration in materials particulars is not sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder under section 34 of the Penal Code.

The appellant was a servant of the State Electricity Board constituted under the . He was charged with having committed offences by obtaining loans from the Corporation. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted him under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On appeal the High Court acquitted the appellant but confirmed the conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal Code and therefore he could not be deemed to be a public Servant within the definition of section 2(1)(d); (ii) the High court had erred in holding that the appellant could not have been deemed to have been a public servants within the ambit of section 3, because (i ) the appellant had been performing only routine clerical duties and cannot be treated as an officer within the purview of cl. 12; and (iii) the conviction was bad for non compliance with the provisions of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. HELD: (1)(a) The officers and servants of the Board are deemed to function in pursuance of any of the provisions Of the . Therefore, the appellant is not a Public servant within section 21(9), cl. 13 of the Act. [690 B] (b) The word 'officer ' in section 21 cl. 2(l) of Indian Penal code means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government. He is either himself armed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is so The decision in Reg vs Ramajirao Jivbaji, ; , referred to. (2) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 2, cl., (12). [691 G H] (3) The words 'public servant ' and 'corporation ' are not defined in the Act, but they have reference to the definition in section 3 of the Indian Penal. Therefore, a person who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty, is one who was appointed to any office for that purpose. [688 B C] (4) The mere fact that he employed under the State Government or a Corporation is not necessarily connected with the entrustment and does not necessarily enter into the later act of misappropriation or conversion which is the act complained of. [687 E F] (5) The question whether sanction of the Government was required for the prosecution of a public officer or not, depends on the facts found in the present case. If the appellant did not fall within the terms of section 5, he could be deemed as a public employee within the term of 21(1), cl.(12). But if he was not acting or purporting to act in pursuance thereof, he would be a Public Servant within section 43 of the Penal Code. [689 E F; 690 A B] The appellant could only be deemed under section 21 (9) of Act, cl.(13) of section 1, cl, (12) of that Act, and not of section 25 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Therefore the appellant cannot be deemed a public man within the expression 'corporation engaged in any trade or industry ' as defined by section 21. [69 G H; 71 A B].

The appellant was convicted under r. 125(9) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ in default further rigorous imprisonment. He was also convicted under section 3 of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1962. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him by the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Mehkar. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: Rule 141 (2) does not matter because section 43 of the Rules requires the rules to be conclusive proof that he was so informed; but a failure to comply with sub r. (1) shall not preclude proof by other means that he had information of the order, (ii) The rule contemplates that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid, they would have effect notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with the existing legislation. [273 G H] In the instant case, r.141(2), is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). Section 3 gives very wide powers to the Collector to seize stocks but does not enable the Court to forfeit the juar. The rule must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [272 B C] In this case, the High Court has not been able to show that the rule was ultra vires as it lays a rule which is contrary to an existing Act but by implication. The rules must fall within the power given under section 33 (1), if otherwise invalid they would be effect notwithstanding the provisions contained in the law. [274 C D] In view of the decision of this Court in the case of State of Punjab vs M/s. Har Shankar, ; , the order of the High court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside and instead of the sentences awarded by the lower courts sentenced to imprisonment already undergone, is illegal. [275 E F] The appellant was rightly convicted under Rule 125(1) of Maharashtra Rules for contravening cl. 4 (b) of sub section (2).

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 109 and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that Sia was not aware of the date on which he had gone to the police station and that he should be put up for being identified in an identification parade. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The High court was dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal in his favour. There are certain important considerations which lend weight to the view of the trial court that it was unsafe to convict Sia on the ground that he knew the accused prior to or at the time of the occurrence. [626 D E] (2) The fact that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the alleged abettor is not enough compliance with the requirements of section 107. A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the crime, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not sufficient if an act on the part of the accused is shown to have been done in pursuance of the conspiracy. [625 E F] (3) The mere proof that the offence charged could have been tried without the participation of the other accused would not necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design. [613 G] (4) In order to constitute abetment, the abettor must be shown to having done an act which is without the common intention of the person committing the crime. Mere proof that a crime charged cannot have been com ported without the consent of the offender is not necessarily sufficient compliance with section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [526 C] (5) The evidence of identification is itself a weak type of evidence. But the point of time when the accused person was supposed to be shown as an eye witness, could not be said that he had abetted the crime and there was no reason for rejecting it. [511 D E]. (6) In the present case, the High Court was dealing in an appeal from acquittal in the first instance. The order of conviction and sentences were set at liberty forthwith.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction of accused 2 under section 307 read with s.34, Indian penal Code. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that when three of the four named accused were acquitted, the court could not convict only one of them on the basis of constructive liability. HELD : (i) It is well settled that common intention within the meaning of section 114 of the Evidence Act implied a pre arranged plan and the criminal act was done pursuant to the prearranged plan. The said plan may also develop on the spot during the course of the commission of the offence; but the crucial circumstance is that the said plan must precede the act constituting the offence. If that be so, before a court can convict a person under section 34 read with sections 149 and 147, it should come to a definite conclusion that the accused had a prior concert with one or more other persons named or unnamed, for committing the said offence. A Court cannot obviously make out a case for the prosecution which is not disclosed either in the charge or in regard to which there is no basis in the evidence. There must be some foundation in the Evidence that persons other than those named have taken part in the commission Of the offence and if there is such a basis the case will be covered by the third illustration. In support of the contention that a court, even in the first instance can acquit three of them, under section 304, read with Ss. 34, 34, I.P.C., though the other three named accused are acquitted, if it accepts the evidence that they acted conjointly in committing the offence, the prosecution must fail. [688 D E] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. (ii) The High court gave conflicting findings on the evidence adduced in the case and the conviction was not sustainable. [687 G] Mohan singh vs State, A.I.R. 1962 S.C. 848, followed. Mohan Singh v State of Haryana, A, I, R. , referred to. (iii) The judgment of the High Court cannot stand. It is visualizing a case where there was evidence on the record from which the court can come to such a conclusion.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron ore, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the levy of duty on the ground that the goods were undervalued and that the rate of duty was higher than the rate applicable to the goods. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had no fundamental right to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the material change in section 15(1)(b) of the Act was only the substitution of the words "the rate of excise duty" and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner as such has no fundamental rights to clear any goods imported without payment at that rate or without having the matter determined by the procedure envisaged and enjoined by law for that determination. [626C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner as a manufacturer was willing to pay the duty when the goods crossed the customs barrier and were in the process of being cleared, but could not be cleared because of the prohibitory orders of the Income Tax Department under section 102 of the . [627D E] 2.1 It is clear that the relief under Article 32 of the Constitution is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. The petitioner has no right to ' clear any ' goods imported after payment at the rate prevalent on a particular date or not has to be determined under the four corners of the , [628F G] 2:2 In view of the language used in section 14(1) of Act, it is difficult to accept that the prohibitory order, arbitrary or not, would postpone the date of clearance and as such would postpone its determination. The provision of section 15 (1)(a) clearly requires that the rates of duty, rate of exchange and tariff applicable to a goods shall he the rate & valuation in the force on a specified date or that the value valuation in respect of the consignments stored in the warehouse prior to the coming into force of the Ordinance has not reached the date under the 4 corners of . [625E F] 2 :3 The petitioner, as such, has no legal right to make any claim within the procedure contemplated by the Act. [625H; 626A] Prakash Cotton Mills (P) Ltd. vs B. Sen & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant, who was the managing director of a company which was in liquidation, applied for a decree against the respondent for partition of his joint family property and possession of his separate share. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court held that the debt was not avyavaharika as there was no evidence to support the finding of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the debt in question was not an accretion to the creditors of the father and therefore, the debt could only be challenged on proof of the debt of the son; (2) the liability of the sons was not dependent upon the father 's power to alienate the share of his sons but on the principle of independent coparti tional rights in the sons which were not immoral or illegal; (3) the claim for partition was not a bona fide one and as such the suit was not maintainable. HELD : (i) The liability of a father to discharge debts of the deceased father is not dependent on the father who has no power to sell his share of the property but on principle of pious obligation imposed on the sons under the Mitakshara law. [557 B] (ii) The debt of a Hindu father is an incident of birth, giving to the sons vested right in the coparcenary property and the remedy of the adopted son is to prove in appropriate proceedings taken by them the illegal or immoral purpose of the debts and partition cannot relieve the sons of their pious obligation or their shares of their liability to be sold or be a means of reducing the efficacy of the attachment or impair the rights of the creditor. [558 C D] (iii) The legal position is that even after partition, the sons could not claim any right in respect of the properties which were allotted to them on partition and the property was sold and the purchaser bought it intending to be the whole coparcenary estate, the presence of the two sons coupled with the attachment itself would not make the joint family estate liable for the debts of their father. [559 E F] (iv) The right of the mother to alienate for payment of personal debt is ended by partition in severalty and therefore the liability to discharge the debts does not arise on proof by the sons or the immoral obligation imposed upon them under the statute. [560 G H] (v) The position of a son who is liable to pay his share in the joint property as to what passes to the auction purchaser is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale, what the court intended to sell and what the purchaser intended to buy and did buy and what he paid for. [561 G H; 561 A] (vi) The words di right, title and interest " occurring in section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code have the same connotation as they had in the corresponding words used in the Code of Civil Procedure existing at the time the Bombay Act was enacted. Therefore, where a pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and the suit is brought on the record and the sale proceeds are to be paid off, there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the attached property. All that results from partition is that the right of father to make an application for partition operated as severance of status takes place pending the execution proceedings because the pious obligation of the appellants to discharge their debts of his father which were never tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious duty imposed on them by the Mitakshara Law.

The petitioners, who were the members of the Bar Association and the Additional Chief Secretary to the Government of Delhi, filed a complaint against them before the Metropolitan Magistrate alleging that they had committed offences punishable under section 178 I.P.C. The learned Magistrate after recording their statements in the case, passed an order directing the filing of the complaints and criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Committee. The petitioners challenged the aforesaid orders by way of writ petitions before this Court contending that the provisions of sections 8 B and 8 C of the Act were not applicable to those witnesses falling under section 8 B of the . Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order passed on 29th June 1988 is set aside and the petitioners are quashed and they are discharged from the Committee as per law. [521D] 1.2 The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8B of the Delhi Administration and its police officers. Taking into consideration all the aspects of the case it is obvious that the Committee should not have in the circumstances of the present case directed the filing the complaints, and the criminal proceedings started against the Petitioners before the committee. [525E] 1:3. The Committee shall have considered the question whether the persons were entitled as persons under section8 B of Delhi Administration to be treat as persons covered by section8B of Delhi Police Act, 1980 before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the end of inquiry. If the Committee had found that the petitioners was covered under section 9 B then perhaps they would not have been asked to get in the witnessbox for being examined till their end of the inquiry. [511B C] 1 :4. The committee should have consider whether the Petitioners were entitled, as persons, governed by Section 8B, before asking the petitioners to get the witnesses examined for being re examined. If they otherwise satisfied it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person. Such person would thereafter be governed by s.8 B. [51C D] 2. The inquiry of the Committee directing the filling up of the complaint and criminal proceeding initiated against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under Section 178 I P.C., is not contemplated under section 6B of that Act. It is enough if at any stage the Commission considers it necessary, to inquire whether the complainants were entitled or not to be considered as persons bound by section 9 A of the , and the Committee would have then asked them to give evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the end Of the inquiry [523D E] 3. The action of the committee in asking for a party has the right of cross examination or not shall make any difference if they otherwise satisfy the conditions mentioned in section 8 A. The issue of such a notice is not envisaged under section 10 C.P.(C) and 8 B. (a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. [500E F] 4. If three persons referred to above to whom notices under section 7 have been issued are to be examined even according to the Committee at the beginning of the enquiry there is no justifiable reason to deny the same treatment to the petitioners. [506F G] 5. The procedure adopted by the Committee in directing the file of the complainants and criminal cases initiated against them should be quashed and the Court accordingly quash the said orders of the Commis sioner and also the criminal proceeding.

The Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, were framed under section 3 of the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Act, 1959. The rules provided that a lump sum payment shall be made in lump sum of which the amount shall be fixed by the State Government from time to time by notification in the official gazette. The petitioners who were partners of a firm, challenged the validity of the Rules and contended that the tax was not laid upon them as they had been assessed to tax on fares and freights but upon "fares and freight" which were different entities and in support of their contention it was urged that the Act did not provide for the levy of lump sum in lieu of tax on passengers and freight. The High Court held that the rules and the notification were invalid as they contravened articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression "passenger" is used in article 301 and not in article 304 of Part 1 of the constitution. [526 B] (ii) The word "pay" was used in the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 and to which reference will be made separately. In the case of goods where the weight, bulk or nature of the goods may be different, and a scale of payments must inevitably depend on the actual fares or freights. [525 C D] (iii) The tax is not one of the taxes but upon passengers and goods. The tax was therefore not leviable under Entry 56 of List II. [500 E F] (iv) The levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301, 304 and 304. [426 B C] (v) The words "taxes on passengers" in article 305 are wide enough to include taxes which are levied upon persons and goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. No distinction between operators and freighters is made between operators who are carried or goods transported without the charge of fares or transportations. If the two Rules and the notifications are read together, the mandatory language is limited to the prescribing of the lump sum rates. [54 D E] (vi) The proviso to section 3(3) lays down that even if passengers or goods are not transported, the tax has to be paid as if fare or freight had been charged. This clearly shows that the Legislature was competent to make the payment compulsory and the imposition of the tax is justified on the assumption of a return in the shape of conveniences. If this be the true import of a tax, it is but natural that taxes will be graded according as they involve more or less of such conveniences. They will be heavy in case of roads requiring greater expenditure to construct and to maintain, than in case where the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan.

The appellant was a private limited company. The raw material for its manufacturing process was tin plates. The appellant served notice of retrenchment on the respondents, who were sought to be retrenched in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. The workmen demanded a revision of wages on the one hand and higher wages on other. The Labour Court, after examining the evidence led before it, held that the reasons stated in the notice were not bona fide and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and, therefore, the retrenchment was illegal. The High Court also awarded full back wages to the workmen as back wages. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective from the day on which they were sought lo be retrenched; (2) the non supply of raw materials or reciles for the livehood could not be a mere pretext or rust to toring the workmen, by depriving the them of the basic right of livelihood, and (3) the failure of the management consequent upon the refusal of workmen to accept the workmen 's demand for revision of their wages would amount to unfair labour practice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was wrong in holding that the retrenchment is invalid and it was motivated and the relief granted by the Labour Court was not only against the dismissal but also against the payment of retrenchment compensation. [571C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant has not shown whether his salary and perks have been adversely affected; whether his wages have been legally protected or the doctrine of unjust enrichment does not haunt him any right to claim relief of back wages, and the direction for reinstatement is not only illegal but also ultra vires. [572F] 1:3 The Labour Law Journal, Vol. I, p. 509 referred to. 1.4 In the present case, there was no material on record to show that the Managing Director had made any sacrifice; whether he was always ready to work but they were kept away therefrom. If the services were not terminated the workmen ordinarily would have continued to work and would have earned their livelihood. The workman, however, did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated. [573F] 2.1 In the matter of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the workman continues to be in service. The employer must establish the circumstances necessitating departure. At that stage the Tribunal will exercise its discretion keeping in view all the relevant circumstances. But the discretion must be exercised in a judicial and judicious manner. [574F] 3.2 The question whether the workmen should be awarded full or partial back wages has to be decided on the facts of each case. In the field of industrial adjudication, a declaration cannot be given by the Supreme Court that the terminated services are bad and/or sacrifice is expected of him. It would mean that the employer has taken away illegally the right to the work of the workman contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived the workmen of their earnings. If it was found that the management had taken away wrongfully the Managing Directors and the Directors shall not charge any fee for the services rendered as Director, no dividend shall be paid to equity shareholders, and if the employer is called upon to pay full back Wages with interest, the Managing director shall not be paid any overriding commission, if there be any, on the turnover of the company since this will account for the pragmatic approach of common sacrifice. [575F G] 4.1 It would be a motion addressed to the discretion of the Tribunal. Full back wages would be the normal rule and the party objecting to it must establish its circumstances necessitating departing from the normal standard. To substantiate the contention that this is an exceptional case for departing therefrom, the Court will have to consider all the facts and circumstances of each individual case.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge for committing murder of his wife. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the confessional statement made by the accused to the police regarding the father of the boy was inadmissible in evidence and no oral evidence in respect of that confession could be relied upon. HELD : (i) It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender are not specially empowered during the investigation of a case. The discovery and the arrest of an accused person is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation. [434 B] (ii) The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house of the accused. It is not necessary to dilate upon this aspect of the matter because, even after excluding the evidence of the witnesses raising hue and cry or going to the Police even though his wife was murdered in his house, the accused would have raised hue and cries. [427 C D] (iii) The confession made by him to the Magistrate was inadmissible under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [ 428 E F] Nazir Ahmed vs State of Delhi, ; , referred to. (iv) The statement recorded by a second class magistrate under section 161 Cr. P.C., is admissible in evidence. [534 G H] (v) The accused was not given any oral or documentary evidence to show that anyone noticed the accused at the film show. He was only with the deceased at the time of occurrence. It was not necessary for him to examine any other person. [416 D E] (vi) The High court altered his sentence into one under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced the accused accordingly. [414 G H; 415 A B] Nazir Ahmad vs State, ; referred to, (vii) The fact that the accused was taken by the rolice to the house at about 9 30 p.m. when he was murdered there with the Khokhri and the fact that he had not been examined as a witness did not affect the guilt of the appellant. [413 C] (viii) The mere fact that a person who was responsible for the murder is charged under section 120B I. P .C., does not make him guilty of the offence charged. It would be an unnatural construction of the section to hold that these safeguards were not thought necessary and could be ignored where the confession has been made to a magistrate of a lower class and that such a Magistrate was free to give oral evidence of a confession made to him. [411 D E; 414 A B, F G] (ix) The appellant had gone to the film showing that the father had been born to her as a result of her adulterous conduct. Had he been the son of the accuse, the crime would have been committed by the appellant and none else who caused injuries to Churi deceased as a consequence of which she died.

The plaintiff sued the defendant for a sum of Rs. 80,507/ with interest at 6 per cent from the date of the mortgage and future costs. The defendants contended that the suit was barred by section 43 Of the Transfer of Property Act, as it was not instituted within three years of the date on which the mortgage was created. Held, that the plaintiff had no right to sue for a half of the amount due under the mortgage from the dates of the mortgages and the only remedy available was by way of suit for recovery of the balance of the property. The provisions Of section 43 of the Transfer Of Property Act did not apply to a mortgage and the suit must be dismissed as barred by limitation. Held further, that in view of the provisions of the Limitation Act, the plaintiff 's suit must fail. Section 82 of the Indian Contract Act does not deal with mortgages but only deals with the rights which are payable under them. The words "the mortgagor who redeems and directs that in the absence of a contract to the contrary he shall be reduced to Rs. 2,000/ . " In the present case the plaintiff was entitled to claim interest on the amount of Rs, 80,057/ with costs. Held also, that section 43 did not deal expressly with mortgages. The suit was therefore governed by section 82 Of the Indian Limitation Act and the question whether the suit mortgage was inartistically worded the plaintiff has no right under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 82 of that Act to claim a sum equal to Rs, 2,00,000. Held per KANIA C.J., PATANJALI SASTRI, MEHR CHAND MAHAJAN and GHULAM HASAN JJ. (FAZL ALI J. dissenting) The suit must therefore fail. The plaintiff had not used the word "subrogation" in section 43 as it stood before the amendment of 1956. It was open to a court to give a plaintiff such general or other relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in costs. In the absence Of agreement be tween the parties as to the figures, I would remand the case to the High Court for determining the amount payable by the plaintiff on the date fixed by section 83 of the Act.

The appellants, who were unsuccessful in the Public Works Department, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that they had been selected for the post of Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) by the Selection Committee constituted under Rule 7 of the Karnataka State Service Rules, 1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3% of the total marks was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 If the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of tho total marks and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appellants were bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [497C D] 1.2 The selection for appointment to the post was made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the Rules are clearly in violation thereof. [498D E] 1:3 The Rules are clear in violation ly in the instant case. There is no allegations of any mala fides in the matters of the appellants ' appointment. However the Rules were clearly in contravention of the decision of this court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. S.C.R. 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors, ; , referred to. 1:4 The Rules were not in existence. No order as to costs. [598F G] 2.1 The selection was made as per the Rules for filling up of Asstts sional posts of Civil Engineers and 100 Mechanical Engineers initially and subsequently added additional posts of 150 Civil Engineers, thus in all 450 Civil Engineers. Both the appellants applied for the posts of their choice. They were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for these posts secured higher marks than the appellant. The appellants filed a petition before this Court challenging their selection on the grounds that the quota prescribed for viva examina tion was 33. 3. The Rules being clearly in breach of the ratio laid down by this Court in Ashokkumar Yadav & ors. vs state of Haryana and Ors., , [1988) Suppl. SCC, 657 and the appellants had already joined the posts, there is nothing to interfere with the rules under which the present selection was held. [500E F] 2:2 The Rules have been clearly in violated by the High Courts. The rules are clearly not in violation or infringement of the principles of the matter. However since the marks were clearly, in violation o f the decision taken by this court on 4th September, 1991, the selection was quashed and the selections were made according to the Rules.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 302 read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the fateful day, the deceased came to his house and informed him that his wife had been murdered by him. On 14th July, 1982, he started giving reli gious discomfort to his wife. He tried to make his followers believe that he had seen God and if they followed him and his preachings, they too could see God. The deceased was taken out of the room of the Collectorate and was chased by P.W.2. On the same day, P.Ws. 3 and 4 were also arrested. The appellants were put on trial along with other accused persons for offences under sections 302 readwith section 120 B of the I.P.C. The Trial Court acquitted all the accused except the appellant No. 1. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State against the acquittal of the appellants. In this appeal, it was contended that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence that the deceased was beaten up badly after being apprehended by the mob soon after the bomb burst and that he was falsely implicated in the murder case. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As this Court pointed out in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , the confes sion of a Co accused is neither substantive evidence nor substantive evidence and therefore, would not be admissible against the other accused person at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. [408B C] 1.2 The confession was voluntary and truthful. It was true that a set of witnesses who were present when the bombs were fired at the deceased, were not examined in the case. Obviously, when Yadav was beaten upto the police station, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in the fight. It is true as argued by Mr. Jai Narain for the State that it is difficult to support the charge of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413C D] Kashmira singh vs State Of Madhya Pradesh ; , followed. 1:3. The confession is not admissible against other accused in the present case. The conviction of the appellant under section 3 of the Explosive Substance Act and the sentence as awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court are set aside. [414D] Kashrik Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; ; KashmiraSingh vs State, ; and Kashmira Kaur vs State (Delhi Administration), ; , referred to.

The appellant company was a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson Private Limited. The last of the companies was governed by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and the workmen were paid dearness allowance on different scales depending upon the rates prevailing in comparable concerns. The appellant company claimed that the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowance should be applied to the industry and that if an employee was dismissed or discharged for misconduct which caused financial loss to the employer, gratuity should be paid to him. The Tribunal held that the workmen cum region was entitled to dearness allowance at a certain rate and that the company had failed to make the comparison between the employers and employees of different categories of employees with which the Tribunal had compared the appellant 's concerns. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant company could not be said to have committed an error in applying the industry ' cum region test for fixing wage scales and dearness allowances. The award relating to wages and Dearness allowance was therefore justified on the ground that it paid scant regard to the exemplars filed before it and did not care to make comparison with the total wage packet of comparable concerns and thus arrived at a just figure for basic wage, for each category of factory workmen. (ii)The Tribunal had no where considered what would be the total wages packet in fixing wages, and dearness and other subordinate staff were concerned. The tribunal was right when making comparisons took into account the total pay packet in fixed concerns and also taking into account its trend in that region. (iii)The award relating back to the appellant for the reason that it had not considered the total salary packet in comparable concern was justified. (iv)The appellant could not claim any interference with the order of the Tribunal fixing the date from which the award would come into force. The first reference was made to the Tribunal on April 8, 1959, while the second reference was pending before the Tribunal. The second reference did not relate to the region aspect of the industry, namely, that it was a comparable concern and had no relation with the same industry. (v)The second reference related to the year 1950 and the Tribunal was in error in putting the subordinate staff in the same category as those of the factory workmen who were engaged in different lines of business for the work of clerical and subordinate staff.

The appellants filed a suit against the mortgagees for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof. The mortgagees resisted the suit on the ground that the mortgage was not a valid one, that the mortgagees were agriculturists and that they were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that as the mortgagors had failed to repay the amount due under the mortgages, the mortgagees could not claim redemption of the mortgaged property. Held, that in view of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as it stood at all material times, the suit was barred by limitation. The provisions of section 73 of the Act were applicable only when there are more occupants than one and the notice of relinquishment must be given by the registered occupant. In the present case, the appellants did not purport to file the same on behalf of annappa nor had they any right to do so; by reason only of his being the registered occupants he could have no right to give such a notice without reference to the other occupants so as to effect their interest in the occupancy. The Rajinama passed by Shiddappa did not affect the right of an heir, if there were more occupants, than one who had the right to take possession. The appellants did nothing more than plead that the Rajinma was the manager and karta of the joint family and that he had no right in the property. Lalchand Sakharam Marwadi vs Khendu Kedu Ughade (1904) L. R. 32 Ind. App. Cas. 703, referred to. The mere assertion of an adverse title on the part of the appellants cannot affect the rights of other occupants. In view of the observations of this Court in Lalchand, Sakharam marwadi vs khendu kedu Ubha Deorah (1906) L R. 33 Ind. Cas, 32 Ind App. Cases No. 22 Ind.App. Cas., No. 23 Ind.app. Cas,. No. 24 Ind. A.I.R. , referred to and distinguished. The order of the High Court in Letters Patent Appeals was correct and the principal contention that annappenna had not been impleaded as a party to the appeal, must fail. Khiarajmal vs Daim (1903) L C. R., 32 Ind Cas. 32 Indianapplies at all materials times.

The respondent, a company, was an accessory anti not a part of the typewriter. The respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry 2 of the Schedule to the Act, but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed under the Notification and (2) ribbon was an integral part of a typewriter, taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966. The Sales Tax Officer held that carbon papers did not contain any technical or doubt as to the contents of the schedule to the Notification but a specialized article used by the respondent in printing and supplying the goods from its head office at Kanpur which was used for obtaining prints and trenches. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% prescribed under Entry 2, List II of the Seventh Schedule to. the Act was challenged by the appellant before the High Court. The High Court held that the carbon paper did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that the respondent had no competence to assess the carbon papers on the basis of carbon papers in question. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of tile denomination of a specialised Article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [840 D] (2)(a) The word ' paper ' in the common parlance or in the com plaint means a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing, or printing or for packing or for drawing on or for decorating, or cover ing the walls. Now carbon paper which is manu facture is not paper as envisaged by entry 2 of Notification No. ST 3124/Xl02(4) dated 1st July 1966 issued under section 3 A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. [881 D] In the instant case carbon paper was not paper within the meaning of serial No. 7A of the notification. The mere circumstance that the words 'dyes and colours ' used in entry 2 were not decisive or a part thereof did not attract tax as per Entry 18 of the Second Schedule to Act.

The respondents were employed in the appellant Mills at Amroha. The respondents were employees of the appellant Mill at Amroha and the mills at Bulandshahr. They were retrenched by the appellant on the ground that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under Standing order No. 1, but the Labour Union, who was a party to the dispute, raised an industrial dispute and made its award holding that the management had no right to transfer the respondents 1 to 4 to the new factory and therefore the order dismissing them was illegal. The appellant contended that the right to have the respondents ' services transferred to another factory was implicit in every contract of service and as such the respondent could not be transferred to a new concern, and that the appellant was not entitled to any of these amenities. Held, that the employer had no power under Standing Orders No. I to transfer his employees to a newly created one of the ordinary incidents of service in the Bank. The employer in the present case has no such right. Mary (Anamalai Plantation) Workman 's Union vs Seliparai Estate, ; , followed. In the instant case, the respondents had been employed in a business or concern and the question that arose was whether the appellant had the right of transfer to another place where he chooses to start his business subsequent to the date of his employment. Mary, (Ananamalai plantation) workman 'S, Memp & Co., Ltd., vs Ali Hasan, A.I.R. 1950 All. 816 and Mary, , referred to. The question whether a person employed in an industry can be transferred under the contract of services or under any statutory provisions depends upon the facts of each case. In all such cases, when a person joined such a service, the latter is transferred to the later employer at a stage subsequent to his appointment and vice versa, according to the exigencies of work. The respondent had no such rights as he had been appointed in the previous season during the relevant period. Mary was an employee of the respondent bank and therefore, the appellant could not have the right under Standing orders No. l(a) to transfer him to a different concern. Mary is anamalaiplantation workman and the appellant is an industrial tribunal. The Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside the finding of the State Industrial Tribunal as it did not give rise to any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. Mary.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948. In 1965, the special contribution was to be made by the respondent employer under section 73 of the . The respondent company was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the Act until the provisions were enforced in the area where the appellant 's factory was situated. The appellant company challenged the liability to pay special contribution under Chapter VA of the , before the High Court, which held that the contribution payable under Chapter IV A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant Company. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contributions payable under Ch. V A were not a fee but a tax and therefore, the Act does not contemplate rendering of service or conferment of an benefit to be quid pro vised for payment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It was not considered fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit clauses are extended should alone make contributions and thereby help to set up a corporation. [1094C] 2.1 The object is to make appropriate provisions for securing the right to work, to education and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of any undeserved want, to make legitimacy or not at all. The payment of contribution by an employer towards premium (what else is it ?) of an employee 's compulsory insurance under the falls directly within entries 23 and 24 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. [ 1094D E] 2:2.1 There is no reason to brand or stamp the contribution as a tax or fee in order to seek to legitimise it. Legitimacy need not be sought fictionally from Entry 97 of List I, but simultaneously with the power entrusted in respect of entries 23 & 24 of list III. Even if the charge is to be construed as a fee as the High court has done, it appears to be justifiable on that basis too. [1194F G] Basant Kumar vs E. S.I. Corporation, ; , referred to.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that they have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a longer period. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [620C D] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position. This Court in spite of the fact that the petitioners are being paid their daily wages in spite thereof, they have not been paid the minimum wage in spite Of there being no work available for them. [625D E] 3. In spite of this conclusion, the question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise. The Court directed that all the 63 daily rated workers including the 54 petitioners mentioned in the Annexure R V to the counter affidavit together with Annexure RV thereto be given the benefit of the voluntary retirement scheme framed by respondent No. 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues. [720E F] 4. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief from this Court on the ground that they were not regular employees, but only kept on rolls and paid in spite the fact of being no worked for them, and as there is a vacancy, available for re spondent No. 1 is not absorb ed against it. [650F G] 5. The writ petition must accordingly fail. [651B C] 6. The direction given by the High Court to the Special Leave Petition is set aside and the special leave petition is dismissed. [662C D]. 7. The Special Leave Petitions are, therefore, dismissed.

The plaintiffs claimed to have purchased the entire property as transferees from the National Agency Co operative Bank Ltd., who had been impleaded as defendants. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court upheld the title of the plaintiffs to the share in the property. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the sale in execution of a mortgage decree obtained by the National agency Co operative bank was valid and extended to the entire interest in the mortgaged property and (ii) even if the transfer was not effective, the suit was liable to be dismissed. HELD : (i)(a) The question whether an alienation is a benami or not must depend on the facts of each case. It is well settled that a sale by a person who has no right to bring a suit or rather has a vested interest in it and such a transaction does not attract section 11 or section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code, as the sale is not a benami one. [211 D] (b) The mere fact that the property was sold at the time when the sale was effected did not affect the right to the full owner of the property and confer on him a right which he was precluded from bringing a suit for the recovery of property. [212 E F] (c) The fact that in the present case the necessary averments were made regarding possession and dispossession of the defendants by reason of their purchase from the several co owners would not make any difference, because, the sale deed was executed on April 18, 1931, without adverting to the antecedent want of power. [213 G H] (d) The suit for declaration of title did not lie in respect of the same cause of action and the suit must be dismissed as incompetent. [214 B C] (e) The High Court erred in holding that the sale by the plaintiff was a benami transaction and was therefore hit by section 11(1)(a). [213 D] In the present ease, the plaintiffs had no right or title to bring the suit for a declaration that they were the ostensible owner of a property with the consent of his co sharers. The mere circumstance that the defendants had no interest in a property was not consistent with the sale being real and intended to pass title. [216 E] (f) The plaintiff 's claim could not be accepted without careful scrutiny of facts.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions judge for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction but on a reference under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court held that the trial had not been vitiated by any irregularity or misdirection in the case and set aside the convictions and sentences passed against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the omission to comply with the provisions of sections 173(4), 207A and 207A of the Criminal Procedure Code, had caused prejudice to the accused; (2) the failure to comply did not vitiate the trial unless the accused succeeded in showing that they had been prejudiced in their defence. HELD : (i) The omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more severe effect than the omission which was curable by reference to section 537(a) of the code. [292 B] (ii) The failure to do so did not affect the trial and consequently ipso facto, a fresh trial became necessary irrespective of whether or not the accused had shown any prejudice. [293 C] (iii) The absence of compliance with the provi sions of section 173(3) of Code of criminal Procedure was fatal to the prosecution case. [294 E] (iv) The defect in the evidence relating to the non compliance with section 162 of the Cr. P.C., could not be cured by reference only to the omission on the part of police officers concerned or of the magistrate before whom the committal proceedings were brought, to see that all the documents necessary to give the accused persons all the information for the proper conduct of their defence were furnished. [295 E] The omission was not fatal and the omission was curing an irregularity which could be cured under section 537. [296 G] (v) The non compliance of the provisions relating to section 173, Cr.P.C. did not render the entire proceedings and subsequent trial void. [297 B] Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor, A.I.R. , referred to. (vi) The irregularity is curable under section 538(a). [298 E] Abdul Rauf Khan vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. (vii) The mere omission by a police officer to fully comply with section 173 does not render his entire proceedings invalid or invalid. Section 537(b) of Cr. Procedure Code does not require that the case should be remitted to the Magistrate for trial in accordance with the procedure prescribed by section 207A. [298 F] (viii) The fact that the omission complained was corrected after the accused were produced before the Sessions Court did not make any difference because the omission alleged in the present case should have been cured by the provisions Of section 537 of the C.P.,C.

The appellant Municipality was constituted under the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901. The respondent Municipality had been consulted and it was found that the water of some of the wells in the surrounding area was not in any way polluted by reason of the effluent being discharged through the existing channels. The appellant filed an application before the Special Officer under section 153A(1) of the Bombay district Municipal Act for permission to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluents from the factory of the respondent Municipality. The Special Officer rejected the application on the ground that the respondent had carried out similar tests and that the appellant was not satisfied with the report of the Special officer. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of section 153 A(1)(a) were not applicable to the case as the permission to carry on the effluent in question was granted by the Municipality only after issuing a notice to the respondent municipality and after hearing the appellant, it held that the Municipal Corporation had no jurisdiction to issue the notice. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Special officer had wrongly decided that lie could not go into the question whether the nuisance in question existed. [398 D] (ii) The provisions of sections 153A and 153B of the Act are not applicable because the person to whom the notice has been issued does not deny the existence of the nuisance. The purpose of section153A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to the existence or a nuisance which was purely a matter for the subjective satis faction of the municipality. [399 E] (iii) The power conferred on the Municipality by section 153B is to be exercised in a capricious manner. If the person concerned objects to the notice and the requisition contained therein absolutely the objection is in substance to the issue of the notice itself, which means he objects to, the declaration of the public shall be made within the subjective conclu sion of the Municipal Council. [397 E] The provisions Of section 153C(1), (3) and (4) are not attracted because the persons to whom notice has already been issued by the Municipal Commissioner do not deny that the nuisance existed. The provision is for the appointment of an assessor to advise the Special Officers on any technical matter. [396 G H] (iv) The procedure under section 154A is not a judicial one and the provisions are not exhaustive. The scheme under section153 A is to make it clear that the objection must be in existence such a nuisance to the satisfaction of a Municipality as regards the manner in which the effluent shall be discharged. If a person to whose notice has not been issued applies for an order requiring him to arrange to comply with the requisition, he may do so without delay in order to preserve the health of the community and the fertility of the soil. The special officer is given the power to make the declaration under section 152A(2) of that Act. [395 G H; 396 A B] (v) The provision of section 154(1 ) is not applicable as it has been done in this case. Section 153A does not require a judicial officer to hold an enquiry into the matter. It is only when he considers that there is such a danger that the words may be ascertained and to give effect to the direction to arrange the discharge.

The appellant was charged with the offence of theft of railway stores. The prosecution case was that the appellant failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods and that he had not offered any satisfactory evidence of possession of goods. On the strength of some information received on 28th July 1964, that some stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a Sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector of Police, searched the premises of the motor transport company at Lucknow and found that the said stolen railway Property was being used for his own use or were intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The appellant pleaded guilty and contended that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The trial court found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the prosecution must prove that the goods belonged to any particular railway administration and that the article was not only the property belonging to a railway administration but also those which were intended for use in the constructions, operation of a Railway Stores. The evidence in the case did not establish that the items seized were Railway stores within section 2 of the Act. The mere description of the articles as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 3(2) of that Act. There was no evidence before the courts to prove that they were railway property within the definition of section. The only description of goods as new was sufficient to show that they belonged to a Railway Administration. The fact that the seized stolen railway properties were being used by a railway administrate and that they had been used for the construction or operation of the railway cannot be established. The High Court was right in holding that the evidence in this case did establish that articles seized are railway stores and not 'goods ' within the purview of section, 2(a). Moyalal Rostagir vs The State, A.I.R. (1954) Punj. 1, approved. Moyalial Rostangir vs State, ; , followed. The facts in this ease were as follows: On the basis of some of information received from 28th June 1964 that some theft railway property had been being sent for trans portation in the market, the appellant was convicted under section 3 of the . The High court held that the case fell within the ambit of section 304(a) of Indian Penal Code and sentenced the appellant to imprisonment. The bail bond of the appellant directed to be cancelled.

The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, but she did not carry on the business with her till date of her death. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent tenant on the ground that she had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent landlord was the tenant and as such the respondent was entitled to the continuance of the tenancy. On appeal, the High Court held that since the appellants had not carried on the 'business with her as family business in the demised property, they were not enti tled to the benefit of the amended definition of tenant under the Act. The High Court also held that the appellant was entitled only to the protection of the amendment of the definition of 'tenant ' under the Rent Acts and that the legal representatives did not acquire any right to remain in possession of the premises. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the lease hold rights of the tenanted premises were heritable and the heirs of the deceased tenant were entitled to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under section 13(1)(a) of the Act, and that since they had not been evicted from the demised shop, the tenancy thereto was heritable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent landlord after termination of the contractual tenancy of the tenant is entitled to continue to remain as a statutory tenant under sub section (1) of section 13. [108G] 2. The term 'tenant" in Section 3(vii)(a), means a person by whom the rent is, or but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any accommodation and includes any person occupying the accommodation as a sub tenant, and also any person continuing in possession after the termination of his tenancy in his favour otherwise than under the provisions of the Rent Act. [109B] 3. The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs or the heirs in respect of commercial tenancies on the death of the sub tenant after termination, does not indicate that the legislature intended that the heirs should be deemed to have acquired the protection under the statute. [110C D] 4. In case of commercial premises governed by the Rent Laws Act, the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard tO tenancy. It may also be borne in mind that in case of a commercial premises the heirs are entitled to succeed, not only to his business but also to his tenan cy rights under the rent Act which protects the heirs from ejectment except in accordance with the provisions contained in the Rent Control Acts and the other Rent Acts continue to enjoy. [111D E] 5. The Legislature has neither intended nor in the absence of any provision restricting the heritability of the commercial tenancies not with standing the determination of the statutory tenancy will devolve on the heirs, in accordance therewith, and no order or decree for eviction shall be passed against the tenant unless any such ground is established to the satisfaction of the Court. [112F G] 6.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund Scheme to all its workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The employees have to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not be covered by the same scheme under the Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Provident Fund. The Board has made no effort at all to analyse the balance sheet of the Board to show the actual results of its working. It has made a no effort to work out the financial implications of its order. It had made no efforts to workout the financial implication of its own employer. It is true that in the year ending March 1969 Board 's gross profits amounted to Rs. 305.12 lakhs and it had been continuously rising from Rs. 59.39 lakhs in 1961. The appellant Board has also made no attempt at all lo explain the actual result of its work. It was contended on behalf of the workmen that this would impose additional financial liabilities which the Board would not be able to bear. Therefore, the main question for consideration by the Tribunal was whether there should be a contributory provident fund scheme on the basis of basic wage or total wages. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Provident Fund is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the respondent Board. That is why the Tribunal has dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [47 D E] 2. The Tribunal has dealing with the matters in a thoroughly arbitrary manner. It does not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the respondent, the interest should be taken into account before the profits could be ascertained. Even with regard to the deprecia tion reserve the provisions of section 68 may have to he taken into consideration. If it is not it would have to been met by loans on which interest will have to go. [46 E F] 3. The contribution to the development reserve is a Statutory obligation and was a definite percentage whereas it was open to the ordinary commercial concerns to credit an amount to depreciation reserve, and interest on stocks so guaranteed. [48 G H] 4. The interest on stock not so guaranteed cannot be deducted in order to ascertain the financial capacity of the employer. [49 C D] 5. The respondent has made any effort at examining the balance sheets of the appellant Board to indicate the actual value of its staff, and it is necessary to dispose them of the matters afresh in accordance with the observations in this Judgment.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligations. The Magistrate rejected the application holding that the appellant had been impotently incapable of having sexual relations with the respondent. In appeal, the High Court held that the wife had been suffering from mental cruelty with a view to deprive her of her legitimate right to live with her husband and hence she was entitled to the grant of the maintenance. The High Court also rejected the contention of the appellant that it was not necessary for the respondent to discharge the marital obligations, and dismissed the application filed by the respondent for maintenance. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the husband had been found to be impotency and was therefore unable to perform his marital duties; (2) the wife was not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live in her husband 's house; and (3) the respondent had been subjected to mental cruelty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have taken a contrary view and have not noticed that the main object and interpretation of the second proviso to sub section (3), of section 125, is to provide an effective and summary remedy to provide for appropriate food, clothing and lodging for a wife. [707B] 1.2 In order to find out whether the husband was justified in refusing to live at the ground of refusal to live, the Court has to consider the grounds on which the wife refuses to live. The expression 'cruelty ' is not exhaustive but purely illustrative and self explanatory and takes within its fold not only the two instances mentioned therein but other circumstances also of a like nature which may be regarded as a just ground for refusal of the wife to live alongwith her husband. [608C D] 1:3. The object of section 488 is to give relief to neglected wife if there is impotence and there are "just grounds" passing such an order. This alteration gives a wider discretion to the Court, which means that in passing such order it is legitimate for it to take into account the relations between the husband and the wife, and the husband 'could be entitled to maintain maintenance from her husband according to his means. [700D E] 1 :4. The Courts cannot compel the wife or the husband to stay with her at any stage of the proceedings under section125 to claim separate maintenance. [ 700E F] 1I2 In the instant case, the husband has a reasonable apprehension that the respondent is not an active participant in the sexual life and therefore, the sexual pleasure to the wife is of no consequence and cannot amount to cruelty. [750H; 751A] 1l3 The High court was wrong in holding that where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a husband is impotified and is unable to continue with his marital obligation, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a just cause for refusal to stay. [751B] 4. In the present case, there was no reason why the respondent should not have been granted maintenance from the appellant.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the city of Bhavnagar. The first respondent Union of India, the Municipal Committee of the appellant 's factory, filed a suit for possession of the said plot on the ground that the structure in question had been constructed by the appellant and that the structures were occupied by the State Government and that consequently the appellant was not entitled to recover possession of such land. The trial court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the suit property till 7th July 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of Saurashtra to the State Public Works Department of the State of Saurashtra. The High Court allowed the appeal of the Union of india and dismissed the suit for recovery of possession. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Article 65 of the Constitution is applicable in this case as the suit was filed on 3rd March 1964 and that on the finding of the Trial Court in favour of the plaintiff on the question of title in respect of 'Parade Ground ', and in the absence of specific plea of adverse possession in his writ petition, the trial court 's decree should have been confirmed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The suit was for possession based on title to a plot based on the title to it but the right to execute the sale deed in respect thereof was transferred or vested in the Municipalities concerned. It amounts conferring an authority or authorising the Municipalities to execute sale deeds in respect o f those lands situated within the Municipality, which should normally have been done by the Government. The subsequent correspondance and orders of the government also show that the Government had corrected themselves in their communication dated 6th May, 1952 and stated that the claim of the plaintiffs that the lands were vested in Bhavnagar Municipality was erroneous and that it was not open to the appellant to rely on the principle that possession follows title. [231E F] 2. The fact that the suit itself is for possession basing on title and the plaintiff have not proved title, does not make any distinction and it refers to only lands and not buildings. It refers to merely lands and buildings. In the instant case, the suit had been filed on March 7, 1964 and the suit has not been shown as a transfer of title. The plaintiff has not proved possession. [232G H] 3. The question whether the plaintiff was handed back by the Union or the State to the Government to reconsider the entire case and decide it is not necessary for the defendant to plead or prove adverse possession. It is only in the present case, that the title itself should have be vested in them. Since a number of Municipalities made representation to the government to reconsider its entire case, and decided that the right of the state to sell plots of land given under Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January 1948 by the plaintiff to the defendant Government only on 7th March, 1952, it is clear that the document was evidence against the Municipality in so far as it treated the properties as belonging to the Defence Department of Government of India and that its right to sell such lands of the Govern ment was with the Government concerned. [230B C] 4. The claim of title itself is not a transfer or an authority to them. The other documents relied on by the defendant in support of his contention that the possession of land was also not taken by the Municipali ties at any time. It does not give a right to the plaintiff. In this case not only there is evidence to show that physical possession was with defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title had been handed over to the Municipality. [229C D] 5.

The appellant was a Class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the Special Judge, Ajmer, for having committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal against that conviction but on a certificate granted by the High Court under article 134 (1) (c) of the Constitution it held that the appellant accepted Rs. 150 from Nanak Singh as and by way of illegal gratification and did not commit an offence within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal code. The appellant contended that he was an officer in the service or pay of Government and was performing a public duty and therefore, was liable to be convicted under section 420 Indian Penal. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was illegal and the appeal must fail. The offence of criminal misconduct was committed by the appellant as a public servant within the terms of section 2(9) Of the Indian penal Code and he was not an officer of the Government within the definition of that term in section 21 (9). The appellant was, therefore, rightly convicted under the Act. The appeal must accordingly be dismissed.
