The question whether a person is an officer or not has to be decided by the Court coming to the conclusion that a person was not in the employ of the government and could not be said to be an officer within the term of section 6(9). In the present case, the appellant had been convicted under sections 5(i)(d), 6(1) and 7 of Act 11 of 1947 and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months. The conviction was therefore illegal. The fact that the salary of the respondent was paid by Government and he had been discharging public duty did not affect his character as a Public servant within section 21, Indian Penal C.P.C. [688 B D] In the instant case, though the appellant 's clerk as such was employed as an officer under the Works Manager who was certainly a public officer, he was neither in the employment of the State Government nor was he employed to assist him in its relations to individual subjects. The respondent was therefore, on a narrow interpretation of section 1(9)(d). He was, however, not an 'officer ' within the expression "public servant" contained in section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II Of 1947.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala for permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga, with a building constructed thereon. The auction was held by the department and the sale was notified for June 14,1977. The Collector, Patiala, by his order dated January 16, 1976 issued a proclamation prohibiting transfer or creation of a charge by the Respondent of his halfshare in an immoveable property consisting Khewat NO. 374. The respondent filed a civil suit against the State of Punjab and the appellant for permanent injuction restraining the Government and the Collectrate from auction ing his half shares. The trial court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The High Court, however, allowed the second appeal by the State. Allowing the Appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that a property is liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree. [847C] 2. Section 61 of the code provides for the mode and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the said Act and the sales which were notified were not exempt from attachment and sold under section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached and accordingly issued a permanent injunction with regard to the portion in whose favour the respondent was residing. [884D E] 3. Section 59 of the Criminal Procedure Code provides for mode and method of recovery of arrear of revenue and declares what properties are liable to he attached and sold in execution thereof. The opening words of sub section (I) of section 60 are "the following property is also liable to attach and sale" The opening word of sub sec tion (1) of Section 60 is "the same as the property which is liable" in the said sub secion. [854E F] 4. Section 62 of the Cr. P.C. provides that the following properties shall not be liable to attached or sold, namely: (a) one main residential house and other buildings attached to it; (b) a building used by him for his residence and occupied by him; (c) a shop constructed thereon; and (d) any building constructed in execution over which such a decree is passed. [864G H] 5. Section 63 of the Act provides that where property is so liable to an attachment and sell in execution, of a money decree, it shall be attached or sale in the execution of such a debt and the said clause (ccc) provides as follows: "The following properties are hereby liable to seizure and sale under section 70. " [851C D] 6. Section 58 of the C.P.C., provides that when property is sold by public amendment, it is not to be so exempted from attachment or sale. In the instant case, the property, if any which are exempt from attached and sale, in revenue recovery proceedings under the said section, would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said act. [874E] 7. Section 6 of the Delhi Rent Control Act provides for a mode and agency of attachment and sales and sale. The two sections are not exempt under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said Acts are concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery to recover arrears of Revenue under the Act. [877F] 8. Section 65 of the Transfer of Property Act provides only for recovery from attachment. The expression "such attachment or Sale" in section 60 of that Act does not apply to an attached and sales under any other law made expressly inapplicable thereto.

The Special Deputy Collector of Land Acquisition awarded a total compensation of Rs. 20,000 to the appellant. The Special Deputy Collec tor determined the value of the lands passing on the death of Rashid in 1963 and fixed the compensation at Rs.20,000. This award was received by the heirs of Rashid on whom the estate of Rashid devolved in equal shares. On appeal, the High Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands which had been undervalued in the original assessment and as such property (meaning lands) chargeable to estate duty had escaped assessment to duty, it was not liable to be re assessed. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the High court erred in holding that there were no two separate rights one a right to receive compensation and other a right of claim for further compensation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding the notice issued under s.59(a) of the Act was valid. [337B] 2.1 The High court was right that there are no two different rights one as a right and property had not been correctly valued in the Original assessment proceedings inasmuch as the lands were lost to the estate by reason of the acquisition of their lands under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. [330C D] 2:2 In the instant case, the assessments made by the Special Deputy collector were for the years 1954 to 1960 and the value was determined on the basis that the acquired lands still formed part of the estate. The lands had vested in the Government long prior to the death and therefore it was merely a right which could not be elevated to the status of an asset or property and as a result of acquisition of his lands under section 18 of the Land Acquisi tion Act, the appellant had only one right which was to receive the compensation for the said lands at their market value on the date of the relevant notifications. [328D E] 2I2 In view of the provisions of section 59 and the fact that the lands in question could not have been valued at an earlier point of time, the notice under s,59(b) was issued by the respondent on the wrong assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to estate because the lands had become liable to estate tax. [326E F] 3.1 In the present case, it is clear that the assessments were made in the year 1958 and the same had escaped assess ment to duty. The Revenue will pay the costs of the appeal to the assessee. [324G H] 3:2. The notice under section 59(a), would have been issued on the assumption that the respondent had acquired any surplus land which was an inchoate right which can not be enlarged to the position of an assets or property. [325A B] 3I3. In the case of a right acquired by the Government, long before the death, but the right to compensation is recognised and vested in it, it cannot be said that the property had escaped taxation and therefore the notice was liable to he quashed on this ground. [322C D]. 4.1 It is well settled that when the original assessments were not made part of assessment proceedings, a fresh notice under Section 59(b), would be necessary to be issued for the purpose of determining the correct value of land revenue. The only right is to receive payment for the land at their proper valuation on the dates of the rele vant notifications and when he accepted compensation fixed by the special Deputy Collector as the proper valuation he must be deemed to have adopted that evaluation as his own estimated value of lands which he wanted to enhance by relying upon the valuation made by another authority, namely, the City Civil Court. [320D E]. 3I4.2.

The appellant, a member of the Cooperative Society, was elected as Director of the Bank on 18.8.1986. His election was not called in question by the Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Nagpur, on the ground that he had defaulted in payment of certain loan instalments on 21.10.86. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the said order was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court holding that section 73FF(1) of the Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development Bank (Amendment) Act, 1960 and Rule 71(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Rules, 1986 were not applicable to him. The Division Bench held that the appellant ' s election was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant"s election as a Director of a bank and that procedure having not been followed the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 78(1). Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions relating to election have to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the Act such as in section 78 (1) which deals with disqualification for membership. Under sub section (2) of section 73F, a person shall cease to be a member if he is so disqualified by or under any other provision of this Act. Section 77(1), which deals regarding disqualification for members of a committee, provides that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section(1 ) shall cease lo be a Member of the Committee and his seat deemed to have fallen vacant. The fact that he has been disqualified to continue as Director or creasing to be Director on account of his having committed default does not detract from special, would apply, because the appellant was in arrear in respect of instalments on the date of his election and till 21. 10.1986 i.e. both prior and anterior to his election on 18th August 1986. [682B C] 2. The proviso to sub section 2 of section 74F says that a person who has suffered any disqualification for being elected as an officer or member shall cease from the Committee, and his office shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant. Therefore, the moment the appellant after election continued to be in default, and, therefore, must be taken to have made default, stood disqualified and thereby ceased to be the member of a Committee and he must be deemed not to have been a defaulter in presenti on the due date. [683C D] 3. The expression "makes default" or "stands disqualified" being in present the default must have been committed after the coming into force of section73FF and that his default continues from day to day until it is repaid. Every day thereafter until payment results in making of default and, consequently, it could not be said that default could be on the account of being defaulter which continued from dayto day until he was repaid. [684D E] 4.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement, the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's services were terminated by giving full opportunity to defend himself. On the conclusion of the enquiry, the State Govt. issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which quashed the order of the government 's reducing the pension by 50% and directed the State government to reconsider the question of reduction of pension by fifty per cent. The High Court held that the State Govern ment had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice on attaining 58 years. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government has power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [188B] 1.2 In the present case, the purpose of the inquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent "s pension". The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. It appears that the attention of the High court was not drawn to these Rules. Therefore, the Government has no authority to initiate any proceedings against Respondent. [189C D] 1:3. The State Government had power to reducing or withhold the pension granted to the Government servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service and after completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government Servant depend upon the good conduct of the Govern ment servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part of the pension payable lo a Government employee for misconduct, which he might have committed whilst in service or after completion thereof. [190E F] 1 :4. The Government had no power to initiate proceedings against respondent as it was not competent to initiate action against the State servant even though his retirement was found guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or After the completion of the service, the order passed by the State Gov ernment is set aside and quashed.

The appellants were the tenants of certain premises in the town. The respondent landlord applied for permission to sue him under section 3(1) of the West Bengal (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, for ejectment of the appellants on the ground that they had applied for the permission to institute a suit against them. The appellants contended that the permission was not valid in law because the permission granted by the Commissioner was invalid in law; but the High Court held that the appellants were entitled to apply under section 6(2) of Act II of 1947, and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the jurisdiction conferred on the State Government by section 7 F of the Act was very wide and as such the bar created by the relevant provisions of the said Act excluding the jurisdiction of the civil courts could not operate in cases where the plea raised before the civil court goes to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to the conclusion that the impugned order was a nullity. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the application for permission was invalid. [560 C] (ii)The bar created under section 7 G of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Act II Of 1947 is very wide. As the appellants had not raised any objection to the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate, the High court was in error in coming to the conclu sions that the same limitation must be imported in construing (a) the provisions of section 3 (4) and (5). [560 E] (iii)The power conferred on a State Government under section 4 is very limited. The power conferred by section 3 is very narrow. As it must be held that a party can move the Commissioner under section 5(1), he has to satisfy the Court that the District Magis trate has acted illegally or with material irregularity, and that would give him the jurisdiction to exercise his revisional power. [561 G] (iv)The High Court had no doubt that the provisions Of sections 3 (3) and 16 of the Calcutta Act II, 1947 were clear and unambiguous and they indicated that the High Courts in exercising their powers under section 13(4) had not intended that before a District Magistrate grants permission to file a suit to bring a suit, he should issue notice to the party affected by the order. [562 E] The power given by section 4 (3 ) is very broad and unambiguous. It must be read as meaning that the Civil Courts which have jurisdiction to deal with civil causes can exercise their powers in cases of this kind.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, physically assaulted his wife and her children. The respondent filed an application before the High Court for quashing the proceedings on the ground that the President of India had no jurisdiction to make this reference as he was not happy with his appointment as a Member of the State Public Service Commis sion. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant could not have been prosecuted under section 3(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, for having committed gross misconduct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the report of the Commission was not in accordance with law and (ii) the High court had no power to examine the evidence recorded by it instead of being made by a Magistrate or a Munsif. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of reference is set aside and the case remitted to the High COurt for disposal on merits after giving an opportunity to the respondent to defend himself. [645D] 2. The report of a Commission is not a part of its own procedure. It is open to the Court in the first instance, to consider whether there was a conspiracy to involve his client falsely or that there were reasons for so involving him. If the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed no grievance can be made that the facts which establish the charge of misbehaviour are found by the highest court of the land and not by the lowest. [643E F] 3. The evidence in this case is not such as to justify an examination and assessment of facts. It would have to be read in the context of the guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court. [641A B] 4. The material on record shows that the Commission had made a reference to the President under article 317(1) of Constitution, but it was not made by him. The opinion expressed by the President is binding on the President. [651C D] 5. The question whether the report submitted by the Commission is vitiated by any examination and re examination of witnesses is a matter which should be decided by this Court during the hearing of the Reference. [661D] 6. The decision of this Court in Dr. A.K. Sharma vs Union of India, ; , followed.

The appellants were the deity installed in the temple. The temple was a public trust and the endowment was held to be of a public nature and, therefore, was to be governed by the Act. The respondent Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Orissa, filed an appeal against the decision of the Subordinate Judge. The High Court reversed the decision holding that the temple and the deity were private temples within the meaning of section 4(2) of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the endowment being a public one, the deity was not a public body or a public institution within the definition of section 2(a) of that Act and therefore, the temple was not an "public" one. HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that it was a circumstance which could be spelt out and held that the dedication to the temple by members of the public was of a private nature. [837 B] (ii) The essential distinction between a private and a public endowment is that while a public or a private endowment is not capable of holding property and the property dedicated to the public must be vested in the beneficiaries and the income from the property is used for the maintenance and support of the family of the founder. [829 C] (iii) The mere fact that members of a Hindu public are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment a public element. [828 D] (iv) The question whether a religious endowment is of a purely private character or of a statutory character, depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The essential features of a Public trust are: (1) that there was no intention to treat the temple as a public temple; (2) that the fact that the members of public were allowed to be worship by themselves would not show that any contribution was called for from members of such public nor was there any averment in the deed to show that there were any stipulation for offerings or contributions to be made by members. [827 D E] (v) The intention which can be gathered from the document is placed beyond doubt by a later document Ext. 1 which was executed on 17 11 1932 and is in the nature of a settlement Deed, the relevant portions of which may be quoted thus: "Out of the property of the temple, there is a temple of the kind described as a family deity and the dedication is made only for a group of individuals who may be connected with the family. The endowment is made out of public funds and not of right. The founder of the endowment has all the powers of management and control over the temple including the temple in question. " [827 E F] (vi) The fact that there is no recital in any of the documents to show whether the members were of a particular community or not, does not make any indication of such a recital. It is manifest that the founder of a endowment cannot be called a family idol and the intention of the settlor or the founder was merely to instal a family temple in the property which would have been dedicated for the purpose of maintenance of the deity. [826 G H] (vii) The recitals in Ext. A. 'and Ext. I clearly establish that the intention was to dedicate their properties to public and that the deity would be of the private nature and not a matter specified in the later.

The appellant Bank originally known as Bharat Bank Ltd. agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. The agreement provided that all powers hereby granted were and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorneys against the bills were made or made hereafter. The appellant was authorised to sue for recovery of and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts with the approval of MaL repatriated Bank Ltd., Jabalpur. On July 19, 1948, the power of attorney recited that the appellant had no right to attach it. The respondent filed objections under section 47 of the Indian Contract Act before the Sub Divisional Magistrate who held that the appel lant was the assignee of the bill and decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no equitable assignment. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The law on the subject admits of no doubt. In construing a power of Attorney, it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, Malhotra and the Bank was that of borrower and lender and that the document was brought into existence in connection therewith. When the debt due to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities, the authority specifically appropriated it for payment to the appellant. (ii) The power of the Attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19. 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill. (iii) The High court was in error in holding that there is no equitable assign ment. In the present case, the appellant was an assignee of a bill and the power was expressed to be irrevocable. [777 E F] Palmer vs Carey, , approved. (iv) The question whether a document amounts to an equitable assignment or not is primarily one of construction but it may mention a few decisions which throw light on the matter. Jagabhai Lallubhai vs Rustamji Nauserwanji, ; and M/s. Khemick vs Candell, ; , referred to. (v) The appellant had an interest in the fund and was authorised by the appellant to receive all monies due or to become due to Malhotra in respect of pending or future contracts with government authorities.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and was assessed to income tax in respect of that assessment year. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the receipt in question being profits in lieu of salary had to be considered as his salary as defined in section 17(1) (iv). The High Court answered the reference against the assessee. In appeal by certificate, HELD: The receipt of Rs. 27948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered a salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17(3)(ii) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income Tax under the head "income from other source" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E '. In computing the taxable income, the receipt of an interest on any investment is a gain made by the investor and therefore the same is exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17 (3) (ii). [445 D E] The respondent was not represented before this Court. It was not shown that the assessee had any interest on the securities. The income from the other sources was brought to tax under section 56. Therefore, the question is what is meant by "profits in lieu" of salary". [441 G H] In defining the expression "Profits in lieu Of salary", the legislature excluded from its scope of that expression any payments received by the assesses from a provident fund, his own contributions to the fund or any interest thereon. From that it follows that the receipts in question cannot be treated as salary though it is an Income. [441 B] In the instant case, the respondent was neither represented before the Court nor was he represented before us. The High court was therefore right in holding that the income tax authorities were not entitled to tax or if it was not exempt under what head the same had to he brought to taxation under section 17. [442 C D] (ii) The receipt by the respondent with which we are concerned is exempt under section 18(1)(iv). Therefore, there was no need to call into aid any of these rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court.

The Bihar Act, in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of cow or buffalo, is valid. The Act provides for the establishment of a committee to make recommendations on the method of selection of cattle of animals of the species of bovine cattle. Section 3(1) of the Act provides that no person shall slaughter a cow without a licence from the appropriate authority mentioned in section 4 and section 6 of the said Act or any other law for the time being in force or in any usage to the contrary. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Acts on the ground, inter alia, (1) that the impugned Acts were not violative of article 19(1)(g) of their Constitution as they infringed their fundamental rights under articles 19(i)(g), 21 and 22 of the Constitution; (2) that sections 3(3) and 4 of the Bihar Act were ultra vires the State Legislature and (3) that section 3(4) was violative of the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19 (1)(f) of our Constitution. Held, that the provisions of the impugned Act infringed articles 19 (i)(d), 21, 22 and 23 of the constitution and are not void under article 13(2). The Act is a law relating to the slaughter and does not infringe the rights of the petitioners under article 19. The provisions of sections 3 and 4 are not violative Of article 19 and are therefore void. The Bihar Act is constitutionally valid in so insofar as it prohibited the slaughter by the impugned acts of the butchers (Kasais) of a cow or cow, and the slaughter animals which are useful for human consumption cannot be supported as reasonable under article 21. The restrictions imposed on the slaughter must not be arbitrary or excessive. The restriction must not only be reasonable but also valid. It is well settled that the power to regulate the slaughter is subject to the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on the exercise of the power. The impugned Acts are not unconstitutional as they violate articles 14, 19(l)(g). The provisions in the Bihar Acts show that the restrictions imposed by them were reasonable and valid. There was no violation of any fundamental right under article 31 (1), (g) or (vi) of Part III of the Constitu tion. The ban on slaughter of animals above a specified age may not be justified as it is not reasonable within the meaning of article 21, but only reasonable. The State of Bombay vs R. M. section Kasais, ; , referred to.

The respondent was a clerk in the appellant company. He was dismissed from service by an order dated January 31, 1956, and on his appeal to the High Court he was informed that the order of suspension had been revoked by the relevant authorities under the provisions of the . The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High court challenging the orders of suspension and termination of his services. The High Court held that the Standing Orders did not apply to him, but only applied to Standing Orders No. 2(a) and (b), and that the respondent was not an employee within the meaning of the Standing Order No. 1. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in the departmental musters" occurring in Standing Order NO. I, and the expression "workman" in Standing Orders 2(b), mean such categories of employees as may from time to time be declared to be workmen, and under Standing Order 1, it is not necessary that every employee should have a ticket before he can be an employee, and if workmen are such categories, they must be so employed. The words " who" in standing order No. I mean such category of employees which may fromtime to time become employees from time lo time be declare to be workman, and therefore, the respondent could not be said to have a contract with him under Standing Orders 1. The Standing Order did make a distinction between "employees ' and " workmen". The definition clause in Standing order No 2(c) of the local Act contemplates the making of standing orders for all employees in respect of matters which are required to be dealt with by Standing Orders. The expression " workman" is defined for the purpose of the Act, and includes a person who has no ticket. The respondent was an employee of the appellant Company and was dismissed by the company on the ground that he had no ticket but only a ticket. Held, further, that in view of the provisions contained in Standing orders No. 3 and 4 of the Local Act, the words 'employee ' in Standing. Order No 2 (a) of Standing Order I must be read as " whose name and ticket number are included" in the depart mental musters ' column. The definition of an employee is employment in the office, Mains Department, eta., of the Company either at Nagpur or Nagpur. The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Bombay vs M/s. Dungore Jute Mills Co. Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellant, a company incorporated in the year 1961, was carrying on the business of manufacturing controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The claim was resisted by the company on the ground that the Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained for each unit and separate profit and Loss account was maintained for every unit. The Tribunal held that alloy steel project could not be treated as separate establishments because under the Act a Company is an establishment which has been in existence for a long period and had been receiving profits, and therefore, it cannot be treated at par with other units. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was wrong in holding that merely because Alloy steel Project is owned, controlled and run by a person or body other than the Government company or a corporation owned by a private company or an undertaking of the nature described in section 3 of the Act, it could not treat the entire unit as separate establishment. (ii) The expression "establishment" in the definition of "establishment " in section 2(a) and (b) of the Payment Of Bonus Act means any establishment which is owned by or under a company. The word "establishment ' is used to indicate something different from a company as defined in the . In the case of separate departments, undertakings or branches of an establishment, it may not be possible to make a deduction at all when the Act itself provides for the same. (iii) The definition of establishment given under section 3(1) of that Act is inclusive and not exhaustive. The expression 'establishment ' in the Act means a establishment which carries on, controlled or managed by persons other than companies. The definition does not apply to establishments consisting of different departments, corporations set up for purposes of section 16(1). (iv) The word 'establishment" used in the section includes all the establishments as defined under the . [633 B C] (v) The words "establishment in a public sector" are intended to indicate some kind of establishment. In the present case, the appellant was a company which had been running its own factories for a period of six years and had a number of undertakings, separate accounts were kept for each separate undertaking.

The respondent assessee is a sugar mill in Karnataka raising similar question of law. The State Government issued a notification under Section 3 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1974 exempting from the operation of the Act and the State Boards from all the provisions of the said Act. The cess was levied on the ground that it fell under item 15 of Schedule I to the Act. In respect of the assessment year 1982 83, the respondent assessee claimed exemption from payment of cess from the sugar factories on the grounds that this industry falls under item No. 15 of the Schedule I of the Cess Act and as such the levy and collection of cess was not justified. The Assessing Authority held that the sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 as "processing of animal or vegetable products" and accordingly levied cess from its factory on the basis that this activity fell under Item 15 of schedule I to The Cess Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that sugar manufacturing industries would fall under item 68 as " processing of animal products industry". The State Board of Revenue in revision set aside the order of the Assessing Authority and directed the Assessing Authorities to take appropriate action for recovery of cess. The High Court also took a similar view holding that sugar manufacture would come under Entry 15 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that sugar industry would fall within Entry No.15 and therefore, the levy of cess could not be said to be an industry within Entry 14 of the schedule I. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Cess is a fiscal enactment, as is held by this Court in Member Secretary, Andhra Pradesh State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd., [1963] Supp. 2 SCR 79. The levy and recovery of Cess is on water consumed by persons carrying on the industries specified in Schedule I. The Act does not contain vegetables which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude. It was also of the view that sugar factories would fall in Entry 15 if they are engaged in the industries enumerated in Schedule 1. [532C D] 2.1 The term "vegetable" is defined in various ways. The term is used in contradistinction to animal kingdom. In the context in which the word 'vegetables ' is used, in Entry No.(6) of Schedule 1 like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and also in its more complicated form involves progressive action in performing, producing or making something. [525D E] 2:2 The term 'veg etable ' has been defined in several ways. In different ways the word is used as a nounter in referring to any and every kind of plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule II like Paper industry and Textile industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry, 15. The word 'crylon ' has not been defined. [25G H] 2(a) The term `vegetability ' means a product of or made of or out of vegetable. It is used to indicate that sense and meaning thereby all that belongs to the world of plants would come in existence which is different from that originally existed in the sense that the thing produced is by itself a commercially different commodity whereas in the case of processing it is not necessary to produce a commercially different article. processing is an activity for certain purposes and vegetables are products of that industry. [26G H; 27A B] 2.(b) The word `vegor ' has to be read as a whole and to the fitness of the matter to the statute. The meaning given to the same word occurring in a. social security measure or a regulating enactment may not be apt or appropriate when the same words are used in common parlance are related to the context with which they are used. [27C D; 28D] 2 (c) The Cess act is a tax on consumed by person carrying on specified and every type of plant, life or processing is to he given then certain benefits must be found out from the language according to its natural meaning fairly and squarely read.

The respondent, an Advocate, filed an application before the Rent Controller for eviction of the appellant 's tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who contended that the practice of the profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a)(iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds that he requires the premises bona fide for the purposes of carrying out his profession. The Rent Controller held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for carrying on the profession as a advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction. In revision, the High Court affirmed the decision of the Rent Control Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression business occurring in Section 10 (3)(a)(i) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of the advocate. [14 E] 1.2 In a broad sense it is taken to mean everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the pur pose of livlihood or profit. In a narrow sense it may be confined to commercial activity. It is confined to business carried on by an Advocate but not section 10 (1) (c) only. [15 E] 2. The expression 'business ' in Section10(3)(a)(ii) is intended to include a practice of business within its meaning. [16 F G] 1:4. In the context of the Madhya Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, section 10(1) provides for the eviction by a tenant where the landlord of a residential building requires it for his own occupation. Section 10 sub section (3)(b) provides that a tenant shall not be evicted whether in execution of a decree or otherwise except in accordance with the provisions of Sections 10, 12 and 13. [17 G H] 1 5. The word 'business occurring in section 10 of the Act is used to include 'business as understood in one Act with reference to their use in another Act; more so, if the two Acts in which the same word is used are not cognate Acts. Neither the meaning nor the definition of the term in one statute affords a guide to the construction of the same term in another statute and the sense in which that term has been understood in the several statutes does not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which it appears. [18 C D] 1 6. The words 'business" and 'profession ' are used in the definition in section 2(a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings, (Lease & Eviction) Act, 1950. [19 G H; 20 A] 7.

The respondent, a limited company, was the creditor of M/s. India Supplies Ltd., and the appellant in the year 1942, filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of Rs. 4,00,000 with interest at 6 per cent from time to time. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree holding that the respondent deposited the sum of Rs 4 lakhs with the appellant and also held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the use of the word " deposit" in the roznamcha, entry No. 30 of the entry showed that the amount was deposited with the respondent 's money; (ii) there were disputes between the partners of the firms and the respondent regarding the payment of the money to M/S India Supplies; (iii) the appellant had no ordinary loan of Rs4 lakhs from the respondent; and (iv) the respondent had not examined himself and did not examine himself. HELD: (i). The High Court was correct in decreeing the suit. [578 D] (ii). The mere fact that money in specie was not paid would not be destructive of deposit. The relationship between the parties, the surrounding circumstances at the time of the transaction, the pecuniary position of the appellant are all overwhelming features to taluqa tion. [579 E] Nawab Major Sir Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., ; , referred to. (iii). The respondent acted as bankers and the money was paid by the appellant. The mere circumstance that money was not given would not make it a case of deposit of the amount. [580 G H] (iv). The fact that the appellant did not pay the loan in cash, would not show that understood their financial position. It is precisely because of the then inability of India Supplies to repay the money immediately. It was precisely because the respondent demanded the money by a letter dated 27 April 1953 (exhibit 7) from the appellant 's account. The High court was correct. [581 F] Nawabfer Hussain Khan vs Dhiyan Singh & Anr., ; and Subbaih Chetty & Ors. vs Visalakshgi Achi, I.L.R.

The petitioner was detained by an order of the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs, dated February 28, 1986 under section 3(1) of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to his detention. The grounds of detention were served on him on March 27, 1986 and he was produced before the Advisory Board constituted by the Central Government on April 22, 1986. On March 23, 1987, the petitioner was taken into custody and was produced at the time of hearing. On February 20, 1987 the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate passed an order under section 11(1)(a) of COFEPOSA directing that the detenu be detained until further orders on the ground that he had been prejudiced in making an effective representation to the Board against his detention in the absence of the summons issued under section 108 of the Customs Act. The petitioner challenged the order of detention by a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The fact that the appellant is in custody when the order was made and produced before him cannot take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making the order. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining author ity was aware of the fact that he was already in custody and yet he was sub jecting the order or that he being sub jected in detention would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention. [849C D] 1.2 The fact remains that the petitioner is in jail, where he has been detained, and the order is necessary for putting him back in jail. This Court cannot be oblivious of the facts of the present case. [850E F] 2.1 In the instant case, there was no warrant for summons under section 109 of the Act. There is nothing to show that the detention authority was aware that the person already in detention when the impugned order was passed was aware about the fact of his being in custody. The fact of the petitioner being in jail is not a matter of jurisdic tion but has to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. There was no force in the contention of the peti tioner that the order would become vitiated.

The petitioners are working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The casual labour consists of unskilled, skilled or skilled workers, who have not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years or more. They were engaged by the Union of India to do the work of the last ten years as casual labour on continuous basis. As an alternative to regular absorption they were denied the benefits of the interim relief. The petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the denial of the benefits claimed. The respondents contested the writ petitions and contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour, the wages paid to them are very low and far less than the minimum pay payable under the pay scales applicable to regular employees may be effected as is at present available to casual labourers working in different departments. The Court allowed the writ petition and directed the Union to pay to the petitioners same salary and allowances and other benefits as were being enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. The Union of india, however, contended that the State cannot deny at least the minimum wages in the pay scale of regular employees on the ground that they are being paid wages far less. Allowing the writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are entitled to corresponding Dearness Allowance and Addl. Dearness Allowance if any, payable thereon. whatever other benefits which are now being enjoyed in the Postal and Telegraph Department. Is it for paying them lower wages? Then it amounts to exploitation of labour. [606C D] 1.2 In Dhirendra Chamoli and Another vs State of U.P., this Court has taken almost a similar view with regard to the employees working in the Nehru Yuvak Kendras who were considered to be performing the same duties as Class IV employees. The said decision is being repeatedly observed by those, who are in charge of economic affairs of the countries in different parts of the world that as far as possible security of work should be assured to the employee so that they may contribute to the maximisation of production. It is again for this reason that managements and the Government agencies in particular should not allow workers to remain idle. [066G H; 609A] 1:3 The petitioners have not been regularly recruited but many of them have been working continuously for more than one year in the Department and some of them are rendering service which is being rendered by regular employees doing the same type of work. There are several types of work such as road making, railway construction, house building, irrigation projects, communications etc. which have to be undertaken on a large scale. Development in these types of activities (even though they do not involve much foreign exchange) is not keeping pace with the needs of society. [076E F] 1st petitioner has not been regular recruited but some of the petitioners have been rendering service for nearly ten years. They are rendering services to many as casual workers, for a long period is not a wise policy. It may be that the casual labourers have agreed to work on such low wages. That he has done because he has no other choice. It was poverty that has driven him to that State. The Government should be a model employer. [706F G] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioners are not regular recruited and they are rendering the same kind of service which can be allowed to be taken as regular trade unions. They have been subjected to hostile discrimination. It has been contended that non regularisation of temporary employees or casual labour for a short period is no justification for doing so. Such a classification is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [806G H] 2:2 The petitioners, therefore, are entitled for corresponding Dearness allowance and Addl., Dearness Allowance, if any. whatever may be poverty that have driven him out during that day. [906H; 609B] 3.1 There is no reason why the petitioners should not be paid dearness allowance at a lower rate. [106C D].

The assessee, who was a partner of an assessee firm, had sold his house to another person. The Income tax Officer included the value of the house in his return for the assessment year 1945 46 and assessed him on it for the said assessment year. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the income tax officer was not competent to issue a notice under section 34(1) of the Act, because, he had failed to give a notice as required by section 34 (2). The Tribunal, however, rejected his contention and the High Court upheld the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The assessee could not be allowed to raise any question of law in this Court under article 136 of the Constitution. [448 C] Under section 22(1), the Income tax Act, 1922, is a complete code providing for the filing of returns and the assessment can be completed within one year of the date of service of notice under sub section (1) or sub section(2). But if the return filed on January 5, 1950, was no return at all, then the conditions under the first subsection of section 34 are satisfied. [449 D] The assessee had not made a full return as required under section 22 (3), and therefore, the period during which action could be taken was the extended one of eight years. [453 E] In the present case, the notice under s.23(2) was issued on January 4, 1950. The notice under that section was valid in law. [454 F G] The notice was valid only for a year and not for a return of income which showed no assessable income. [451 A B] The Income Tax Officer could have avoided the result by issuing a notice tinder s.34(1). [452 C D] In view of the fact that the assessee had failed in his appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, it was not open to him to contend that the notice was invalid because he had no jurisdiction to issue the notice. [452 E F] The question whether the notice issued under section 23(2), was valid or not, was a mixed question of fact and law. It was open to the assessee if there was sufficient justification for it to hold that the amount noted in the footnote was really the assessee 's income, in which case an assessable income would have been found and the tax could be charged thereon. [444 A B].

The first petitioner, a registered Central Trade Union, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi. The second petitioner, who was a registered central trade union, challenged the Circular dated 23 8 1982 ( Annexure A) on the ground that it violated the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act 1970, as amended by the N.B.S. & Co. (Amendment) Act, 1970, and the N .B. Series being a self contained code, the circular was ultra vires section 9 of the Act unless it was so read as to be in harmony with the provisions of the said Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the Circular is to neutralise and dis criminate the Directors who will truly represent the interests of the various persons manning or dealing with the bank as an industry and a commercial enterprise. [855C] 1.2 In the instant case, the object of Circular is not to neutralize and disengage any officer of the Bank to be appointed by the Central Government as the true representative of the employees. The object is to give the Board a truly representative character so as to reflect the genuine interests of all persons specified under section 9 as well as the larger and wider interest of national economy as postulated in Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43A of the Constitution. [862E F] 1:3. In the light of the rival contentions, it is clear that the object is not only to neutralises and disenchance the employees but also to reduce the choice of their choice in the selection of their representatives. That means, it would be perfectly in order for the Central Govern ment to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repre sentatives of the concerned employees, and, if necessary, to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose. [861F G] 1 :4. The Circular dated March 23, 1982 (Annexure B) is ultra vires the Act and the Scheme and it is null and void and of no effect. [863G H] 1 5. The transfer cases are directed to be conducted in a manner as specified in the scheme. The Central Government must in this regard act in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India for it is the latter that has the necessary expertise and intimate knowledge in the field of banking, finance and other connected matters. [864A] 1 6.

The appellant assessee was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The Appellate Tribunal declined to order any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The power to stay is incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. [67D] (ii) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Tribunal with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise of those powers, fully effective. In the present case, the Appellate Tribunals were given the power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal before the Tribunal. [69F] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had the power to impose penalty as incidental or ancillary to it. [70G H] (iv) The Appellate Tribunals must be held to have the power under section 254(1) with widest amplitude, and have in some cases been held similar to and identical with those of the powers of an appellate court under the Civil Procedure Code. [71A B] (v) The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is not a court but it exercises judicial powers. [72F G] (vi) The provisions of section 255(5) do not expressly confer a power on the Income Tax Officer who can give the necessary relief to an assessee. The right of appeal is a substantive right and the questions of fact and law are at large and are open to review by the Appellate Authority. [73G H; 74A] (vii) The Tribunal must be hold to have been the power in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. A certain apprehension may legitimately arise in the minds of authorities administering the Act that if the Appellate tribunals proceed to stay recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in the disposal of appeals by the appellate Tribunals. [74E F] (viii) The appeal must be dismissed.

The respondent was appointed a constable in the U. P. Police Force and on his appointment he was promoted to the rank of Head Constable and in May 1952, he was posted as Station Officer. On September 16, 1952, the Superintendent of Police made an endorsement on the report that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of dishonesty and therefore the order was invalid. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High Courts in India have not expressed their opinion on other questions raised and argued before them. In view of that finding the departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondents in regard whereof the respondent had no jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph (1) of para 486 of the Police Regulations. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries did not affect the validity of the order. (ii) The departmental inquiry is only a continuation of the enquiry and the departmental trial was validly held. If so, the question is whether para 486 would govern the present case or it would fall out side its scope. (iii) The fact whether in the meantime the police receives further complaints, or that it would fail within the express terms of para 487(2), does not affect either the question whether substantially the subject matter of the departmental proceedings and the department is the same. In this case the departmental enquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the magisterial inquiry and therefore it falls within the specific terms of Para 486(2). The fact, that in a interregnum the Police received further complaint or that there was no prejudice caused to the respondent the non compliance with the said regulations would not affect his validity. (iv) The order of the High court is set aside and the case remitted back to the High for disposal in accordance with law. (v) The State of U.P. vs Babu Ram Upadhya, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 861, followed. (vi) The respondent 's contention that para 486 could not affect him was not accepted by the High Courts and the order passed by them was set aside.

The appellant was appointed to supertime grade II in the Super time grade II of the Indian Medical Education Service. He was promoted as a Professor in the Specialists 'Silicon Hospital, and transferred to the said hospital on July 17, 1978. The promotion of respondents 4 to 24 was challenged by the appellant before the High Court by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. A Single Judge of the High court allowed the petition holding that the promotion of respondent 4 to super time grade 11 was in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules and that the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion as he was not qualified for being promoted to super Time grade II. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal preferred by the State. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appointment of respondents four persons in super time scale II was made by way or through a proper channel and (ii) the Government had acted mala fide in issuing the promotion order to the appellant at Simla instead of making an unspecified Specialists. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of promoting service into five different categories is to promote departmental candidates from amongst those who qualify for the same as provided for in rule 8(3). It is clear that when a post is created in a certain grade, category or cadre and it is to be filled in by promotion, that would only be from amongst persons belonging to Specialists Grade II. [53E] 1.2 The object is to encourage posts in the service into a specified post which means specified in the speciality in which a need has been felt from amongst the members of the specialists ' grade belonging to that speciality and in order of their inter se seniority a promotion could be given. In passing a contention, it is not open to him to urge that the post at Willingdon Hospital alone must have been filled by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. But it was very much possible for him to contend that whenever unspecified specialists were appointed on a particular grade, it could be filled up in either by promotion. [54F G] 1:3 The object being to encourage post of manningdon hospital at Willeddon, speciality and to promote the defence services, it must be held that whenever an unsadhent is created, a post in converted to a specified grade which means a specified higher post in the same speciality. [55G] 1 :4 The object was to encourage the post of a specialists cadre at Willningdons speciality and not to create posts for upward promotion service rendered as probationer. [56A B] 1 5.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about agrarian reform. The object of the Act was to provide for the ceiling on land ownership and for matters connected therewith. Section 19B provides that where a person is in possession and has no interest in any land acquired by him exceeding in the permissible area, he shall within the period prescribed, furnish to the Collector a return indicating the permissible areas he desires to retain. The Act was amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High Court had upheld certain patterns of alienations and acquisitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the land inherited by an heir by inheritance is saved from utilisation by the State. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Act has been enacted because the High Courts have taken the view that area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 is not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures Rules, 1953. [632 B] (2) Section 19 B provides for the acquisition of land in excess of permissible area. The excess land will be used for re settlement of tenants ejected or to be ejected under clause (i) sub section (1). The surplus land will he used for reopening the issue of a fresh notification and the court is not the anti hero in the drama of limping land reform. [32F G] (3) Section 10A provides that even if the source of the excess area is inheritance, bequest of gift, the capacity to own is conditioned by the permissible limit. Indeed section 19 B had to be enacted because, the High court took the view, that area was not hit under the ceiling set out in section 19 A and section19B were left untouched. [33G H] (4) The legislature has taken the policy of the law which brought about agrarian reforms. The courts are 'finishers, refiners and polishers of legislation which comes to them in a state requiring varying degrees of further. processing ', said Donaldson J., in Corocraft Ltd. vs Pan American Airways Inc., ; , referred to. (5) Section 9B provides for compensation for the surplus area to be distributed by the respondent in excess. The surplus area shall be at the disposal of Government for utilization under section 10 A. [34H] (6) The provisions of section 19A and 19B provide that the time lag is statutorily given for executing gifts and transfers to defeat the law itself. [35E F] (7) Section 20B provides a machinery for determining the surplus land. The legislature, while interpreting the saving clause, has used the words "any surplus area" in its widest connotation. The Legislature has not intended to convert the surplus pool into an opportunity to pervert and to thwart the substantive object of law. [36F G; 37A] (8) Section 17B provides the mode of recovery of land revenue by the Collector. The power conferred on the State Government is wide enough for executing any order under section 19. It follows that the appeals have to be allowed, which we hereby do without hesitation, without hesitation.

The appellants were the sons of one B, who was the eldest among the five sons of B. The respondents claimed that the property in suit originally belonged to B and the estate was divided into three categories: (i) his father 's share in the Zamindari; (ii) his brother 's interest in the estate; and (iii) his mother 's son 's family properties. The trial court held that the respondent had acquired occupancy rights in the lands and that the appellants were entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the Trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i ) the State Government had acted in exercise of the power conferred by section 3 of the Act and therefore the order of the Governor recognising Dayaram as Zamindar was not binding; (2) the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding the mutation was erroneous because no suit challenging the decision was instituted within two months from the date of the order, and (3) the decree of the Trial court was not barred by the decision in the present case. HELD : (i). The High Court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded to the appellants. [334 B] (ii).The High Court had no power under section 14 to determine rival claims of persons claiming proprietary rights to the property vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3. Section 14 is intended to determine only the proprietary rights in land, qua the State. The power is exercisable in accordance with and not in violation of the custom of the family. [336 C D] (iii). The order of Governor was in the form of a memorandum addressed to the Deputy Commissioner, Chanda, who had been authorised by the Governor to make his order. The order was made by the State Govern ment only in respect to the proprietary right in the property vested in the proprietor. The Collector was invested with quasi judicial power and if there be a dispute regarding the succession, the question of title could not arise. [328 D E] (iv). The decision of Governor did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. The High Courts were in error on the face of the terms of section 35(7) of Act 1 of 1951 which provides that the payment of compensation under this Act to the creditors of a proprietor or to the proprietor in accordance With the prescribed manner shall be a full discharge of the State government from all liability to pay compensation for the divesting of proprietary rights, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect thereof to which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom compensation has been paid as aforesaid.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the appellant was in arrears of rent from 1st September, 1964 and also on the grounds that the appellants were in arrears. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenants were in arrear of rent for more than six months. On appeal the appellate court confirmed the decree. In an application under article 227 of the Constitution the High Court held that the provisions contained in section 12(3) (a) and (b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 did not apply to the suit. The appellants contended that they had raised dispute about the standard rent by their letters dated 17 November 1966 and 19 December 1966 and therefore there was a dispute as to standard rent and the provisions in section 11(4) (b), of the Act were applicable. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that since the appellants had not complied with the provisions of section 12 (3) of Act, they could raise the dispute as they raised dispute regarding standard rent or permitted increases. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was in continuation of the tenancy and the notice terminating the tenancy was dated 1st December 1956 and therefore the period of one month after service of the notice under section 12 had expired. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts have not agreed with the view of the Gujarat High Court in Ambalal 's case. [633 B] (2) In the present case the appellants did not raise any dispute regarding the standard and the provision contained in sections 12(4), (a), (b). of the said Act, are applicable to the suits filed on 15th March, 1956. The suit for ejectment was filed on the 16th March 1956 on the basis of the letters dated 1 11 1966 and 20 December 1966. The notice terminating tenancy was issued on 18th April, 1966. On that date the appellants raised a dispute about standard rent. The respondent landlord did not file any application in terms of section 11 (3). The High court held that to limit raising a dispute within one month from the service of notice would render the provisions under section 11 of the Rent Act nugatory. [625 G H] Ambalala Pannalal vs Gajanan Vithoba Bobhate & Anr., ; , followed. Ambalai 's Case, (1911) 1 K.B. 171 and Chunilal Shivlal vs Chimanlal Nagindas, A.I.R. 1959 Bom. 177, approved. (3)(a) The Bombay High Court was right in holding that when the respondent paid all arrears of standard rent he did not comply with the provision of section 13(3). [637 B C] Amalal vs Badaldas, A, I. R. , referred to. (b)(i) In a suit filed on a notice under s.12(2) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates control Act, the respondent landlord raised a contention that the contractual rent was excessive and that the standard was excessive. The Trial Court found that the notices were not genuine and that there was no dispute about rent within one months of the service. The appellate court also held that there is no limitation of time during which a dispute must be raised and none can be implied from the Explanation to section 12 of the Amending Act.

The respondent company was a limited company incorporated in Canada, and its shareholders were the directors of the respondent company. The Aluminium Ltd., a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in India with effect from December 31, 1939, and in exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the company, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of respondent company, one of whom was a director of the Aluminium Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the Respondent company. One of these directors was Mr. L. G. Bash and the other directors had between them during the chargeable accounting periods ending December 31st, 1941, to 1943. The question for determination in this Court was whether the directors were entitled to be regarded as a company the directors whereof had a controlling interest therein. Held, that the Aluminium Limited was a subsidiary of the Indian Company and was not liable to tax under section 2(21) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, as amended by the Finance Act, 1951, read with section 66(1) of that Act. The shares in question which give the controlling interest are neither held by Mr.L. Gibby & Sons Ltd., nor were they subject directly or indirectly to his will and ordering and, therefore, he cannot apply either of the tests mentioned above. Commissioners of Inland Revenue vs Jamed Hodgkinson (Salford) Ltd., applied. Commissioner of Income tax vs Bipin Silk Mills Ltd., , referred to. Commissioner Of Income tax, Bombay City vs The Aluminium Company Ltd., ; , relied on. Commissioners for Excess Profits Tax vs J. Bibby and Sons Ltd. , distinguished. Commissioners, of Inland revenue vs Jamedar Hodgson, (1910) 14 I.T.R. 667, referred to, Commissioner of Inland Reve nue Income tax v. Bipin Silk Mill, , distinguished, Per Sarkar, J. The decision of the High Court in Commissioners of Income Tax vs Bipin Textiles Mills Ltd. was not applicable to the present case as well as to the facts found in the present ease. Commissioners on the other hand were entirely different from the case of directors who held the majority of shares as trustees and the votes they cast are their own votes.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant, Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st November, 1956 he was allotted to the new State of Karnataka with effect from 1st October 1957. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former state of Mysore, was abolished by the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. On 21st November 1972, some person junior to him were promoted as Assistant Engineer Grade II on their being found guilty of misconduct. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970. On 22nd November, 1972, the Board framed Recruitment and Promotion Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December, 1966. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I division clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their acquiring higher qualification and for promotion. On 31st October, 1957, some others junior to respondent were reverted as he had not passed the examination. The Respondent made several representation one such representations being on 25th December 1969. On 23rd January, 1970, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of reversion. The Single Judge dismissed it and the Division Bench held that the writ petition could not be thrown out on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the grounds that in view of the later Resolution dated 5th January,1970, it was no longer open to the Board to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court found that the earlier resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the question of seniority and was therefore not applicable to the respondents.

The petitioner, a widow of one of the deceased son of the petitioner, was taken from his home in police custody on January 1, 1987 by respondent No. 6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Station, Bishalgarh, for the investigation of an offence under section 379 I.P.C., which was registered at 8 P.M. on January 2, 1987. The petitioner was arrested on February 1,1987 by respondent Nos. 6 to 8 and his dead body was recovered from the railway track. The case against the petitioner was that she had died in police service on March 1, 1988 due to multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police lock up after he had escaped from police custody. In her petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for compensation for contravention of fundamental rights to life, it was contended that the death of her son occurred as a result of injuries inflicted by him while she was in judicial custody at the Police Outpost and his death was unnatural. The State of Orissa contested the petition on the ground that the petitioner 's son had been taken into police custody when he sustained fatal injuries. It was further contended that it was not a case of custodial death but of death of the son, as such, the petitioner could not be apprehended thereafter in spite of a search and seizure. The District Judge rejected the contention and held that the liability of the State for payment of compensation to the petitioner for violation of fundamental right to life under Article 21 of the Constitu tion was not established. The High Court also rejected the plea of sovereign immunity for tortious acts of its servants, and directed the State to pay a sum of Rs.1,50,000 to the wife of the victim. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The defence of 's husband is that he had managed to escape from police arrest at about 3 p.m. on the night between 1st December 1987 and 2nd December 1987. It is not a fit case for grant of compensation in exercise of its power under Article 142 of the Consti tution. [608D] 2. The right to relief under Article 226 of the Con stitution is a remedy available in public law and is based on strict liability for violation thereof, but this does not necessarily render the court powerless and the constitutional guarantee a mirage. It follows that 'a claim in public Law for compensation ' for contravention or violation of human rights, when the only practicable mode of redress available for the contravention made by the State or its servants in the purported exercise of their powers, is to be found in private law or for damages for the tortuous act of its servant. [508D E] 3.

The petitioner was convicted by the Chief Justice of India for committing an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court dismissed his petition for commutation of sentence on the ground that he had not been informed of the application made by him asking for a similar permission. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed is willing to be interview. [1187B] (2) It cannot be said that the Press is entitled to express any particular view or opinion but the right to means of information through the medium of an interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to life imprisonment. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for the Court to say that the two convicts are ready and willing to function. [1108C D] (3) The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President of India rejected his petitions for commutation. He is not the right in law to express no particular view of the matter. [1087D] (4) It is not a matter for this Court to decide whether the two petitioners are ready or willing to serve. [1018E F] (5) The petition is dismissed. [1009C] (6) If it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview a prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. There is a provision in the rules that if a person sought permission to be examined is a female, she can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. Taking an overall view of all the matter, it would not be possible to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be allowed to interview them.
