[1001D E] (7) The Superintendent of Jail shall allow the petitioner to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who are under a sentence of death. [1000E F; 1018A] (8) If in any given case there are weighty reasons for doing so, which we expect will always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore the petition is allowed.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., on January 19, 1950. On January 20, 1950 the appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. On August 26, 1950, the respondent moved an application requesting for damages from the Receiver and the appellant prayed that the receiver be appointed as Receiver. The trial court decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but the High Court dismissed it on June 29, 1970. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor court. The surety bond was executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District Judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Thus, by virtue of section 150, the Subordinate judge was entitled to exercise the same power in the matter of the enforcement of the bond as the District judge himself. [359 B C] (2) Under the terms of the surety bond, the appellant rendered itself liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the Court. Therefore, the order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the Receiver could be executed against the appellant to the extent to which it rendered itself personally liable under the terms thereof. [360 C D] (3) Under Section 150 of Code of Criminal Procedure, except in certain cases where the firm had become liable as surety for tho fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of the Court in any suit or in any proceeding J consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed either by the District Court or his successors, successors in office and assigns. [361 D E] (4) Under s. 150 of that Code, the court for the time being is seized of the proceedings. Under section 151(c), save as expressly provided, when the business is transferred under the Act to any one Court, it has the power to perform all the duties as are respectively conferred on the transferee court.

The appellants who were dealers in food grains, supplied wheat to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants and rejected the contention that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. In appeal the Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning of the U .P. Act, 1948. The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge. The appellants appealed to this Court with special leave. HELD : (i) Under section 4 of the Uttar Pradesh Wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959, the occupier of a sugar factory had to buy sugarcane from cane growers in conformity with the directions issued under the Act and the purchase order was not made in pursuance thereof. The power of the occupier to sell goods is conferred on him by the Control Order. Under section 21 of the Act the occupier may, by a written order require any person holding stock of iron or steel, acquired by him otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of clause 4 to sell the whole or any part of the stock to such person or class of persons and on such terms and conditions as may be specified in the Order. The State Government was competent under section 21 to impose tax purchases of sugarcane for use, consumption or sale in a sugar mill. [677 E F] (ii) Under the Act, the owner of a factory had a right to sell to the State Government 50% of the wheat held by him at the commencement of the Order and thereafter 50% Of the wheat sold was to be delivered by the dealer to the purchaser. The sale price was fixed by the State Govt. and the appellant was bound to deliver 50 per cent of the quantity of wheat purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of Order. [678 F G] (iii) Under clause 5 of the Control order, the State Govern ment had power to tax purchases in respect of goods specified in Schedule I. The appellant could not claim that the supplies were not sold as required by the order. The High Court was wrong in holding that the sales were made without any authority of law and that the transactions were not exigible to tax under section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act. [679 G H] (iv) Under cl. 5, the appellant could authorise a producer or stockholder to dispose of wheat from the dealer. If the cane grower made an offer, the factory was to take delivery on his behalf. The sugar cane growers were not given any option to sell it at the controlled rate. The Cane Commissioner had no option but to purchase 50 per centum of the sugar purchased by the appellant every day. [680 G H; 681 A] (v) Under r. 5 of U. P. Sugarcane (Levy ) Order, 1960, the cane growers could only be allowed to 50% in their sale price. The effect of the super imposition order was that the stocks of wheat supplied to the appellant were not to be sold by him to the Government or his authorised agent every day 50% thereof and that he had also to supply to the respondent State Government 100% of its quantity of foodgrains. [681 G H, 681 A B] (vi) The High Courts erred in holding the sales made by the respondent to the authorities were not liable to tax. [682 C D] (vii) Under s.4 of the , the occupier could sell to a Government or a stocahrolder only at the price fixed by him and not any other transaction which was deemed to be sale in accordance therewith. The expression "sale" in section 2 (h) means a transfer of property in goods for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration.

The appellant was detained under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him and he was informed that he was not to be taken at the place before the Advisory Board within three weeks from the date of detention. He was also not so released. The Advisory Board made its report on September 26, 1986. It found that there had been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22(4) and therefore, the appellant was entitled to be set at liberty. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the second order of detention dated August 7, 1986 contending that there has been a violation of the Constitutional protection afforded to him under Article 22(1) of the Constitution inasmuch as he was arrested and deprived of his person liberty long before the date on which the order of his detention had been made. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant is entitled to have been set at free, since no reference had been given to the Advisory Committee within the period of three weeks. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 Article 22 (4) of Constitution is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the day of hearing and therefore the detention should be upheld. [209C] 1.2 The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the Court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The procedural requirement are, there fore, to be strictly complied with if any value is to be attached to the liberty of the subject and the constitution al rights guaranteed to him in that regard. If a reference to an Advisory Board is to he made within three months, it is no answer to saying that the report though not obtained within three month, was obtained before the hearing of the case. If the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it would be not answer to that say that there was no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry of a period of 12 months from the dates of detention under the earlier detention order. [208D E] 1:3. The procedure prescribed by article22(4), is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of 3 months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. [207E F] 1 :4. The requirement of law under article 22 (1) is that the Advisory Boards set up under the relevant statute, are to render the protection of article 22.(4) nugatory and therefore section 15 has to yield. But by reading down the provision, the colli sion may be avoided and sec. 15 may be sustained. So avoiding the collision course, we hold that if the report of the Advisory board is not made within 3 months of the date or the second detention order, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three years from the d ee of the second impugned order of conviction. [206F G] 2:1.2 In a habeas corpus proceeding, it was not a enough answer to claim that the procedure prescribed in article 22 has been complied wi th by section 15 of the Act. The period of limitation for making a subsequent detention order under the Act against the same person, subject to the proviso that if there were no fresh grounds for such detained, the detaining authori ty becomes illegal unless he is satisfied about the sufficiency of the cause for detention. This implies that the question whether a law providing 'for preventive detention ' shall authorise detention of the person for such longer period as may be specified in the order has been considered before the expiry o f three months from that date, and this decision must be avoided. [205G H; 206A] 2.3 The procedural provisions are the most important for the purpose of this case.

The petitioner, a student of the respondent University, was established Vaidyas in Rajkot. He had intervened between them and the respondent. The respondent applied for filing an award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (the Act). A notice was issued to him by the petitioner calling upon him to appear before the arbitrator on 18th January, 1977. The application was converted into a Special Civil Suit No 84 of 1977. In the award it was stated that he had torn off the award and therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. The petitioner filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objection on the ground that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the arbitration agreement, and (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the respondent against the order of the trial Judge raising almost all the disputes which had been raised in this civil revision application. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award, it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to arbitration of the named arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award; secondly, by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter addressed to the arbitrator wherein it was mentioned that both of them had appointed him as an arbitrator to resolve the disputes between them. The award was signed by both the parties, about which there is no factual dispute, reiterated the fact that the respondents had agreed that both the petitioner and the Respondent would abide by the award dated 20th January 1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the Arbitrator himself. It was clear from the narration of facts that the conduct of both the sides that there were an arbitration agreements and by entering the agreement in question, the parties have agreed to referred the dispute for arbitration. The arbitrator had also agreed that the petitioner made an award. All these are in writing and signed by all the parties. This, in our opinion, is clear from his narration of events.

The appellant, a sub mortgagee of the respondent 's property, instituted a suit for recovery of money on the ground that the mortgage was not in execution and that the decree holder had become the successors in interest of the mortgagors. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the judgment debtor having made special request to the decreeholder for an amicable settlement of the properties, the decree holders were protected by sub section (5) of section 36 of the Act. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent as a bona fide assignee for value of the mortgage debt was protected by section 36(5). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the application for withdrawal of the suit under section 36 was not maintainable because (1) the decree in question was passed in execution proceedings and (2) the attachment was continued by a special order made under Order XXI, rule 57, as amended by the Calcutta High Court. HELD : The appeal must be dismissed. (i) The expression "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in section 36 (5), is not confined to assignment of debts and the entire interest of a mortgagor is not assigned to the sub mortgagee and that he has not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section(1) of Section 28. [586 H] (ii) The words "all rights of a mortgagee" are used in the widest sense and include all the rights which are incidental to the mortgagor 's interest. In the present case, the appellant was not an assignee within the meaning of sub s.(5) Of section 36. [591 B C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that there was no inconsistency between Promode Kumar Roy vsRupees and all the right of the mortgagor to recover the debt from the original mortgagor. [601 D E] (iv) The order of the executing court dated 30th January, 1937, which purported to dismiss the respondent from execution was not a final order of dismissal but an order of discharge under Order 21, rule57, as it stood before the amendment by the High Courts in the last sentence of that rule. [611 D] (v) The word "dissolved" in section 2(22) of the Indian Income tax Act means "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after the 1st day of Janu ary, 1939, or pending on that date and includes a proceeding in execution for any of the purposes mentioned in clauses (a), (b) or (c) or both. The word 'dissatisfied ' is not defined in section 3(22). It is not restricted to cases where the original mortgage debt is in the form of an English mortgage, but only with respect to a mortgage which was in the Form of an Indian mortgage. [621 D F] (vi) The respondent 'could not be allowed to take advantage of the order dated 30. January, 1939 passed by the executing Court on 30th Januar, 1939.

The appellant was the karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The properties were divided by metes and bounds in 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 and A 2 there was a disruption of the joint family and a severance of the Joint status between the members. In 1954, he transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint Hindu Family. In 1950, he sold the properties to the respondents. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court dis missed the suit on the ground that the transfers were made by the respondents under exhibit A I and A2. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree in O.S. No. 62/54 but held that the transfer was not supported by any consideration and was invalid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The properties sold by the appellant were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras School of Mitakshara law by which Venkatacharyulu was governed he had no power to make a gift of the coparcenary properties, the two deeds being in reality gift deeds. [46 C] (ii) The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts. The gifts were not hit by section 6(h) of the . [47 D E] Balo vs Parbati, I.L.R. , referred to. (iii) The transfer was without consideration by way 'of gift and as such was invalid under section 6 (h). [48 C] Balos vs Parbata Subba Rao, I, L. R. , approved. (iv) The gifts are not hit or invalid because they were made in consideration of past illicit cohabitation. [47 E F] Balio vs Parbatlal I. L.R., , referred. (v) The gift was valid but in holding that the gifts were invalid, the court found that the alienations were without any consideration by the respondent and were invalid. [48 D] (vi) The High Court rightly held that past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for the transfers under exhibit. A 1. [49 E F].

The appellant was the owner of certain properties. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the said properties on the ground that the appellant had not been in possession of them and that the suit was barred by limitation under section 116A of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the period of 30 days prescribed for filing the appeal was not applicable to the case as it was filed beyond the period prescribed for an appeal under the Limitation Act. On appeal the High Court held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time and dismissed the suit. In this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that (i) the first part of section 29(2) of the Limitation act did not apply to an appeal filed under the Indian Law; (ii) the second part of the section did not prescribe any period of limitation for an application under the Code of Civil Procedure and (iii) the words "where any special or local law prescribes a period of time different from that prescribed therefor by the First Schedule" occurring in the first limb of sub section (2) would also apply to a case where the first Part of the Act does not prescribe a period within which an appeal lay; and (iv) the third part of Section 29(1) was independent of the first, part reading "for the purpose of determining any period Of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special, or local laws" as being wide enough to include a suit, Appeal or application under a special or Local law which is of a type similar to that prescribed by the first schedule. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The second part reading section 29 (2), of the Code, in so far as it provides for an exhaustive and exclusive code of limitation, makes it clear that the procedure applicable in an appeal against an order made by a civil court under section 98 of the Civil Procedure Code is that prescribed in the First schedule to the Limitation Acts. [166F G] (2)(a) The first part reading 'for the purposes of computing any period or limitation prescribed ' for any suits, appeal and application by a special law makes it plain that the general provisions of the , are excluded from the operation of the second parts of section 12(2). [167G H] (b) The expression "appeal" in article 156 of the First Part means an appeal governed by the Code or the Code. The first limb is wide enough in its ambit to include appeals under the Letters Patent and the second limb of section 5 of the Limita tion Act. [168H; 169A B] (c) The words " where any special" or local Law prescribes a time limit for an appellate court, mean that though a right of appeal is conferred by section 116 A(1), the appeal thereunder for the purpose Of sub section 2 will be deemed to be an appeal from an original decree passed by a Civil Court situated within the local limits of its civil jurisdiction. [169F G; 170A] (d) The word "appeal", in the context of the limitation Act, means an application made under the Civil Courts Act and not a suit or an application for an order of any kind. [170G H; 171A B]. (e) The High Court was right in holding that section 29 of the 1963 Limitation Act would apply only when a special 'or local law prescribed a period. [171E] (f) The object of the 1908 Act is to provide a speedy or local interest for any particular appeal and not to confer on the court an appellate jurisdiction and that it is sufficient if the procedure prescribed by section 29 is followed in order to render the provisions of section 3 thereof nugatory, indicating thereby that the special law is applicable only when the special or ' local law prescribing a period is prescribed in that Schedule. [172F] (g) The question whether for the purposes Of computing the period under section 12 of the .a suit or appeal governed under the special ,or local laws for which a period Of time is provided in the Act, is one of mixed questions of fact and law, depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. [173G] (h) The provisions of sections 9 to 18 of the are applicable only to suits, appeals or applications for which no period of Limitation is prescribed by a Special or local statute.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate, Mathura under section 76 of the (Act) on the ground that the power to fix any area as a bus stand was vested in the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76(2)(r) of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magis trate to fix places for the bus stand/halting place '. It further observed that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get down and pick up the passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as one of the bus routes. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The Regional Transport Authori ty has passed the impugned orders in question with the object of establishing a bus stands in the area in question. That appears to be so from the order passed by District Magistrate and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of the Town Area Committee. [717D] 2. The District Magi trate has passed an order in question without prejudice to its providing a bus service for anybody who chooses to use it voluntarily and to such person being required to pay for such use. [700E] 3. Section 76(1) of Act empowers the State Government to make rules regarding the maintenance and management of parking places and stands and the fees, if any, which may be charged for their use. Section 77(2) (r) provides that no person incharge of a motor bus plying for hire shall for the purpose of taking up or setting down passengers, park or stop his bus anywhere within the limits of the municipal ity except at the Municipal Bus Stand. The other bye laws provided for a levy of a fee of Re. 1 for every 8 hours or part thereof in respect of the use of the Bus stand by such buses and for the issue of a permit on such payment. [617F H] 4. Section 68(2), (r ) of the , provides that the State Govern ment may, by notification, specify places within the limit of any municipality notified under section 68(1), or the area notified thereunder or in places other than duly notified stands or halting places and requiring the driver of a stage carriage to stop and remain stationary for a reasonable time when so required by a passenger desiring to board or alight from the vehicle at a notified halting place. [72B C] 5. Section 73 provides that a bus permit shall be issued in such a manner as may be specified or public service vehicles may stop for a longer period than is necessary for the taking up and setting down of passengers. The power to issue a notification fixing a bus Stand is vested on the State Govt. specifically to make Rules regarding the maintaining and management, of parking place and stands, and the fee, ifany, which might be charged by such person in respect at the municipal Bus stand. [71C D] 6. Section 75(2 (r), r/w. 349(ii) of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 provides that any area or a halting place may be notified by the State Gov ernment to have the up or set down passengers.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the . The prosecution case was that on October 19, 1961 Sub Inspector of Food and Supplies Department was present at Smalkha Barrier along with Head Constable, who was driving a truck. On the way the truck was intercepted by the police and the driver was found carrying 75 bags of paddy. The truck was seized from the truck as also the bags of rice. It was alleged that the consignment of paddy was booked from Lakerkotla on October 18, 1961 by Qimat Rai on behalf of M/s Sawan Ram Chiranji Lal. The consignee of the paddy was Messrs Devi Dayal Brij Lal of Delhi. The consignor of the rice was Messrs. Sawan Singh and others. The goods were seized under a search warrant. The appellants contended that there was an attempt on the part of the appellants to transport paddy to Delhi, and so there was no export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. Held, that the appellants should not have been convicted under Section 7 of . The appellants were rightly convicted under para 2(b). The truck with the loaded paddy was seized at Samalkha Barriers which was 32 miles from Delhi and it was found that the goods were being watched at Samalsha Barrier which is 32 miles away from Delhi. It could not be said that there had been attempt on account of an attempt to commit the offence of export. The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. The sufficiency of the actus reus is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission Of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempting to commit a crime he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit that offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the act.

The Sassoons entered into a contract with the Sassoon for the supply of their Managing Agency to Messrs Agarwals and they were assessed to income tax on the basis that they had earned the commission in the hands of the Sassoon Agencies. The Sassoosons agreed to transfer their managing agency to M/s Agarwals at the same rate as the Managing Agency Agreement and the transfer was made by the Sasawall Agencies to the respective transferees. The transferors were to be paid the remuneration for the period of actual services rendered by them to the company and the portions of the remuneration or commission which were earned by the companies during that period. The managing agency agreement provided that the remuneration payable to the Sasseosons would be the income accruing to them in the chargeable accounting period, but that the company would not be entitled to any commission or remuneration for such remuneration. The company was assessed to tax on its own income and the company claimed that the managing agency commission was earned by it as a result of the agreement between the Sasomans and M/S Agarwals. Held, that the transaction in question was one of the Managing Agents of the respondent company and not of the managing agents of the company. The Managing Agency Agreements were independent contracts and the remuneration received by the respondent from the companies under the managing Agency Agreement could be taxed only as income accruing directly to the respondent and not as a part of it. Held further, that in computing the taxable income of the assessee the profits and gains of the whole year must be taken into account. The agreement was independent of the business of the Company and was the source of the income. The mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source or character of income. Held also, that on the facts of the case it could not be said that the commission received by M/ s Agarwals from the Companies under the agreement was income accruing in the course of the year and therefore the profits of the firm were liable to tax. The assessee was entitled to the entire remuneration as a business expenditure. Held accordingly, further, the agreement did not amount to a transfer bearing asset within the meaning of section 2(d) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and the transaction was one which was one for the purposes of taxation.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A statement made by a witness within the meaning of section 157 of the Evidence Act should be in the first instance fully established. [90 D] (2) It is not necessary that the statement must be proved beyond doubt. The probative value of an admission or confession does not depend upon its communication to another, though just like any other piece of evidence it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. This proof in the case of oral admission or a confession does no depend upon the communication to other than they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. [91 E F] (3) The High Courts have consistently accepted the circumstantial evidence adduced in the ease and have held that the word "statement" used in section 157 meant only "something that is stated" and the element of communication was not necessary before "sthing that is said". [92 G H] Pakala Narayana vs R. , referred to. (4) The evidence of an admit ted statement or confession can be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or confessions, as in the present case, but it cannot be used as a corroborative piece of Evidence. [92 F G] (5) In the instant case, the High Court was right in holding that the accused must have committed the murder. No other reasonable hypothesis was or could be suggested. [93 H] (6) The confession made by the appellant is not a substantive piece of substantive evidence and it cannot therefore be admitted as a confession under section 30 of the . [94 C D] Pakla Narayana vs rant, A.I.R. 1959 Supp. 1 S.C.R 310, referred to, (7) In this case, P.W.s 11, 13 and 15 deposed that they clearly heard the accused say when he opened the door of the house and came out at 60 'clock in the morning of the fateful day. The evidence was not corroborated by any other evidence.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. He was kept under suspension from August 9, 1973 pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973. The appellant submitted his reply on december 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The said order was challenged in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Rule 5 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Service Regulation, 1976 is ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution and that the rule is ultra rites of Article 14 of The Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 5 is ultra vivour of Article14 of the Constitu tion. [225B] 2. Rule 9 of the Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate the services of a permanent employee by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. It was not the contention therein that the Rule was capable of two constructions. It is settled law that there is a presumption of constitutionality of the rule. The Court ought not to interpret the statutory provisions, unless compelled by their language, in such a manner as would involve its unconstitutionality, since the legislature of the Rule making authority is presumed to enact a law which does not contravene or violate the constitutional provisions. Therefore, there is no valid opportunity to interpret Rule 5. [226C D] 3. The rule is valid and it cannot be said that the language in Rule 5 would be capable of both interpretation. It may be correct to say that the Board may unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there was no need for the services. A perusal of the rules shows that the Rules make authorityisation or revision of pay scales and other conditions of service of Development Authority employees whether permanent or temporary. [227D E] 4. Rule 8 is valid. But from the facts it is clear that the Legislature of the rat ed Government has to enact the law which did not contravene nor violate Article 14. Therefore there is nothing in the Rules to show that the rules were capable of one interpretation. [228E F] 5. The expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee 's service" whether permanent, or temporary, which shall be decided by the Board" means that the board of management may form an objective opinion on the basis of the material, that the post which the officer or the employee is occupying no longer is in need. Thereby, the post would be abolished. [229F G] 6. The words "in this event ofthe Society not being having any other need" thus have to be construed from the language employed would be that the Boards of Management may form a different opinion on its basis. [230B C] 7. Rule 10 of the Central Road Transport Service Rules, 1976 which came into force on May 1, 1976, is valid as it does not violate or violate Article14. [231C D].

The appellant State issued a notice on February 3, 1970 inviting tenders for the grant of li cial rights for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. The appellant was declared an elected candidate and his name was entered in the prescribed register and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. On February 3. 1970 the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the bid at the auction was not approved by the State Government as required under section 22(1) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the State Govern ment had no power to interfere with the auction held by the Collector after it had been declared as the State Govt. had issued instructions to him not to issue the licenses. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the State had no authority to issue such a notice; (ii) the notification dated August 19, 1970 was invalid as the authorities for fixing the procedure under the amended section 29(2)(b) had not been specified the Government was competent to accept or reject any tender without assigning any reason therefor; and (iii) the High court erred in holding that since the appellant was the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his names were entered in a bid register and he was a licensee for several liquor shops, amended it in the light of the subsequent developments. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government issued a special order under section 29 (2) (b) of Bihar andOrissa Excise Act 1915 in so far as it directed that fees for licences for retail sale of country liquor should be fixed by auction. [703C] 2. Section 22(i) provides that the Government may grant to any person, on such conditions and for such periods as it may think fit, the exclusive privilege or privilege in respect of any intoxicant. The power to accept a tender without specifying the authority which was to be exercised is conferred by section 22 (1) and under such control as may be specified. [803D E] 3. Section 29(1)(b), which has been amended with retrospective effect, itself provides that no grantee of any privilege shall exercise it unless or until he has received a license in that behalf from the Collector or the Excise Commissioner. The respondent State had issued a notification under section 5 of the Act for the purpose of granting licence to the appellant for selling country liquor. The Government had issued another notification dated February 3 1, 1974 under section 9(2) of Act 17 of 1970 for grant of license for the retail sale in favour of the respondent. The Collector 's tender notice was quashed by the High Courts on the grounds that the appellant had no right to collect and re auctioned the liquor and that the respondent was not entitled to any order for its refund. [788E F] 4. Section 5 of Act 18 of 1970 provides that a grantee of such privilege shall be deemed to have been granted in the interest of the Excise revenue, if he has obtained a licence in that respect. The grant of an exclusive privilege under section 20(1), is not a privilege of a citizen of India and it is not subject to any other provision of the Constitution. [789G H] 5. Section 8 of the Amending Act of 1970 was amended with effect from August 19 1970 by adding a new sub section (2). The amended section also provides that "no grantee of a privilege shall grant licence for sale of liquor or to grant that right to its license holders on payment of consideration, with such conditions as may he necessary in the public interest". [702B C] 6. Section 7 of the amending Act provided that no grant of any licence under section 21 of the amended Act shall be made except in accordance with the provisions of sub section 2 of section 29. The proviso to this section provided that "the State Government may, after giving an opportunity to the licensee or the excise commissioner, make such orders as it thinks fit" and that "shall not be liable to any penalty for any reason whatsoever". The High Courts held that the amended Section 29 (1)(a) did not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and naked power in determining the sum payable under section 28(1). [704C D] 7.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 302 read with section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on 19th December 1967 one of the accused, a friend of deceased Narendra and his wife, had gone to Bombay for his business in the manufacture of medicines. The Manager of the said house searched the house of the appellant and recovered a cycle from him. The appellant was further charged with having committed theft of articles in the house. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 120 B read with sections 302, 454 and 201 of the I.P.C. On appeal by special leave, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no corroboration of the actual participation in the murder and that the evidence of the deceased was not corroborated by the evidence against him. HELD: (i) The appellant had been rightly convicted under section 201 read with s.120B of I. P.C., [619 A] (ii) There was no motive for the appellant to commit theft. The evidence of PW 2 that he and his son were seen alive by Kewal Ram, owner of the betel shop on 26th December, 1967, is not corroborated in material particulars. The High Court found that there were no corroboration in regard to the crime. [620 B] (iii) There is no corroboration as to the actual complicity in the crime with the crime and the evidence must confirm that part of the testimony which suggests that the crime was committed by the accused. If a witness says that the accused and he stole the sheep and he put the skins in a certain place, the discovery of the skins would not corroborate the evidence. [625 E] (iv) The High court found that the death of Narendra and the theft were proved beyond doubt. There was also no corroboration to the evidence regarding the crime as well as the common intention by way of a pre conceived plan to murder Narendra. The nature of corroboration is that it is confirmatory evidence and it may consist of the evidence in material details to connect the accused with the time. When it is said that the corroborative evidence must implicate or tend to connect an accused with his crime, the court must satisfy that there is nothing inherently impossible in evidence. The rule as to corroboration is based on the reasoning that there must be sufficient corroborative evidence in materials particulars to connect a person with the offence. [613 E F] (v) There are no independent corroboration of evidence in the material particulars and that it was proved that the murder or theft formed the same transaction and were committed by accused No. 2 and 3. The mere fact that the deceased had been murdered is not conclusive. It is necessary to find out whether there is sufficient corroborative Evidence in material facts to connect accused with crime. In the present case, the evidence on record was that the appellant was responsible for the theft of his articles. [512 G H] (vi) The conviction and sentences were set aside by the High court.

The appellant was the owner of a Hindu undivided family. He had been granted a sanction to the draft scheme under section 22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 (Bombay Act No. 1 of 1954) for the purpose of acquiring his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. yard. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2 per sq., by his order dated November 4, 1971. On appeal, the Town Planning officer held that the appeal was not maintainable as the Act did not provide an appeal from a decision of the Town planning Officer on matters dealt with by him in his order. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Gujarat High Court which dismissed the same holding that the Act does not provide for an appeal against a decision by the Town Plan officer on matters dealing with by the parties and that the provisions of sections 32, 33 and 34 have a direct bearing on the question of appealability of the town planning scheme. The High Court held that section 32(1) provides an appeal only to the Town planner who is given a plot in the final scheme and not to the final plot holder. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the Town Commis sioner 's decision was appealable under clause (viii) or clause (xiii) of section 32 (1); (ii) the Act specifies a principle of compensation, and (iii) the High Court erred in holding that enactment of a rule determining compensation payable to an owner for loss of land has to be determined on the basis of market value of the land on the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating the compensation payable by persons interested in the scheme estimated on the market value on the dates of the declaration of the intention to making a scheme, and section 64 (1) prescribes an additional amount of loss to be paid to an owners of land who are injuriously affected by the making of a town planning Scheme. [92F] 2. The object of determining compensation is to make provision for estima tion or adjustment of price of land of which the owner was deprived by the scheme estimate on the valuation of the lands under section 66. Section 73 provides that the owner shall, after notice given by him, pay to the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the par ties. The rate of interest is fixed at 6 per cent and the rate is fixed for a case where the amount payable to the owner exceeds the amount due from him. [93G H] 3. Section 65 provides that where the owner fails to provide any land in excess of the value of land which is injuriously effected by the taking of a Town planning scheme, he shall be entitled to obtain compensation from the local authori ty or from any person benefited or partly from the Local authority and partly from such person as the Town Development Officer may in each case determine. [94H; 95A] 4. The provisions of section 65 (1)(f) are applicable only to cases where the total of the values of the original plots included in the revised scheme exceeds the market price of the same plot when taken into account without the improvements. The increment is a principle applicable to all cases in which by virtue of operation of the Act a person is deprived of his land whether in whole or in part. It may be recalled that section 33 provides for an enhancement of compensation from Rs.

The appellant was the brother of his grand son, who died in 1934 leaving two daughters. The widow filed a suit for partition of land according to her share and for mesne profits. The appellant contended that the daughters were entitled to their lands taking into account the provisions of the will to select their respective shares and that the appellant was entitled to the lands taking them as his son. Held, that the testator 's heirs had no right to make a selection in respect of the properties which they were entitled. The testator 'had only an option to select the land to be given to each son and therefore there could not be any question of the legatees making the selection. Narayanasami Gramani vs Hindle, Mad. 981, approved. Narayana Krishna Moideen vs Hinde, Mad 980, referred to. The will was a will by which the testator appointed his brother as guardian of his minor daughters as well as his foster son as also two other sons. The question whether the legate were entitled under the will was one for election to the Court and not for the daughters to make the selection, but only for the daughter to make it clear that the intention of the testator was clearly to select her son and not to appoint a third person to make selection. The words "he shall give to the female children " in section 89 were intended to cover the selection of the daughters and did not mean that the legate would get their lands after taking into consideration the good and bad quality of the land. Narayansami Grami vs Hindles, Mad., 981 and Narayanaswami vs Hindling, Mad, 980 referred to, distinguished. The vattam was not intended to be a gift for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, but it was intended to make an artificial rule of construction that in such cases the testator intended the legatee to select should be applied in India also and the decision in Narayanashanasami vs Hindley, Mad 881, referred only to the interpretation of the words " he shall give the widow with a right of selection to the legatee. The case fell under section 89 and was not applicable to the facts of the present case. The first appellant had indicated the selection or appointed a third party to make her selection but still the gift could be made certain by selection.

The appellant, a widow of one B, filed a suit for joint possession over the land in dispute. The respondents contested the suit and pleaded that the defendants were in separate occupation of the land or plots in dispute and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to any share out of the produce and, therefore, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. The District Judge decreed the plaintiff 's suit for a joint possession of the lands in dispute but the High Court set aside the decree on the ground that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in law in holding that there had been no evidence on record to prove that the appellant was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the respondents assured the plaintiff that her name shall be entered in the record during consolidation proceedings. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Court erred in Law in holding the suit was barred by section 49 of the Act. [867D] 2. The possession of B apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of his sons as co sharers would be deemed in law to be the possession thereof. [886E] 3. In the instant case, the High Courts had held that the possession was not given by the defendants because they were co sharer of plaintiff 'S ' and the respondents had absolutely any concern with the appellant giving her an assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. [876G] 4. The fact remains that the District Judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during consolidation operation either by the respondents or somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. In this connection, the District Court found as follows: (a) The possession was never given to the plaintiff by the defendant, as the defendants had no concern in the rent and profits of the suit land of a co shar holder; (b) the plaintiff has not been informed about the consolidation proceedings and was assured by the plaintiff. [877B C] 5.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Haryana. The first respondent filed an affidavit in support of the petition stating that he had been appointed Deputy Prime Ministers and that the oath administered to him as Deputy Prime Minis ters was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution. The petitioner also stated that he was still functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to the petitioner. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Minister is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Ministry. [219G H] 2. The prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. This Court in Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., ; , held that the prescribed oath must be divided amongst the Ministers and the description of the Prime Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Chief Secretary, along with his other submis sions, but the description as longas the other Ministers are required to take. He has no power of the President to make the affirmation of the sovereignty and integrity of India. [319H; 319A B] 3. The expression "Chief Minister" in section 2(1) of the Act means a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Minister. He is a member of the council of Ministers although he has not been described by him as Ministers and hence the first contention raised by the petitioner that he is just a Minister cannot vitiate the appointment of the oath as such. [ 319C D] 4. The question whether the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty, integrity of the India does not vitiate his oath.

The appellant, a company which was carrying on the business of running and maintaining work, stopped work in the factory on 1st November, 1948, and closed it on that day. The dispute between the workmen and their employers was referred to the Industrial Tribunal under section 10(1) (c) of the , for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the continuity of service of the workers was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers who participated in such strike were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B(1). On appeal, Held, that the appellant was not entitled under the Act to carry on the work so as to amount to a strike. The provisions of the Factories Act were similar to those contained in section 49 A of the Act and it was an illegal strike. Section 49 B provides for a strike which is not a lock out by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal, or under a common understanding of any number of persons who are or have been so employed to continue to work or to accept employment. The expression "strike" in section 2(q) of that Act includes a cessation of work by a person employed in an industry acting on the part of a large number of workers. The word "stciliator" in the present case, is not defined in the Act as meaning "a cessation of duty by a party of persons engaged in the industry acting within the scope of the definition. Section 2(p) of tile Industrial Disputes Act defines "stquisite" to mean "a cease and cease to be a workman on the happening of any event which may occur by sickness". The word 'strike ' is defined in section 3(q), as meaning a cessation or cessation of employment, in the case of an illegal strikes. Section 4 is not applicable to cases where the interruption in service is brought about by an illegal lock out and the workers are acting in concert. The workmen were granted exemption from the provisions of Chapter IV A of that Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1947, on the ground that they had been acting in a strike and could not be regarded as being a concerting action on the night of 1st Nov., 1948, but that the stoppage of work on 1.11. 1948 was not a concerts in the company 's service.

The appellant, actor, was charged with offences under section 292 I.P.C., for having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censors. The prosecution alleged that the famous picture was misleadingly foul and he had arrived at the scene of offence. The Magistrate after examining some witnesses, took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused under section 79 I. P.C. The appellant contended before the High Court that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the Act, there is a justification for its display thereafter and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 of the Penal Code, the public exhibition, circulation or distribution or the production of the film even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals are liberally certificated. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the film had been certified by the Central Board of Film Censor and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious was a valid certificate under section 80 of the Code. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The trial court when it hears the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under the provisions of the Constitution and once the special law polices the area it is pro tanto out of bounds for the general law. At least as a matter of interpretation, section 79 does not come down to the ground that the certificate granted under it by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 293 I.p.C.[515D E] 1.2 The High Courts in their judgment have taken the view that the facts stated in the complaint prima facie attract the offence under Section 292 I P. C., and therefore, the film having been certified as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292I.P.,C. to punish such exhibition unless the ground covered by the two laws be different. [515E F] 1:3 The High court has not committed any error in its judgment in the present case of the motion picture. [525F G] 2.1 Section 79 of I. p. C. does not confer a certificate on the successful candidate. It is an ex pression, not a moral tailor setting his own fashions but a statutory gendarme policing films under article 19(2) from the angle of public order, decency or morality. [500G H] 2:2 The question whether the film has become "not a menace and a guarantee" is a valid classification as was held by this Court in K. A. Abbas vs State of Andhra Pradesh, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as an Advocate on the ground that he had suffered from a acute shortage of work. The petitioner challenged the power of the Government under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court. The High Court declined to dispense with his personal appearance and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Government Pleader was not a party to the writ petition, (ii) the Advocate General had no locus standi to file an affidavit; (iii) the State Government was in error in holding that the Government pleader was not entitled to seek or cling out any other litigant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Government Pleader is only an ordinary litigant and is not bound to encourage monopoly within the profession. [766D] 2. The Court cannot ignore the fact that the government Pleader of this Court is a party in any case. It is inconceivable how he would have discharged his duties to the court and to his client if this crowd of land acquisition cases were posted in several courts more or less at the same time. [764E F] 3. The State, appreciating the need for a Government pleader, should engage competent lawyers without hunting for political partisans regardless of capability. Public offices and Government Pleaders are the best judges to be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [753G H] 4. The practice of filing affidavits is not a legal right apart from the fact whether they do so or not. [774A B] 5. The Supreme Court has no power under article 32 to issue any writ, order or direction which would have the effect of prejudging the legality of the action and subvert the rule of law itself. [773G H; 771A] 6. The court is expected to evolve a policy in regard to its Law Officers which admits of lawyers convenience becomes a part of the profession and the office must be held not to be private. It may be that the courts are more competent to decide what they should do so, and further peculiarities have been made while functioning in the State. [ 771B C] 7. The very nature of the matter is important. A bunch of Government pleaders are the nucleus about which the professional class of the nineteenth century was to form. It would be difficult for them to urge that lawyers should not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf, for the sake of convenience. [763C D] 8. The courts have a numberof other duties to discharge. Besides, they do not contradict Government 's power to appoint more than one Government Pleader. [765D] 9. The Courts have a large number of lawyers with their vilemma and a large scale of work is an internal arrangement and the Court must be satisfied that there are adequate number of other duties. [661E F; 765A B]. 10. The Judges of the High Courts are expected to decide on the quality of the product or service, control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the people who are the third world clients and practice partisolution in court. These principles make poor appeal to those who count, which is a pity. [ 765F G] 11. The time has come to examine the quality and duties of Government Pleader and in this Court there is no error even in that behaviour. Not to have provided more government counsel when the volume of litigation demanded it, would have clogged the lawyers in court and helped them to foot the bill. [ 767G H, 767A] 12. The question whether a Government lawyer is an agent of the State or is a private party depends on the facts of each case. If the crowd of government Pleader is entangled out from it large scale, there would be no need for adjournment for adjournment because of absence of counsel and, lastly, sets a limit on the total fee payable for government work executed. [ 768D] 13. The number of counsel who are Assistant Government Pleader should be fixed by the administrative rules of the state. [ 769E F]. 14.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Mills held on May 6, 1948, a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the bank and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by the shareholders. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd., which was a public limited company. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50 per share and the shares were allotted at a lesser rate. The respondent No. 1, who was a Public limited company, filed an application under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the issue of bonus shares on the ground that the release by the Mills of the shares of its shareholders amounted to distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income of the seven appellants and of other shareholders of their company as dividend on the footing that the releasing by the mills of the share holders amounted to a distribution of dividend within the definition of that expression in section 2 (6A). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the distribution of the right to apply for and obtain two shares of a company was an distribution of dividends within the scope of section2(6 A) of Act and in answering it in favour of the appellants, the High Court took into account both the normal and the extended meaning of that word. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the distributed by the appellants amounted to "dispute" within section 2.(6A), and in rejecting the contention of the appellant that the shares had been distributed as dividend within its ordinary meaning, it was open to the Mills to renounce the offer. [587 F] (1) The High Courts were right in taking into account only two normal and extended meaning, namely, (a) distribution of a capital of an assessee could not be regarded as dividend for the extended definition of "Dividend". It was open under section 2 of the Act to nominating persons who were to take over the shares and that is what the Mills did. The mills had three options, (1)[1957] S.C.R. 888, 888 and (2) to decline to accept the offer made by the appellant. [588 G H; 589 A B] (b) The mills could not therefore be compelled to obtain this benefit if it did not desire to do so. It could accept the shares or decline to take the form of a resolution for distribution of bonus, but it was not distributed in money; it may be distributed by delivery of property or right having monetary value. [589 C D] (2)(a). The High court was right that the distributable dividend would undoubtedly have been distribution of profits within the ordinary meaning of the expression "difference" in section2 (6 A), and the High court had to take into account two normal or extended meaning.

The appellant was defeated. The election petitioner filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent, the returned candidate, on the ground that the names of the witnesses whom he desired to produce were already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election petition and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present in Court without any order of the Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that except the appellant, no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the appellant was recorded, the Court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidates; and thereafter, the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the parties. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf the appellant that (1) the purpose of section 87(1) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 must satisfy the requirements of section 83 and 84 of the Act, and (2) the Court must ascertain how far sub rule (3) would carve out an exception to the enabling provision contained in Rule 1A of Order XVI. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The scheme of the various provisions of the , is that after the court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list of witnesses with the gist of evidence of each witness in the Court within the time prescribed by sub rule(1). But where the party would be in a position to produce its witnesses without the assistance of the court, it can do so under Rule 1 A of Order XVIII. [532C D] (b) The purpose of the Rules is to provide for the examination of witnesses within the period prescribed under sub rule 1 of Rule 1 of order XVI and Rule 22 of the High Court Rules would not have omitted to mention that only those witnesses kept present could be examine whose names are mentioned in a list prepared by subrule (1). [533E] (c) The consequence is that where the witness summoned either to give evidence or to produce documents fails to attend or to do so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings, the court on being satisfied of the service as provided therein and is further satisfied that the person has without lawful excuse failed to honour the summons, the trial as provided in sub rule 2 of Order XVII would be a proclamation requiring him to attend to give his evidence or produce documents without applying for summons under Rule I. If it was implicit in Rule IA that it only enables the party to examine only those persons whose names were mentioned in that list, the person who wanted to produce the witnesses could not be allowed to do such witness on the date of hearing and the court cannot decline to examine the witness unless the Court proposes to act under the proviso to sub rule.(1) or (2).

The appellant, a teacher of the Intermediate College, was appointed on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay of Rs. 550 1200. The appointment order stated that he had assumed charge of the post of Principal and he had convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on April 12, 1981. The appellant submitted his application for appointment to the post. The Manager of the College informed him that as per the communication received by him from the Manager of his college, he had been appointed as Principal and that he has convened an emergency meeting of its staff to consider the question of his appointment as Principal. The manager of the college wrote to the Manager that since the appellant was not willing to hold the post, he should be given one year 's notice. The management did not pay any salary to the appellant though he functioned as Principal, and ultimately the appellant approached the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying for a writ of mandamus directing the 5th respondent to ensure non drawal of pay of teachers appointed after his date of appointment. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the radiogram dated April 7, 1981 contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore the Committee of Management had no power to set up a selection committee nor the selection committee had any power to make appointment. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the date on which appellant was appointed as principal, the Committee had no right to select the appellant nor the Committee could make appointment and therefore it may be declared that the appellant continued to hold a post of principal in contravention of the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power conferred on the committee of management to make appointments is suspended for the time being. [975D] 1.2 In order to avoid forestalling of governmental action by private managements, the power to appoint teachers including Principals has been left untouched. But there is no power of appointing any person having a scheme of administration as envisaged by section 16A and the scheme of Administration envisages setting up of a Committee of management and the Committee has the power under sub section (1) of section 9 to set aside the appointment. [979E] 1:3 The power of wide amplitude will comprehend the power of making appointments including of the appointment of a Head of an institution and of the teachers. Sub sec. (10) is not attracted in this case because, the order made by the State Govern ment under sub sections (1), (2), (3) preceding sub section(4) of sec. 9 gives power to the Committee to make such appointments. The power is being regulated by the regulations, which are enacted by the Board with the prior sanction of the state Government. [980F G] 1 4.

The respondent, a textile mill, was assessed to sales tax on the ground that it had wrongly escaped assessment. The Sales Tax officer rejected the contention of the respondent and held that the goods were not the "end product" within the meaning of the Act so that the appellate authority could go into the whole evidence and decide disputed questions of fact. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court was right in not interfering with the decision of the taxing authorities at this stage. The taxing authorities had the power to decide the question before them either rightly or wrongly. The High Court could not interfere under article 226 of the Constitution on the grounds that no disputed questions arose. The respondent was entitled to raise a preliminary objection as regards the maintainability of the writ petition, because, it was not so much the point of manufacture at which the Mills sold their own product which determines the nature of goods which are entitled to exemption, but it is the stage reached by this product in the process of manufacture of fabrication of a "textile" which should decide the questions satisfactorily. The interpretation of the High Courts that unless the taxing authority had committed error apparent on the face of record, it could not be decided whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to the exemption, was correct. The definition of "textiles" given in the Oxford Dictionary is "a textile". A textile fabric does not cover everything which could be made into a fabric. Mere cord does not become a textile fabric just because it requires some skill to make it. Mere fact does not cease to be a textile fabrics just because they require some skill, to make them. Mere history does not constitute a fabric which is also a textile. The question whether the commodity for which the Delhi Cloth Mill claims exemption is a textile was a "silk" and not any other kind of fabric. The term 'textiles ' has a wide meaning. Its first meaning given in Oxford Dictionary, is: "A textile fabric; any kind of cloth". It must acquire a body and a texture. Presumably it is more than that. But against pushing this point of view too far it may be urged that in the technical and commercial parlance it means a fabric, though not mere cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric. A textile fabrics does not fall within the definition of 'textile ' given in section 2(C) of the . The High Courts were right in holding that the taxing Authorities should be left to determine whether the "tyre cord fabric" is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or as merely cord pretend to pass on off as tul ar textile fabrics.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising out of the said incident was referred to Labour Court, Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered a reference under section 10(1)(c) of the , and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. The appellant contended that it would be difficult for him to attend the labour court regularly at Dhanbad and that transfer of the case from the Labour Court to the Labour court, Patna should have given an opportunity to the management before transferring the case to the labour Court, Patna. The Management contested the petition contending that no reasons were stated for passing the order. The High Court did not agree with the contention and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that no reason was given for passing an order transferring the cases from one Tribunal to another without hearing the parties, and that the Government had withdrawn the pending case from Labour Court Dhanbad and transferred it to another Labour Court at Patna. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that the government was misled by the representation of the workman. [297G] 1.2 In workman of Punjab State vs Labour Court; , ; , the Calcutta High Court had expressed the view that for application of rules of natural justice the classification of functions as quasi judicial is not necessary. The principles of natural Justice are fundamental in the concept inherent in the exercise of a judicial power. [298H] 1:3. In work man of Punjab Chheharta vs Varty, ; , referred to. 1.4. The principle of natural justi fication is that in a democratic set up, the fairness of procedure should be fair and not arbitrarily or capriciously. [300A B] 1.(i) It is a rule to ensure the vast power in the modern state is not abused but properly exercised. The doctrine of natural law is flexible and it is intended for improving the quality of government by ensuring that the statutory authority arrives at a just decision either in promoting the interest or affecting the rights of persons. To use the time hallowed phrase "that justice should not only be done but be seen to be done" is the essence of fairness equally applicable to administrative authorities. [301C D] (ii) The doctrine has been evolved by this Court as a result of which the concept of natural right is virtually made a rule of implied by the duty to act fairly and fairly. The concept of rule of law would lose its efficacy if the instrumentalities of the State are not charged with the duty of discharging their functions in a fair and just manner. [302E F] (iii) The principle that justice must not only he done but also be seento be done is the foundation of justice. A case with a not dissimilar problem was in Pannalal Binjraj and Anr. vs Union of India, ; at 765; State of U.P. vs Tulsi Ram, ; ; Pearl beresing Corporation of Calcutta vs Workmen, ; and M/s. New Brunk Coal Co. Ltd.

The appellant company was the manager of a hotel and its workmen were the Chief Commissioner, Delhi. The dispute between the appellant and its employees related to the payment of bonus to them. The company contended that the reference was incompetent as two grounds had been urged in support of it; one was that the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , and the other was that there was no dispute between it and its workers, and the second ground was that no notice of dismissal had been given to the workmen. Held, that the question whether the reference is incompetent was a mere technicality upon technicality, for the union not being a living person can only be served through some officer or servant of a trade union connected with, or by any other workman employed in the industry in which the workman is employed. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy (A.I.R. , approved. State Of Madras vs V. C.P. Sarathi, A.I R. and State of Madura vs C P Sarathy, A I R. , referred to. Held further that the dispute was not a mere legal one and the reference did not become incompetent merely because it was mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the dispute. The nature of the dispute is also specified in the terms of reference. State vs C, P.S. Sarthy, A,I R., , referred only to the dismissal etc. of particular workmen as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi, and not on any other union. The present reference was therefore bad merely because in the order of reference the words "as represented by a Hotel Workers" were added. State Bank of India vs Cp Sarathy ; , referred. State Electricity Board vs CP Sarathy; , , distinguished. State, Madras vs G. Pappayya, A.,I R, and State Of Madura v C. p. Sarathnam, A,.I. R. (1954) S.C.R 334, relied on. State o/Madras vs C . P.Sarathy, I.L.R , referred not to.

The appellant imported a part of the engines mentioned in Heading No. 8406, and claimed benefit of Notification No. 281 Cus/76, dated 2 8 1976 as amended by Notification No, 281 C. Ex., dated 1 9 1976. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the said Notification. The Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appel lant. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the imported parts of the engine or engines mentioned under Heading No 84.06 were exempt from payment of duty as provided in the Notification. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Notification grants exemption in part from payment to a certain extent of the customs duty. [225B] 2.1 The Notification does not mention 'parts thereof '. Non mention of 'part ' in Heading 84.07 is excluded from the benefit under the Notification and, therefore, even if bushings are the same as bearings, still they would come within the purview of the Notification, provided they are parts of such engines mentioned thereunder. [226C D] 2:2 The Notification will apply to parts of a engines mentioned at Heading No., 84.05.
