[227D] 3.1 In the instant case, there is no material or evidence nor was there any finding that the bushes which have been imported by the appellant were parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading Nos. 84.04.06. The notification will apply only to parts in respect of which the exemption is claimed, are parts thereof. [228D] 2 :3. In view of the finding that a part has not been mentioned under heading No.84.06, the Notification will be applicable to parts, will be to amend the Notification which the court will not do. [229F] 3:4. The intention of the notification is clear enough to provide that the parts of engines, mentioned under Entry No. 83.06 would get the exemption under the notification and in the absence of any provision to the contrary, it is necessary that the Customs authorities should embark upon the question and decide whether the bushes imported by them are really parts of those engines.

The right of management was divided between the two sons each taking six months ' share in the offerings made by their father and the son. The first defendant was a Mujawar and was receiving the offerings by right of inheritance. After his death, the plaintiffs 1 and 2 were entitled to 3/4th share each. The second defendant was also entitled to one half share each in the profits of the Dargah. The plaintiffs filed a suit against the defendants for declaration that they were entitled only to the property of the said Dargah. According to the plaintiffs, the said property belonged to their father who had two sons and one daughter. The trial court decreed the suit and in appeal, the High Court held that the courts below proceeded on an erroneous assumption that the Courts below proceeded upon an erroneous conclusion as if it was the duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster has been established. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts proceeded on a wrong assumption that if really the rights of Fathima Bee had become barred by limitation, all the rights had become extinguished; (ii) the defendants were entitled under section 14(1)(c) to have their own management of the suit Dargah and (iii) the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathina Bee had lost their right by ouster. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Courts committed a serious error in reversing the finding and in taking a wrong approach in holding ouster on the basis of judgment and decree given in Suit No. 116 of 1909 and on the ground that Fathita Bee was a co sharer in the right of possession of the respondent Dargah. [525F] 2. The appellants and their counsel were totally mistaken in taking the ground of exclusion of Fatima Bee 's title at the time of the judgment of the High court in 1909 and another ground taken is that neither Fathoni Bee nor the plaintiffs had at any time received a share in it. It was also not a party in the said litigation and any judgment given in that suit cannot be held as res judicata or binding on Fathuma Bee or the present plaintiffs. [526G H] 3. The Trial Court has considered all these aspects in detail after discussing the entire evidence placed on record and had clearly recorded the finding that there was no proof of ouster in the facts of the present case. It is a settled rule of law as between co heirs there must be evidence of open assertion of hostile title, coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of the other so as to construe ouster. [500B C] 4. The written statement filed by the appellants in the present suit was totally lacking in the particulars and thus apart from the want of evidence, there is no proper pleading of ouster. There is no specific denial of Futima Bee as well as the plaintiffs. It has been admitted that Fatina Bee was living and was being looked after by her broth er and she was in fact paid portions of income from the Dargah and on that account she was satisfied in allowing the brothers to enjoy the office of Mujawar on her behalf also. [511C D] 5.

The first respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. He was charged with house rent allowance for 10 months and dearness allowance. The first respondent contended that the house rent allowances were not wages within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the , as it was not payable to an employee who occupied Government quarters or to those to whom accommodation had been offered by the Government but who had refused it, and that therefore the claim for house rent was allowed by the Authority. The Authority held that the first respondent 's house rent could not be said to be "wages" within the definition of "wages". On appeal the Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Authority and directed the Authority to pay house rent at certain specified rates. The appellant contended that (i) the terms of the contract between the parties included the rule of " Rates" as defined in section 2 (vi) and therefore the position in law was that there was no absolute right in the first respond ent to claim the house allowance; (ii) the rules which must be included in the terms Of the contract were inconsistent with some of the terms thereof and therefore, the rule could not apply. Held, that the rule laid down by the Railway Board in its letter dated 1st December 1947 was inconsistent with any provision of sections 7 and 11 of the Act and was not ultra vires the provisions of section 7 and the Authority had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim which should be dismissed in limine. The House Rent Allowance Rules framed under the Act provide for the payment of house rent and allowances at rates specified therein. The house rent Allowance is admissible only so long as an employee is stationed at one of the specified places and has not been offered Government quarters. The rules clearly provided that the allowance will not be ad raisable to those who occupy Government quarters, or to the employees refuse to take advantage of the offer. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it he ceases to be entitled to the house rate allowance. In the present case, the first Respondent 's employment was not a permanent one but was only a temporary one. The rule clearly provided in section 7(i) that the employees should be posted at one or those to which accommodation had already been offered but who have refused it and no such order could be made unless the house accommodation had actually been offered to him.

The detenu was detained under the . The grounds of detention were served on him. He filed a writ petition in this Court challenging his detention mainly on the ground that he had been denied an opportunity to make an effective representation against his detention. This was dismissed by a single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the detenu that (i) the grounds of the detention were as elaborate as possible and that the supply of copies of all the relevant documents had not been supplied to him; (ii) the supply was conclusions drawn from facts and not matters of detail or any other matter which is not referred to or relied upon in the grounds; and (iii) the detenu 's representation dated March 24, 1980 was considered by the Advisory Board constituted under section 3(1) of the . Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The detaining authority without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies of which were asked for by the detenus mechanically refused as desired by the Collector, to supply the copies. [351 D] 2. The detenu had asked for copies of the full text of those statements. It was on receiving a direction from the Central Government that the copies were supplied. On account of this chill indifference and arbitrary refusal, the detenu, who had applied for copies on February 18, 1980, could get the same only on March 27, 1980 i.e., after more than one month. Thus there was unreasonable delay of more than a month in supplying the copies to the detenus. [352 E F] 3. The mere fact that the grounds were not supplied to the detenu with reasonable expedition to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest, did not absolve the detaining authority from its constitutional responsibility to supply all the basic facts and materials relied upon or referred to in those "grounds" to the detenue, and it was on this short ground that there was inordinate delay of nearly three weeks. [353 G] 4. The failure to apply its mind vitiates the order of detention. [354 A B] Khudiram Das vs State of West Bengal & Ors., ; , referred to. 5. The representation dated February 18 1980, made by the detenu to the detaining authorities was considered and rejected on April 8, 1980. The first ground for non supply of the copies was that the latter had acquired the gems in question from those persons. The second ground was that there were only the substance of the statements, while the detenu had requested for copies thereof, and that it was not possible to say that the disclosure of the same would endanger their safety or harm public interest. [355 E F; 355 A B]. Khudi Ram vs The State of Bihar & Ors. ; , followed.

The appellant State filed a joint appeal against the acquittal of several accused persons, and the High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by the sections was against the maintainability of a joint appeals by the State against an order acquitting several accused person. The question for determination in this appeal was whether several accused were acquitted by the trial court, and if the High court rejected the appeal without going into the merits. HELD : (i) Section 419 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not in terms cover the case of an appeal by the state against several accused. [878 C] (ii) The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Courts by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C. and r. 6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code. [873 D] (iii) Section 417 which provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal empowers the State Government to direct the public prosecutor in any case to present an appeal from an order of acquittal. This section also does not appear to indicate any bar or prohibition against presentation of a Joint appeal against several persons acquitted in a ease. [874 E] (iv) The High Court was wrong in holding that the joint appeal by several accused was incompetent. [872 G] (v) Section 418 of the code on which the High is said to have been made applicable, does not contemplate a joint application for a joint hearing by all the accused persons jointly tried and acquitted by a common order, but if an appeal against more than one accused person is competent, then on principle it is difficult to negative the maintainability. [878 E] The power under section 554 (2)(C) Cr P. C. on which a joint trial is commenced, is specifically provided for an application being made in the case, for joint trial by two or more persons. Such a restricted order of admission being invalid, the appellant would be entitled to insist that his appeal should be heard on the merits and this was not done. [877 G] The plain reading of section 419 shows that the High 'Court was wrong when it held that a joint Appeal by several persons convicted at one trial must be upheld.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in India and in the former Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The income of the assessee from the said business was not liable to be taxed by reason of section 25(3) of the Act. The Income tax Officer accepted the fact that the entire profits of the foreign business came to be assessed in the hands of the appellant under the 1918 Act and it was also charged under the 1922 Act read with the appropriate Finance Act, resulting in double taxation in respect of the income for the year 1921 22. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25 (3) Of the 1922 Income tax Rules, 1922. On a reference made by the High Court, the High court held that the foreign income could be deemed to have been charged under section 3 of the 1918 act only when there was an assessment to tax on the foreign profits and there was no tax on such income. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the appellant was entitled to the relief under s 25(4) of 1922 Act except for the income received from the house properties in Malaya which was discontinued in the year of account, and that the income derived by the assessee in respect his activity styled foreign business was liable to tax under the provisions of the 1922 act. HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that section 25 of the Income tax 1961 Act was applicable even if the person assessed under that Act was different from the person who claims relief under that section provided the former was the predecessor in interest of such person in relation to the business. [910 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M. Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, , followed. (ii) The income derived from foreign business is not liable under the 1961 Act because the assessee received the entire profit of the Indian business at Penang, and Kambar. Therefore, the assessee is entitled to both parts of relief contemplated under section 2(2)(a) of that Act in respect Of the foreign 'business in British India and the income from the foreign firm which was discontinuance in the previous year of accounts. [936 D] (iii) The question whether the foreign company was liable under section 5(3), of the 1961 Income tax is not relevant to the present case because, the income was received by the appellant as a receipt under section 6 of the earlier Act. [981 C] Commissioner Of Income tax vs sectionV.R., M. Palanappa Chettiar & Ors., , followed and applied. (iv) The assessee was entitled only to relief in respect the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign partner which was continued under different heads only for the purpose of computation of the total income. By virtue of the provisions Of the 1918 Income tax 1922 Act, the charge was made on the receipt of income in British Indian and as the income had been discontinued in 1955, it must be taken to be impliedly over ruled by the recent decision of this Court in Commissioner of Incometax, Madras V. section V R.M., Palaniappan Chettiar & Others, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R, 912.

The respondent assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of a capital project. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959, on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, to determine whether the supplies of bricks were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supplies were not sales and that the supply was for the best quality and in strict accordance with the specification and price specifications. The respondent appealed to the Tribunal which held that supplies of brick bats were sales and works contract and therefore, the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department was a sale or works contracts. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction contemplated by the Contract entered into between the applicant and the Public Work Department of Government was a works contract, and not a works contracts and therefore the transaction was a contract of sale and not works contract; and that as the contract was for sale or work contract it had to be handed over back to the Government after manufacturing of the brick work is completed. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The contract in this case is a contract for sale and the works contract is not a Works Contract. The appellant is liable to sales tax. [165G] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. 2.1 The contract entered between the appellant and the public works department of the Govern ment was a transaction of sale of bricks and not work contract. There was no contract for the sale of brickbats. The Government in its overall interest and anxiety for general welfare could insist on compliance with certain beneficial legal measures. It could also insist on certain terms which will ensure efficient production of the material. provision against subletting when the land was given free by Government is also understandable. All the features do not negate the concept of a contract. [166H; 167A] Chandra Mohan Gosain 's case, ; referred to and all the features did not negate tile concept of contract of sales of bricks that are ultimately manufactured. The true test in this ease is whether in making the contract to brick produced was transferred as a chattel for consideration and we are clearly of opinion that this has taken place in this appeal. [167B] Chandra Bhushan Gosain & Ors. vs State Of Bihar, ; , distinguished.

The President of India promulgated the Emergency Commission on March 25, 1971 under Article 352 of the Constitution. The President issued a proclamation of emergency on March 3, 1977 in exercise of powers conferred by sub clause (a) of clause (2) of article 352 of Constitution of India. Clause (1) of Article 352 was substituted for the original clause (c) of the said Article which provided that if the President was satisfied that a grave emergency existed whereby the security of India was threatened, whether by war or external disturbance, he might by proclamation make a declaration to that effect. Clause 2 of the Emergency Com mission provided that the period of five years in relation to the then House of the People shall be extended for a period of one year "on such terms and conditions as may be determined by the President. The petitioner who was an assessee under the Income tax Act, 1961, challenged the validity of the proclamation on the ground that the duration of the House of People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under Article 356 of the constitution of India and since the proclamation of Emergency had ceased to be in operation on March 31, 1977, it was not necessary for the President to make it before it was passed by the Legislative Assembly. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the two Proclamations of Emergency were validly issued or not. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1)(a) The proclamation of November 30, 1974 which was issued under Article 118(1) was valid and did not require any further amendment. [448C] (b) The President 's order dated March 3.1977 was passed in the Lok Sabha and not in the Legislative Council of India as contemplated by clause (3) of that Article. [492D] (c ) The proclamation issued under article 118(i) was a valid proclamation for the period during which the first meeting of the Assembly was about to come to a close. The proclamation had been duly published in the official Gazette and it could not be challenged on the basis of the non publication of the resolution of the two Houses of Parliament. [503E] (2)(a). The President acting as President of the Lok Union approved the two resolutions passed by both the Houses of the Legislature approving each of them had not been published in official Gazette. The Lok Sabha Debates and the Rajya Sabha Debates contain the proceedings of the Legislative Committee of Parliament and the State Legislatures. [513G] (3)(a)(1) The Assembly of Parliament was dissolved on March 1, 1977 and the President 'Speaker ' acting as the President of Parliament passed the House in 1977. The Legislative Assembly of the State of Uttar Pradesh was not a member of the Rajya Sabhas of the States of Punjab and Haryana.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the authorities. The High Court held that the property was a public temple within the meaning of Madras Act II of 1927, and that the suit was not maintainable under section 84(2) of the Madras Act 11 of 1927. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the question whether the property in dispute was a private or a public trust could have no market value and therefore was incapable of valuation. HELD: The High court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that the properties were private or public temple. [156 B] (a) The question whether a private property is incapable of valued depends upon the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the respondents the property is the private property of the family capable of alienation, the High Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to them the property belonged to the Thoguluva family capable Of alienation. [157 C] (b) The appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit is the public temple and not a public Temple as held by the High court. The question for consideration is whether the High Courts were right in holding that the land in question belonged to Thoguva family or was a Public temple. The appellant had also relied on the observations made in the judgment of this Court in the case of G. R. 155, which are not applicable to the present case. [158 D E] (c) The High Courts have proceeded on the basis that the disputed property belonged exclusively to the family and it was incapable for valuation. But as observed earlier the appellant ' s claim was that he had in his possession municipal receipts showing the property tax paid to the Madurai Municipality. According to him, property tax for the half year ending September 30, 1950 was Rs. 94 0 6 and for the first time it was increased to Rs. 1,672.32nP in 1961. If that be so, capitalising that value at twenty times the annual rental value would come to more than Rs. 20,000/ . [158 E F] (d) The property was not a private one and therefore capable of valuation as it could have in either case no market price. It was incapable or indirectly a claim or question res pecting property of any value of Rs.20,000 or more and the appellant had to pay court fees as it would in the ease of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. [155 E F].

The appellant, a non gazetted employee of the respondent company, was appointed as a clerk in a clerical staff. On an application made by him under section 33 of the Factories Act, 1948, the Industrial Tribunal granted him the relief claimed by him. The appellant contended that the practice started by the appellant of re employing retired persons should be discontinued and that the said practice was being followed in many cases and that it was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiffinition of its employees. Held, that the appellant 's grievance against the direction in the award that as a result of the demand made by the respondents, the appellant should be paid wages in lieu of the workmen who were entitled to look forward was not justified under the Act. The fact that the re employed persons had made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appel lant could have no bearing on the point. The question whether the practice of employing retired person was a matter which was within the discretion of the Tribunal and the appellant could not be blamed on that account; but there were some other factors in relation to this problem of re employment which cannot be ignored. The history of the relations between the parties coupled with the prevailing practice in the comparable concerns in the region strongly supports the view taken by the Tribunal that in the appellant company it was an implied condition of service that in addition to the wages and dearness allowance, a provision for tiffs should be made in that behalf. The result is that the question posed by the respondent 's demand must be considered. The dispute between the appellant and its workmen was not a matter relating to the re employment of retired persons but it was referred to the Tribunal under section 10 of the Act which held that the dispute was one relating to wages for t he re employed person and the dispute raised by the workmen was an industrial dispute within the meaning of the . The question posed in the appeal was whether the appellant was justified in making a reference on the ground that it had not been obligatory on its part to make a provision regarding the tifinition. Held further, that when a dispute is made on the basis of reduced salary, that really means that the employer is introducing a wage structure in respect of the reemployed personnel which is definitely inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the appell lant by the award and that clearly cannot be permitted under industrial law.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Bank of India 's Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, the respondent applied for transfer of the money from the Reserve Bank of lndia to the Reserve bank. The Union of India claimed immunity from attachment of the cheques on the ground that they represented provident fund money long before they were attached and hence they were not immune from attachment. The Central Government rejected their claim holding that the money was immune from attach. The respondent thereupon applied for removal of attachment on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that they represent provident fund moneys which by section 3 of the , was immunefrom attachment; (2) that the Union of lstia had no interest in maintaining an application for removal and the attachment was illegal as it was not made out to his credit in the Provident Funds. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1)(a) The Union 's claim that they were immune from attached under section 3 was not barred from attachment because the Union had no interests in maintaining the application for removing attachment. [32 B] (b) The respondent 's case was a trustee for the subscriber of the amount standing to his account as the agent of the Railway Administration and not as the first intimation at Liverpool by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the bankers of the Bank. [33 C D] (c) The Central Govern ment had no right in maintaining application for remove ing attachment. But the Union 'of India was a Trustee for the subscribers of the moneys which were converted into sterling and were transmitted by the ReserveBank to Browne, the money remained at the disposal of the railway Administration. [34 E F] (d) The Bank was in respect of the provident fund amount on retirement. The Reserve Bank was the agent. of the Railways Administration for conversion of the amounts into sterling. The debt was discharged as soon as the money became payable. The payment was required either under the first information report or under section 60(1)(k) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. [35 G] (e) The High Courts were in error in holding that money in the hands of the Reserve Officer of the appellant had ceased to be provident fund and was liable to be attached. [36 C D].

The appellant was employed as a pump operator in the respondent company. He was charged with misconduct of misappropriation and misappropriation of certain amount paid to him by the company without damning, as distinguished from dismissing him for misconduct. The management found that the appellant had failed to prove his guilt and dismissed him for mis conduct. The Labour Court held that the termination of services of the appellant was illegal and therefore the respondent was not guilty of any misconduct. On appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of dismissal but on a further appeal by the Management, the High Court held in favour of the management. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the termination was legal and immune to judicial interference; (ii) the respondent had lost confidence in the employee; (iii) the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the Labour court; and (iv) the appellant has merit on merits. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in setting aside the impugned order of the Labour 'Court. [497G] 2.1 The respondent workman was an intolerable person undesirable to be retained for misconduct as a colourable exercise of power by the management and the appellant could not have any merit on that score. [498A B] 3.2 In the instant case, the termination order was not bona fide. The termination was in accordance with the provisions of the Standing Orders. The respondent had not dis closed the grounds oil which this suspicion arose in 1968. Further after 1968, the appellant remained silent and did not even file a counter affidavit. Therefore, the management could not be said to have lost confidence on the appellant. [500C D] 3(i) In the present case, there was no specious attempt by the employer that he had lost faith in the appellant 's employee. The appellant was merely an intempering party in the dispute and without the former, though circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of the power of simple termination. [501C D; 496A] (ii).The Labour Court has misled itself on the law land. It is manifest therefore that loss of confidence is often a subjective feeling or individual reaction to an objective set facts and motivations. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former. [ 497F G] 3.(iii) The management could well have disclosed his own conduct and the ulterior purpose be to dismiss the employee because he was an evil to be eliminated. But if the management, to cover up the inability to establish by an enquiry, illegitimately but ingeniously passes an innocent looking order of termination simpliciter, such action is bad and is liable to be set aside. [ 496A B; 497C] 4. The Management has not dis closing the grounds on which this allegation was based. It has not been done. There is only the ipse dixit of the employer in the present cases. The Industrial Tribunal had misled itself by the appellant, a termination simpliciter may be bow fide, not colourable but colourable exercise or unfair labour practice. [50E] 5. In the circumstances of the instant appeal, it is clear that loss has been caused to the respondent by the termination. The order of reinstatement was not mala fide. It was manifest therefore, that the impugned action was not bonafide. [51F G; 497A B].

The petitioner, a retired Government employee, was appointed as an Assistant Surgeon in the District Hospital. On 21st April, 1986, he was posted at the Campus of the hospital. He was transferred to Delhi where he was on deputation and continued to work as such till his discharge. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the transfer order contending that the victims of this medical mishap were not given any opportunity of being heard and that the doctors, who had been allowed to go back immediately after the operations, had been injured in the hospital by the doctors. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the patients were entitled to get a fixed percentage of the scale possible and evolve proper guide lines for the conduct of eye camps. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the guidelines laid down by the Union Government on 9th February, 1988 had been violated as the doctors were allowed to hold free eye camps in the hospitals and that they were not entitled to claim any additional payment. Dismissing the writ Petition, HELD: 1. The Revised norms issued by the union Government on September 8, 1986 have been updated and revised. [234D] 2.1 The Revised guidelines dated 9th2, 1988 with the suggested modifications are these: (a) The doctors should be given some monitary relief by the State Government; (b) the doctors should also be afforded some monaster in emergency; (c) the medical treatment should be provided to the patients with attraction of the improved facilities. [235E] 2.(i) The guidelines for conduct of the eye camp are necessary and whether failure to do so would be action able. The aspects to which the present proceed ings are confined are: (1) Whether the guidelines prescribing norms and conditions for the conducting of eye camps are sufficiently comprehensive to ensure the protection of the patients who are generally drawn from the poorer and less affluent section of society or whether any further guide lines would require to be evolved; (2) Whether in such cases of mass use, a pre test for safety and purity of the article was necessary and if so whether failure of doing so would attract punishment under any of the existing schemes now in force in the State. [236F G] 2(ii) The Revised guideline dated 9.2.1988 with the suggestion modifications, can be held to be satisfactory.

The appellant No. 1, a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1984, was elected to the State Legislative Assembly in March 1983 and elected to be a member of the Samiti from the very inception. The appellant No 1 filed an election petition before the High Court challenging the action taken by the respondent No. 2 on the ground that the election was vitiated because of the dissolution of the Society declared and declared as a result of which the President of the Samities had been elected. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned Act and the Rules framed thereunder were passed in contravention of the provisions of the Bidhan (Constitu tion) Order, 1984 inasmuch as it was passed on 17.7.83 after the passing of the Act and that a fresh Government came into existence in the Samiti in exercise of his powers under section 16(G) of the said Act. The appellants have come to this Court by way of special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant No 2 that since the election had been brought about by the President amendment, the impugned order could not be granted and fixed 13.8.84 as the date for showing cause. On behalf of respondent No 1 it was submitted that the procedure stated in the Act was followed and the Chief Minister of Assam was the ex officio Chairman of the Committee appointed under section 3 of the Bihar Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (taking over of Management and Control) Act,1984. It is further contended that since there was mismanagement, delay in examination and results, it was because of that that the President could not have been allowed to function as the ex Vice Chancellor. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned Act is silent and although as quoted above it talks of being temporary measure but it talks about being temporary act, it continues and even as stated above there appears to be no intention of the State Government to restore the body back to its elected bodies and office bearers, despite the fact that the Court has not expressed any opinion on this question. [175F] 2. The Act and a noti fication issued under this Act taking over the management of the Rashtra bhasha prachar Samiti could not he accepted to be in accordance with the Constitution. Apart from this it is also clear that although when the Act talks of a temporary measure in fact, the Act does not provide for as to how when the temporary measures come to an end the elected Byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalika would be restored.

The respondents were married to one of the sons of one Ram Kishori Lal, a resident of Asansol in Bengal. The appellants filed a suit for a declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10, 1940 executed by her was void and inoperative under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the marriage was settled at Deoghar and the terms which were settled between the parties were: (a) that Sumitra Devi would arrange for the gift of four houses at Asanso in favour of her daughter as her share on partition; (b) that she would pay to Kamala Devi Rs. 20,000/ as expenses for the marriage; (c) that the gift was not binding on the reversion; and (d) that there was no compelling reasons for the High Court to differ from the appreciation of the oral evidence by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the proper finding should have been that the deed of partition was a valid gift under section 14 of the Indian Contract Act and that the appellants were not entitled to the reliefs claimed. HELD: (i) The question whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be judged according to the state of the family at the time of the gift, the extent of the property immoveable property, the indebtedness of the members of the gaddi, and the paramount charges which the family was under an obligation to provide for; and after having regard to those circumstances if the gift can be held to be reasonable such a gift will be binding on both the parties irrespective of the consent of the persons of the party. [477 G H] (ii) The High Courts were in error in holding that there is a moral or religious obligation of giving a portion of the joint family property for the benefit of the daughter and the son in law, and a gift made long after the marriage may be supported upon the ground of personaluptial agreement. [476 C D] (iii) The evidence on record did not establish that the possession of the house in question was made over to Kamala. It was also not proved that the house was ever in the possession or after her marriage. There is no consideration nor any discussion of the texts bearing on the question whether there was a moral, obligation of the widow to provide a portion thereof for the family property. [466 D E] (iv) The gift was made after the father 's death and subsequent to the marriage, and it was open to a widow to make an effective gift in favour her daughter subsequent to her marriage if the conditions laid down by Hindu law were fulfilled. [478 F G] (v) The fact that one of sons had become indebted cannot take away the power of the father to make such a transfer. It is not necessary to decide whether a person has got any right to get a declaration which he has asked for. [479 A B] (vi) The mere fact that the son has become indebted could not take away his power of alienation. There was no consideration or any discussion on the circumstances if it was held that there were no compelling reason for the same. [480 C D].

The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The first respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices as alleged by the appellant, and that the proceedings were taken ex parte against him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice indulged in by Tej Singh had been clearly proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the first respondent that the appellant had actually paid for the posters which were printed not by Ruplal but at the instance of Tej Singh, on a perusal of the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties, that the allegation of corrupt practices indulged in was clearly proved and that therefore the result of the election would have been materially altered. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh was guilty and not guilty of a corrupt practice as contemplated by section 123(2) of the Act having been adopted by the first Respondent, which has been fully proved. [419F] 2.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of the respondent would have gone to the appellant (Ahsan Singh) and, therefore, the result would have come down. [416G H] 2:2 The conclusion is that the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Kaur had actually received the posters by Bhum Raj from the constituency wherein he had mentioned that Ruplar was not collected with the printing of the posters. [414A B] 3. In view Of the very wide margin of ballot votes ( 123) between the defeated and the returned candidates, a great presumption and likelihood that the voters polled in favor of the candidate would have went to Avtar Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result. [413D E] 4. The result is that there is no force in the contention that Tej singh had actually made the conditions in the country. The evidence on both oral as well as documentary adduced before the trial court, clearly established that Tejinder Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing was done by a strong inference that the vote polled in his favour would have go to Avtar Sing Singh cannot therefore be ruled Out and that will have doubt less materially altered its result. The conclusion of the High Court is therefore correct.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was defeated in the legislative assembly election held in 1982. The Chief Minister of the State filed an application for contempt against the respondent, who was then the Chief Minister, alleging that one Shri Devinder Sharma, a forest officer, had been prosecuted and convicted under section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1982, by the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with the due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the application on the ground that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. The High Court dismissed the application holding that there was no punishment imposed on the respondent by the appellant, and discharged the rule neces sary. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that when the High Courts do not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High court does not exercise its jurisdic tion or power to punish for contempt. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the High Curt is to punish a person who has been punished for contempt of itself. [893C] 2.1 In considering a question whether the alleged contemner is guilty of contempt or not, the court may look into the materials produced before it and, if necessary, examines witnesses and, thereafter, passes an order either acquitting or punishing him for contempt.[893D] 2:2 A contempt is a matter between the court and the alleged offender. Any person who moves the machinery of the court for contempt only brings to the notice of the Court certain facts constituting contempt of court. After furnishing such information he may still assist the court but it must always be borne in mind that in a contempt proceeding there are only two parties, namely, the Court and the contemnor. It may be one of the reasons which weighed with the Legislature in not conferring any right on the petitioner for contempt, and as there is no exercise of jurisdiction or power by the Court to punish able for contempt it is difficult to say that the High COurt has exercised its jurisdiction or powers to punish the for contempt [894E F] 2 :3. The power of the Supreme Court is to impose a punishment for contempt on the contemnor or by acquitting him. It is true that in considering a matter whether the allegation is guilty or not the court, hears the parties and considers the materials placed before it, and if necessary examines them, the materials produce before it. If necessary, examination of witnesses and thereafter passes an Order either acquitting the contemnor, or acquitting him for Contempt. When the HighCourt acquits the contemnor after hearing the parties, and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the order does so also in the exercise of its jurisdiction as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution. [889F H] 3:4.

The appellant was the daughter of one V. R. who died in March, 1941. The widow filed a suit for possession on the ground that she had become a tenant by forfeiture of rent and also agreed to pay the agreed rent in monthly instalments. The trial court granted a decree for ejectment against V.R. on the grounds (1) that she was entitled to the whole compensation money as the tenant 's rights had ceased by forfeiture; (2) that the notice under section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, was not necessary for terminating the lease in suit and (3) that there was no forfeiture because no rent was fixed in respect of the suit property. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the statutory provisions of section 111 (g) as well as section 114 were not applicable to leases executed prior to the coming into force of the . HELD : (i) The provision as to notice for determining a lease for non payment of rent was not based upon any principle of justice, equity or good conscience. It is one thing to decide what is the true meaning of the language contained in an Act of Parliament. It has to be decided by itself, the delay, the conduct of the parties and the difficulties to which the landlord is put should be weighed against the tenant. This was the view taken by the Madras High Court in Tatya Savla Sudrik vs Yeshwanta Kondiba Mulay (I.L.R, , distinguished. (ii) The provisions as to notices for determining the lease for bona fide requirement of a tenant would not be based on any principle or rule of equity and good conscience which must govern even agricultural leases. [1023 B C] (iii) In the present case the appellant was a recalcitrant tenant and is a habitual defaulter. Rent has been in arrears at times for six years, at other times for three years and at other time for four years and so on, and every time the landlord had to file a suit in ejectment which was always resisted on false defences. [1123 C D] (iv) The appellant cannot be allowed to take advantage of his own wrong and plead relief against forfeiture on every occasion particularly when he was warned by the Court of appeal on a previous occasion. [1102 B] (v) In view of the fact that the tenant is a recalci nationless defaulter, the provisions of the Rent Act are not applicable in this case.

The appellant, a union called Kymanna Pradhan and others, was dismissed from service by the management on 13.9.1968. The Management served a notice on the management to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against them for the alleged misconduct committed by them. The respondents filed their reply denying the charges levelled against them. They also stated that while they were working as casual workers in the appellant 's factory, the Management had decided to terminate the strike without giving any reason and that since before the commencement of the strike two meetings were organised by the Respondents, one at 4 p.m. on 19.9 .1968 and the other at 11 A.M. on 20th September 1968, the management had by leading evidence proved their misconduct. The Labour Court dismissed the respondents ' writ petition holding that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to them before inflicting upon them the punishment of dismissal. The High Court confirmed the order of the Labour Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the inquiry was vitiated as no second notice was given; (ii) the concept of second opportunity being given to a delinquent which obtained under section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 or article 311 of the Constitution prior to the insertion of the proviso to Article 311(2), could not be invoked or applied to the instant case; and (iii) the principle of natural justice was not attracted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The first part of para 3 merely casts a unilateral obligation on concerned authority or the officer to give due consideration to the gravity of the misconduct and the previous record of the delinquent in awarding the maximum punishment. It is true that the Arbitrator has undoubtedly taken the view that the opportunity spoken of by para 3 OE S.O. 17 was not given but was availed of by the concerned four workers (including Rama Shankar and Burma Pradhan). The question is whether when paragraph 3 of the Standing Order No. 17 provides for second opportunity to offer explanation in regard to the alleged conduct charged against him, it is necessary that the only ground on which inquiry was held to be invalid by the Arbitrator and by the High Court must disappear. [368C D] Hamdard Dawakhana vs Badri Das & Ors., ; , applied. In the instant cases, the first part Of para 3 clearly lays down that the second opportunity of showing cause against the proposed punishment is contemplated either expressly or by necessary implication. The second part of Para 3 merely cast a unilateral responsibility on concerned authorities or the officers to give proper consideration to gravity of misconduct and previous record in awarding maximum punishment; it is the alleged act of misconduct that is to be explained by him and not the proposed penalty. [369E F] Hamadard Dawkhana vs Lakshmi Narain & Ors. ; , referred to. 2. The word "opportunity" in para 3 of OES.O 17 is the opportunity to be given to the delinquent to meet the charge framed against him. In this connection it will be useful to refer to the decision of this Court in Hamdards Dawakhan vs Badri Dass & Ors, ; , relied on. In view of the construction which we have placed on section OEs.O 3 and 3 of Para. 3 it must be held that the first portion of para. 3 merely creates a unilateral right and does not confer any second opportunity in respect of the proposed action. [370F G] Ham dard Dawkshana vs Laxmi Narain & ors., ; applied.

The appellant was the owner of a portion of land leased by incompetent persons to the competent persons. The lease deed purported to be a lease deed executed in favour of incompetent persons. In the suit filed by the respondents, the appellant contended that he was himself the owner and had not actually transferred possession of the land to the respondent. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the benefit of section 7D would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin and not to persons m unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible entry. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section7D. Allowing the appeals by special leave, HELD: 1. The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to person whose posses sion had a legal origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believe it to be the property of the Government. [114E F] 2. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7A must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". In the present case, the finding of fact entered by the High court is that the appel lant had come into possession of his lands by trespass. His plea before the Courts below was that he had come to possess of the lands by adverse possession. His contention was that the respondent was himself, the owner 's title to it by adverse posses tion. In such circumstances the High Courts were in error in holding that he could not be entitled to protection of Section 7D. [115G H] 3. The finding of the High courts is that there was no benefit to the appellant and the respondent had come in possession of those lands by encroachment or forcible possession based on unlawful entry or forcible Entry. It was not within the contemplation of the legislature to confer the benefit on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The High Court was fully justified in holding, that the appellants were not entitled tO the protection under Section 7 D.

The appellant was convicted under Section 135(b) (ii) of the . He was convicted and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The appellant had not produced evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. His case rested on his bare assertions in a written statement. Of course no one had come forward to state or allege that the goods found, in the circumstances stated above, were smuggled into India without payment of duty. The appellant 's explanation was that he had not given any evidence to prove that his Sub tenants had place in India and that there had been misdeclaration of the goods. [541 D E] In a written state ment it is immaterial whether the goods are legally brought into India or brought into the country without payment. [542 F G] The appellant was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods. It was immaterial that the appellant was found in possession of the offending goods on 21 4 1967 there was some evidence to enable the courts below to come to the conclusion that the gold must have been known to the appellant to be imported even if he had been not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty, and his case rested entirely on his mere assertions in the written statement which was filed on 30 10 1968. [543 G H] The State of Punjab vs Gian Chand & Ors., ; , referred to. In the instant case, there was no evidence that the appellants were found in the possession of goods on the 21 4 67 and that they had not offered any evidence either to show the goods being legally brought in India or smuggled. [544 G H; 545 A] Collector of Customs, Madras & Ors. vs D Bhoormal, ; , relied on. The State 's appeal was dismissed by this Court on 2 4 1968. In view of the fact that the complaint itself was filed after a long interval of time of about 3 1/2 years, the appellant had been convicted only under section 135(a) and (b) of . [544 B C] M/s. Kanungo & Co. vs The Collector of customs, Calcutta & Ors, ; and M/S.

The appellants were the Presidents of a registered association which was dissolved and the members of the Association were joined as respondents. The Association was formed in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and its members were not entitled to any share in the profits made on the sale of yarn. The appellants filed a suit for accounts and claimed that they had been guilty of an illegal association with the object of carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further claimed that the suit was maintainable under section 4 Of the Rewa Act, as it was not registered as a company under the Rewa state Companies Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Under section 4 of the Madhya Pradesh State Companies ( prohibitory in nature) Act, 1936, the appellants were entitled to bring a suit within the meaning of that Act. [776 D] (ii) The provisions of section 69(3)(a) of , are not mandatory and they do not require the investigation of any facts. Therefore, the suit for account must fail. [771 C] (iii) Under the , an unregistered firm is not illegal; there is no direct compulsion that a partnership firm must be registered, though the disabilities consequent on non registration may be extremely inconvenient. The fact that in order that illegality may be a defence, it must affect the contract on which the plaintiff is compelled to rely so as to make out his right to what he ask. It by no means follows that whenever money has been obtained in breach of some law, the person in possession of such money is entitled to keep it in his pocket. If money is paid by A to B to be applied by him for some illegal purpose, it is competent for A to require B to hand back the money if B has not already parted with it and the illegal purpose has not been carried out. [777 E F] (iv) The suit before the High court was not one for accounts of a dissolved firm but for accounts. Therefore the preliminary objection must fail, because, the analogy does not really apply. [779 C D] In the present case, the question is whether the suit is barred by section 4 (2) Of the Act. It is enough to point out that whenever a money has already been obtained, in breach thereof, such a defence must be allowed to prevail in a court of justice.

The respondents were charged with offences under sections 447, 429 and 379 IPC read with section 54 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and ordered issue of process to the accused. The respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C., for quashing the proceedings against them on the ground that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognisance of the offences and issuing summons. The High Court quashed the proceedings holding that the complaint was barred by sec. 210(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the High Courts were not competent to take cognizance of an offence under section 9(1), read with sec. 50(l) of Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1974 and that the offences envisaged by secs. 9(i) read with Sec. 50 (l) are the same or substantially the same as Sec. 429 IPC and that after due investigation and police had filed a final report that no offence was made out and that initiation of any fresh proceedings against respondents would be impermissible. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not committed any error in taking cognizance of offences under sec. 51(1). [467C] 1.2 The expression "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act ' in section 56 of the Act merely imports the idea that nature and intent is "a series of complex biotic communities of which a man is an interdependent part" and that it should not be given to a part to tresspass and diminish the whole. [467D] 1:3 The expression 'any act, or omission ' in sec. 56 of Act means any allegation made orally or in writing to a Magistrate. [468F] 1.(a) In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence. [466B C] (b) The expression `any act ' in Sec. 56 means any act or omissions which constitutes an offence and includes acts done orally or substantively. The expression has not done much to lessen the difficulty in applying the tests to identify the legal common denotification of the criminal. [470D E] 1(c) The word `any ' is used in sec tion 2(16) of Act, which means any one who is an aggrieved person 's specific or multiple punishment for the same offence. But where a Magistrate takes cognisance ous of an offense instituted otherwise than on a police report and an investigation by the police is in progress in relation to that offence, the two cases do not lose their separate identity. [471D E; 471A] 1 (d) The words `any Act or omission" in secs 56 and 51(2) of Chapter I have not done so as to attract the protection of article 20(1)(c). [470F G] 2.1 In order to find out whether the allegations in the complaint are likely to be established by evidence or not, the Court has to exercise its power under sec tion 9(I) of Cr.P.C. [473G H; 474A] 2:2 The High court was right in holding that it would not be correct to infer that the two respondents were made aware of the position that cognizance of such an offence can only be taken on the complaint of the officer mentioned in that section. Even where a magistrate takes cognition of an act instituted otherwise, than on police report, and an enquiry by the Police is in operation in relation thereto more than once, and accordingly section 210(2)(a) has no role to play.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on the ground that he had committed a breach of his liberty by indulging in his activities in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order, and was released on bail. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner that: (1) the provisions of section 439 Cr. P.C. should be construed liberally so as to ensure that the 'bailee ' does not flee justice; and (2) the High Court under section 439 Criminal Procedure Code, enlarge the petitioner on bail, should have been within its power to reject a surety because he or his estate is situated in a different district or State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law is being followed by the courts not only for juvenile justice but also for a large number of other minorities and distant densely minorities who are to be given bail. [343G] 2.1 In order to secure release on his own bond, the court must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deter mination for releasing the petitioner. [344A B] 2:2 The law, not the money tag, must be read 'bail ' to mean that it popularly docs, and lexically and in American Jurisprudence is stated to Mean, viz., a generic expression used to describe judicial release from custodia. [346C D] 2I1 In the instant case, the petitioner was rightly convicted for offences under section 307 I. P .C. and sentenced on his application for bail. He could not be released on his personal bond without sureties. [347D E] 2l2 The High Courts have been in error in imposing the sentence of death on him. [349G] 3.1 The law does not require that the magistrate should release the petitioner, on his self bond, in a sum of Rs. An after word 'bail` with or without sureties, and that the proviso makes a contradistinction between 'bail and 'own bond without surety '. Even so, an accused in judicial custody, actual or potential, may be released by the court to further the ends of justice and nothing in section 441(2) and (3) use the word ' bail ' generically because the expression is intended to cover bond with orwithout sureties. The proviso makes it clear that a murderer, concurrently found to be so, may not be able to furnish bail on account of their poverty while a convict is found guilty if during trial when the presence to instruct lawyers is more necessary, an offence would stultify the sub section; for then, an offender released on probation or on his being convicted and sentenced. [345H 346A] 3:2. The language of sections 439 and 440 Cr.P C. shows that the legislature has used the words 'bail" and 'forthwith ' in the American Jurisprudence. The word 'EMA ' suggests ' with or after sureties ' is comprehensive enough to cover release on one 's own bond with sureties '. [348C D; 349A] 4.1 Section 439 Cr, P. C., does not contemplate bail but only applies to bail bonds. It does not say that it commonly falls within the meaning of section 437(2).

The assessee, a registered firm, had at various places in India branches one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle Amritsar, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the assessee to include in the computation of capital invested for the purpose of section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but the Income tax Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment order and directed the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court. The High Court declined to require the Tribunal, on the view that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from non inclusion by the Income Tax Officer in the assessment in question of the income of Eastle 's and that "the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Tribunal in coming to its conclusion, was a relevant factor. The Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner and held that the findings of the Income. tax Officer were one of facts as it had been based on inference arising out of the non inclusion of the amount advanced to 'Castle. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Courts in India have jurisdiction to call upon the Tribunal for the opinion of the High court whether the question of law arises and the High, Court being approached by the aggrieved party within the period of limitation prescribed, is not satisfied about the correctness of the decision of the appellate Tribunal refusing to state a case for the reasons that no question of fact arose and the finding on matters of appreciation of evidence cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. In so advising the High 'Court must accept the findings on matters such as the one of the fact, even if on a review of the evidence the court might have arrived at a different conclusion. The decision of an appellate Tribunal on questions of appreciation is not conclusive. The finding of fact, if there is some evidence to support the finding, must be accepted as the Appellate 'Tribunal 's finding. In the present case, the refusal of the appellant to state his case and reference to it was not justified by the High.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was appointed as a party to the writ petition filed by him. The Minister was directed to file his affidavit. In the writ peti tion filed by the appellant, he stated that he had not been impleaded as a respondent. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding that the Minister concerned should file an affidavit in regard to allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The Minister concerned is the Minister responsible for the decision of the High Court directing that the minister be impleaded as respondent. [972 B] (2) The High Courts were in error in directing that a Minister should file his personal affidavit. [963 C] (3) The direction for impleading of the Minister as a necessary party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made against him and thus, to afford an opportunity to the parties and thereafter pass the necessary order in the matter. [952 D] (4) The Secretary of the Department should file affidavit in respect of allegations made by the Minister himself. [943 C D] In the instant case, the High Courts had not committed any error in direct ing that the Ministers concerned should be impleaded. [ 943 E] (5) The order passed by the Governor was set aside and the Minister was impleaded as the party. [922 G] (6) The State Government should file its affidavit in the Court on or before the date fixed for hearing of the case. [932 A B] In view of the fact that the HighCourt had not persuaded itself to interfere with the order of the Governor, the order adding the Minister to the array of parties was set at naught. [ 933 C E] The High court was in error on the part of the State Government in directing the Minister not to file an affidavits. [992 D F] (7) The Court directed that the Secretary be impleaded in the writ Petition as a proper party. The order for impleading is set aside.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application for recovery of arrears of rent under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1924, was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala Cantonment, on January 7, 1960. The respondent contended that the provisions of the Act and Rules were not applicable to him as he had committed a breach of the provisions contained in the lease. The trial court held that the appellant had no jurisdiction to recover the arrears of the rent due under a lease. On appeal the High Court held that (i) the Rent Controller had the power to recover rent under s 259 and (ii) the rules were not ultra vires the powers of the Board, and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (1) the provisions Of section 259 were not intended for recovery by a suit as an alternative as a matter of abundant caution to avoid an argument that the application to a magistrate under s.259 was not maintainable; (2) the words "rent" in section 259 meant only a sum which was recoverable by the Board under the Act or the rules made thereunder and therefore, it did not bar the right of the board to recover such arrears of land as were recoverable by it under the provisions. HELD : (i)(a) The words "recoverable by a Board" in s. 259 are not intended to be included in that expression in section 258. [346 B] (b) The word "rent " in section 256(1) is used in connection with those cases and it cannot be said that there was no case where the Act did not provide for claim of rent by the respondent under the lease or the Rules. [347 C D] (c) The expression "recoversable by the board" in the context of the section means "any sum which is due to the Board". Therefore, the words 'recoverablesable by any Board ' or the Military Estates Officer under this Act or rules made under the section are not meant for recovery. [349 C D]. (d) The provisions of s.260(1), read with s. 257(1). do not bar a right of appeal to the civil court against a decree passed in a suit filed by the appellant, because, the liability to pay rent arises purely on the basis of a lease between the Board and the tenant. [348 E] (e) The term "rent ' is defined in section 2(10) as meaning a sum paid or payable by a person under an agreement for the management of the Cantonment Board. Section 259 provides that where any such sum is due from a person to the Government, the Board may require any occupier of such property or of any part thereof to pay it instead of to the owner, any rent payable by him in respect of such land as it fails to pay. The word 'rent ' in section 260(1)(c) means a sum payable by the lessee to the lessee on account of the lease and includes a sum recoverable under an ordinary contract between the lessor and the lessee. [350 F G] (f) The definition of "rec Overable by" in cl. 259 is not exhaustive. It does not exclude money due under an express provision of the statute which expressly makes rent claimable or recoverable by either of the two authorities specified therein. [351 C D; 351 A B]. (g) The High Court was right in holding that the rent in question was not a claimable by virtue of section 259 and therefore the suit was not barred by limitation.

The appellant was terminated from service on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. At the instance of the appellant the Government referred to the Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal/Labour Court/Tribunal/Industrial Disputes, which held that the appellant was not a "workman" and therefore, the reference was incompetent. The Labour Court also held that there was no evidence under section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act to prove the fact of misconduct. In appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that since the appellant had been employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company, his services were illegal but dismissed the application only on the grounds that the was not applica tion in the nature of workmen 's case. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the Tribunal on the nature and circumstances of the case is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour court. [474F] 2.1 A long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. In the instant case, the Tribunal found that the appel lant was not an "workman". The finding is therefore not sustainable. [473G H] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah shell Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, ; ; DS.Nagraj vs labour officer, Kamal & Ors., ; ; G.Sivarathin Chemicals and Chemicals Ltd. vs Burmahu Shell Management and staff; , , referred to. 2.2 The finding that the termination of the appell lant from service was illegal but not treated as precedent is not sustainable in view of the fact that a long period o f over 16 year had passed, it would he unjust to Leave the appellant with any remedy. [475B C] Burmaha Shell Oil storage and Distribution Co. vs Hindustan Development Corporation Ltd., ; , referred tO. 2:3 The finding on the question whether the termination itself was illegal is not a case of dismissal or discharge from the wholesaler or retail dealer.

The respondent Company was a Government lessee under the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Samvat 1999. On the expiry of the lease period, the respondent company filed a suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Additional Collector dismissed the suit holding that the land in question was held by the Company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. The High Court confirmed the order of the Additional Collector. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant State it was contended that the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant and that the company was not an occupancy tenant under section 185 of the M .P. land Revenue Code 1959. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [179F] 2. The order of Additional Collector is set aside. The findings of the subordinate authorities are set aside and the order passed by the Additional Collec tor is restored. [180G] 3. The respondent company was a person holding the land from the State Government. This is so whether or not the Company is deemed to be holding over under the old lease or holding, upon termination of that lease under and in terms of the fresh conditions agreed upon between the parties to enable the Company to remain in possession of the land as a lessee. [181A] 4. The Company has been successful in showing that the respondent Company never acquired the status of a Gair Maurusi tenant in respect of the lands in question at any time prior to the coming into force of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007. The fact that large amounts are due and payable by the company as rent and that rents have remained unpaid for a period far in excess of three months from the dates on which they became due, is not liable to be questioned in these proceedings. His finding shows that large amount are due, and payable, by the respondent as rent. [182B C] 5. The appeal by the State is allowed with costs throughout. [183C] 6. The judgment of the trial court is setaside and the High court restored the order dated 20.9.1980 in Misc. Petition No 84 of 1978.

The Kerala Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for the acquisition of any land in an estate. The object of the Act was to provide that the surplus land should be acquired or held under personal cultivation of the holder, and to provide a machinery for compensation for the property so acquired. Section 47 of the Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1965 provided that the provisions of the Principal Act shall apply to the lands acquired and held by any person through inheritance, request, gift, family settlement, purchase lease or otherwise, together with the lands in his personal cultivation at the time of such acquisition. The State Government amended the principal Act by adding a proviso to article 31 A providing for compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent. The Amendment Act provided that no property shall be compulsorily acquired or requisitioned save for a public purpose and save by authority of law which provides for compensation in respect of the interest of the owner, compensation shall not be less than the market price of the lands if such land be within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. The petitioners challenged the validity of section 47 of Act 13 of 1965 on the ground that it was inconsistent with or takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution and that the impugned Act was void as it contravened article 31 B of the Constitu tion. Held, that the expression "law in force" in article 31A of the constitution is not a law in force when the State legislature was formed but until the power is exercised by the Legislature to issue an appropriate notification, the provisions Of Ch. IV could not be deemed to be law in existence unless it was brought into operation by legislative enactment or by the exercise of authority by a delegate empowered to bring it into operation. The theory of a statute being "in operation in a constitutional sense" though it is not in fact in operation has no application. Held further, that section 47(1) of the , which provided for payment of compensation at a rate which was less than that originally fixed under the Act and the guarantee of the second proviso to Article 31 A of the Consti tution, is on that account infringed article 14 of the Con stitution. The right to compensation which is not less than tho market value under any laws providing for the acquisi tion by the state of any estate in an Estate in the personal cultivation or the right to possession of any property owned or controlled by the Government cannot be limited only in the constitutional sense and not in the sense of its actual operativeness. Held also, that article 31(A) was not applicable to the present case because the impugned law relating to the ceiling limits viz. IV of the principalAct was never made operative by a notification, and was repealed by the Amending Act 15 of 1965.

The widow of her husband, who had inherited the property from his widow, was in possession of the same by adverse possession against the widow. She died in 1924 leaving a son, the widow, and a daughter, the respondent. The widow filed a suit for partition of the properties on the ground that the widow had acquired a title by adverse Possession against her. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the reversioners could not claim possession so long as the widow was alive.
