In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the widow could not make a surrender of the property during her lifetime without any valid extinction by any act of surrender; and (2) the respondent had no interest in the property which she could convey under the Hindu law. HELD: The widow 's estate was in fact acquired by adverse posses sion against her, and the widow became entitled to recover possession from the widow or his spiritual benefit. [355 E] The widow, when he takes the estate on surrender, takes it subject to the interest already created. A surrender is a voluntary act of self effacement by the widow and she is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. [356 F G] In the present case, the reversioners had not acquired any title from the respondent but only from her husband who had acquired title by reason of a subsequent voluntary act on the part of the widow; and the reversioners were entitled to claim possession of those properties during her life time. [357 B C] The fact that the reversioner had paid valuable and substantial consideration for a property on the expectation of enjoying it so long since she was alive, did not affect the title of the reversioners. [358 E F] In view of the provisions of section 5(1) of the Hindu Law, the alienation by a Hindu widow of his property without any legal necessity, could not be said to have been made in contravention of the provision of the general law as a result of self immemorial usage. [359 B C]. The widow had no right to alienate her property without a valid surrender and she was entitled to sue for possession at once. [360 E] Sulaiman J. (dissenting) vs Subbamma, I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile State of Uttar Pradesh as a limited company. The Cotton Mills Company Ltd. had acquired 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 each. On February 15, 1984 the appellant became the Chairman and Managing Director of the Cotton Mills company. In 1970, the Cotton Mill Company filed a petition under sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 before the High Court for winding up of the appellant company. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton mills Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the Polytex Company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver under section 169 of the Act and therefore, there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the cotton Mills Company suffered any diminution or curtailment in its rights as a shareholder in respect of the shares so attached. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the special general meeting was not validly called because the Cotton Textile Company had not become paralysed and that if those shares were omitted from consideration then the shares held by the other requisitionists would not have been eligible to requisition the meeting. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the Cotton Textiles Company could not be treated as the holder of the office of Receiver in view of section 153A of the deal with the contract of pledge and that the power of the company and its directors to deal with property comprised in the appointment (both property subject to a floating charge and property subject only to a fixed charge) except under certain circumstances, was not sufficient to take away the right of the cotton mills Company to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under section 170 of the Income tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of winding up is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of Receiver under the Land Revenue Act. [887C] 2.1 The power to wind up a company is not absolute and it can be exercised only when there is no other creditor of the pawner had any right to take over the shares. [889D] 2(a) The power conferred by section 169 (1) (a) (b) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 has no effect on the voting rights of the Textile Mills Company. It is also significant that the Directors of the polytex company who what that a Receiver had been appointed in respect thereof, have not been excluded from consideration. [879E] 2.(b) The resolution of the Board of Directors of a company which has not been duly approved by the Central Government under section 18AA (1)(a) of Industries ( Development and Regulation ) Act, 1950 takes over six industrial units of the textile mills Company held by it at the time of deposit of the requisition. [877F] 2 (c) The Cotton Textile Mills Co. Ltd.

The petitioners, who were plaintiffs in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, filed a suit for declaration that they were owners in possession of the suit land along with some others. The Gram Panchayat contested the suit and raised preliminary objections that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. The Trial Court framed an issues relating to the maintainability of the suits. The petitioners filed revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court because the land in question was shamlat deh and it had been vested in it. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. Section 13 of Punjab Village common Lands (Regulations) Act 1961 provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain or adjudicate upon any question whether any property or any right to or interest in any property is or is not shamlat land vested or deemed to have been vested under the Act. The Act was amended by the Punjab Act No. 18 of 1961 which came into force on April 1, 1961 and the original sections 11, 12 and 13 read as follows: "11. Decision of claims of right, title or interest In shamlat or patties, pannas and tholas and used according to revenue records for the benefit of village community or a part thereof or for common purposes of the villages; . . . (1) Any person claiming right, titles or interest therein, may submit to the Collector within such time as may be prescribed, a statement of his claim in writing and signed and verified in the prescribed manner and that the Collector shall have jurisdic tion to decide such claim in such manner as may he prescribed. " The petitioners had not claimed a declaration that the land was shamilat deh and they had no right or title in it and therefore, the suit property had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the suit. [834C D] 2. The suit had not been filed cleverly by claiming a declaration of right title or interests in shamlat lambi and used for common purpose. They had, however, questioned the correctness of entries in the Revenue records which shown that the panchayat was entitled only to the land.

The respondent Board, a public limited company, had been in the business of supplying electricity to its consumers. The Electricity Board demanded interest on the amount payable by it under the provisions of the Orissa State Electricity Board General Conditions of Supply Act, 1948. The Board challenged the demand on the ground that the Electricity Board was not obliged to pay interest on such deposit and also for supply of energy to the consumers. It was contended that the Board had no power to charge interest on a deposit made by it in terms of the agreement between the consumer and the Board. The High Court held that the electricity board was entitled to adjust its tariffs against the security deposit as the Board was bound to pay surcharge at 18%. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Electricity Supply Act was not applicable to the supply made by the Board; and (ii) the Board has a statutory right under section 49(1)(f) to charge the interest on security deposit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The electricity supply is a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. The billing time taken by the Electricity Department is to the advantage of the consumer. Since the amount is held as security, it is intended for appropriation. [262D] 2. The purpose of the deposit is to secure the payment of consumption charges. It serves not only to secure interest of the Electricity Boards for any such violation but also to serve as a deterrent on the consumers in discharging their obligations towards the Board.[263F G] 3. The supply of electricity by the respondent Board is to be made under proviso (a) to section 49 of the Act. [264G H] 4. The conditions and terms of supply of the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Supply Undertaking are basically different from fixed deposit. The consumption security deposit is not only a part of the money which is payable to the Board on the bill being raised against the consumer, but also a security towards payment or satisfaction of any money (for example, theft), which may become due and payable to a Board by the consumer [264A B] 5. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. It stands to reason that if there is a revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in it. If there is revision in a rate, it will be necessary for the Electricity Undertaking to ensure that the intentions of Parliament shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates somewhat harshly on a small section of the public, taken in conjunction with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19 (1) (f). [264C D] 6. The nature of consumption deposit is such that it represents only a component of the amount which is paid to the Electricity Company on account of the consumers ' security deposit and not also a consumption of the electricity. Therefore, the Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumers with the Board to secure their own interest. [265E F] 7. The question whether the Board can be held as a trustee or not depends upon the facts placed before it and the amplitude of the consumption security deposits since it has direct bearing to the level of supply in consumption of electricity. The fact that the amount was held as the security does not affect the conscience or reasonableness of the court. [267G H; 268A] 8.

The petitioners, who were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre, were promoted to the posts of Assistant Directors or Deputy Director. The petitioners challenged the promotion orders on the ground that they were not competent to do so and that the same special pay which was granted to them under the Recruitment Rules was not being paid to them. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Indian Telecommunication Service Officers who are working in the Telephone Research Centre are being given Special Pay of Rs. 300 Rs. 200 and Rs. 150 per month in addition to their pay scales in the grades of Deputy Director, Assistant Directors and Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.11.1973. [1011C D] 2.2 The Indian Telegraph Service Officers, who are functioning in the telephone Research Centre were being given special Pay of RS. 300 per month. They are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is not deputation allowance. It was paid for the arduous and special nature of the functions to be discharged in the telecommuni cation Research Centre. The Special Pay is not being given to a few graduate engineers recruited specifically for TRC when the qualifications, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and transferred officials and that they have to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay in addition tO their scale of pay which is the same. [1001D E] 2:3 The Indian Telephone Research Institute is engaged in the research and development Centre and is being given a special Pay in lieu of Special pay in addition lo their scale. The transfer officers who are selected by the Union Public Service Commission after a rigorous competition examination need to be given Special pay. It does not mean that persons who are directly recruited and working in tho centre are inferior to those who enter the centre by transfer. It cannot be said that persons appointed to the post of Assistant Director, regarding whom the petitioners belong, are not given any special Pay. [1002C D; 1013E] 2 :4 The Indian Communications Service Officers (Class I) Association is engaged to perform functions for which they are recruited while on the other hand, the officers drawn from the ITS cadre when posted in TRC. are required to perform duties which are not in their general line. In another part of the same answer it was also admitted that many such transferred officials were in the service of the Indian Telecommunications Service who are appointed by the Government after a thorough competition examination followed by an interview, and that many of such transferred official were in their service conditions.

The appellant, a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara, was employed as a mourshi in a Mill. The appellant had framed a charge sheet against him under section 7 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, and the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965. The Labour Court held that the charges leveled against the third Respondent were proved, but did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approach the Labour Court and directed reinstatement of the third respond ent with full back wages. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the order of the Labour court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the third respon dent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not take any application under s.42(4); and (2) the finding of the Tribunal was perverse, because (a) the second respondent had failed before the Labour 'Court to comply, with the provision of law, in that it did not give notice of such intention in the prescribed form to the representative of the employees; and (b) the findings of the Industrial Court were perverse. HELD : (1)(a) The scheme of Chapter VIII is that a Labour Court is to have power to decide all the disputes covered by section 42 (1). Section 44 provides for an appeal against the decision of a Labour court in respect of a matter falling under clause (a), or cl. (c) of paragraph A of sub section (1), of section 78 except in the case of lock out etc. or a decision of such court under para C of sub s.(1) of section 7. The question therefore narrows down to this i.e. whether the legislature by inserting paragraph D in section 78(1) intended to chalk out a wholly different course of action to that prescribed in Chapter VIII dealing with changes. [738 B C] (b)(i) The Legislature wanted the provision to be a comprehensive one and contained all the powers of the labour court in the matter of all disputes mentioned and given it jurisdiction to punish certain offenses under the Act. It did not lay down the procedure for the attraction of such jurisdiction. [ 738 E F] (ii) The provisions of section 42 of the are mandatory and do not lay out the procedure which is prescribed in section 79(1). [737 G H] (iii) The provision of section 44 is to be read as a whole, while there is no doubt left in our minds that the legislature wanted the provisions to be made applicable in Chapter X dealing with change.

The appellants filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 for eviction on the ground that they were the successors in interest of the lessor company. The respondents contested the application contending that the appellants had formed a partnership, as a result of which a new month to month tenancy was created and the respondents were liable to vacate the premises on 31st July, 1971. The Rent Controller held that the respondents are the successors of the original lessor company and the legal representatives of late S.M. Ganguli who had executed a lease for 20 years in favour of one S. M. Ganguli, who on his death was succeeded by his legal representatives. The appellants filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the grounds that they are the successor in interest as a sub tenant under the lease after due attornment and were liable for eviction after the expiry of the period of lease on 31 7 1971. They also stated that the heirs of late s M Ganguli had formed an partnership, and the appellants were not liable to eviction. The trial court held that they have been the successorsin interest of lessor company, and therefore, were not entitled to evict them under section 11 of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the Judicial Commissioner agreed with the findings of the trial court on merits and concluded that in absence of a month 's notice under section 13(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsif. The High Court also held that since the respondents had failed to seek extension of the term of tenancy, they were not bound by the terms of the lease deed and hence the entire proceeding was mis conceived. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that (i) the application under Section 12 of Act before the civil court was maintainable and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise; (ii) the question of dealing with the eviction of tenants under section II and extension of period of tenancy under section12(3) of the said Act could arise only where the matter is covered by section 12, and as such the decision on that point was not open to the High court to reverse them under Section 100 C.P.C.; (iii) the questions involved in the eviction application were concluded by the first appellate court in favour and against the appellants instead of confirming the decree of the Munsif directed them to file a fresh application under s 12(3). Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an application for the purpose of section 12 should be treated as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. [975C] 1.2 In view of the circumstances of the present case, the proceeding arising out of the appellant 's application before the Munsiff should be regarded as a suit and the judgment of the High Courts as a decree therein. A further question may arise as to the effect of the Judicial Commis sioner, Ranchi declining to pass a formal decree of eviction and directing the appel lants to make an application tinder section 12( 3) for that purpose.

The appellant, a registered society, filed a suit for an immovable property through its then Secretary. The suit was later transferred to the court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1, Jaipur City where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami who was elected. The trial court allowed the application holding that the appellant had not been elected as Secretary and had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. The High Court, however, held that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the trial court had committed several serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the elected Secretary and that the Trial Court had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting withdrawal of the Suit under its inherent power, and that since the case had been remanded for reconsideration of the evidence on merits, the application filed by the appellant under section 14 1 of C.P.C. was not competent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the suit had been transferred to a prayer purported to have been made on behalf of the plaintiff does not make it clear that the court had no jurisdic tion to recall the order permitting the withdrawal of suit under its intrinsic power and the High Court should have exercised its revisional power on the ground that the case has to go back for reconsideration. [236C D] Sadho Saran Rai & Ors. vs Anant Rai & Others, AIR 1923 Patna 483; Vilakathala Raman vs Vayalil Kavonia, 27 Madras Law Jour 238; Vlakatha Raman vsVayalil Kochu, 27 Mad. 483; and Basangowda Hanmantgowda Patil and Others vs Churchigirigowda Yogangowda & Anr., AIR 1923 Pat 483; referred to. 2. The factum of the consent can be investigated in summary proceedings, but the reality of the joint application cannot be so investigated. [237E F] Sadhukhan Rai & others vs Anant Raj & Ors., AIR 1924 Patna 483 and Basanta Hanmant Gangowda Patil & Others vs Pillai, A.I.R. 1923 Pat.

The appellant was the accused No. 1 before the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, and was charged with having committed an offence punishable under section 7 read with section 4 of the Ordinance read with sections 5 and 6 of the Defence of India Act, 1946. The trial ended in conviction and sentence of imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 8,000 each. On appeal by the appellant the High Court agreed with his conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the Ordinance promulgated under the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the Government of India Ordinance, 1946, was not in operation at the date when the offence was committed by the accused and (2) the ordinance had been promulgated after the emergency was declared to have ended on April 1, 1946; and (3) the Act was not applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir as it stood prior to its enactment. HELD : (1)(a) The Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the period between June 27, 1940, and April 1. 1946, the date on which the offence in question was committed, was a perpetual one and continued in operation until it was repealed. [645 B] (b) The emergency under which the Governor of India was invested with the power to make laws is distinct and distinct from and must not be confused with the emergency which occasioned the pawing of the Act and the clear effect of the words of the statute on section 72 is that Ordinances promulgated under that subsection during the currency of the Emergency were to continue in force until it is repealed. The Ordinance was therefore a perpetual piece of temporary legislation intended to meet an emergency. [643 C] (c) The Emergency Provisions which were promulgated by the Governor were not applicable in the present case because they continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India, though the Ordinance had been passed before April 1., 1946, and the Ordinance in so far as it was not extended to the territory of India. [641 D] (d) The words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" in section 72 were omitted from section 72 during the pendency of the emergency and were not synonymous with the Emergency which occasioned a contingency. The emergency on account of the expiration of the period specified in section 3 of the Indian Ordinance was not confined to the space provided by the Emergency Powers vested in him under section 73 of the General Clauses Act, 1940. [651 D F] (e) The provisions of section 72 with the omitted words restored to their original position after April 1,. 1946, while determining the duration of the Ordinances which had been enacted between June 28, 1940 and April I, 1946 were not limited to the place of not less than six month from its enactment but was perpetual in its duration with the result that it continued in force till it was repeal. [661 D E] (f) The effect of section 7 of the , as amended by the Indian Independence Act, 1947, was that Ordinances passed by the Federal Legislature were to be deemed to have been in operation on July 11, 1953, and were operative from April 1 1946, when the emergency had ceased.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that death sentence should be reduced to life imprisonment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of Code of criminal procedure 1973. [1072B] 1.2 In the instant case, the High Court was justified in affirming the death sentence imposed on the appellants. [ 1073C] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. 1.3 The conviction and sentences passed by the Additional Sessions Judge are liable to be reduced from life imprisonment to life term of imprisonment for life. [1172D] 2.1 In the present case, there was no need to expand or circumscribe the connotation of the expression 'special reasons ' occurring in section 354 (3) Cr. P.C. by indulging in classification of murders such as white collar offences and non white collars or laying down guidelines for imposition of the extreme penalty. [1272E] 2:2 The High court was justified on the facts of the case, in confirming death sentence passed under s. 368(1) Cr P. C., being satisfied that there were "special reasons" within the meaning of section 354, sub section (3), of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 so as to bind all courts in the country. [1372G H] 3.2 The question whether the death penalty should be awarded or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such cases. When a sentence of death is passed it is subject to confirmation by the High court under section 366(1), and the accused also has right of appeal to the High, Court under 5. Article 136 of the Constitution. [1472B C] 3:3. The question as to whether the capital punishment should be imposed or not need not be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend on the circumstances and circumstances of each particular case and the law applicable. But the professed view does not stem from a firm belief in dignity of human life for they themselves advocate the death Penalty for certain classes of offenders, (1) when a sentence is passed, it is open to the court to decide the accused 's sentence on the basis of grounds of compassion and humanism, and such subjections are not for the Parliament to decide. [1572C D] 3 :4. The legal position in this case is that death penalty and the judicial discretion vested in the Court regarding its imposition on an accused are constitutionally valid. [1673E F] Rajendra Kumar 's case, ; and Rajendra Prasad 's Case, , referred to.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Clerk in the erstwhile Punjab State. He was compulsorily retired on 30th September, 1953. His case was that he had been exonerated of the allegations and imputations made against him on each occasion. The High Court refused to grant special leave to appeal to this Court. In appeal to the Supreme Court it was contended for the appellant that the State Government had not given a reasonable opportunity to produce nine witnesses in his defence with some documents, and that the High Court had considered at some length all relevant questions raised by the appellant. HELD: (i) The High court had given its judgment eight months after it had been passed. It was not possible for the High court to see whether the exclusion of evidence was justified or not. [583 E] (ii) The State Government could have made a revocation of special leave under article 136 of the Constitution after hearing arguments of the appellant and delivery of a judgment. But this could not stand in the way of the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed and fully inquired into by officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged. [584 F] (iii) The question whether the appellant was given a fair opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. [585 F] Smt Ujjam Bai vs State of & Anr., ; , referred to. (iv) The appellant was not given any opportunity to meet a new case and there was no reason for the first respondent to have failed to do so. [586 G H] (v) The fact that the appellant had been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries, did not affect the validity of the departmental proceedings. [587 C D] (vi) The plea that the enquiry was null and void was not accepted by the High Courts. The State of Assam & Anr. vs J. N. Roy Biswas, ; , followed. (vii) The respondent 's defence was not open to be taken into consideration in asking for certification which had not been argued at the time when the first appeal was heard by the Division Bench.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. The appellants contended that their contracts were identical, and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. The High Court held that the contract between the appellants and the M/s. T.K. Wadeyar was integrally connected with the contract entered into by the appellants with their foreign buyers and that the contracts were different. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The contracts between the appellant and the foreign buyers are different contracts and it is the S.T.,C. which entered into independent contracts with their other foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis. Under the contracts between a foreign buyer and the S .T. C. the merchants were required to bring the goods on board the ship. The actual exportation of the goods was an unconditional appropriation which passes the property. This is not because of any peculiarity of F. O.B., contracts but because in this type of contract the seller 's duty is to place the goods "free on board" a ship to be named by the buyer. When the seller delivers the goods for loading on board he normally obtains a mate 's receipt which he transmits to the buyer and then it is natural that they should thereafter be at the buyer 's risk. Now a days a party which has contracted to sell goods to a foreign buyers may itself buy the goods F.o.B, Indian port from Indian seller in order to fulfill F.0.B contract with a foreign seller. This Court in the case of Serajuddin etc. vs State of Orissa, [1975] Supp. S.C R. 169 held that in all cases where the goods were inter State and the export sales were effected by the foreign buyer to the importer, the foreign seller was the M .M. T.,C., which entered in the independent contracts of export. The delivery of the good sold to the foreign sellers was the last purchaser within the State. [444B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the contract is not identical and there cannot be two imports. There cannot be both the last sales in the course of export and export. There could be two exports in the present case. The first contract was referred to in the High Court. The second contract was also referred to. Serajul Chand Rataria vs Bhuwalka Brothers Ltd., [1975) Supp. SCR 169, followed.

The appellant was employed with the respondent company as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974. The respondent moved an application for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate in the proceedings. The Labour Court held that the termination of the services was in accordance with the standing orders justifying the removal of the employee on successful probation during the initial or extended period of probation; that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the probationary period, his service was terminated by notice dated 12.10.1974. The appellant filed an appeal before the Labour Court which held that there was no retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 and therefore the termination in this case was neither illegal nor improper or unjustified and the claim of the appellant for reinstatement was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The termination of service of the appel lant was ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits. [532C] 1.2 In order to invoke the fiction enacted in sub section 2 (a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant date i.e. the date of termination of his service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date, if the workman has been given one month 's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the period of notice has expired or the workman had been paid in lieu of such notice wages for the period he has been paid at the time of retrenchment compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days ' average pay (for every completed year of continuous service) or any part thereof, in excess of six months. [525D E] 1:3 The termination is ab initio illegal and inoperative. He must, therefore, be deemed to be In continuous service for a period of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in section 25B(1). [526E F] 2.1 It is not necessary for the purposes of sub section (2) (a), that the workman should be in continuous service within one year or six months, as the case may be, if he satisfies the conditions in clause (a). The condition is that commencing the date with reference to which calculation is to be made in case of retrenchment the date on which the workman is actually working for not less than one year under that employer who has retrenched him from service. [500F G] 2:2 In the instant case, admittedly the appellant had rendered service for six more than 240 days within a period Of 12 months and, indisputably, therefore his case falls within section 25A(2)(a) and he shall be deemed not to have completed one year of service. The termination was ab facto void and ineffective. [51B] 2 :3 In order that the retrenchment may be effective by a certain date, it is sufficient if the workmen are in continuous Service for not more than one years. If they are in service for more than six months under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until (a)(1) the workman 's services are terminated; and wages for such period of six month shall be payable equivalent to 15 days ' service, or (b) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government. [52E F].

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. On his report to the Deputy Commissioner, Bhatinda that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and had demanded Rs. 30/ as bribe from one Ude Singh, the appellant was called upon to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him if the allegations in the charge sheet were proved. The appellant submitted his explanation on February 22, 1955, but the Deputy commissioner by order dt. March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and in lieu thereof he was asked to showcause why disciplinary proceedings should not he taken against the appellant if the allegation in the chargesheet were proved, and if the charges were proved the appellant would be guilty of misconduct. The Deputy Commissioner by his order dated March 17. 1955 ordered the services to be terminated with effect from the date mentioned in the order. On February 22. 1955, the Settlement Officer submitted his report on the evidence recorded in respect of alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in view of the fact that he was satisfied that the appellant had received a sum of Rs.150/ as illegally gratification from another person and had demanding illegal gratification, the Deputy Commissioner recommended that the respondent be terminated. The order was confirmed by the Deputy Commis sioner on March 17 and the appellant 's appeal to the High Court against the order of dismissal was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The enquiry against the respondent was for ascertaining whether he had been found guilty of the misconduct or inefficiency or for some similar reason, the termination of service was by way of punishment. [723 B] (ii) The appellant was given no such opportunity and article 311(2) was not complied with. [ 719 C D] State of Orissa vs Ram Narayan Das, ; , followed. (iii) The order of termination was not a result of any stigma affecting the future career of the public servant by the order terminating his employment for unsatisfactory work and conduct. [700 E F] (iv) The respondent was given an opportunity to make his defence and it was open to him to show that he should be confirmed, but no such notice was given.

The appellant State Government issued a notification dated November 15, 1968 for selection to the posts of Professors in the colleges. By another notification dated July 25, 1969, the Commission was consulted and it was brought to its notice that the Commission had considered the suitability of candidates for promotion as Professors in accordance with the law. The Commission submitted its report on June 25,1969, which made it quite clear that the State Government referred the selections to the Commission for the appointments. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the impugned notification. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The selection was not vitiated on account of the writ petitioner 's writ petition challenging the validity. [875 B] (ii) The Commission was also consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another, and it had been specifically stated on behalf of the State that it consulted the Commission under section 133 of the Constitution and as the writ petitioners have not ventured to take a plea to the contrary, the High court erred in taking a contrary view. [873 E] (iii) The High court was right in holding that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. [874 G H] (iv) The State Government had also placed on record the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969 which makes it quite obvious that the appellant had not venturing to take any plea to its contrary. Had the Commission de facto abdicated its power in favour of some committee composed of strangers to the commission, the position might have been different. [872 G H; 873 A] (v) The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed that the commission was consulted. [871 B C] (vi) The appellant State had also produced a copy of the minutes dated July, 22,1969 which makes the selection of Professors, which were called the "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules 1969. It has been specifically mentioned on behalf the Commission that it consults the Commission in regard tO the principles for making promotions in question, or to make promotions and transfer from one Service to another and on the suitability o f candidates for such appointments promotions promotions or transfers.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . The petitioner challenged the validity of the proceedings taken by him under article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution on the ground that the speech was published in its entirety without any reference to the contents of the news item in question, and that the publication of the speech, if it had included the portion which had been so directed to be expunged in the eye of law, amounted to a breach of privilege conferred by article 19 (1) (a). Held, that the petitioner was not entitled to succeed. The expression "the right" in article 194(3) of Constitution means the right to freedom of speech guaranteed under article19(1) of that Article and that even if the privilege was not expressly made subject to the provisions of the law, it did not necessarily mean that it was not so subject. The petitioner had the fundamental right under article 194 (3) to freedom from any action in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in the Legislature or in committees thereof and the expression " the House or Houses of such Legislature" in Article 194(1), could not be construed as including a citizen 's right to move the Court for a writ of prohibition. The provisions of article 194 were intended to protect the freedom of expression guaranteed under that Article, and the petitioner had no right to complain against any alleged irregularity of procedure. The fundamental right was preserved despite the provisions in article 19. The Constitution expressly declares that the powers, privileges and immunities of a House of the Legislature of a State and of the members and committees thereof shall be such as may from time to time be defined by the legislature by law. The power conferred on the Legislature by article 194 of the constitution is subject to reasonable restrictions within the ambit of article 19 and it cannot be said that the fundamental rights under article 14 were infringed. The right guaranteed by article 197(1). Article 19(2) does not import into India the law made by Parliament in pursuance of the earlier part of article 105(3), but only applies to laws which are made in exercise of constituent power like the law which was considered in the previous part of that part of the clause. The Act is a law made under the provisions Of the Constitution and it does not make any difference whether the privileges, immunities or immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons of the United Kingdom at the commencement of the Act are such as were ordered to be removed by the Speaker, and therefore, if the House has the power or privilege to prevent the publication, of its proceedings or portions expunged by the Committee of Privileges, it cannot claim a privilege in respect thereof. The privileges, privileges, immunitys and immunities enjoyed under the latter part of Article 194 (1), are not such as are expressly madesubject to the provision of the Constitu tion or to those of article19. The petitioners were therefore entitled to the fundamental freedom guaranteed by articles 19(i)(a).

The appellant State Government took over the management of a College on 5.5.1971 and appointed the respondent as Reader in that college on 7.4.1971. The services of the respondent were terminated by the appellant on the ground that he was drawing a salary of more than Rs.600/ per month. The appellant filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the termination orders, which were dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the requisite qualification is eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Service (O.E.S.) for appointment as Reader and not five years ' service, the respondent was entitled to be considered by the Public Service Commission for appointment to the post of Reader. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The requirement of eight years teaching experience is a matter entirely different from that of the requisite qualifications. [777G] 2.1 The condition of draw ing of Rs. 600/ or more on the date of taking over, which has been laid down in the circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment, is arbitrary and discriminatory. This condition has no nexus, whatev er, with the object underlying the qualification test in an educational institution having regard to quality, efficiency and progress in all respects. It is not unknown that private institutions generally have great handicaps in the matter of finance and oftener the teaching staff in a private college has not the same scales of pay and sometimes even has much lower scales than that of Government colleges. [778C D] 2:2 The requirement for eight years of teaching experience as mentioned in the Circular is a serious grim issue. It has to be administered on sound lines having regardto quality, efficient and progress. In view of the fact that the respondent had to join the new service under the Government, it is not merely taking over the land and buildings, tables and chairs. It had to tackle, at the same time, a human problem, that is to say, the fate of the teachers and the staff serving that institu tion. The institution with which we are concerned was taken over by consent, as a going educational concern and it goes without saying that it must be administered in accordance with law.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority granted three temporary permits to the appellants. The appellants made applications to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A) consequent upon the scheme being published by the Corporation under section 69 C, the Corporation alone could not grant temporary permits and if such application is made by the corporation and granted no one else is entitled to obtain a temporary permit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court fell into an error by interpreting section 68 G(1) only to mean that even though there are 7 vacancies for temporary permit, once the Corporation made an application for temporary, not for the full strength but something short of it there was no power left in the State Government to grant temporary permit to any one else. [985C D] 2. The correct approach would be that keeping in view the strength of the vehicles fixed by the competent authority, the authority should first examine the application for number of temporary permits made by it and if they are found to be competent, eligible and qualified they may have to be granted permits for the benefit of large travelling public. That is why power to increase strength of fleet operating on the route is conferred and has to be exercised in public interest meaning transport facility to travelling public.[985D E] 3. The authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling public, and it would be squarely attracted. [89F G] 4. The decision of the State Road Transport Corporation is upheld both by the High Courts as well as by the Supreme Court. [90G] 5. The true approach would have been that keeping In view the ratio laid down in section68 F(I A) and section 68 I.C. the authority under tho Act must first examine, the application of the present appellants for the remaining 4 vacancies and grant four permits according to law.

The appellant was the son of a Hindu undivided family. He executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of certain properties in favour of his maternal grandfather, the ancestor of respondents Nos. 1 and 2. The said property was ancestral property and he was entitled to challenge its alienation by his father respondent No. 9. Respondents Nos. I and 2 filed a suit for possession of the said property on the ground that they were not born at the time when the mortgage deed was executed and so they were entitled to question it. The trial court held that the property in dispute was ancestral and he had no right to challenge it. On appeal, the High Court reversed this finding holding that the properties in suit did not bind the appellant 's father as his family was governed by the customary law prevailing in the Punjab. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral or not depends upon the nature of the property which is capable of being partitioned and the court establishing the rule, even though the court before whom the matter arises afterwards might not have given the same decision had the question come before it originally. [59 E] (ii) The High Court was in error in holding that a property inherited by a person from his maternal grand father was not ancestral property as he had succeeded her father in default of male heirs. [60 C D] (iii) The fact that the appellant had no title to the property did not affect the question of the courts being of co ordinate jurisdiction, a decision which has been followed for a long period of time and has been acted upon by persons in the formation of contracts or in the disposition of their property or in legal procedure or in other ways will generally be followed by courts of higher authority than the court established by law. [61 D E] The question as to whether property acquired from a paternal grandfather is agricultural property or not was not raised for the first time before this Court and it was urged that the High Courts were in error on the point of law in holding the property inherited to his maternal uncle was not an ancestral property. [62 F G] (iv) The decision of the High court of Punjab as early as 1895 was reversed by the Privy Council in Parlia Ram vs Garu, A.I.R. 1945 P. 110 and Narotam Chand vs Mst. (1908) L. R. 35 I.A. 151, disapproved.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under sections 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of the 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants entered Ebir Ali 's house with the common intention of killing him and caused injuries to him. The Sessions Judge accepted the verdict and convicted them all under sections 448 and 307 read with section 34 of the Code. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted the appellants but convicted the appellants under section 449 and section 307/149 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307 readwith section 34. The appellants contended that there could be no conviction under section 450 read with s.34 of Indian Penal code because the offence committed by a number of persons was actually committed in order to the committing of an offence punishable with death, and that the offence under section 302 read with S. 34 was not sustainable in law. Held, that the words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 of the I.P.C., but also in the two succeeding sections, namely, 450, 451 and 457 of the Criminal Procedure Code and section 457 of I. P. C. The word "in" in section 448 of the Cr. P C. is used where house trespass is committed "inorder to the commission of any offence punishable under section 448". In the present case when it was found that the four appellants attacked Haji E brar Ali, the appellants attacked him with dagger while one used the dagger on him, each of them held that he down while one using the dagger was in law considered to have done the entire act of holding Ebber Ali down and applying the dagger. If Matiullah by himself had held Ebris Ali down, and struck him with the dagger, with the intention of causing his death and injury had actually resulted in his death he would have been guilty of murder except in some special circumstances as mentioned in section 300 of the IPC. The act did not result in death. The acts did not amount to murder but only caused by the dagger which was not committed in the order to be committing the offence punishable.

The appellant was the nearest male holder of a property in Gurdaspur district. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that he was entitled to succeed to the properties mentioned in the plaint as well as to the sum of Rs. 1,539/7 0 as the daughter of the last male holder. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court modified the decree by reducing the amount of compensation from Rs.1,538/7 to Rs. 1000/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had discharged the initial onus in two ways namely, (a) by producing a Riwaj i am of Gurdial Singh who was also a member of the same family of Gurdial; and (b) by adducing evidence showing that the collaterals of the first holder excluded the collateral from succession to the self acquired property of her father. HELD : (i)(a) The appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was cast on him by producing Riwraj i am as a result of the production of Riwj i am and this was a reliable and trustworthy document. [153 B] (b)(ii) The evidence in the present case was not very sketchy, that it did not appear whether the properties left by Gurdial Singh were ancestral or self acquired or whether the collateral had been excluded from succession. [154 C D] (c) The High Court erred in holding that the appellant had discharged this initial onus and that the respondent was entitled under the law to succeed on the basis of the evidence produced by him. [155 E F] (d) The fact that Riwaji am was not a party to the suit, could not affect the presumption arising on the proof of the presumption. [156 G H] Mohammad Khalil vs Mohammad Bakhsh, A.I.R. 1935 Lah. 340 and Nazarun vs Mt. Aimna Bibi, Mad. 276, referred to. (2) The statement in a Rivi am that she was excluded from inheritance to the father was not admissible under section 8 of the Evidence Act because it was not supported by any evidence. [157 B] Mohammad Ali vs Abdul Rahim, A I.R., 1940 Lah. 157 and Namat Rai vs Mt, Harnam Kaur, A,I. R.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company which was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. He applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney in respect of certain properties. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) Of the Indian Stamp Act to the High Court and the reference was heard by a Bench consisting of three Judges. The first two judges held that the instrument in question was a deed of settlement which comprised several matters, but the second one related to distinct matters and must be stamped with the aggregate amount of duty. The second judge held that though the instrument was executed by one person, if he fills several capacities and the authority conferred is general, there would be distinct delegations in respect thereof. The third judge held against the respondent. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the words "distinct matters" used in section 5 Of the Stamp act refer to different classes of instruments which might be executed either by one individual or by another and not by a single individual when he is acting as an executor or administrator. The word "distinguished" in section 4 Of the Act means something more than "categories". It is well settled that when two words are used in a statute in two consecutive provisions, they must be construed as distinct matters. In the present case, the instrument did not contain distinct matters but consisted of one matter only and that matter was the execution of a general power of Attorney by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the donee. Chaudhury vs Chaudhury ([1879] A.C. 848), referred to. The question whether a power is of a attorney or a combination of several of them depends on the nature and extent of the authority granted thereby. In deciding whether a Power of Attorney relates to distinct matter, it is necessary to consider the terms of the instrument and the nature of the authorship conferred thereby. Where several donors have separate interests in different classes, they are not separate persons. The fact that the donor has executed a power in respect Of all the matters in which he could act, does not necessarily mean that he must be held to be distinct matters for purposes of section 5. The transaction is a single transaction whereby the donor constitutes the doneer of the deceased and his attorneys for him and in his name and on his behalf to act for him in his individual capacity and also in his capacity as managing director, director, managing agent, secretary or liquidator of any company in which the deceased was or may at any time thereafter be in terested in any such capacity as aforesaid and also as executor, administrator, trustee or in any capacity whatsoever as occasion shall require. The deed does not contain a distinct matter but comprises one matter, namely, that declaration is made by the husband of the estate of the testator in respect whereof he could exercise all the powers which he executes in favour with the donee. He may also be accountable to the beneficiaries for the due administration of the affairs of the trust but that does not mean that his personal estate or interest in the property vests in him alone. The document does not comprise distinct matters, and is the execution thereof.

The assessee company was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was an Indian State. In 1948, the Raj Pramukh of the newly formed State instituted a Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949, and the said Ordinance was repealed by the Finance Act, 1950. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the depreciation allowed under the Saurashtra Income Tax Ordinance, being a deductible amount in computing the written down value of the assets of the assessee company could be deducted from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which was allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, even though not claimed. Held, that the provisions of the Finance Acts were applicable to the present case and the depreciation availed of by the assessee under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act was a deductible deduction in computing written down values under the said Act. The words "of a Part B State" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be applied according to its terms. The word "of any law relating to tax on profits of business" in para 2 of that order means and includes not only leave no doubt as regards the intention of the authority but also the fact that it is within the competence of the Central Government to make the removal of difficulties. The expression "of such Part B States" in Paragraph 2 of this Removal of difficulties Order must mean that the Income tax Officer, in determining the written off value under section 10(5) (b), has to apply the provisions in computing its written down Value under section I3(5)(b) of the Indian Incometax Act irrespective of whether any difficulty had arisen in giving effect to the provisions. The Commissioner of Income tax vs Kamala Mills Ltd., ; , followed. Held further, that if the intention had not been to include depreciation allowed by the Income Tax Officer under the proviso to cl. 2 of para 2, the order operated under its own terms and so in giving it retrospective effect to its order it was not necessary for the Income. tax Officer to see first whether any difficulties had arisen. The second proviso to section 10 (5) of Taxation Laws (Part B States) (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 1949. The third proviso to that section provided that where an assessee had been allowed to appeal under the Act before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the Income ' tax Officer determining in some cases any difficulty arose in giving effective effect to this provision, it was unnecessary for him to give such a part of the paragraph which would have read as "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part A State relating to income tax and super tax or any law pertaining to tax.

The appellant was a contractor of the respondent Corporation. The respondent Corporation invited tenders from registered contractors for laying civil and structural works, including construction of a Main Station Building. Paragraph I of the notifi cation listed three "Minimum qualifying requirements" as also the "commit tive minimum qualifica tion" as provided in para I of Part I of Schedule II to the . The appellant 's tender was accepted by the respondent corporation and the contract was terminated on 3rd January, 1989. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award of the contract. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the prequalifying conditions set out in para 1 were only the three conditions set forth in para II and that all the documents referred to in para V were only for information and not information as required by it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the clause requiring pre qualification for submitting a tender for the contract had been merely an enabling ten per cent of the documents to be furnished along with the application for tender forms; (ii) the terms and conditions set up in para IV were not complied with; (iii) the respondent was bound to furnish such information as may be specified by it and that the appellant was bound under the contract to assess the value of the certificates furnished in this regard and if the K.P.C. considered them sufficient to warrant the issue of a tender form, the appellant would be precluded from doing so; (iv) the appellant had no right to act arbitrarily in accepting the tender of the 4th respondents, but was bound by the terms of the tender notice only stated that it had done 35,000 cubic metres per month of concrete and not 30% of brick work at one site; (v) the supply of some of the materials referred to therein was indispensable to assess whether the applicant fulfilled the pre qualification conditions set in para VI; and (vi) the performance of the terms in para III was also essential for the supply. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The requirement of para I is a note on the tendering system in K. P.C., and the application other than the mini mum qualifying requirement should be prerogative of K.p.C.[239D] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had no doubt that the contract would be issued only to those who comply with the pre qualificato ry requirements. The stipulation in para 11 was not a condition precedent for the grant of the contracts and the appellant could not have been considered for the Contract. [239F] 1:3. The requirement for submitting the tender forms was that the applicant should have submitted the tender form and the conditions could be fulfilled before finalisation of the award. It is not known on what grounds the applicant had submitted the form. The only ground for delayed supply or omission to supply, any one or more of the details referred to herein is that he would otherwise have had one competitor less. But, it is not clear on what ground that application was rejected nor has that party come to Court with any such grievance. [240G H] 1 :4. The question whether the course adopted by K. p.C was justified or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If there was no acceptable tender from a person who satisfied the condition of eligibility, the first respondent could have rejected the tenders and invited fresh tenders on the basis of a less stringent standard or norm. But it is clear that if a party does not strictly comply with this requirement, the Court will decline relief. [241H] 1 5. The second consequence indicated by this Court in earlier decisions is not that the KPC should be stopped from doing anything which would be against public interest. The fact that a document was belatedly entertained from one of the applicants will cause substantial prejudice to another party who wanted, likewise an extension of time for filing a similar certificate or document but was refused the benefit. It may perhaps be said to cause prejudice also to a party which can show that it has refrained from applying for the tender documents only because it thought it would not be able to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rule was likely to be relaxed. But this is not the position in the instant cases. [242H; 243A] 1 6.

The appellant was the owner of a house. He had a house in which he had a shop. The house was let out to him for residential purposes and the appellant was put in possession of the land. In pursuance of an agreement between the parties, the appellant made an application before the Additional Custodian under section 5 A of the East Punjab Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, for confirmation of the exchange and other consequential and incidental orders made in connection therewith. The Additional Custodian rejected the application on the ground that the order of confirmation was not appealable under section 27 of the Act. The appellant then filed an appeal to the Custodian General which was dismissed. On a revision petition by the appellant, the High Court held that the decision of the Additional custodian was final and conclusive and that the orders of confirmation were binding on the Additional Controller. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order under appeal was one passed by virtue of section 27(3) of the Central Act of 1950 which purports to indicate the effect of repeal on previous matters. Under section 58(3), the application made by the person affected thereby is not subject to an appeal or revision but only to the appellate court. [1138 B] (ii) The appellant was entitled to a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of Constitution for setting aside the order passed by the Additional Deputy Custodian. [1039 C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the Additional Administration had no jurisdiction to confirm the order confirming the exchange. It is well settled that the power exercisable thereunder and the nature of things that may be done or action taken thereunder are different from those conferred on the competent authority under the Act of the appropriate Government. [1102 C] In the present case, the Additional Commissioner was not empowered to revise an order passed under section 25A of the , if he had made a reference to him and the order was therefore without jurisdiction. [111 D E] (iv) The power exercisable by the Custodian under the East Act of 1947 is not confined only to matters of jurisdiction or illegality as is contended, because under section 58 of the General Clauses Act the powers exercisable thereunder are exercisable when there is an appeal provided but no appeal is filed against such order. In the instant case, it was clear that the appellant had a genuine interest in opposing the confirmation sought, which related to a large tract of agricultural land and which would reduce the pool of agricultural lands available for rehabilitation of displaced agriculturists and that confirmation was opposed to the policy and directives of the Government. The Assistant Custodian who appeared before him in support of the notice for revision or to the allottees of the property in whose interest the revisional order appears had been passed, could not have filed an application under section 20A of Act XXXI of 1950 for confirmation which was made by him in 1948. [112 E F] (v) The Additional custodian himself in his order under section 26 of the Punjab Evicuees ' (Administration) Act 1947, had stated that the allottees were at best lessees for three years and that they came into possession much later after the orders were passed by him. He also stated that even when the rules in this behalf came into force, he did not know them as to who were the authorities that could deal with it.

The appellant company, a locality in Bombay, was a factory. Its factory consisted of workmen employed in the tiny, but were getting on well in their business and in their relations with their workmen. The dispute between the parties related to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishment before 1965. The Tribunal held that the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata as it did not provide for those categories of bonus and confined itself to profit based bonus only, but also included certain other categories of employees in the industrial dispute. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Bonus Act speaks of a whole Code, on the sole subject of profit based wage, to consider whether any festival or festival is called for by the employer to his workmen or not. [605 D] (2) The object of the Bonus Act is to provide for bonus to persons employed in certain establishments not in all establishments. The Act does not bar claims to customary bonus or those based on conditions of service. There is hardly any doubt that custom has been recognised in the past as a source of the right to bonus, as the several decisions of this Court show that it relates to a case of profit bonus urged under the by two sets of workmen, employed by establishments which are either excluded or exempted from the Bonus act. [505 E F] (3) The question whether a particular festival is a complete Code, depends on the context and terms of that custom or the tradition on which the claim for bonus based on profit to employees employed in establishments. For this reason it is not necessary to show that such bonus has been paid even in years of loss. [407 F G] (4) The fact that the Bonus ' Act speaks, and speaks as a whole code, on both sides, does not detract from the claim of customary or contractual bonus. The governing principle is that profit bonus not founded on the provisions of the bonus Act and by resort to an adventure in industrial dispute under the is no longer permissible. [405 G H] (5) The scheme of the Act shows that the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of payment of bonus based upon profits or the financial results of the employers but the workmen fall outside the ambit of the legislation by express exclusion or exemption. The relevant portion of the definition of "industrial dispute" in section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is as follows: "Industrial disputes" means any dispute between employers and employees whether employed in industrial establishments or not and all but four of them are (i) an industrial dispute which is referred to the Tribunal; (ii) a dispute for the years. [409 G H; 409 A] (6) The bonus Act speaks and speaks, as a matter of pleading, that the workmen who have entered before the Tribunal are entitled to bonus by way of collective bargaining and pragmatic justice claim precedence over formalised rules of decision based on individual contests, specific causes of action and findings on particular issues, but it is clear from the definition that the dispute is one which falls within the general Code. [411 B C] (7) The Tribunal understood the former way and followed it up with a rejection, on its own accord, in respect of the dispute between them. It took the view that if the Bonus Acts deal wholly and exclusively with profit bonus, it cannot operate as a bar to a different species of claim merely because the word bonus is common to both. It also held that since the bonus has not been related by reference to any festival by the workmen in their pleadings, they are entitled only to a consolidated sum of money which does not depend upon the profits or their financial results.

The petitioners were appointed directly by the Haryana Superior Judicial Service of Punjab in December, 1976. They were promoted to the Higher Judicial Service on the basis of a competitive examination held for recruitment to the Superior Judicial Services of the State. The High Court of Punjab and Haryana declared that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by the length of continuous service on a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the ratio of 2:1 between the promotees and direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that the High Court acted upon the amendment made in the Punjab on December 31, 1976 with retrospective effect from April 9, 1976, including the amendment to rule 12. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The seniority of members of service is to be determined with reference to the dates of confirmation without applying the rule of rotation. [1046C] 2.1 The High Courts were not justified in applying the Rule of rotation at the time of confirmation of the promotees. [1147D] Haryana State and Haryana vs State of Haryana, ; , followed. 1.2 In Punjab, the High Courts never consulted on the question whether the Governor in the exercise of power conferred by the proviso to Article 309 has the power to frame rules regulating the conditions of service of judicial officers of the States. [1104E] 2:3 The High courts were not right in applying rule 12 to the seniority list of the Service, because, the rules must now be understood to mean that the decision which is taken by the Governor of Punjab on the recommendation of the Governor for the first time shall be final and conclusive. [111A B] Haryana Government vs State, ; referred to. 2.4 The High court was not justified on the ground that the rule had been amended in consultation with the High court. [112C D] Haryana Public Service Commission vs Punjab Civil Service (Civil) No. 9228/77 dated 31st December, 1977, followed. Haryana State & Haryana vs S.L.P. (Civil ) No. 8228/76 dated 1st December 1977, referred to and applied.

The respondents were appointed as Junior Assistant to the post of Senior Assistants in the Commercial Taxes Department. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated February 18, 1986 passed by the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad, directing the State Government to examine the legal effect of the Government Order in G.O.Ms. No. 1648 dated November 20, 1982 and to consider the legal consequence of the said order. The Government allowed the representation of the respondents and directed that the order of appointment, seniority, promotion etc., be maintained. The High Court held that the zonal seniority was the criteria. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the State Govern ment had no inherent power to bifurcate or reorganise a zone within a zone for equitable opportunities and facilities for the people belonging to different parts of the State, in the matter of public employment and in the matters of public appointment and in matters of employment, and that the impugned order was bad in law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Government had no authority to bifurcated or reorganised local cadre within a Zone, i.e., the division into the local cadres except in accordance with the provisions made in GOMs No. 77 dated November 1, 1975. [574D] 1.2 In exercise of the power under paragraph 3(1) of the Order, the State Govt. framed the order organising local cadres and zone Vizagis for the purpose of recruitment, seniority and promotion etc. The expression "constituted otherwise" occurring in para 2(e) is of wide amplitude but is only relatable to the power given by the Presi dent to the State Gov ernment whenever he considers it expedient so to do to have the power to divide or reorganize a zone into local cadres for different parts. [575F G] 1:3 The State Govt., in exercise of its power under para 3(2) of Order, 1975, framed the impugned Order organising local cadre and zoneVizags within the zones and issued through GOMS No. 728 dated November lO, 1982, a fresh Notification was issued on April 1, 1982 amending the order to provide for the continuance of local cadres in respect of Class or classes of posts in any department in that district. The State Governmen tial has no inherent powers in creating a zone or organising local Cadre within a zones except in accord ance with the provision made in the Andhra pradesh Public Employment (Organisation of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order, 1974. [576F G; 577A] 1 :4 The State Gov ent Board had no power to bifurcation or reorganis ing local cadre into local cadre or cadres therein. In exercise thereof, the Government issued a Notification dated November 2, 1982 abolishing local cadres. Para 3(7) of this order provides that "nothing in this order shall be deemed to prevent the State from organising or continuing more than one local cadre for such part of the state". The High court held that GOM was not vitiated by any manifest error of law warranting interference. [577F H] 2:1. It is true that the clause 'or consti tution ' occurring in paragraph 2(a) of GOM.Ms No. 795 dated November 10, 1982 has been treated as a special provision made under the Constitution (Thirty second Amendment) Act, 1973 peculiar to the state of Andhra Pradesh due to historical background. Therefore, the creation of local cadre is related to the concept of unit of appointment under the service rules and the part of State Government has been declared as a local area for the purposes of recruitment seniority and promotions etc.

The appellant was the owner of Gadi Sirampur in execution of a mortgage decree. The respondent No. 1 obtained a permanent lease of four villages from the appellant for a term of ten years and the appellant purchased the said lands on payment of Rs. 1,10,631/ . The appellant 's father had executed a mortgage deed in favour of the respondent No 2. The appellant was not a party to that suit. The trial court held that the respondent was subrogated to the position of the Bank and that the appellant was entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants. On appeal, the High Court reversed this decision holding that the plaintiff was sub bound to pay the permanent lease in respect of the lands and mesne profits from the date of the mortgage till the date on which the suit was filed. Held, that the question whether a mortgagor in possession has power to lease the mortgaged property depends upon the authority to deal with the property in the usual course of management. The mortgagor in Possession is not liable for destructive waste is acts which are destructive or permanently injurious to the mortgaged properties if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by such acts. The true position has been stated in the following terms by Das, J., in Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumar (I.L.R. and Balmukund vs Motilal (I I.L R. , referred to.
