Held further, that it is for the lessee if he wants to resist the claim of the mortgagee to establish that the lease in his favour was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of administration. The question whether the mortgagor in posses sion has power under section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act to lease a mortgage property depends on the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee. The real position is that the mortgagor may make a lease conformable to usage in the normal course of his management, but this right cannot be restricted by the terms of the English Law of Real Property. Balmakund vs Ram Kishore (I L.R,. and Balkund vs Sons (I 1.L., R. and Cres. 245) referred to, Held, further that the suit for possession was not maintainable in view of section 66(2) of the Act.

The petitioner, a contractor, filed an arbitration suit in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The respondent filed an application before the Calcutta high Court under Sections 5,12 and 33 for setting aside the arbitration agreement dated November 23, 1990 in respect of the first time in July 1979. The learned Single Judge of the Calcutta Division Bench dismissed the application on the ground that the claim was barred by limitation. The Division Bench held that it was not proved that the petitioner had sent any claim in July, 1979 and that the respondent had abandoned the contract, even assuming that any claim was as a fact made in July. 1979 and payment was not made, the petitioner could not take recourse to arbitration under section 8 of the Act for appointment of an arbitrator. The High Court quashed the arbitration clause 68 of the contract in matter Nos. 1326, 1364 and 1365/90 dated November 3, 1990. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the petitioner having made the claim for the first lime in July 1978, the arbitration could not be proceeded with; (ii) the respondent having sent the bills on July 12, 1979, and payment being not made there, the respondent could not have taken recourse to the arbitration under sections 8 and 12 of the Arbitration Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Court is entitled to permit a contracting party to rescind the contract or the court can revoke, the authority to refer the disputes or differences to arbitration. [368C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Court exercised its power under sections 15 and 12 for appointment as arbitrator and cause of action had arisen between the parties at the instance of either party to the contract. The petitioner did not take any action from then. It was open to him to plead in the proceedings before him of limitation as a defence. [369D] 1:3.1 In the context of the present case it is clear that the Court may be justified to exercise its discretionary power under Sections 15 and 16 to grant leave to the applicant to rescind, the contract agreement or to rescind it. The question therefore, as posed earlier is whether the court would be justified in permitting a contracting parties to rescind a contract or to rescinding the arbitration agree ment. [370E] 2.2 The Court has discretion to exercise the power under Ss. 5 and 12(2) (b) to permit the respondent to rescind an agreement or the Court can revoke the authority of the arbitrator 's consent. In the present ease, the parties slept over their right for more than 10 years. Statutory arbitrations stand apart. [371F] 2:3 The Court cannot be justified under section 37(1) to grant permission to the respondent in exceptional circumstances to rescind or rescind the arbitration agreements. [372A B] 2 :4. In these circumstances it is an exceptional case and the courts below have justifiably exercised their discretionary power, and jurisdiction under sections 6 and 12 (2)(b).

The appellants in the appeal were the estate of a Zamindar. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of section 2(1) and the notification issued under section 3(1), as amended by Act 1 of 1964, provided that where a suit is wholly or partly dismissed under rule 8, the plaintiff shall be precluded from bringing a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action. The appellants contended that the objection raised by the judgment debtors was barred by the principles of res judicata and also on the ground that the decree could not be executed in view of the provisions of the Act. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the objections were barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. On appeal the High Court held that the plea was barred under the principles laid down by this Court in Raj Kishore Pratap Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh (1962) Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564 and that the bar of resjudicata would not operate as res judicata against a plaintiff in a subsequent suit on the same point. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The contention that the judgment debtor was entitled to get compensation under the Act is unsustainable. The objection of the judgment creditor is unsustainable because it is only a part of the mortgaged property has vested in the State absolutely free from all encumbrances. [914 D] The question whether the decree cannot be executed against the estate or not depends on the plea taken by the parties and the decision of the claims officer or the Board has been made final by the Act, and it is not open to the appellants to proceed with the execution. Their only remedy is to get the compensation under Act. [936 D] In the present case, the decree holder had a right to proceed against the properties of the mortgagor in view Of section 4 (d) and section 4 of the Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1964. The High Court was not correct in holding that it could assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection of the . [936 G H] Ramnarain vs Basudeo, ; , followed. The true effect of the decisions of this Court is that where the whole of the property mortgaged is an estate, there can be no doubt that the procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed in order that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officers and the decisions are made final.

The respondents, who were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ', challenged the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the Civil Services Examination Rules (O.As.) on the ground that the said proviso was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and was not ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. The Tribunal dismissed the O.As. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the second Proviso to Rule 3(4) of C.S.(E) Rules is unconstitutional as it makes a discrimination against the candidates appointed to the Indian Police Service Group ' A ' and who have been allocated to that service in the same manner, without having to resign from the service to which they are allocated, nor would he lose his original seniority in the service, to which he was allocated. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The second proviso is unconstitutional against the appellants. [972C] 1.2 The second Proviso is not ultra rites Regulation 4(iii) of the C.P & Berar Police Regulations, 1962, as it does not restrict the candidates who are otherwise eligible in terms of clauses (i) to (iii) thereof. The proviso is not invalid on the grounds that it makes the candidates ineligible who are therefore entitled to appear at the next Civil Service Examination. [992D] 1:3. The second Explanation to Rule 2(4), which insists that a candidate who has been allocated under the I P.S., or Central services Group 'B ', on the basis of the previous C.A.T. examination can either join in the next civil service Examination, but subject to the provisions of Rule 17, and that the proviso to this rule is not unconstitutional. [982E F] 1 :4. The first proviso to r. 4(i) is valid and does not offend Article 14. [1003G H] 1.(a) The second provisos are constitutionally valid and do not violate article 14. The impugned second proviso has been struck down as invalid on account of the failure of the Government to justify the introduction of the impugned second Proviso in Rule 4(ii). [1004B C] (b) The proviso to rule 4(1) is unconstitutional, because it makes no distinction between candidates who otherwise eligible and those who on the date of the earlier examination had been allocated and appointed to a service. [1012C D] (c) The first part of the proviso is valid as it stands. It does not violate any prohibition or embargo imposed by the second sub rule (iii). [1013E F; 1014G H; 1015A] (d) The impugned proviso is void because it does no discrimination against candidates appointed through the same open competition to appear in the first C.B.S./C.T., or any Central Services, Group 'C ', and who are permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to so appear. [104G] (e) The expression "may be allowed to sit at the first Civil Service examination" in Rule 17 of the said C.R. Rules does not travel beyond the intent of the main rule putting any unjustifiable embargo on the number of attempts at the examination. [114A B] (f) The provision is made for a candidate, who has already been allocated, to the service and is appointed to that Service, and is entitled to compete for appointment in services mentioned against that service. The expression 'may be allow to sit in the second C.T./S.C. Group ' or 'C.P., and who has not been permitted to participate in the examination in view of the power conferred by Rule 4 on the first part, is not only placed on the candidates, who on that basis, have qualified himself in the preliminary examination but also on the candidate or candidates who have appeared in Civil Services Main Examination of a subsequent year under the interim orders of the Tribunal for the Civil Service Examinations. [124G; 125A B C] 2. The provision of Rule 4 is not violative of Articles 14. It is not discriminatory and violative of article 14, because, it makes discrimination against persons appointed to service and who on account the basis that the result of the first D.P./S., is not placed on a higher footing than those who have otherwise eligible.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The Advisory Board, after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, rejected the request for assistance of a friend. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court and that application was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, the detenu would have been better placed before the Advisory Board. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Advisory Boards had no justification to refuse assistance of the Deputy Collector as a friend was bad and continued detention of the appel lant became vitiated. [790B] 2.1 In the instant case, the detaining author ity has not taken into consideration the allegation that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant his case would have be better placed. The Board, therefore, is not justified in refusing assistance of an Advocate. [789D] 2:2 It is true that while section 8(e) disentitles a detenu from claiming the assistance of natural justice as afriend '. But what cannot be permitted directly should not be allowed to be done in an indirect way. Sundararajan, J., speaking for the Court, explained the position and held that if a person was not a friend in the normal sense could be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. [788E F] 2 :3 The Advisory board has no justification for refusing assistance to the appellant in such circumstances. The rule in A. K. Roy etc. vs Union of India & Anr., ; applied. 2:4 In the facts of the instant cases, the refusal by the Advisory Boards to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan as a lawyer was bad, and continued incarceration of the appellants became vitiated, and the order of detention is quashed. [781E F; 792A] 2(a) The detenu was not given any legal assistance for the purpose of seeking assistance of his friend at the hearing and for reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit filed by the detaining authorities. [780B C] (b) The Advisory Advisory Board has no reason to refuse to permit assistance of A.K. Roy, J. [779C D] 2.(a) What cannot be granted directly should be allowed directly to be do indirectly; and no one should be enabled to take shelter behind the excuse that such officers are not "legal practitioners" or legal advisers. [777D E] (c) The word 'friend" used in the judgments of this Court was more in this sense than meaning 'a person known well to another and regarded with liking, affection and loyalty. ' A person not being a friend is not being "an ally or enabled to act before the Board through a legal practitioner". [777E F]. (d) The term 'friends ' used in section 8 (e) does not mean that the detaining Authority or the Government should have the facility of appearing before the advisory board with the aid of a legal practitioners. [774F G] 2 (a) It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellanant on account of such denial. This Court has reiterated the position that matters relating to preventive detention are strict proceedings and warrant full compliance with the requirements of law. In view of the position of law and the facts, the denial of A reasonable opportunity to the detenu in such circumstance is not unjustified. [783F G; 785A B] (2) The rule is not permitted directly to have the liberty of a lawyer. [784C D]. Nand Lal Bajaj vs State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

The appellants were the owners of certain premises requisitioned and acquired under the Defence of India Act, 1939. The requisition orders provided that the goods requisitioned and requisitioned were to be delivered by endorsement and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they related and as the mills were not informed of the order of requisition the appellants filed a suit challenging the validity of the requisition on the ground that the delivery orders did not pass on September 30, 1946. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but the High Court held that the requisition orders did affect the property and that the properties in question had passed to the owners as provided by r. 75 A (2) Of the Defence Of India Rules, 1939, which provided that where a notice of acquisition has been served on the owner of the property under section 12(1) of the Act, the property shall vest in Government free from any mortgage, pledge, lien or other similar encumbrance and the period of requisition shall end. The appellants contended that the orders of requisition were invalid as they had not been properly served and therefore there was no acquisition of property. Held, that the order did not affect the properties and the requisition was valid and binding on the owners. The provisions of r. 77 (2), of the Defence Rules, do not apply to the case. The words "the owner of a property" in r. 2(a) of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure are wide enough to include an order in writing as is the case in r, 75 A(2). Held further, that under r. 1 (1) Of 0. XXIX, r. 3 of the Rules, the requisition order must be brought to the knowledge of the person whose interests are being affected by it and that this was not done in the present case. Held also, that as the requisition were duly served on a corporation, the properties could not be requisitioned under r, 77 (1). The requisition order did no doubt provide for the manner in which documents may be served on any of the owners but it was not necessary to serve them with notices under r., 75 A. The notice of requisition was properly served on all the owners and the mills had been in law the owners ' property.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned was 1963 64. In the assessment relating to the assessment year 1963 64, the assessee claimed that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not agree with the matter and held that no action could be taken against the assessee under Section 23A. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Tribunal. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax under Section23A was made on or before the date relevant to the assess year 1963 63, the said amount cannot be treated as a provision and not a reserve. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessee itself called it a provision. It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve for the purpose of the Income Tax Act. [113E] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. In Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , this Court held that the provisions made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision which was a provision, and not an reserve. [114F] In VIrshad Sultan Tobacco Company Ltd. vs Commis sioner of Income tax, Andhra pradesh, , this court held that since no order imposing additional tax is made on the anticipated loss and contingency are charges against profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L. accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand, reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are repre sentable being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. [115E F] Vazir Qasim Sultan Tobacco Cooperative Ltd. & Ors. etc., vs Commissioner Of Income Tax Andhra Pradesh, etc. , referred to. In these appeals, the Revenue obtained the reference and the High Court answered the question against the asses see. The correctness of the said view is questioned in this appeal by special leave. [116F G] Metal box, which has been followed in Vazir (Pegler 's Book keeping and Accounts, 15th Edn. p. 42), was followed in the Vazir Ol 's book keeping and accounts, 15 th Edn. P. 42). The assessee did not called it "a reserve nor" was it sets apart or appropriation as a Reserve. [117G H] In the instant case, the High court was right in holding it to be a provision of section 23A and not the reserve. The appeal accordingly fails and is dismissed.

The petitioners in the writ petitions, who were working as Assistant Engineers (on a later point of time) in the erstwhile State of Rajasthan joined service in the year 1955 and continued to be on the cadre of Assistant Engineers. They challenged the validity of the seniority list dated December 17, 1965 issued by the Government of India on the ground that officers appointed to temporary posts on the basis of interview alone were subjected to competitive written and personality test and in the nature of things only the very best could emerge out successfully. The petitioners contended that they were recruited in Class I service and supported their claim on diverse grounds so as to obtain the result that all Assistant Engineers formed one class under the Indian Railway Establishment Board. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification of temporary Assistant Officers into those that were recruited on the same day by selection was not discriminatory but violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [1025C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners who were appointed to the cadre posts in Class 1 service and supporting their claim for permanent Assistant Engineers joined service much later than the results of the competitive examinations were placed above those appointed on the date of selection by the Union Public Service Commission. The requisite direction was thus made and carried out. [1125D] 1:3. There is no provision in the Rules which excludes the rule of constructive res judicata. It is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a Service. Similarly when the dispute raised between the officers in a representative capacity and Engineers not so represented, in Katyani Dayal 's case (supra) still it was a dispute raised before this Court which has already been decided finally. [1102E F] 1 :4. The distinction between the two services was well marked in Kattyani Dayal & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors., ; and Katyni Dayal ' Dayal ' vs Union Of India, [1990] Supp. SCC 688 at 691, referred to. 1:5. The rule of weightage also appears to be reasonable and this is a system which has not been challenged by mere passage of time. It may be that the dispute between the Officers in a representa tion capacity and engineers not so represents, in the instant cases, in view of the bar of re agitation erected by Direct Recruit 's Case (supra). Equally when absorption had been made possible and its pace quickened with weightage, it is difficult to find fault with the scheme at this point oftime to look for a substitution at our end, as that would unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprehensible now at this stage to dig up old issues. [1014G H; 1025A] Katyabhai Dayal & ors.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 I.P.C., and section 11 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but on appeal by special leave it was contended that section 11 Of the WestBengal Special Courts (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1949, violated article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the offences alleged to have been committed by the appellant within the specified areas were required to be tried by the Special Court under the special procedure. Held, that the provisions of the Act were not discriminatory in character and could not be held to offend article 14 Of the Constitution. The State Legislature was competent to enact a law relating to "any other matter" within the meaning of article 13 of the constitution as it stood before its amendment by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956. The West Bengal Act, being a special law, was open to challenge on the ground that it contravened article 14. The provisions of article 14 were not unconstitutional in view of the decision of this Court in State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar, [1952] S.C.R. 284 and State of Bihar vs Anwar Sarkar, ; , followed. Held further, that section II Of the Ordinance was valid and did not offend article 13. The Act was a special one and was intended to be a special procedure for the trial of offences or cases in any way they like without regard to any objective and as such the statute was open only to the legislature to classify "offences" or "classes of cases" and that recourse to a simplified and less technical method of classification was not justified. The object of enacting the Saurashtra State Public Safety Measures (Third Amendment) ordinance, 1949 was to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State of Saurashtra and to provide that such offences shall be tried as expeditiously as possible in accordance with a special procedures evolved for the purpose. The Ordinance was not discriminatory and did offend article 19(1)(f) of the Constitu tion. The preamble to the Act showed that it was intended by the Legislature to provide the procedure which was followed in the present case. It was not necessary for the State Government to decide whether any class of cases or offences should be tried under the Special Courts constituted under the West Benoarilal 's (Second) Amendment Ordinance, 1948, and as the provisions contained in the Act had been made applicable to the State, it was competent for the legislature, to classify offences or classes of cases into "offenses" or class of offences for the purposes of the Ordinance, for the state Government is in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the State and the Court will not lightly interfere with the decision. The fact that the deviation from normal procedure prescribed by the Ordinance were not so many or vital as in the Bengal case did not affect the result, as the defect of the absence of a reasonable or rational classification was still there.

The prosecution case was that the appellants along with two others were tried for offences under sections 302, 396 I.P.C. and section 396 I P.C., and convicted by the Sessions Judge, Kanpur, under section 396 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the other four accused but convicted the other five accused under section 302 I. P. C. and the sentence of imprisonment for life awarded to them by the learned Sessions Judge was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that having regard to the size of the eastern kotha of the house of the deceased, it is not probable that the assailants armed with various weapons could have been present in that kothas at the time of the occurrence and that the evidence of P.W. 2 and P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 to the extent that their evidence was corroborated by the evidence on record, were not convincing. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts have rightly rejected the evidence regarding the presence of the appellant in the kothad village at the relevant time and it is well settled that there is no reason whatsoever for rejecting the evidence relating to the presence or participation of the accused in the incident. [574 D] (2) There is no justification for rejecting evidence of the witnesses who are injured witnesses to the effect that their testimony has been corroborated by their evidence. The evidence of a witness who has been examined to corroborate the evidence is not convincing and it cannot be said that from the mere fact that none of the members of the village had been recovered from any of the houses, it could be held that the appellant was not the culprits in this case. [575 D E] (3) The evidence on the record shows that P. Ws. 1 and 7 and others were injured witnesses. There is also no reason for rejecting their evidence as to who were the assailants. The learned Sessions judge has rejected the testimony of P,Ws. I, 7 & 8 in so far as it goes to prove the presence and participation of appellants in the occurrence. [576 D E; 576 A] (4) The reasons given by the trial court for rejecting this evidence are not convincing because they have been corroborated from the evidence.

The appellant State Road Transport Corporation created under a State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to run its business as an undertaking and the employer terminated the employment of some of the employees during the initial period of probation. The respondent Corporation terminated the services of some employees during that period on the ground of unsuitability. Thereupon, an industrial dispute was raised by the appellant. A Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance with section 25F. The employer Corporation came up before a Division Bench which held that the termination of service was not retrenchment within the meaning of section 2 (oo) but was retrenchment within its ambit, and that the discharge of the employee was bad for non compliance with section25F. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the services were terminated on the grounds of unsubsity and therefore did not amount to retrenchment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'termination ' in section 25G of the has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation of the word. It means the discharge or dismissal of the workman by the employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. [790B] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent Corporation had Bank 's stand that section 25 F of the Act did not apply to it and was not a case of disbanding surplus labour force and, therefore, did not attract retrenchment. The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that in these cases the order terminating the service was bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour Court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief. [789D] 1:3. The expression "termination" in section2(oo), does not include a termination of any service by an act of the employer. The underlying assumption, of course, is that the undertaking is running as an industrial undertaking and that it would be retrenchment within section 2 of the Corporation Act. [788E] 1 :4. The question whether the discharge on account of surplusage ' is valid or not depends upon the facts of each case. If due weight is given to the words 'the termination by the employers of the service of a workman for any reasons whatsoever, the employer would be entitled to take advantage of non compliance of section 25FFF. [ 788E] 2.1 In the present case, there was no dispute that the respondent had terminated the service on the basis of surplus,ageage '. The order of retrenchment was bad as it did not fall within any of the excepted categories. There is thus termination of services for a reason other than the excepted category.

The assessee, a dealer in unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration, filed returns of sales effected by it of unclaimed and unrelated goods year after year and paid sales tax pursu ant to the assessment made by the Sales Tax department. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed the assessee 's turnover under section 56 of the Indian Railways Act, 1941. The Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes rejected the claim on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed or unconnected goods was a regular feature of the assessee"s activities and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the same. In second appeal, the Tribunal held that the sale effected by the assessee was a "dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1940 and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. On reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the good. It seems to South Eastern Railway was a 'dealer for the purposes of the Calcutta Finance ( Sales Tax)Act, 1941 and therefore the sale took place. The Board of Revenue, West Bengal and simi larly, it is an act which may he regarded as obviously incidental or subsidiary to its commercial business as carriers of the same goods. It appears to South eastern Railway was the 'dealer ' for the purpose of the said Act. [781E F] 2. In the instant case, the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. [780F G] 3. In view of the fact that the assessee has been a carrier of goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of So disposing of goods was necessarily incidental to the main activity of carriage of the Goods by the railway. It was an activity, which may, be regarded in the nature of business as carried on carrier of 'goods. It has been activity which might be regarded a necessary incidental or analogous to its own business as soft ternctive to its trade as carrier or if at all claimed for such period the railway was entitled tO dispose them Of.

The appellant, a Director of the Insurance Company, was appointed as Managing Director on March 1, 1949. He resigned from the office in 1942 and was succeeded by his brother J. Dalmia. The appellant filed a suit against the Union Agencies for recovery of certain sums of money which were due to them from the appellants. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mere fact that the funds of the company were diverted to Union Agencies by the transactions proved that the amount was received in cash and not through transfer which transactions had to be adjusted. [387 G] (ii) The fact that J. was a Director in the appellant 's firm was not conclusive as to whether he had any knowledge of the transaction with respect to the full working of the scheme to provide for the losses of the Union agencies from the funds. [388 C D] (iii) The evidence on record showed that the money of the appellant company was diverted to the Union Agency by the transaction proved by the prosecution. It could not have been possible for the prosecution to lead direct evidence about the source of the money to be paid to the appellant. [389 E F] (iv) The appellant had no knowledge of his knowledge with respect of the full running of the funds received by J. [390 G H] (v) The High Court was right in holding that the falsification of the journal vouchers related back to the original diversion of the amount out of the fund of the insurance company to the respondent. [391 C D]. (vi) The presumption under section 409 I.P.C. is not rebutted by the evidence on the record. It is only when the court accepts the evidence that would be sufficient to rebut the presumption. In the present case, the appellant had nothing to do with the movement of the securities held by the respondent Agencies and was merely acting in his own behalf. [392 G H; 393 A B] (vii) The question whether the appellant was guilty of any knowledge or not having been established it would be difficult for the Court to draw an inference that he had no know about the whole affair with the Insurance company or that there was any knowledge about the affairs of the respondent agency. [393 C D; 393 E F]. (viii) The conduct of J. in dealing with the transactions was not such as to amount to a criminal conspiracy. It was not possible for him to believe that the appellant did anything to do so and that he was misled by the withdrawal of money from the Bank.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. The Government of Bombay sanctioned certain rules called the Allocated Government Servants (Absorption, Seniority, Pay and Allowances) Rules, 1957. These rules provided that "the ministerial staff in the Secretariat service shall be deemed to have been allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of a State and were allotted to serving in connection therewith. " The appellants were not absorbed in the Ministerial Service of a Secretariat Service but were transferred to the Secretariat of the Government of Gujarat and assigned duties in various districts in Saurashtra and Kutch. The respondents Nos. 2 to 148 who were holding the permanent posts of the secretariats of the Part B State of Saurashtra and the State Government of Saurashtra were allotted the posts of clerks in the secretaries of the part B State. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of transfer on the ground that it altered the conditions of service of applicants for the Secretariat services from other departments to other departments and that the order violated the proviso to cl. (6) of section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1956 which altered the condition of service applicable immediately before the appointed day in the case of any person who was allotted to another State cannot be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. The High Court held that since the impugned order purported to amalgamate the former Saurashtra and Gujarat States personnel with the Gujarat Secretariat Service contrary to the terms of r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules, the order did not violate the proviso. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transfer of the former State and Kutch States Secretariat personnel to the Gujarat secretarians were not open to objection. HELD : (i) The order of transferring the former Bombay Reorganisation Tribunal does not violate any statutory right vested in the personnel of the latter States which they acquired under the , to hold posts in connection With the affairs. [522 B] (ii)The expression " repatriating" has not been used in the order, but that will not justify an inference that there was no intention to absorb the former. The expression " repatriated" has also not been defined in the orders of the Union Government. [525 C D] (iii)The mere fact that they were posted (in the Secretariat) did not make a final decision, it is not open for the officers of the Secretariats to challenge the authority of the Govern ment of Gujarat either to transfer officers from the Districts and to post and assign them duties in theariat or to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the department. [500 E] (iv)The order of the High court was contrary to law, because, it altered conditions of serv ice of applicants; and that it did not prevent any additional members from being amalgamated in the subordinate staff in a service. The order was therefore bad.

The Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 was passed in 1948. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Haryana General Sales tax (Amendment & Validation) Ordinance, 1967 on the ground that it contravened section 15 of the Central Sales Tax Act, as amended by the Punjab General sales Tax (Second Amendment and Validation), Act, 1969. The High Court dismissed their petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the provisions of the Punjab Amending Act and the Validation Act were not discriminatory and that the levy of tax on sale or purchase of declared goods within a State was violative of article 14 and was also unconstitutional being in violation of articles 14 and 19. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Haryana General sales tax (Second amendment and Validation ) Act, 1968 is valid. [553 B] (2) The provisions of section 15(a) of the Act are not discriminatory as they are violative of Articles 14 and19. [554 C] (3) The Act has been made retrospective but no machinery is provided to discover if the declared goods were assessed to tax more than once. As there was a discrimination between the imported goods and local goods, the stage of tax is the sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to pay the tax and in the case of purchase tax the stage is purchase by the first dealer liable under section 5(2)(a) (vi). [554 E] (4) The levy of sales tax on declared goods is not discriminatory. The rate of tax same in every case is the price of goods manufactured or produced in the State and similar goods imported in the course of inter state trade or commerce. [555 G] (5) The question as to how far a party can ask for refund, without the order of assessment being set aside by appropriate proceedings is highly doubtful. [556 B C] In the instant case, the petitioners were dealers in cotton and they had been assessed to sales tax under section 3(a)(vi). They challenged the levy on the grounds that it was discriminatory and violative of articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The contention was rejected by the High Court. [557 D E] State of Punjab vs M/s. Ram Kishan & Co., ; , followed. (6) The petitioners were not dealers in Cotton or oil seeds. They had been selling cotton for manufacturing yarn and selling it to other dealers. The only levy was on sale of declared foods within the meaning of section 2(a), (vi) and (vii).

The appellants who were the mortgagors of a joint family business filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain amount due from them on account of mortgage. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed that decree holding that the mortgages were not binding on them or on their shares in the joint family property and that the debt was scaled down by the High court in favour of defendants 2 to 7 only and that they would still be entitled to avail himself of the benefit of the scaling down of the decree. The appellants contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and exceptions to this rule were admitted in special circumstances where the integrity of the mortgage had been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; and that, as the decree holders were bound under the terms of the compromise they could not be allowed to take into court all the documents in their power or possession relating to the mortgage and reconveyor. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that a mortgage decree is one and composite and exceptions are admitted in Special circumstances where there is severance of the interests of the mort gage has been dis disruption at the behest of the mortgagor himself; but the fact that in such cases the mortgagors are not an agriculturist himself being entitled to the benefit under the scaling over of the debt does not make any difference. The High Court was right in taking the view that the compromise decree should not only have stated the amount payable by defendant No. 1 and that by defendants 2, to 7 separately but should have expressly directed that on payment of the amount directed to be paid by defendants 8 to 7 their interest alone in the mortgaged property would not be liable to be sold. The fact that the decree contains no directions does not affect the correctness or otherwise of these deci sions. Ramier vs Srinivasiah, (1940) 2 M. L.J. 39 and Srikanta Pillai vs Seetharam, (1929) 1 M.L.J 39, referred to. Held further, that in view of the fact the decree contained no directions regarding the amount of interest on the mortgaged properties and consequently there was no question of the pur pose of scaling down the mortgage decree under the Agriculturists ' Relief Act. The judgment debtors are not entitled to get the benefit thereof as they have been scaled over under the provisions of the Agriculturists Relief Act, but there were purchasers of the mortgaged land who were not agriculturists and the question whether a purchaser could get the benefits of the said debt scaled up under the Act in spite of the provision of general law which prevented a mortgagor from denying his liability to pay interest which he owns in the mortgage property to satisfy the entire mortgage debt. The decree in the present case should not be disturbed on the ground that it was not possible for the defendant No 1 to contend that the mortgaged debt remained indivisible and could not, therefore, be any objection to a decree for reduced amount being passed against an agriculturist debtor while the same relief is not given to his co debtors who do not fulfil that description.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of rent and damages. The respondents contended that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The trial court held that the first plaintiff was entitled to recover possession of the premises as sub tenants, but the High Court in appeal reversed this decision holding that the City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Courts were not competent to entertain a suit for the recovery of arrears of rent where the relationship of landlord and tenant existed between the parties. HELD : The suit could not be determined by the City civil court. The suit was essentially a suit between a landlord and a tenant, and the suit did not cease to be a suit in which a question of title to premises arose and was determined. [373 B] The suit under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, was not one between a lessor and a sub tenant. The plaint in the present case showed that the defendants were landlords of the suit premises at various stages and the plaintiffs were their tenants. The suits were essentially a claim for possession of premises to which any of the provisions of Part 11 of the Act applied. [374 C] The City Civil court was therefore, not competent under section 29A to entertain and try such a suit. [375 D] The Bombay Rents. Hotel and lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1944, was enacted by the legislature clearly intended that no finality should be attached to the decision of a Court trying a suit under s 28 on a question relating to recovery of rents or relating to possession and all claims to such a status would have to be determined under the provisions Of the Act as they would be claims arising out of the statute. [376 D] In the present ease, the suit was not between a tenant and a landlord merely because the defendants denied the claim of the plaintiffs. The claim of defendants was that they had been inducted into possession by the plaintiff in a competent court to establish his title to such premises. Even if it be assumed that a claim to a right to tenancy of premises is a question which arose out of Act or any of its provisions, the jurisdiction to try such suit was exclusively vested in the courts specified in section 28 and no other.

The appellant was appointed managing director of a private company in the year 1955. He was appointed as the managing director by an order dated July 7, 1955. The respondent was appointed the managing directors on January 14, 1957. On July 7 the appellant filed a suit against the Company and the respondents for the following reliefs: (a) that the appointment of the appellant should be made after the commencement of the Act; (b) that he had not ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the meetings of the Board of Directors; (c) that his appointment was illegal and inoperative; (d) that in any event, the appointment was void. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant had been validly appointed as managing director and therefore the appointment could not be made by the company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the word "assignment" in section 255 of the new Act, which has reference only to an appointment by a director, does not mean merely "appointment". The word "revocation" does not include appointment; (ii) the words "assign" and "assigned" are used in section 312 of the old Act, and therefore, the word 'assignment ' does not refer to appointment. HELD : (i)(a) The word 'resignation ' does mean "appointment", and it is clear that the word has been used in the main part of section 86B of the Indian , which has taken the place of the first proviso to section 86 B of the . [334 C] (b). The word `assignment` does not necessarily refer to a transfer. It refers only to appointment, and it cannot be said that the words 'assign ' in section 313 of the present Act are intended to include "appointment" and thereby make the assignment subject matter of the proviso redundant or otiose. [335 D] (c). The expression "assignation" in the first Proviso does not indicate that it is intended that the term 'assigned ' must be held by a person who is a director of the company, but for the proviso, it means that the section would apply to such an appointment. The appellants are the tenants of the respondent firm. The respondent filed an eviction petition being H.R.C. No. 641/75 against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the Respondent sublet the shop let out to the said M/ s. Adeshwar glass Mart and were liable to be evicted for contravening the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the respondent was not a tenant within the meaning of section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Act. In an appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction petition was filed against the appellant firm and one another partnership firm and that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellant had sublet the premises to M/S. Adeswar Glass Mart and was liable to he evicted for contravention of the provisions. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that it is only by virtue of the provision of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. [420C] Chhotelal Pyarelal vs Shikharchand, ; , relied upon. In the instant case no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise this contention at this stage at all. This contention must fail. Had this contention been raised in the Trial Court or even in the first Appel late Court, it would have been open to them to amend the eviction petitions and join the partners as re spondents. [426D E] Chh landlady Pyarelal, the partnership firm is carried on business at the said premises and that firm was carried on the business in that premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the same business. Moreover, although a notice was given by the respondent to the appellant and M/ S. Adhirajlal, it could not be said that the partnership deed and ledgers were produced. It is also not one which would have shown that rent was received by the appellants from M/ SS. Adarayan Glass Industries, the firm or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence the ratio laid down in Chhotelals Pyarelal 's case is directly applicable to the case before this Court.

The Andhra Pradesh Act was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of its powers under Entry No. 1, List I of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The Andhra Pradesh Legislature enacted the Central Act with a view to provide for the imposition of ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling limit. Section 2(n) defines "vacant land" to mean land which is used or is capable of being used for purposes of agriculture, or for purposes ancillary thereto including horticulture, forest land, pasture land, waste land, plantation and topeaking of such plants as may be prescribed by the Rules. The Act was enacted with a purpose to provide that if any land situated within the limits of an urban agglomeration other than land which was mainly used for the purpose of agriculture and agriculture in this connection includes horticulture, but does not include raising of grass, dairy farming, poultry farming, breeding live stock and cultivation or the growing of such crops as may he prescribed by rules, the whole of the Andhra Pradesh shall be deemed to belong to category D in that Schedule. Section 3(j) defines 'vacant lands ' to mean "land which is capable, of being use for purposes Of agriculture, but includes land deemed to be agricultural land under this Act". The Andhra Act was amended by the Andhra Act No. 1151 of 1976 and a new section 2(p)(A)(ii) was introduced in 1976. Section 4 provided that if the extent of the holding of a person is in excess or to exceed two acres, he shall be liable to surrender the land held in excess. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of the Act was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Andhra State Legislature had no competence to enact the impugned Act; (ii) the definition of "vacants" in section 2 (n) of the Central Acts was not ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the State, and (iii) the entire Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1976 was ultra vires. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of 'vacants ' in section 3(f) is materially in the same terms as the definition in the Andhra Land Reforms Acts. Section 7 sub section (2) of that Act defines " Vacant land". Sub section (3) provides that if a person or family unit holds land in excess, of the limit specified in column (1) of Schedule I, he would be liable for surrender to the State Government. The entire Andhra State Act is ultra vires the State legislature. [1155D E] 2. The expression "vacancy land" in Section 2 (o) (A)(i) of Central Acts is not defined in the Act. The word "land" is a well known concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified as an urban land under section 2. [1105E F] 3. The term "vacation land" is used in two different senses, namely, (a) the expression "land holder" means the owner of a land which has been used for purpose of agricultural and agriculture; (b) any land within the meaning of the definition clause in the Central Land Act, but until it is so notified it would not be an urban area and the Andhra pradesh Act would apply to land situate in such area. [1055F G] 4. The State Legislature would cease to have competence to legislate with respect to ceiling on land situated in such areas even though it is not an urban township at all. [1256C D] 5. The Central Act imposes a ceiling on holding of land in urban agglomerations other than agricultural land which, as defined in section (1)(A) of .has the meaning assigned to one standard holding and so also in the case of a family unit with not more than five members, the ceiling area is the same, but if the family unit consists of more or less than five persons, the maximum permissible limit will be fixed for each individual unit. [1355E F; 1356A] 6. The provisions of section 4 are in pari materia with the definition contained in section 5 of the . [1357F G; 1358G H] 7.

The appellant company was ordered to be wound up by the Company and the workmen were directed to report for duty. The company terminated the services of the workmen on the ground that they had not been given any notice or opportunity of being heard before terminating their services. On appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the discharge of the workman was justified but it set aside the order of dismissal and ordered reinstatement with full back wages. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Industrial Tribunal did not act as a court of appeal and substitute its own judgment for that of the management. It had considered the justification for absence without leave and found that the company had decided to terminate the services by giving notice to the workmen. [677 E] The question whether the discharge and/or suspension of the employees was justified or not depended upon the circumstances of each case. In the present case, the Tribunal found that there was no consideration for the condition imposed and the company could change its mind and ignore the condition. It did not consider the effect of the condition on the part of the appellant in terminating the services. [678 F G] The Industrial Tribu nal had considered all the circumstances and came to a conclusion that the respondent workmen failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence, and that was the reason why they were not taken back. [679 D E] In the instant case, though the Tribunal had found that it had decided that the appellant company had given notice to show cause against the dismissal of the respondent, the Industrial Tribunal found in favour of the company on the basis of its finding that the workmen themselves tried to coerce the Company by theirlow down ' tactics and that the Company was not justified in refusing leave. [680 E F] The fact that the workers were suspended during the lock out did not detract from the conclusion reached by the Industrial Tribun al that the charge sheet on which Chattoraj was suspended had not actually been proved. The Tribunal found, therefore, that the charges against the appellant were proved and the Industrial Court should have interfered with the decision of the Company unless it found that its decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. [681 E F; 681 A B] The Labour Appellate Tribu ties did not give any finding on the question whether there was a violation of the provisions of the Standing Order in as much as the respondent had failed to adduce satisfactory evidence to prove his case and the Tribunal was, therefore in error in holding that the order terminating the appellant 's services was justified.

The respondent University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 recommended the names of Dr. G.S. Nathawat for the said post. The appellant Dr. Urea Kant was selected and appointed as Professor in the department of Bot any year. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by a common judgment dated March 6, 1991. The Division Bench held that the purpose of preparation of the reserve list was that if the person selected at No. 1 did not join then he would be appointed against a future vacancy. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment of Dr UreaKNK was made in order to curtail the ad hoc appointments and also because the regular selections take place after the post had been filled up on the recommendations of the Selection Committee. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a clear error in restricting the scope of reserve list only against the post for which the selec tion was made and which according to the High court could only be available to the incumbent in the reserve category if the persons selected at the said list did not joining such post. Such interpretation is not borne out from any of the provisions of Section 3(1) of the Act of 1974. [426C D] 1.2 The Selection Commit tee in the present case was constituted for the selection of Professor, in Botsany and such Selection Committee had approved and recommended the name of Dr, Urea KNKKN KNkwat on 20th June, 1989. The Syndicate in its Resolution dated 10th July, 1978 had resolved that the reserve lists be prepared by the Selection Commis sioner for selection of a Professor in a University, there fore, it was held that once a person selected by the selection committee has joined that post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve select list is of no avail and becomes extinct. There was no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve List alive for a long period of one year as no person selected for the posts can at all be expected not to join for such a long time of one y year. If we examine the matter from another angle, it would be clear that according to University such a procedure is in vogue in all the universities of Rajasthan that a reserve list is used for the appointment on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the reserved list and numerous appointments had been made in the last decade from the reserve panel. The university has also submitted that if it is held to be correct, it will create chaotic situation in the University as all appoint ment so far made from the Reserve List will become assail able.

The petitioners challenged the validity of certain sections of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, on the ground that they had been discriminated against by the provisions of section 9 of the Act in as much as they had applied for permission to change their existing user of their lands by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose. The petitioners contended that the provisions Of sections 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 of the said Act were ultra vires the Constitution of India. The respondents contended that they applied for sanction under section 10 of the aforesaid Act in respect of their land as reserved for industrial purposes and that the permission was not obtained by them within the meaning of section 19(1) of the . The petitioners also contended that section 9 Of the Act did not apply to the area which was not a notified area. Held, that the petitioners had no right to challenge the validity or the notification issued under section 9. The provisions of sections 9 and 10 of Bombay Town planning Act, 1955, were in terms applicable to the land in question and they had no application to the areas which were notified for public purpose. Section 11(3) of Bombay Act did apply only to such areas as were notified by the Municipal Corporation and not to those areas which had been developed and augmented by the designation of their original authority. The power given to the local authority under section 13 of that Act was unguided, arbitrary and uncontrolled and as such it violated the fundamental rights of the petitioners under articles 14, 19(i)(f) and (g). The provisions Of section 9 were not unreasonable and were therefore violative of article 14. The object of the impugned notification was to provide for the establishment of a town planning scheme in respect to the whole or any part of land which was likely to be used for building purposes or had already been built upon. The provision of sections 4 to 16 of the City Town Planning Regulation, 1954 was not unreasonable as it did not provide for any regulation of the right of owners of land to erect or proceed with any building or remove, pull down, alter, make additions or any substantial repair to any building, or change the use of any land or building unless he had obtained the necessary permission from the local authori ty. The scheme was a simple one and was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local autho rity. The preparation of a development plan for Greater Bombay was an immense task and the authorities proceeded with it in a manner to which no exception could be taken. The Act did provide for a maximum period of ten years for the acquisition of any building designated for public purposes under section 7 of the , at least for 14 years and thereafter indefinitely. There was nothing in the Act to limit the maximum period for the purpose of making an application for permission. The procedure prescribed by section 13(3)(a) was not one which could be said to be a reasonable restriction on the right to hold property under article 19(l)(f). The preparation or the final development plan was not anything which was within the scope of the restrictions imposed and therefore the provisions regarding the levy of contribution towards cost of the scheme and all other matters relating to the working of the Scheme were unauthorised.

The appellant was a Part B State and had always been so in the territory of India. In 1947, the State of Kutch merged with the Dominion of India and by article 1 of the Agreement of Merger, the Maharao of Kutch became part of the State. The State of Saurashtra merged with that Dominion on August 2, 1948. On May 4, 1948, the Government of Bombay issued a notification under section 290A of the Government Of India Act, 1935, appointing two persons as the Part B States to be the territories which, at the date of the passing of this Act, were included in the State List. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the Constitution and that the notification was invalid. Held, that the decision of the Tribunal was correct and must be affirmed. The dispute related to the boundary between the two States and the question whether the territory in this State belonged to the Kutch State or not was a matter which could be decided by arbitration under article 1 read with the First Schedule to the Constitution. The award did not purport to nor did it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory. The Government of India had exercised effective administrative control over Sind and the dispute related only to the location of the boundary line, and the operative part of it declared the alignment of the boundaries between the State and Pakistan. The agreement between the parties was reached purely as an executive act and no legislative sanction was obtained by the Government for its implementation. The Union of India could not treat it as part of Indian territory and therefore the notification issued by the Bombay Government under section 2(2) of the Act was invalid, because, in giving effect to the award of the tribunal, cession of India into a Part C State was involved. The decision to implement the award was not binding on the Government but was binding on it. The question whether in implementing the award the executive Government is ceding territory of the Union or not did not arise for consideration. The jurisdiction of the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution was limited to the enforcement of fundamental rights and could only be exercised if the cession of what was now part of India was Indian territory, and not in respect of India, as the dispute was one between the Dominion and the Government. The reference to the Tribunal did not amount to a declaration of sovereignty of India by the State but merely governed the matter. The claim made by the claimants that in implementing an award of International Tribunal an area was part of Pakistan was not correct. The Award did not refer to any dispute as to the existence of the territory and it was not necessary for the Tribunal to decide whether the dispute fell within the territories of India or not. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to determine the boundaries of the area in question, because the dispute relating to the boundaries was a part of British India and was governed by the provisions of the , which it was claimed that the territory was part and parcel of Pakistan.

The mortgagor 's interest in the mortgaged property was sold by the mortgagor to the auction purchaser on April 7, 1925. The mortgagor 'died a mortgage on June 14, 1922 and after his death the mortgagee became entitled to transfer encumber or sell the whole property including the interest of principal or interest thereafter. On October 2, 1927, the mortgagor purchased from the mortgagor 'the mortgaged property and after the date on which the mortgage amount was payable, sold it in favour of the auction purchasers who were the heirs of the mortgagor and certain alienees of the mortgaged properties. The mortgagee 's right to redeem the mortgaged land was extinguished by the sale of the mortgage property. On August 16, 1934, the appellant obtained assignment of his interest in a portion of the mort gage and assigned his interest therein. The mortgagees then sold the remaining portion of their interest in favour on April 14, 1937. The mortgagors filed a suit for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of their interests in the mortagage property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the mortgage was partly simple and partly usufructuary and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon it, the mortgagee 'different portions were in the covenants with the mortgagor. On appeal the High Court held that the mortgagor had lost his interest by reason of the sale deed dated June 14. 1922, and that the suit to enforce the mortgage on August 27, 1922 was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that: (1) The mortgagee had in her possession a part of the property which included within the said Tauzi No. by virtue of section 20 of the Limitation Act; (2) The suit to enforcement the mortgage dated August 27 was barred under the law of limitation as the mortgagor could not sell the mortgagedeed at the date of the suit without obtaining a fresh cause of action for the suit, and (3) the suit was barred because the mortgagee had lost all his interest. HELD : (1)(a) The right conferred by section 68 is again not a right to enforce a mortgage but a right of defence to sue for the mortgage money on the personal covenant or to claim compensation when the mortgagee is deprived of his security. [642 B] (b) The mortgagor had parted with his interest during the period of limitation in satisfaction of the debt and was not entitled to sue any time beyond the date fixed by him for payment of the amount due under the mortgage. The right to sue where the mortgagee was deprived of the whole or part of his property, was wholly or partially destroyed or the security was rendered insufficient within the meaning of section 66(1)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act. [643 C] (c) The appellant had not relied upon any other part payment in respect of the first mortgage before the mortgagor was transferred to the mortgagee and the endorsement regarding payment was made on the mortgage deed recording such payment, and on that date the period for limitation for a suit to recover the mortgage debt was governed by article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act. The appellant 's claim to enforce payment of money under section 68 of the Act was barred as he had not filed any fresh cause for action for enforcing it. [641 D F] (2)(a). The right granted by section 69 is again subject to the limitation prescribed by article 136 of the Constitution. Similarly, the right to file a suit in four different classes of cases and no others. These classes are (a) where the mortgagor binds himself to repay the mortgagemoney; (b), where, by any cause other than the wrongful act or default of the mortgagee or mortgagee, the mortgaged is wholly or partly destroyed or, the security is rendered insufficient; (c). Where the mortgagee in possession of the land is deprived by the wrongful acts or default or by the mortgagee, such loss is one for compensation and the period during which the suit is to be instituted has to be excluded. [651 D E] (3)(a), The right under section 69 of the transfer of property was again not an interest to enforce it but a claim for compensation when it was deprived by a wrongful act of the owner or mortgagee. [661 F G] (4) In the present case, the mortgage deeds were placed in the possession of four tenants who had settled the land and were paying rent to them. The mortgages were not extinguished under section 20.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Vadig and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. The appellants contended that even if a nominal charges were realised from the employee that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, the point has now become more or less academic. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act 1958 is a statute which authorises the levy of passenger tax. This Act has been amended several times right from the year 1960 to 1975. Before analysing the relevant provisions of the said Act it may be necessary to extract the Preamble to the Act. Section 2(7) defines 'stage carriage ' thus: "stage carriages" means a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which carries passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey and includes such a carriage or other omnibus when used as a contract carriage within the meaning of the . Rule 2(i) of the Bombay Motor Vehicle Rules, 1940 framed under the Bombay Act is a statutory definition. [361 E F] 2. The word 'public ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. Thus qua public the employees form a separate class and cannot be said to be public as contemplated by rule 2(1). [361 H] 3. The words 'public servants ' have got a very wide connotation and mean a carriage, to which no member of Parliament can have Free access on the payment of usual charges, and it cannot by no process of logic or stretch Of imagination be said that the transport vehicle provided to the employees by the appellant could be a public servant in any sense of the term. [362 A B] 4. The definition of 'stages carriage ' as given in section 2(6) of Bombay Motor vehicles (Taxation, on Passengers), Act, 1958, includes that the Transport concerned must carry passengers by road and (2) that such passengers must be carried in stage carriages. It is true that the term 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that however does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the statute it cannot be deemed as a necessary for the purpose of charging section 3, which is, the charging Section of the , which is a charging section.

The appellants, who had objected to the grant of a licence for a "no objection certificate" filed by them under Rule 102 of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1952, challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that there was a mosque, a public cinema licence and a temple in the vicinity or the place where the cinema house is to be constructed. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there were two stages through which an application for a license had to be processed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that if before granting a licence, the licensing authority had satisfied himself that there existed no impediment to the granting of such a licence and was therefore perfectly justified in granting the same, and that the order granting a license was not a fit case for interference by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right to object is at the initial stage when a no objection certificate is applied for by the intending applicant for such a certificate. But there is nothing in the Act or the rules which requires advertisement of such an application inviting objections and consideration of the objections before grant of licence. [799C D] 2. Rule 102 empowers the licensing author ity to grant a cinema licence on being satisfied that all the relevant rules have been complied with and the licence may be granted on such terms and conditions and subject to such restrictions as the licensing Authority may determine. The power to grant licence is not absolute but is discretionary. [899E F] 3. Rule 103 confers power on the licensing authorities to refuse a cinema license if the cinema is likely to cause obstruction, inconvenience, annoyance, risk or damage to residents, or passers by in the proximity of the cinema. Rule 105 provides that no objection Certificate shall be granted unless it is accompanied by an affidavit stating that any objection certificate has been obtained and that such objection certificate will not be valid for a period of two years from the date of issue in the case of permanent cinemas. [800G H] 4. The appellant did not file any objection at that stage "no objections" certificate was granted to him. He filed an application under Rule 103 which was rejected by the licensing autho rity on the grounds that there is a mosque and a place of entertainment. The Rules envisage issuance of a license for a permanent cinema and quasi permanent cinema as well as a touring cinema. The licence was not renewed. The licensing authority, therefore, granted a licence to the appellant. [900D E] 5. Rule 104 confers power upon the licensing au thority to grant such a license on being satis fied in the prescribed manner. If after taking into consideration the objections a noobjection certificate is granted, there ends the matter subject, of course, to any properly constituted legal proceedings conceivably a writ petition under Article 226. But sub section (3) of Section 5 provides that an application may be made before the expiry of the period for receipt of a notice of hearing and if the authority has reason to refuse such application or to grant the same it shall record its reasons in writing. If the duty to give notice and hear objections is not mandatory, the actual order passed on a matter must be shown to have injuriously affected the interest of the party which was given no notice of the matter. [901E F; 801A B] 6. The appeal is allowed.

The respondent executed a contract in respect of the mining lease. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent for the transfer of the lease to the respondent. The respondent wrote to the appellant that the lease was concluded on September 2, 1957 and that the appellant had not agreed to purchase the mining leases. The lease deed provided that the lessee would have a possessory right before execution of a conveyance of the mine. The respondents filed an appeal against the decree. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) the respondent had failed to establish the new case; (2) the contract was concluded by an oral application for shares in a mining lease, and (3) the appellant was at liberty to revoke the offer at any tune before its acceptance by the respondent, and that as the Government had not made the offer, the appellant could not get a possessory rights before execution. HELD: The plaint was not an acceptance of the offer but was intended to be an acceptance. [583 D] (a) The letter dated September 2. 1957 written by the appellant to the respondents clearly stated that the contract in question was concluded and that in breach of the contract the respondent failed to apply for and obtain the necessary consent of the Central Government. [584 E F] (b) The plea that the respondent made a concluded contract on September, 2,1957 was not accepted by the High Court. The letter written by appellant dated September,2, 1957, did not amount to an acceptance and the appellant 's offer was not supported by any consideration. The pleadings and issues raised the question whether a con tract was made on September. 2, in a suit for specific performance should be decided first.
