[585 F G] (c) The respondent had not established the new Case. In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded. The offer as well as acceptance should Pr=& the institution of the suit and the approval of the central government to the assignment of the ' mining lease could not be specifically performed and on this ground the High court dismissed the appellant suit. [585 H] (d) The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not a suit under section 46 of the Contract Act for specific performa tion. The plea of the respondent that he had agreed to assign the mining leasehold rights under a mining leases was not taken by him before the filing of the Suit.

The appellants were office bearers of a company. A complaint was filed against them under section 3(1) of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1955 alleging that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued process. The appellants challenged the validity of the investigation in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 3 (1) provides for taking under cultivation any waste or arable land whether appurtenant to a building or not for growing thereon of food crops generally or of specified food crops and section 3 is a specific mandate. HELD : The power conferred on the Government under section 4(2) of Act cannot be challenged as invalid. [655 F] Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , followed. Ch.Tika Ramji and Ors. v The State, ; , referred to. In Ch.tika Ramji 's case the Bihar Act was a pre Constitution Act and it could have continued to be in force only till it was altered, repealed o.r amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [677 G] Chota Ramji & ors. vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Ors., ; referred to, distinguished. Chota Ram & Ors., vs The Sate of U P. and Ors, , referred. Chhika Ramji, and Ors,. vs The Stale General of Punjab, ; referred. In the instant case the Parliament intended to bring under control the cultivation and sale of food crop. In view of these provisions it was open to the police to investigate the same. [678 F] The power given by section 3 of the Act cannot he challenged as valid because all this was in exercise of the concurrent powers of legislation under Entry 33 of List III. [676 G H] Chichi Ramji and ors. v State of Bihar, ; and Chika Ramji vs State, A.I.R. , referred, distinguished and applied. Chita Ramji & Anr. vs the State of UP, ; at page 432; referred to and distinguished. The Bihar Act is a pre constitution Act and the Parliament had declared by law that it was expedient in public interest that it should exercise control over foodstuffs. That being so it was not necessary for the police under section 7 of the , to have taken up the investigation of that complaint. [673 A B] Chite Ramji & Others vs The state of U .P., and Chita Ram & Anr., vs State Of U.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order was issued by the State Government granting concessions to entrepreneurs for starting new industries in Mysore State. The Government of the State issued another order which recited that the reasons for making the said order were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th June, 1969 when the order dated 12th January 1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given under the said orders. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and granted relief on the basis set out earlier. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the concession granted under the order of 30th May, 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory estoppel is not applicable to the instant case because the Government wants to resile from a promise or an assurance given by it on the ground that undue advantage is being taken or misuse was being made of the concession granting the Court may permit the Government to do so but before allowing the Government, would have to be satisfied that allegations by the government about misuse being made or undue advantage being taken. [950C D] 2. The fact that the order passed by the High Courts on 12th February, 1977 did not specify the power under which it was issued will make no difference because such a power is clearly there in Section 8A and where the source of power underwhich it is issued is not stated in an order but can be found on examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. The second submission of the learned counsel for the appellants must also fail. [951D E] 3. In order to test the validity of the order, one has to see the substance of the Concession granted under Order 30, Rule 3 of the said Rules. It is clear that in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of sales Tax or reduction in the sales tax liability to the extent stated in the order. In view of this, there is no substance whatever in the contention that the State Govern ment had no authority to provide for the grant of refund. [961F G] Union of India vs M/s Indo Afghan Agencies Limited, ; , referred to.

The appellants were charged with offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. for causing the death of one of the persons belonging to the group of the accused. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 and A 3 but convicted A 2 under Sections 148 and 307 read with section 149 I P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 1 to A 3. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 148 and on applying 149 I .P. C. cannot be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I. P. C., and they were acquitted by the High court. [8B] 2.1 In so far as the presence and partic ipation of the assailants in the attack on the deceased is concerned, it is not the prosecution case that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime. The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A 1, A 2 and A3 were armed with spears, A 4, A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 was armed with sticks and knives and they had rioting between the two factions. There was no dispute that A 3 were unidentified person who were implicated in the occurrence. The High Court rightly held that it would be safe to accept the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2 to the extent it is corroborated by the evidence 6 of the eye witnesses and the number and nature of injuries, which are caused by the accused persons. [88C D] 2:2 In so much as the appellants formed an unlawful com mission with common intention with common object of murdering the de ceased, the prosecution has not established that apart, from the 7 accused there were other unknown persons who had been involved in crime. There is no question or dispute that apart the seven appellants could be convicted under Sections 302 read along with 34 I.p.C.[88D] 2 :3 The High court was clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam, which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965 the assessee sold the house to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 was completed on 30th December 1966. In the course of proceedings under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1922, the assessee claimed that the value of Rs,. 16, 500 should be included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold by him at the same price at which it was purchased and no capital gain accrued or arose to him as a result of the transaction. The Income tax officer issued a notice under section 147 of the Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for its assessment year 1967 67 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within thirty days of the service of the notice. The assessee submitted a return on 4th April 1968, but it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected by the assessee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. 48 The assessee 's appeal against this order was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. In further appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (1) the fair market value of the property as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assesses in respect Of the transfer; (2) the assessee had an honest and bonafide transaction where the consideration for the transfer had been correctly disclosed or declared by him, but was intended to deal only with cases where the real consideration received by the asses see was not disclosed and the consideration declared in respect thereof was shown at a lesser figure than that actually received by him; (3) the object and purpose of section 52(2) as on date of the Transfer of Property Act before the amendment, namely, reaching those cases where there is no under statement of consideration in respect to the transfer, was not to strike out or ignore the amount of consideration shown by the respondent assessee only if the following two conditions are satisfied: (1 ) the transferee is a person directly or indirectly connected with the assessee and (2), the Income Tax officer has reason to believe that the transferor was effected with the objects of avoidance of his liabilities under section45. (3)(a) The proviso to this sub section provides that where an assessee transfers a capital asset and in respect, of the transferred property, the value thereof is reduced by the amount or value declared by such assessee, but the assessee has actually received more than what is declared by it, he shall be taxed on capital gains on that basis. (b) The assessee has to pay tax on capital gain which have not accrued or arisen to him. (c) The consideration for transfer is shown at the lesser figure as the value actually received or disclosed by the transferor and it is also specified in sub section (2).

The appellant was charged with offences under section 16(1)(a)(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the appellant had gone to "a shop to make purchases" without giving either the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. He was found in possession of the tin plate and a sample of Til seeds was sent for analysis. He admitted that he had purchased the til seeds from the shop. The trial court convicted him under section 7(1) (a)(i) of that Act and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court acquitted him but convicted him on the ground that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human consumption. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the whole purpose of the act was to preventing adulteration, sale or storage or distribution of certain types of food '; and (ii) the use of the article sold was not entirely irrelevant. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what was stored or sold was "fruit" at all. [329 B] In the instant case, the appellant was not present at the time when the seeds were sold by him to the Food Inspector. He did not even remember who made the cash memo when he sold these Til seeds. Therefore, the conviction of the accused must be set aside. [330 C D] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , applied. The fact that the sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis does not affect the prosecution case. It is more likely that the article of adultered food was either manufactured for sale or stored in a shop. Therefore the appellant must get the benefit of doubt. [328 D] In view of the evidence led by the prosecution, it could be said that the entire object of section 7 was to protect "false" meant only for human use and not for human being. [332 E F] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Admin. ; , referred to. The appellant must got the benefit under section 10(7) of Act.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966. He filed a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. The suit was decreed in his favour on 30.9.1969. On appeal, the Divisional Commissioner confirmed the decree holding that the dismissal was bad and he had continued to remain in service and that the appellant continued to serve. He continued to hold the post till the decision of the State Government on his appeal and beyond three years from the date of the order. The High Court dismissed the second appeal filed by the respondent. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the order dated 30.10.1969 was not passed in accordance with Article 58 of the First Schedule to the . Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the dates of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is passed. [54F] 1.2 In all these three cases after the appellate authority has disposed of the appeal the operative order is the order in accordance therewith. [55G] 1:3. The cause for action first arises when the remedies available to the public servant under the relevant service rules as to re instate are disposed of. The question whether it should be disposal of one appeal or the entire hierarchy of reliefs as may have been provided, is a condition precedent to maintaining of claims under the . [55H] 1 :4. In all such cases only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of actions shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from the order passed in revision, it is the right to sue shall first accrued. submission of just a memorial or representation to the Head of the establishment shall not be taken into consideration in the matter of fixing limitation. [58H] 2:1. The period of one year for making of the application and power of condonation of delay of a total period of six month has been vested under section 20 of the .

The appellant, who was the owner of an immovable property consisting of himself and his father, instituted a suit for partition in forma pauperis in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittoor. The trial court rejected the contention that the alienations made by his father as well as sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in all the said properties was not affected by them. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether an appellate decree passed by the High court affirmed the decision is one of affirmance or not depends on the nature of the subject matter in controversy in the suit which is intended to be brought to this court under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution. If the appeal court makes a variation in the decision, it is not a decree of affirmence and this is not affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is made in favour of the intending appellant and not against him. [470 E F] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the appellate decree must be considered as a whole in relation to the decision in the case of a matter in dispute in the final hearing of the suit, so far as it related to the question of the validity of the claim for interest before the trial Court. [471 G] (iii) The finding of the High Courts on the question as to whether the appellate court had jurisdiction to pass a variation decree was not a pure question of affirmation and could be raised in an appeal under article 136. [472 C D] Chitturi Subba Rao vs Vela Mankanni Rao, A.I.R. (1955) Mad. 953, approved. (iv) The decision of this Court in the present case was not one of affirmation but a finding of fact and could not be challenged on the ground that it was not supported by any evidence or that the HighCourt had acted improperly or wrongly in passing the decree. [473 D] (v) If the appellate judgment is wholly confirmed, the intending appellants would not be entitled to come to this Supreme Court as a matter of right unless there is a substantial question of law which has been referred to it by the trial judge. The appeal must be allowed and the order passed by High Court must be set aside.

The provisions of section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, read with the proviso to section 115 of the Code of civil Procedure, are in pari materia with those of the original section 115. The High Court has exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in cases arising out of original suits of a value less than Rs. 20,000/ and in other cases the revisional jurisdiction was concurrently shared between the High Court and the District Court. The provisions of sections 96 to 112 of the Civil Procedure Code read with section 115 are in identical terms. Section 25, in its application to Uttar Pradesh, retrospectively provides that any amendment made or provision inserted in the Code by a State Legislature before the commencement of the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1972, if pending immediately before 1st August, 1978, would continue to be governed by section 115 as it stood before that date. The proviso thereto also provides that in respect of cases arising from original suits or other proceedings of any valuation decided by a District Court, the High Courts alone shall be competent to make an order under this section. Section 7 of the Act merely embodies the general principle against resort to remedies outside the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act. The language of the successive amendments made in the bifurcation of revisional jurisdiction is clear and unambiguous. The legislative intention behind the amendment was to relieve the High court of the burden of exercising revisional power in respect whereof a District Judge or Additional District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes would be competent under section 25, and no question could have arisen of invoking the revisional power of the High Commissioner under section 5, Civil Procedure. All the indications point to the conclusion that a case falling within the 42 Provincial Small Causes Courts Act was never intended to be subject to the remedies provided by the Code, and therefore, the expression "case arising out from such suit" occurring in section 115 does not cover orders passed in revision. The word "case" is used in the wider sense of the words "case decided by the District Judge" and not in the narrower sense in the latter sense. [38C D] Har Prasad Singh & Ors. vs Ram Swarup & Ors., ; , followed. In the instant case, the suit itself had been disposed of by a Single Judge, who was not a court constituted under the Act. It was not possible to proceed outside the Act to avail of a superior remedy provided by another statute. The expression " case arising out Of an original suit" in section 5 of the Provincial Civil Courts Act, is not confined to orders passed before the coming into force of the Amending Act. [39D E] In the present case, it was not vested with revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, Civil Code, because, the trial court had no jurisdiction to entertain the revision petition against a revisional order passed by the district Court arising out the suit of the value of Rs.20,000 and above, and exclusive jurisdiction thereunder. [40E] The expression 'case arising from such original suits ' occurring in Section 115 does refer to orders made in revision under the foregoing provisions of this Act by a court of Small Cause Court.

The respondent, a private limited company, was incorporated in the State of Rajasthan under the . The State Government issued a notification under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, declaring its intention to acquire certain lands belonging to them. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi were not maintainable as the ad interim exparte prohibitory order secured by them had been issued by the State Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under section 51(1 ) of the Act arose within the State 's State of Jaipur i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the State. [602C] 2. The notification dated February 8, 1984 issued by State Government under section 53(1), or the Act, on the basis of which the notification was issued became effective the moment it was published in the official Gazette as thereupon the notified land became vested in the state Government free from all encumbrances. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer under section 54(2) for the grant of an appropriate writ, direction or order under article 32 of the Constitu tion for quashing the notification issued by it under section 50(1). If the respondents felt aggrieved by the acquisition, they could challenge the validity or the issue of the notification. [063D E] 3. The expression ' cause of any territorial jurisdiction ' is a bundle of facts which taken with the law applicable to them gives the plaintiff a right to relief against the defendant. The mere service of the notice under section52(2), on the respondents at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road, Calcutta i. e., within the geographical limits of the state of West Bengal could not give rise to a cause of ' action within that territory unless the service is an integral part of the cause of the action. The whole cause of actions culminating in acquisition of land under s.52(1 )(a) on the at their Registered office at18 B , brabourna Road, and within the jurisdiction of State of WestBengal could not given rise to the cause 'of action within the territory unless tho service of such notice was an integral parts of the ' cause '. The High Court had no jurisdiction to issue a rule n0oisi on the petition under article226 of the Consti tution or to make the ad interlocutory prohibitory order restraining the appellants from taking any steps to take possession of the acquired land acquired. [507E F] 4. The word 'cause of action ' is tersely defined in Mulla 's Code of Civil Procedure: "The cause of a suit wholly or in part arises". It is a composite form of defence and the cause is wide and the Judges must ever be vigilant to protect the citizen against arbitrary executive action. [ 607F G] 5. The power of the High Courts under article 227 of the constitution is not limited by the clemency of self ordained restraint. There has to be in the larger public interest an clement of self order.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in dispute on the ground that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises by a co operative society and that the building was not covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had failed to prove that the spent Rs. 1000 towards repairs of the building, and that he had failed in the payment of rent despite notice dated 24th March 1977. On appeal, the Additional District Judge affirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding about arrears of rent. The High Court confirmed the findings. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the building in question had been constructed by a cooperative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the view taken by the Judge that the buildings were not ten years old on the date of suit and, consequently, the new rent Act had no application to the building; and (ii) the appellant had failed before the trial Court to prove the arrears of the rent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent landlord was in the witness box payment by cheque dated August 16, 1976 but when the plaintiff was in his witness box he was in a witness box to payment and it has not been established as to for which period the payment by cheques was made. [340D] 2.1 In the instant case, admittedly a sum of Rs.1000 had been paid by the appellant to the landlord on 15th September 1976. But when the respondent was in witness box the date on which the assessment of house tax and water tax came into effect is not mentioned in the proviso to sub section (4) of section 20 of the Act. [334E] 2(a) The High Courts have found that the payment through cheque dated 16th March, 1978 was a sum paid by way of loan or advance from the State Government or Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a co cooperative society or the Uttar Pradesh Multipurpose Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. and the period of repayment of such loan or advances exceeds the said period or ten years then the reference in this sub section to the period prior to April 7, 1976 comes into effect. [341B C] (b) The respondent had purchased the building on June 30, 1971 from the appellant and, thereafter, he was informed that the house should be fifteen years old to attract the provisions of the new Act. He also filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the demand for payment of Rs 3,158.30 as arrears of land and damages for use and occupation of the said premises. The learned Single Judge of the High court held that the Building in question was not ten year old on that date of the suit and therefore the new landlord had no jurisdiction to make the right or remedy claimed by him against his liability for eviction on that ground. [343F G] 2.(c) The appellant had also failed before this Court to establish that the amount of Rs, 1000 was due from him towards rent as directed by the High Courts. [344G H] 2 (d) The building in dispute had been completed and the building should be deemed to have been completed on the dates of assessment which was 1st October 1971. The appellant 's claim for adjustment of arrears of rents and damages was not accepted by the trial Judge. The appellate court, however, held that it was not necessary to examine the submission in any detail or to express any concluded opinion about it for disposal of the appeal. [345H 346A] 3(a). The High court did not agree with the finding of the Additional Distt. Judge that he was not entitled to make any payment of the arrears and remanded the case to the trial judge for redetermining the amount by cheque. The Trial Court, however. rejected the defence of the respondent that the premises were constructed in 1968 and that it would be deemed that the landlord was entitled to get the benefit of section 39 of the old Rent Act, and directed the appellant 'to deposit the arrears within a specified time. [346B C; 347C D] (c) In the present case, the building had become more than ten years from the date when the assessment was made and the trial has not concluded. The Additional District judge found that it had been in fact completed ten years.

The appellant filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The respondents contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that therefore the arbitration clause in the agreement did not apply. Held, that the appellant was entitled to the decree. The agreement dated February 6, 1948, was executed by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor and in consequence there was a valid reference to arbitration. The award was not a certified copy of the order under section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, but was an original instrument. The appellant had been authorised to execute the agreement on behalf of the Governor, and in pursuance thereof he paid the requisite stamp duty under section 35 of the Stamp Act and had it validated. The High Court was right in holding that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon was a nullity and that no decree could be passed thereon. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated by notification in the Official Gazette, but there is nothing in section 175 itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person, and when that is established the requirements of the section must be held to be satisfied. The fact that the arbitrator had been authorized by the Government acting through his Secretary to execute a agreement for reference to an arbitration does not preclude authorisation from being conferred as it was not required by section 175 (3). The appellant could not therefore rely on a notification dated February, 6,1948, issued by the Govern ment of India. The Collector of Tripura vs Lall, A.I.R. , referred to. Held further that the objection raised by the appellant that the instrument actually before the court was not an original document and that under section 176(3), there could be validation only of the original, when it was unstamped or insufficiently stamped, that is, the original and not a copy of it. The Government had failed to produce the same. Held also, that as the copy was un stamped, no decree can be passed on the original document which was unreturned and the appellant could have been validly substituted in place of the respondent.

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department. On various dates in the State of Punjab, he placed orders for purchase of sign boards and import lincences. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of these orders. In the year 1980 some complaints were received against the respondent pertaining to the purchase of the sign boards. Vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau. The respondent filed a complaint before the Special Judge, Punjab, who quashed the First Information Report on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of such sign boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume II, and consequently was liable to be quashed. The State filed an appeal against the order of the Special judge, which was allowed by the High Court on the view that the said rule placed an embargo on prosecution as a condition precedent for launching criminal proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that since the respondent had retired as long as on December 13, 1979, he could not be prosecuted after his retire ment even though guilty of committing a grave misconduct or negligence during the period of his service, after the lapse of four year period, and that the prosecution was barred by limitation under article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly quashed the first information report as against Kailash Nath, respondent in criminal appeal No. 422 of 1988. [922B] 1.2 In view of the fact that Rule 2(a) of the Rules dealing with "Ordinary Pension" is a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the rule has been framed, it has to he interpreted by taking recourse to the well settled rule of reading down a provision so as to bring it within the framework of its source of power without, of course, frustrating the purpose for which such provision was made. [ 922C D] 1:3 The object of the Act is to provide for the compulsory retirement of Government servants on the completion of four or years of service after the expiry thereof and the right of ordering recovery from a pension of the whole or part of any pecuniary loss caused to government if, in a departmental or judicial proceeding, the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct. [936F G] 1 :4 The High Courts have taken the view in the present case that the rule having been enacted for the purpose of bringing within the purview of Article 309 and the purpose behind it was not to place an embargo upon prosecution.

The respondent company was a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The authorised capital of the company was Rs. 100/ each ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs.100/ each were held by the directors including Ramayamma. On April 1, 1946, the respondent company took over the business conducted by Nageswara Rao Panthulu for Rs. 5,50,0001 paid in the form of 2,500 ordinary shares. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to vote at the meeting of the Company each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings for the three years ending March 31, 1948, the Income tax Officer found that for the 3 years ending June 31, 1949, the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and 61 per cent as against the ordinary shares which was considerably less than sixty per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the income tax Officer but the Tribunal held that the undistributed portion of the assessable income of the respondent was not liable to be distributed as dividend within the meaning of section 23A and reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the company in respect thereof. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent Company was one in which the public were substantially interested and there was no person who could hold twenty five per cent or more of the ordinary share issued by the respondent. [17 E] (ii) The expression "twenty five per centum of the voting power" would mean not twenty five percent of the total voting power but power exercisable in respect of shares other than shares entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. [18 G] (iii) The words "thirty five per curium of the capital of such subsidiary company" in section 23(1) are wide enough to include directors from the remaining members of the 16 company. If a director does not belong to the controlling group, he will be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the third proviso and the Explanation to section 23 (A) even though such director was directly entrusted with the management of the affairs of the companies.

The appellants were the sole selling agents of the respondent Mills. The goods were delivered to them by the respondent on behalf of another person, who was a registered firm and carried on business in Bombay. In pursuance of all this delivery was made to Dharsi Moolji. The respondent paid Dwarkadas Khetan and Company as their agent. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of sales tax on the ground that the bales remained in the physical possession of the first appellant at all material times and were not physically delivered to the second appellant. The trial court held that the delivery was not true and correct, but the High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the goods left by the appellants were delivered under the control of Dwarkadis, because, they had reached the quotaholder in the end, or rather his proper agent, and so with a del credere agent, because such a person was the agent of the seller only up to a point. The delivery was without any straining of language as the person to whom the goods were actually delivered. Dwarkadash Khetan could not be regarded as having been delivered by the first appel lant for the reason that ultra technical notions regarding the concept of possession were to be incorporated into the case, and the fact that the respondent had no direct dealing with the transaction was immaterial. Dwaraklal Bairathi vs The State of Bombay, A.I.R. (1954) S.C. 929, followed. Dwarkamal vs The Government of Madras, A I. R. (1956) S C. 835 and Dwarkadasi vs The Commissioner of Textile, A 1. R., (1957) S T.C . 834, referred to. The fact that a person is in such a relation as the agent does not necessarily mean that he was not in physical possession. It is true that the order which is to affect the business of hundreds of persons, many of whom are small petty merchants and traders, the sort of meni who would not have lawyers repeatedly at their elbow; but the fact remains that the person who pays the goods for them from out of the goods actually delivered, does so in a way inconsistent with his law.

The appellant was a Professor of a Government College. He was charged with having accepted gratification of Rs. 500/ as bribe for showing favour to a candidate whose name was not mentioned in the prospectus, practical examination for the first year B.Sc. and his name was included in the Physics practical examination. The Special Judge convicted him under section 165A of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to two years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs., 1,000/ . On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the last part of the Ninth clause as it stood before its amendment in 1964 was applicable to the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression "public servant" is not defined in section 21 of the Penal Code but has a wider connotation and if no limitation is placed on it, the words "corrupt", "illegal" and "otherwise" mentioned in section 5(1)(d) are wide enough to include every person who is remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty. [321 B] (2) The word "obtains" has wide connotation and it includes every person in the service or pay of the Government or remunerated for the purpose of any Public duty. It is not necessary that the public servant while misconducting himself should have done so in the discharge of his duty. Section 5(i)(d)(1) provides that a public servant shall be deemed to commit an offence if he is holder of an office. He cannot be said to be holding any office when he is appointed for the purposes of examining certain answer books even though that may fall within the performance or a public duty, and in which capacity alone he could fall within section 21. [320 C D] (3) The use of the word "other wise" in section 6(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, shows that the words 'corrupt ' and 'illegal ' are used in section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But it is not possible to put on clause (d) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. According to the High Courts, a reading of section 5 (1)(a) as it stands before its Amendment in 1964 shows that connection with Government was necessary either in respect of the payment of remuneration or in respect Of the performance by the Government. [322 C D; 322 A B] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration ; , referred to. (4) The words 'abusing his position as a public officer ' qualify the word 'other wise ' and do not form two clauses. If that is so, the abuse of position as public servant would be essential whether the means are corrupt or illegal or are of the nature covered by the word `corrupt or illegal ' mentioned in clause (a) of section 6. [323 C D]. Dhaneshwar Narayan Saxena vs State of Delhi ; , followed. (5) The definition of "public servants" in the Prevention Of Corruption Act is not confined to public servants but includes a person who has been remunerated with fee orcommission for the work of any office or pay or commission. Therefore, the use of word 'obtains ' on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of a receiver. [324 E F] (6) The abuse of positions as a Public servant would not amount to public servant within the meaning of section 21(1). [327 B D]. (7) The High Court was right in holding that the abuse was not one of mere academic or administrative character and that it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the accused had been guilty of any offence with which he was charged. [328 C] Dhaneswar Narain Saxena v Delhi Administration, ; , applied.

The petitioners, who were casual labour engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 and 16 years in the construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Northern Railway, challenged the validity of the orders of their absorption. The Court granted interim relief to the petitioners. In the writ petitions filed by them under Article 32 of the Constitution, the Court directed that the scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative, should be implemented. A number of documents and circulars issued by the Administration have been produced in support of their claim. The petitioners have also furnished written submissions. In addition to the directions given by this Court, they have also produced written submissions, particulars of service of each of them, which was the previous requirement. The respondents have filed a counter affidavit stating that the petitioners have put in more than 360 days of service. The affidavits have been placed before this Court to show that the Administration is requiring continuous service for purpose of eligibility, and that the casual labour in open line as well as willing project casual labour are combined for the purpose of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in. In view of the submission made by the respondents, this Court directed the petitioners to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued from time to time. The Union of India has filed a rejoinder. It is stated on behalf of the respondents that the Court had not been given any direction to treat them at par as temporary servants and that they were now entitled to all the privileges as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. In reply, it was contended that the claim of the petitioners for equal pay has been considered by this court in the Writ Petition No. 147 of 1983 (Granting relief) dated 14.12.1983 and the Senior Signal and Telecommunication Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed an affidavit stating therein that the administration is requiring continuously service for purposes of eligibility. The learned Additional Solicitor General also stated that since prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984 project casual labourers were not entitled to any privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled only to all privileges as admissible to temporary railway employees. The counsel for the respondents has stated that by the time these writ petitions were filed, the Railway Administration had not treated them as temporary ones and that their case was similar. Allowing the Writ Petitions, this court, HELD: 1.1. It cannot be said that the pensionary benefits are admissible even to temporary Railway servants and, therefore, that retiral advantage is not available to casual labour acquiring temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc. Service prior to absorption against a regular temporary/permanent post after requisite selection will however not constitute as qualifying service for pensionary benefits. [143G] 1.2.The respondents shall have a direction to consider the claims of each petitioners promptly and make appropriate orders for their regularisation. For over ten years, litigations of this type have been coming to the Court. about three years back, this is admitted by the Union of india. This Court directed a scheme for absorbing in temporary status the casual labourers with regular scales. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railways Administration and cannot be avoided. The writ petitions are disposed of with the directions indicated above without any order for costs. [144H; 144A] 1:3. It would not be necessary to create temporary posts to accommodate casual labour acquired temporary status, since there is break in such continuity, the previous service is also taken into account. [145B] 1.(a) The petitioners shall have an alternative claim over others to permanent recruitment and they will be considered for regular employment without having to go through employment exchanges. Such of them who join as casual labourers before attaining temporary Status after requisite selec tion will however, not constitute a qualifying service. [146C D] (b)The respondents are directed to consider their claims of the each of the Petitioners promptly and making appropriate orders in respect of their regularisation within their respective years.

The appellants, who were members of a Association carrying on business in partnership, entered into an agreement with the Forward Markets Commission for the settlement of certain types of forward contracts. The terms and conditions of forward contract contained in the said agreement were governed by the provisions contained in clauses (3), (4) and (6) of Bye laws of the Association which provided that "the members shall be at any time controlled under the provisions of the , if the Forward markets Commission is of opinion that continuation of trading in hedge transactions for any delivery or deliveries is detrimental to the interests of the trade and the public interest or to the larger interests of general public". The appellants, a member of the said Association, entered upon certain contracts with other members of the association for settlement of forward Contracts. Clause (3) provided that the Forward Market Commission shall not, on a proper construction of the bye laws, take effect in any way prejudicial to the public safety or the larger interest of the economy of India and so no notification was issued under section 12(1) of the Act prohibiting the commission of any contravention of the provisions thereof. The appellants challenged the validity of the impugned bye law on the ground that it contravened articles 14 and 19 (1) (g) of Constitution. Held, that the bye law was not ultra vires the Government as it had no power under section 11 or 12 to make a bye law with retrospective effect and therefore the byelaw was beyond the powers of the Government under section 13(1). The provisions of sections 11 and 12 were applicable only to such bye laws which were not in either case subordinate to the Act. The bye law did not contravene articles 14, 19 (i) (f), 31 (g), 31(2)(a) and 31 (3)(b) of Schedule VII of the Constitution. The provisions Of section 12 (1 ) of the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952, were applicable to such a bye laws. The contracts entered into by the appellants purported to be one under the bye Law for the time being in force and any dispute arising between them could not be referred to the Government. The Government had no authority under section 1(1)(a), to frame bye law and that the rules made thereunder were not ultra rites.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The shares were held by the company as dividend, and compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes was paid to it. In appeal before this Court, the question was whether the distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to the land acquisition compensation received by the Uka Sugar Mills Ltd., after 31st March 1948 was in the hands of the assessee company. HELD : (i) The High Court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami or premia received by it from the company out of those capital gains, to which the dividend must be deemed to be capital gain, and whether any part of the compensation received for compulsory acquisitions of land was capital gain. [34 C] (ii) The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the case remanded to the High court for disposal according to law. [35 D] (iii) In the instant case, the High Courts had not recorded final answers on all the questions in favour of the assessees. [36 E F] (iv) The question whether any amounts of salamis realised by the assessee from the Company were still income liable to tax under section 12 as dividend income liable for the purposes of section 2(6A) of the Income tax Act, 1922, was not a question of "capital gain" and whether the amount of Salami received for the compulsory acquisition could be considered exempt from liability to tax. [37 F G] (v) The expression "any part of it" in section 2 (6A), of the Indian Income tax ACt, 1922 is of a capital nature. Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income tax, Assam, ; , referred to. (vi) The assumption made that the entire amount of compensation is deemed to he capital gain cannot be sustained. [38 F] Commissioner of income tax, Punjab & Haryana vs Delhi Cloth and General Mills, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Patiala, , followed. (vii) The conclusion of the High 'Court that the distribution of dividend out of capital gains was taxable must be set aside. [39 G H] (viii) The decision of the Supreme Court in Income tax Reference No. 131 of 1961 and other references to the above said decisions is set at the instance of the Revenue.

The appellants were charged with offences punishable under the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act. The prosecution case was that Sandalwood oil was not a wood oil as defined in section 2(f) (1) of the Act and therefore it is not a forest produce within the meaning of section 2 (f) of Act. On the basis of the information received by the Forest Department, the High Court convicted the appellants under section 5(1)(a) (i) of Kerala Forest Produce (Regulation of Production, Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for short). The High Court held that Sandals were not 'wood oil ' as defined under section 2. (f ) (i), (ii) and (iii) of that Act. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'agricultural produce ' in section2(f)(i) must be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner it cannot be restricted in a narrow circum stances to include what was ordinarily and in common parlance be spoken of wood oil. [156F] 1.2 In the interpretation clause, it is stated that an interpretation clause should be used for the purpose of interpreting word which are ambiguous or equivocal, and not so as to disturb the meaning or the meaning which are plain. It is stated therein that the construction of the word 'industry ' in Section 2(j) would require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be gathered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [157G H] 1:3 The dictionary meaning of the term is "to prevent, prevent or avoid" or "disproducing" or from being injured by any process. The dictionary means to prevent, promote or manifest legislative purpose, or to bring about a change in the mind of the people. It cannot be limited in such a manner so as not to disturb or prevent manifest legislative intent from being carried out. [158A B] 1 :4 In order that the word may be construed according to the meaning given in the Act, when there is nothing in the context or the subject matter to the contrary, to be applied to some things to which it would not ordinarily be applicable. [159E F] 2.1 It is well settled law that the words 'materially altered the accommodation or is likely substantially to diminish its value" in the construction to a shop, and therefore, both would deal with the same offence.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code but acquitted. The High Court convicted him on appeal to this Court, Held, that the evidence in the present case was not sufficient to sustain a conviction and the conviction could not be set aside on the ground that it was not "reasonable" for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder. The mere fact that the deceased was to be produced as a prosecution witness did not mean that he was guilty of the offence charged. The evidence in this case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn from the evidence of an expert unless it was corroborated in material particulars in his statement made at various stages of the case and which had been pointed out by the High Court. The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution were not sufficient for sustaining the conviction. The recovery of the kassi was a wholly neutral circumstance because it had not been proved that it belonged to Bhagwandas. The appellant was therefore guilty of an offence of murder under section 307 I.P.C. and sentenced to transportation for life. The sentence of death passed on him was set aside by the Rajasthan High Court in appeal. Sundarlal vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, A.I.R. 1954 S C 28 859, followed. The fact that a facile fluent liar had been asked to mention it, was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. But it could not therefore be said that the opinions of these authors were given in regard to circumstances exactly similar to those which arose in the case now before this Court nor was there any such reasons justifying interference with the findings of the High Courts because their conclusions were based on no evidence, taken as a whole, upon which any Tribunal could properly come to a conclusion that the appellant was guilty. The conviction of the appellant under section302 I. P. C., was therefore not set aside. The appeal must accordingly be allowed and the sentence of imprisonment reduced to transportation. The question for determination in this appeal was whether there were compelling reasons for setting aside the judgment of acquittal. Held, further, that there was no sufficient reason for interfering with the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the courts below because the High court had not taken into account any such exceptional and compelling reasons which would justify interference with a conviction.

The appellant company was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. The workmen employed in the factory were represented by the Indian Oxygen Workers Union. The dispute between the management of the appellant company and its workmen related to the employees of the factory at Jamshedpur. The Tribunal held that the workers of the Company had been given special leave with pay to attend the meetings of the executive committee specially held for the purpose. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the company that the Tribunal was in error in making its award operative not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at Jamshedpur and that the reference extended to them also and the Tribunal had rejected the demand for special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has not committed any error in holding that the constitution of the union prior to its purported amendment contained amongst other Articles, Articles 1 and 3. [558C] (2) The scheme of the Act is clear and unambiguous. It provides that a trade union would not be entitled to registration under the Act unless the executive thereof is constituted in accordance with the provisions of the . In considering such a demand, the first question which strikes one is as to why the meetings are set out in the said agreement and the statement and no other disparities social or economic. [559E F] (3) The fact that the union had been allowed certain of its workmen to attend without loss of pay proceedings before conciliation officers and industrial tribunals, does not detract from the position that the executive Committee meetings of a registered office shall not be changed except by resolution of the General Body meeting specially held in view of the express terms of that section. [560F G] (4) The statement made by the parties to the dispute that the workmen concerned were at liberty to work beyond 48 hours per week as provided therein, does also show that the company 's intention was validly amended on either January 6, 1963 or that it had not been given any notice of the Registrar notifying the fact of his having registered the said amendments. [561G H] (5) The word "dispute" in section 18 means a dispute between two employers and their employees inasmuch as it does not include an individual dispute but includes disputes arising out of or connected with that dispute. [562A B] (6) The expression "dividend" in the definition of "difference" in Section 2(g) means a claim for bonus. The concept of "claim" is a concept based on socio economic equality and which endeavours to resolve conflicting claims of employers and employees by finding not a one sided but a fair and just solution. A demand for Special Leave has, however, nothing to do with any disparities or inequalities social or industrial. [563C D] (7) The claim for special Leave is justified as the Tribunal has been given the discretion to grant special leave demanded by the union.

The assessee was dissolved on March 31, 1939. The timber business of the firm was taken over by two partners of the same family. In 1934 there was a partition between the two families and the firm came into existence. The forest business of M/s. Hakam Mal Tani Mal Tai Mal Toni was taken up by two partner of the assessee firm. An instrument of partnership recording the terms of the partnership and reciting the dissolution of the earlier partnership was executed on June 29, 1939, and the business in timber which was carried on by the undivided family was taken to be carried on in the name of M. Mal Tami Mal Thani Mal Tipper. The assessee was reconstituted in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm M/S. Hakham Mal Tni Mal Tali Mal Tana Mal Kuthiala, Abdullapur Depot, Simla, had been dissolved on April 1, 1939 and the timber business was taken by two of the partners of M 's firm in 1934. The departmental authorities held that succession to the family firm M was not carrying on business and that it succeeded to the business on April, 1, 1943. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession was not governed by section 25(4) or 25(5) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court in reference held that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25 (4) and the second proviso to section 25 of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had no application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the business of Messrs. Hakum Mal Tan Tani M Mal Tauthial A, Abdulapur Depot Simla, was carried out by two partnerships and that the timber was dissolved in March, 1939 when the assessee 's name was entered into. HELD : The assessee firm was constituted to carry on the timber in the business carried on at the time of dissolution from April 1 , 1939. [648 D] The business of a firm is an old and a running business and an intention to maintain continuity of the business and its transactions may reasonably be attributed to the assessee. It must therefore be held that it was not necessary for the assessee to carry out business on the date of dissolution of that firm in March , 1939, to have the business at the commencement of the Act 7 Of 1939. In the absence of other evidence, it may be held, that the income of the partner had become a separate from April I, 1939 or it may mean that from the end of March 31 , 1939 there had been separation. When a deed recites that the accounts were settled upto March 31 1, 1948, and upto March 30, 1939 the business was brought into operation and was on that account entitled to the benefit of section 25 4 of the Incometax Act.

The appellant was granted stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimogarh. The Secretary to the Regional Authority, respondent No. 29, filed an appeal before the State Transport Appellate Tribunal against the order of the State Road Transport Appellate Tribu nal and obtained stay of the order. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the said order was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Secretary to Government, Regional Transport Authori ties, Shmoga, had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963, after a lapse of such a long time from the date of grant of the permit. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The order granting the permit is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of a permit. The appeals before the High court were therefore not competent under section 64 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no juris diction to entertain the appeals and interfere with the order passed by the State transport Appellate Tribunal. [189 D] In the instant case, the Regional Trans port Authority granted the permit to the appellant on the same day. The Transport Authority did not have jurisdiction to entertain such appeal and to interfere with it. [190 E F] The High Court was therefore, in error in dismissing the writ application of the appel lant. [192 G H] In view of the fact that section 64(1)(a) of the Motor Vehicles Act is the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant o f a permit and other matters with which we are not concerned here, there was no error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunal as well as the High Courts. [194 G H; 194 A] The order of State Transport Appel late Tribunal of January 29, 1969 is set aside and necessarily the order granting it to the appell ant stands restored. [195 B C] In this case, there is no appeal provided for under section 65(1) of Act No. 64 to the State Government against an order issuing a permit in pursuance of the earlier resolution of the Regional transport Authority granting the permits. The High court was therefore not right in dismissing it on the ground that the appellant had no locus standi to file the appeal and there was, therefore, a clear error of law apparent on the face of the record.

The appellant was elected to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in 1967. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practice under section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no meeting was held at Hapur and there was no evidence to show that the respondent was guilty of any corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 (3A). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the election petition was not signed by the respondent and the news item in the newspaper had been published on 7 February 1967; (2) the meeting was not held at the time of polling; (3) the respondent had not filed any report about the alleged corrupt practice; and (4) the appellant was denied opportunity to meet the respondent. HELD: (i) The High court rightly observed that no notice was given to the respondent before Hapur on 7 2 1967, that he was denied an opportunity to participate in the election. [905 D] (ii) The publication in the newspapers 'Vir Arjun ' Exhibit 22 is a general diary of Thana Hapur bearing the date 7 February, 1967 and the newspaper report shows that the meeting which was held on 7 1 1967 was a meeting organised by the supporters of the Congress Party. The alleged incident at Chhajjupur was unacceptable because, first information report given by the appellant to the Election Commission was not lodged with the police station. Secondly, the news items in the daily newspaper were published on 8 February 1967 and secondly, the newspaper publication said that a constable was sent to the Town Hall Maidan at Hapur on 19 2 1967. [900 G H] (iii) The respondent had filed an affidavit in support of his case that he had been denied opportunity of meeting the appellant 's election. The evidence on behalf Of the appellant is not acceptable for two reasons: Firstly, the publication in newspaper 'Vil Arjun ' exhibit 22 was an appeal on behalf the respondent but the newspaper published on 2nd February 1967 gave the news about the attack on the office of the Republican Party on 7th February,1967 and the newspapers publication said to have been made with the consent of the respondent Prakash Vir Shastri. The appellant also relied on the oral evidence of PWs. P.W. 1, P. W. 2, P, W. 3, P and P.Ws.

The respondent filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. The appellant decree holder auction purchaser filed an applica tion under Order 21 Rule 90 read with Article 134 of the Constitution of India before the District Judge, Jaipur City, Jaipur, praying for delivery of possession of the property auctioned by him. The application was opposed by the judgment debtor on the ground that as the application was filed more than one year after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under article 134 of . The District Judge held that in view of Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1908, an application for setting off the sale could not be made within three years from the date of decree and as such, Article 134 stood impliedly repealed by section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code. The District judge also held that since the application for delivery was filed beyond one year from the time of confirmation, it should be held that the application under O. XXI Rule 95 of the C.P.C. was barred. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the judgment debtors it was contended that: (1) The auction purchaser having filed an appeal against the order of the District judge, the judgmentdebtor was not entitled to compute the period of one year under Article 134 and as there was no attempt to support the judgment creditor 's contention, he could not have filed the application within a period of 12 years from date of the decree; (2) The application for set aside the order dated 21.1.1979 passed by the District Court confirming the sale was made more than two years after the dismissal of the appeal and (3) The High Court had erred in holding that Article 134 would apply to an application filed under O XXI Rule 92 of the code of Civil procedure, because: (a) the auction purchaser will be deemed to be a party to the suit in which the decree is passed; (b) all questions relating to delivery of posses sion of the properties shall be referred to the executing court; and (c) all question relating to the delivery of pos session of the immovable property to such purchaser or his representative shall be deemed not to be questions relating, the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the debt within the meaning of Article 134(1)(b). Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The High Courts will have placed reliance upon the decision of the Privy Council in Chandra Mani 's case and the decision in Chandra Mahaswami vs State of Orissa, [1962] Supp. 2 SCR 829. In view of the provisions of section 47, C. P.C., it is clear that the period for limitation under Article 135 of the , should be computed from the dates of dismissal of second application for the setting aside of the sale and not from the first confirmation of the second application. [368E F] 2.1 The High courts will have to consider whether the application filed by the 4th judgment debtor praying for setting it aside on grounds other than those mentioned in Rules 89, 90 and 91 is barred by the execution of a decree for possession so as to invoke the provision of Article 135(1) of the . [368F] 2:2. The period of limitation under Articles 134 and 136 of Limitation Act cannot be computed after the date when the sale becomes absolute on the dis missal of the application. In the instant case, the High Court has not held that Article 136 was attracted to an applicatio n for setting the sale in question. [369F] Chandra Mani vs State, ; , referred to. 2:3. The order of confirmation passed by a executing court either allowing or dismissing the application will be final and effective subject to an appeal that may be made under the provisions Of Article 134. But after a sale becomes final on the passing of the order, neither the judgment debt was extinguished nor any objection was raised that it was not maintainable in law.

The appellant was the candidate of the first respondent. The first respondent filed an election petition claiming a declaration that the appellant 's election was void and that he was entitled to be declared duly elected from the constituency. In support of the petition, the first Respondent alleged various corrupt practices on the part of the appellant. However, the High Court dismissed the petition holding that both these acts amounted to corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act and were sufficient to void the election. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The publication of a wall poster by the first res pondent was not a valid notice under RSC Order 18 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [732C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had not stated that it was because he was a Marxist leader and was also arrested for harbouring the murderers. The evidence in the petition did not disclose any such fact as to how many facts related to the defec tive poster. It was only when the first respond ent himself knew that the offending poster was affixed prior to the election, that he had reasonably calculated that the voters or at any rate the voters in and about the locality where the theatre was being put up had knowledge of the fact that it is a murderer who was not known to him. [764D E] 1:3 The first Respondent had also deposed that he knew the contents of the wall poster on the day prior to his election, but he did not state as to why it would create an impression in the mind of the voters of the said wall that it had happened to be a murder. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the publication of the notice was intended to create an apprehension and did create an belief in the minds of the electors of the constituency, that it must have been so. [774E F] 1 :4 In the present case, there is no reference to the appellant in his written statement as to what was the nature of the work done by him. The publication was intended only to create a impression and did not create an intention to bind the first respondents.

The respondent No. 5, a public limited company, was granted the land in question by the State Government under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay, issued a notification under section 20 of the Act on April 30, 1974, declaring the disputed land to be reserved for recreation ground or recreational ground in the interest of general public. The respondent No 2 set aside the said order of the Commissioner and directed the sanctioning of the plan on certain conditions which were not complied with by the appellant. The appellant challenged the legality of the said action before the High Court, which dismissed the petition holding that the whole of the land should be kept reserved for parks or recreation ground in view of the clear provisions of sections 46 and 31(6) of the Maharashtra Municipal Corporation Act, 1976. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent No, 2 had misunderstood the provisions of section 46 and had misapplied the provisions thereof. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly rejected the contention of the appellants against the order of exemption granted to respondent No 5 under the Urban Land Ceiling Act. [928C] 2.1 The ground for rejection of the proposal submitted by the respondent no. 5 was not tenable and the appellate authority was justified in allowing the appeal. It is, therefore, not open to the appellant to contend that the order granting exemption should be quashed. [936D E] 1.2 In the instant case, the High court did not consider whether the respondent had applied for other relevant factors including the contemplated revision of the scheme, apart from those mentioned in section 46. The said grounds of challenge to the order were considered by the High Courts and the High courts. The contention that the High 'Court was justified on the ground that after the Municipal Commissioner rejected the plan submitted by respondent No: 5, there was no draft revised development plan in existence, could not be accepted. [ 925F G] 1:3. In view of this Court 's decision in Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another vs Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay and Others, Writ Petition No. 2944 of 1932 disposed of on 6.3.1984, the question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved under a park or recreation grounds for the benefit of the members of the public was a fraud on the Urban Ceiling Act, does not stand in the way of such material or fact being considered by Municipal Corporation for granting exemption to the respondent NO. 5 under section20 of the Urban Lands Ceiling Act.[928D E; 929F G H] 1 :4.

The employers contended that they had been guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out which under the law was illegal. The employers contended before the Industrial Court that they were guilty of contravening the provisions of section 28 read with Items l(a), l(b) and 2(a) of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 ( 'the Act ' for short). The Industrial Court held that the employers had committed an unfair labour practice. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The findings of the Industrial court are set right. [66D] 1.2 The complaints of the union were that the employer was guilty of imposition and continuing the lock out as resumption of production is gradually expanded and that till all the old workmen who were in service of the employers at the time of alleged closure, that is upto and inclusive of April 8, 1980, will be re inducted in service. There will be a continuous watch by the ministerial officer to be appointed by the Industrial Tribunal till all those old workmen are re inducted into service. [67D E] 1:3 The complaint of the employer that they have committed an illegal lock out is not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, and with a view to set right the matter proceeded to examine the same in this judgment. [68F G] 2.1 In examining whether the employer has imposed a lockout or has closed the industrial establishment, it is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closure has to be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lock out was necessarily temporary or for a period. The employer may close down industrial activity bonafide on such eventualities as suffering continuous loss, no possibility of revival of business or inability for various other reasons to continue the industrial activity. There may be a closure for any of these reasons though these reasons are not exhaustive but are merely illustrative. To say that the closing down of the industrial undertaking is a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the appellant employer at the stage when it resorts to lock out or claims to have closed down the industrial undertakings, the Industrial Courts before which the action of the respondent in order to determine whether the closure was a bona fide one or was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the appellants employer.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which were to be considered by the Income tax authorities and to make a fresh statement of its case. The assessee company made a claim for deduction every year being treated as a dealer in investments and properties but this claim was rejected by the Appellate Tribunal on the ground that it was not a 'dealer ' within the meaning of section 2(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the assessee was a dealer and not an investor and that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities and immovable properties of the assessee company could be taxed as business profits. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the question whether the assessee 's income was a 'business ' or an investor was itself a question of law; (2) the High Court had no jurisdiction to make the fresh statement under section 66(1) of Income tax, 1922 and (3) the Tribunal had erred in holding that the appellant company could not be treated as an investor. HELD: The questions actually framed by this Court on the last occasion were not appropriate and the question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or properties acquired by the assessee companies could not he taxed as profits of a business involving the application of law to the facts found in the setting of the particular case. [52 E] The questions which arose for decision were (1 ) whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the assessee could be treated a dealer or an investment Company, and (2 ) whether the profits of the sale, securities, and immovable property of the assesses company can be taxed. [53 G H] (2)(a) The question as regards the nature of the question can be considered only in respect of a finding of fact that the question could be properly framed "as to whether there was material to support the said finding".
