[54 B C] (b) The questions so referred were questions of law and the High court was right in holding on the basis of these questions. [55 D] (c) The High Courts must not interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the Tribunal on a question as framed at present. [56 E F] (3)(a). The question whether profits and loss arising from sale of share, securities etc. cannot be taxed is a pure question of fact and if it is so, the finding of facts recorded by both the Tribunal must be regarded as conclusive in a proceeding under section ' 66( 1) of Act.

The appellant was a member of the Madras Provincial Judicial Service, and was officiating as District Munsif in the State of Andhra Pradesh. He was suspended by an order dated January 28, 1954, pending enquiry into certain charges against him. The Government passed an order on January 28. 1954, suspending him until further orders, and the same was communicated to him on January 30, 1954. On April 28, 1953, he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the order of suspension. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the enquiry into the conduct of Government servants was without jurisdiction and that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the High court is not a mere administrative order and does not amount to an order of dismissal or removal from service within article 311. [419 D] (ii) The Government was bound to hold a fresh enquiry and decide for itself whether the charges were well founded. No such question was raised in the petition or in the writ petition. It was also contended that the High Courts had no jurisdiction under article 311 to suspend a judicial officer pending final orders of the Government. [420 D] The order passed by the High 'Court on January 29, 1954 was merely one of suspension pending final order by the Government and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor of removal from the service within Article 311 of Constitution. It could not be said that the concluding proviso in Rule 4(1) (a) of the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953 had subsequently been amended by G. 0. No. 938 dated April 11, 1955. The order in fact was passed on October 1, 1953. [416 D E] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that read as a whole the Rule did not show an intention to depart from the procedure laid down in the Madras Civil Services Rules and that it was neither one nor more dismissal or of removal within article 31 of the constitution. [414 C] (iv) The fact that under the proviso to r. 4(i)(a) the Government may, subject to the provisions of rule 5, also refer to the Tribunal which is constituted as the authority which may impose suspension pending enquiry in a matter. [413 D E].

The appellant was a registered holder of shares in a company which owned shares of the company. The company had obtained probate of the said letters of trust from the estate of one of its directors, a private limited company and appointed the respondent as the respondent, James Anderson. The respondent claimed that the dividends deemed to have been distributed under the order dated March 26, 1953, were distributed in his individual name by the appellant and pursuant thereto the relevant share certificates were delivered to him. The Income tax Officer included the dividend deemed to be distributed in respect of those shares and no question arose as to whether the dividend was assessable to income tax for the year ending 31st March 1949. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the dividend could not be taxed under section 23A of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because the company had failed to establish that it was liable to pay income tax on the dividends declared by the respondent. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the expression "shareholder" in section 2(2) of the Income tax (Second Amendment) Act, 1950, means a person by whom income tax is payable and may be enforced against him or his legal representative in the manner and to the extent the statute permits. The expression "assessee" in the said section means a shareholder registered in the books of the Company and such shareholder alone is liable to be taxed in respect thereof if he had not died, but for the death of the legal representative although he was himself not a member of the family. Amarchand Shroff vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, , referred to. The word "assessee " in section 24B of the Act means a company registered under the Companies Act and such share holders alone are liable to assessment as income of the deceased person. Amar Chand Shroff 's case, (1923) I.L.R. 59 Mad. 312, distinguished. The definition of "share holder" in s 2(1) of Income Tax Act, 1961, includes a shareholder who has died and his legal representatives are not a legal representative of the estate in place of the person whose estate is vested in him but because as a representative it is his duty to discharge the obligations enforceable against the estate.

The appellant was the Ruler of a State of Baster. He entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the acquisition of his rights in estates, mahals and alienated villages and alienated certain lands in Madhya Pradesh and to make provisions for other matters connected therewith. The appellant contended that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler and was within the class of persons who were by name specifically included in the definition of "proprietor" and therefore clearly within the scope of the Act. The expression "maufidar" as defined in article 366(22) of the Consti tution means a person who is the holder of land which has been separately assessed to land revenue, whether such land revenue be payable or has been released, compounded for or redeemed in whole or in part; and the word "maui" includes an ex ruler. The definition of 'proprietor ' contained in section 2(j) of Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, does not make him a Ruler for purposes outside the Constitution and his case must be regarded as a whole by virtue of which he was entitled to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village. The word "amahal" is used in article 367(22), which states that "mahal" includes any person who for the time being is recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler". The expression 'maufidars ' is not necessarily confined to a grantee from a State or a Ruler of an Indian State. A maufidar could be a person, who was the holder, of land, which was exempted from the payment of rent or tax. In the present case, the appellant had given no evidence that he had any right to recover the rent or property in his villages. The burden was on him to prove this fact which he never attempted to discharge. It was not necessary for him to establish that the lands in question were assessed to the land revenue. The High Court rightly held that the respondent was an "ex Ruler" and that article 366 (22) did not make the appellant a Ruler, for the purposes of the Madhya Pradesh Act.

The respondent was working in a Garden Curator in the office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India. He was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh). The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the order of transfer on the following grounds: (i) that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the C.A.T., (ii) that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago, and (iii) that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. The Tribunal quashed the order on the ground that the decision of the Courts establish that the power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued by the Government. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines say that as far as possible husband and wife must be posted at the same place. [431C] 1.2 In the matter of considering transfer of an individual officer, the Office Memorandum dated 3 4 1986 has been issued by a Bench of which one of us (J.S. Verma J.) was a member. On a perusal of the judgment, it is evident that the constraints and norms which the High Court observes while exercising the said jurisdiction apply equally to the Tribunal created under Article 323 A. (ii). The guidelines do not confer upon the government employee a legally enforceable right. [ 431D E] 1:3. In this case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by the transfer. [ 432E F] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta ; , followed. Bank of lndia vs Jagjit Kaur Mehta ; and J.S Verma J.P.V. State of Punjab vs Jagjit singh Mehta ; referred to. 1.4 The guidelines issued by Central Administrative Tribu nal are applicable to the case of the respondent. [ 433F] Bank Of India vs Jaswant Singh Mehta, ; , referred to 2.1 In the instant case, there is no doubt, the guidelines require the two spouses to be posted in one station, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authori ties should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouse to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. [42F G] Bank, of India V. Jagjit Singh & Ors., ; , relied upon.

The appellants were charged under Section 304 Part I read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder of one Jawahar. The Trial Court convicted them under section 304 Part 1 read with section 34 I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1 and A2. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of A3 that the participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of P.W. 2 was proved beyond doubt. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the accused was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34 I PC. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of P,W.2. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while granting special leave to appeal was not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. [635C D] 2.1 A common intention is to cause simple hurt and, as such, the offence punishable under Section 325 I.p.C.[636D] 2:2. It is also held that the intention of appellants was to caused grievous hurt. As such the conviction and sentence of the appellant under Section 302 read with Sections 109, 1.P., C. read with Sec tion 34, I PC are set aside. [625E F] 2 :3. The conviction and sentences of the appel lants under Section 323, I P. C. and the sentences passed on them are maintained. [613F G] 2 .4. The appellants shall deposit Rs. 7,000 each before the Trial Court within four months from today. [526G] 2 5. The appeal is disposed of in terms of the above directions. [600H] 6. The sentence of imprisonment already undergone by the appellants is reduced to the period already undergone. [599F G) [636A] 7. The fine amount of Rs. 21,000/ shall be paid to the father/mother of deceased Jawahar. In case of non payment of fine, the appellants shall undergo rigorous imprison ment for five year.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of certain amounts due to it on account of loan together with interest. The respondent No. 3, the father of the appellant, was the owner of a motor vehicle which was purchased by the appellant after its nationalisation. The appellant had two partners, one of whom was a partner in another, and the other a firm consisting of three partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, and another section Doraswamy, since died. The suit was decreed by the trial court against the respondent No 3 and its partners. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Bank against the decree of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Bank that (i) in view of section 4(e) of the Act, the provisions of the , were not applicable to the Bank and as such the Bank was entitled to recover the entire amount without the same being scaled down as provided under section 13 of the . HELD: (1) The words `special Indian law ' have a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is no reason why the expression should be interpreted in the light of the setting out of the same in the words of the provision of section 3(27)(a) of Act. [966 D] (2) The expression `special ' has a clear, and unambiguous connotation and there can be no doubt that the expression ` special Indian law" must be construed in the context of a statute and not by the law itself in order to come within the purview of section four(e). [967 G H] (3) The word `special" is used in two different senses, namely `special or `law '. It is not defined in the Act. In the face of the provisions Of section 4 (e), it would be quite clear that the words ` special ' law ' must be interpreted to mean a law enacted by the British Parliament specially for India. [969 D] The expression 'special Indian Law ' has been used in the sense of special Indian Law and the word 'special ' is not restricted to a special Indian statute. It would be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by or under a special III law and not in pursuance of such a law, it will be quite unreasonable to think, that `special IIlI Act ' must also be held to have become void as making invidious discrimination in favour of the British Corporation offending against the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution. [970 D E] (4) The intention of the Legislature is very clear from the language of section 2(27) (a) which defines `special word ' to mean any Indian law enacted or by a special Act. It may be that interpreting the words in pursuance Of the provision, of a Statute, the setting in which such words are placed may be taken into consideration, but that does not mean that even though the words which are to be interpreted convey a clear meaning, still a different interpretation or meaning should be given to them because of the set. The expression "special Indian" has a wider connotation and includes a `law enacted by Parliament '. [971 D E; 972 A B] (5) In view of the fact that the Banking Companies Act is a special law and the provisions in regard to the payment of interest are not applicable, the appellant Bank was not entitled to any scaling down the debt due to the bank by the respondents.

The petitioners, who were sugar factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, challenged the validity of the notification issued by the Government under section 3(1) of the , on the ground that it contravened article 19(1)(g) of Constitution. The High Court held that the impugned notification was invalid as it violated articles 14, 19(i)(g), 19(6) and 31 (2) of India and was bad as it contravened articles 19(l)(g). Held, that the notification was valid and must be struck down. The object of the Act is to secure essential commodities for the general public, which is the consumer, at a fair price; but it does not follow from this that the Government should fix wholesale or retail prices in any particular area. It is well known that there are three kinds of prices prevalent in the market for a commodity like sugar, namely, ex factory price, wholesale price and retail price. The first class of prices fixed by the impugned Notification is controlled by the Central Government under s.3(1), and the second class of price fixed by cl. (c) of section 3 (2). The third class of rates fixed by cls. (a) to (e) are controlled by cl.(c) and there is no reason why the Government must fix wholesale prices for the whole of India. The third category of prices are controlled in certain regions only. The price of sugar in Punjab depends upon the price of the factories in Uttar Pradesh, Uttar Bihar and North Bengal and it is not necessary to consider whether the Government could fix wholesale and retail prices at which any essential commodity may be bought or sold. The fact that the factories are being compelled to sell at below the cost of production does not make them liable for the maximum price fixed under section 31 (1) (c). The petitioners have not even alleged that as a matter of fact the wholesalers and retailers are profiteering and making it impossible for them to be available for the common public at fair prices. The prices fixed are just as much as they are controlled and controlled by an artificial class, and therefore, there is discrimination between different regions or between producers and middlemen in view of what we have said above. The petitioners cannot claim that the prices fixed were below the price fixed.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956, referred to the Second Industrial Tribunal certain disputes between the appellant and its employees. The Tribunal held that there was a rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 and that the Tribunal applied wrong criteria. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the award of 1951 was not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act, and therefore the reference was bad in law. Held: (i) The Government made the order of transfer on April 9, 1957, i.e., after section 2 of the Amendment Act, 1956 came into force. Under that section, the appropriate Government may by notification in writing and for reasons to be stated therein, withdraw any proceeding under this Act pending before a Tribunal constituted under the Act before the commencement of the Amending Act, which was deemed to have come into force on the 10th day of March 1957. The provisions of sections 19(1) and 30 of the , were not applicable to the case. (ii)The award of the Tribunal was binding between the parties as it had been made in violation of the principles of natural justice. Pritam Singh vs The State of Punjab, ; , followed. (iii)The Tribunal had jurisdiction to transfer proceedings pending before it from a tribunal constituted under section 7A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to another tribunal and that was not a case where the award was made in contravention of the provisions Of section 19 (6). Pritam Singh v The State, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, followed. The fact that the existing rate of dearness allowance was increased by the Amending Acts did not affect the effect of the amendment of the definition of "Tribunal" contained in section 2(r) of Act 18 of 1957. Pritam singh vs The Union of India, ; and Pritam Singh V. State of Pepsu, [1954] S. C. R. 1065, referred. (iv)The fact that there were certain references to the Industrial Tribunal did not mean that the Government acted well within its powers in transferring the dispute pending before the Tribunal. The award was binding on the parties and could not be modified or modified by a subsequent notification under section 19 of the .

The appellant was the Matadheen of Sri Gavi Mutt, which was a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The predecessor in office of the appellant filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the scheme was valid, but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the actual administration of the Mutt and its properties, it was partly because the appellant had been obstructed by the respondents in courts of law. his property rights had been taken away. [260 B] (ii) The conclusion that the Scheme was valid is correct. The scheme as framed was a whole, and the challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed. [262 C D] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that since the scheme had not been implemented till 1952, it continued to operate as though they were framed under the provisions Of the earlier Act. [263 E F] (iv) The order of the Central Government was valid and did not contravene article 19 (1)(g). [262 D] R.S. Sharma vs Finsbury Borough Council, ; , referred to. (v) The contention that since in the present case the scheme has not been completely implemented till 1953, it is open to the appellant challenging its validity on the grounds that it contravenes the Mathadhip Act, 1947, was without substance and must be rejected. [264 G] (vi) The effect of the scheme is to provide for the continuance of rules, notifications etc., in so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions thereof. Section 103(d) provides that any scheme settled or modified by a Court under the earlier law shall be deemed to have been settled or modify by the court and shall have effect accordingly. [265 G H] (vii) The appellant 's property rights were taken away, and it was open to him to challenge the validity of the Scheme on the basis that it deprives him of his fundamental right under article 19. Such a plea does not appear to have ever been raised and, in our opinion, cannot be validly raised for the simple reason that the further damental rights are not retrospective in operation. [267 G H; 268 A] (viii) The fact that the order was not implemented did not make any difference to this legal position. If a scheme governed by section 103(a) is deemed to be made or sanctioned under the Act and thus continued, modifications in it can be effected by adopting the procedure prescribed by section 62(3). [267 B C] (ix) The result of the fundamental rights guaranteed to the appel lant under article 14 is that he has continuously challenged the implementation of the schemes by legal proceedings and partly because he has been obstructed in courts. His property rights have been taken over for a long time in 1952 and as such it is not open to challenge on the score that they contravened the Matadi provisions of the earlier Acts. [268 G H].

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982 and continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. He was not paid the salary for the period of summer vacations during all these years. The managing committee of the school rejected his claim for regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as English Teacher with effectfrom July 121982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act on the following reasoning: (i) The appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989; and (ii) The services of the appellant were terminated by the managing committee after 1986. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in denying the benefit to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [995B] 1.2 The High Courts erred in deny the benefit on the grounds that his initially appointment for89 days was con cerned by the stipulations that he will continue until replace by a candidates from the Select List. The State Government is expected to function as a model employer. "We are of the view that the State Government has failed to discharge that duty in these cases. [996C D] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, A.I.R 1987 S.C. 478; Rattan Lal V. State of Punjab, AJ.R. 1987 S C. 478 and Rattan Lal v State of J & K, A J.R., 1987 S .C. 477, referred to. 1.3 The HighCourt erred in denied the benefit by the appellant to the respondent on the plea that his appointment was made otherwise than in accordance with procedure laid down in the Education Act and the Rules and Regulations framed thereunder.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Vidhan Sabha from a constituency in which he was elected. The respondent, who was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti, challenged the election on the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 3 to 7 of the Rules did not convert the office of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti into an office or profit, and that the appellant was entitled to draw a monthly consolidated allowance in lieu of travelling allowances. HELD : (i) The payment to a Chairman, Panchayat Sanstha, is described in the rule as 'a monthly consolidated amount in lieu thereof '. Under those earlier Rules of 1961, the Chairman was entitled only to Rs. 4/ per diem when a Member of the Gram Panchayat performs a journey in connection with his official duties outside the district. The appellant was therefore entitled to the allowance under rr. 3 and 7 of that Rules. [427 B C] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the allowances paid under r, 3 were in addition to the payment under r 3. [447 D E] (iii) The expenditure incurred by a member for travelling allowance or daily allowance is in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duty. [ 428 C] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 653 at p. 656 and Ravanna subanna vsG.S Kaggai, A I.R., 1954 S C. 653, referred to. (iv) The appellant had failed to establish that the allowance payable under r . 3 was in addition lo the payment thereunder. [539 G H] (v) The amount of travelling and daily allowances under r., 3 is not liable to compensate the Chairman for expenses incurred in connection therewith. [ 427 C D] Ravindran Subanna v G. S. Kanggeer, A, I. R. 1954 SC 653 at P.

The appellant tenant filed a suit for eviction on the ground of sub stantial construction. The respondent landlord filed a written statement and pleaded that the appellant had made constructions materially alter ing the accommodation without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tin shed was sub ject to the provisions of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952 (Act 10 of 1952). On appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the trial Court 's order and dismissed the respondents ' suit on the findings that none of the construc tion constituted material alteration. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decision of the Trial Court and decreed the eviction petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant tenant that (i) the tin sheds were sub stances which could be removed without causing any damage to the building, and (ii) constructions so made had materially altered the accommodation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The material alterations contemplated in section 3(1)(c) of U. P. Cantonment Act, 1949 do not constitute material alteration as the determination of this question depends on the facts of each case. In S.B. Mathur vs K.P Gupta, ; , this Court held that construction which converted the tenanted premises into two rooms and tin shed marked by letters CDGH on the Eastern side on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion, is not a substantial change in nature and they alter, the form, front and structure of the accommodation, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out to the tenant. The construction so made would furnish ground for eviction only when they bring about substantial change of the building as contemplated by section 3 (1)(C) of the Act. [975G H; 977A] 2. In the instant case, the disputed constructions which the High Court has found to be 'material alteration ' consisted of a partition wall of 6 feet height in a hall converting the same into two room and a tin shed with letters CGDH on a open land adjoining the accommodation adjacent to it. The Trial Court as well as the first appellate court both have recorded finding that the respondent landlord was not material alteration of substantial character either in the form or structure of accommodation. There is no material on record to sustain the findings of fact recorded by the High court that the appel lant had constructed pucca constructions on three sides. instead the Commissioner 's report is contrary to it and therefore, the finding recorded by him is not vitiated by any error of law apparent on the face of the record. [ 977C D] 3. The question whether disputed constructions constitute material alter ments is a mixed question of fact and law. The courts below have recorded concurrent findings that the Respondent landlord was entitled to file suit for ejectment of a tenant without obtaining permission of the District Magistrate, but the High Courts in second appeals interfered with the findings arrived at by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition were temporary in nature which could not be removed within the mischief of material alteration, [977D E] 4.

The appellant company had filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of damages to the tune of Rs. 26,000/ on account of alleged non delivery of certain goods. Summons in the suit was sent to the registered office of the company in Calcutta and was said to have been served on one Shri Navlakha on 17 3 1975 asking the company to appear at Indore on 25 3 1975 for settlement of issues. The respondent firm filed a revision petition against the order of the Trial Court before the High Court under section 115 C.P.C. The High Court allowed the revision and set aside the ex parte decree. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that since the respondent firm had no knowledge of the exparte decree for the first time on 29 7 1975, the application filed by the appellant company under Order 9 Rule 13 C. P.C., could not be entertained as there was no error in that judgment much less any error of jurisdiction entitling the High court to interfere with it. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can under this rule, be on a juristic person. [1032C] 2.1 In Rule 17 of Order 5, C.W.P., the word "Principal officer" has got to be understood with reference to the other provisions of the Code. In Rule 18 of Order G, it has been provided that where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered Office of the Company and make a report to that effect. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous Case that the service of the summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of rule 2 of Order 29, C., P. C. was not due to any legal representative or any other principal officer of the Corporation because either he refuses to signed the summons or is a corporation is valid under clause (c). [1033D E] 2:2 The appellant under the orders of the Court had furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount. It has agreed to continue the same till disposal of the suit. [ 1032F G] 3. In view of the provision contained in Order 5 Rule 17 C.p.C, the High Courts went wrong in interfering with it and set it aside.

The Magistrate recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of peace existed even in the final order. The Magistrate passed an order under section 145(5) Cr. P.C., declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the said order on the ground that there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the preliminary order that there existed a breach or peace and that there had been apprehension of breach of the peace. The High Court held that as there was an allegation that there were disputes between the parties, the Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145 the Magistrate passed the final orders in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that the final Order of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of such peace existed at the time when the order was passed nor was such a case set up by any party before the Magistrate or before the High, Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the High Courts is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [962C] 2. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach. He has to record his satisfaction in the initial order, that there is a breach not of peace. That being an error of procedure would clearly fall within the domain of a curable irregularity which is not sufficient to vitiate the order passed under sub section (5) of section 145. [952D] 3. The objection raised by the appellants was not accepted by the Sessions Court and the HighCourt rightly allowed the petition. [942E] 4. The contention that there has been a clear finding of existence of breach cannot be accepted. If such a finding arises the proceedings have to be carried to their logical end resulting in the finality of the final decision under sub s.(6) of s 145. As already indicated, the contradictory stands taken by the parties clearly show that there Was no question of the dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under sub sec tion (5). [943C D] 5. The appellants had a clear remedy in the civil court. They could not be said that no prejudice was caused to any of the parties who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court.

The appellant, a public limited company, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn and yarn. The company sold its yarn to its old customers who paid it as shown in its accounts. The appellant contended that the company had earned more profits than was disclosed in its books of account and that the sales were not liable to tax under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the question whether a particular transaction is a sale or not must be decided on the facts of each case and it is not necessary for the Tribunal to decide it on the evidence adduced before it. The finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal was final and conclusive as to the legal effect of those findings was a question of law which could be reviewed by the High Court under section 11(1). Commissioner of Income tax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai & Co., ; , referred to. In the present case, the appellant had been found to have sold its goods to its new customers and received the price therefor. The question as framed by the appellant did not specifically raise this point but it was urged that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to assess the sales in question under section 67(1)(a) of Income Tax Act, 1961. It was also contended that there was no need for the intermediaries to purchase from other manufacturers when all their needs were met by the company and that there could be no question as to who found the capital for the intermediary was. Held further, that in the present ease the appellant was not liable as it had not been treated as a dealer under section 14(2) (c), and the Tribunal erred in holding that the intermediaries were benamidars for the appellant. Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Stanley, , referred lo. The decision in Cooper vs Stoart, ; , distinguished. In re: Granite Co., Ltd., [1964] S C R. 840, followed. Commissioner Of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmed Bhai Umarbhai and Co., [1965] 1 S.C.R. 946, referred to, The appellant had a right to have it referred to the court under section 6(1), which was not a question in the proceedings before the Tribunal. The Tribunal had only to find whether any price was paid by the intermediaries for the sales and not to whom the goods were sold and for what price they had earned as commission, and that it was not necessary to decide whether any amount was payable by the intermediary or non resident persons.

The assessee, a manufacturer of blankets and other woollen cloth, was assessed to income tax on the profits of the firm for the assessment year 1948 49. The assessee claimed deduction of this amount from the assessable income. By his order dated June 30, 1949, the Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish, a member of the family. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that Rs. 5,000 as reasonable amount payable as commission to Shri J.P. Vaish was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income tax Officer. The High Court on reference, held that the entire amount of Rs. 75,465 paid to the General Manager was an income of the appellant and was rightly disallowed by Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question as to whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out wholly or partly for the purposes of business of assessee is a matter which must be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each particular case. But, as observed by this Court in Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; , the final conclusion on the admissibility of an allowance is one of law. [529 B D] (ii) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the assessee the entire sum of Rs 75,467 paid to him was an expenditure wholly and exclusively for purposes of the Business of the assesses within the meaning of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income T.P . Act, 1922. [ 530 C D] Swadesha Cotton Mills Company Ltd. V. C. I.T. U. P., ; and Swadesh Cotton Mills Ltd.v. C,.I. T., U.[1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 986, referred to. (iii) The High Courts were not called upon to decide whether the Income 'tax Officer could exercise the power he exercised under section 10 (2)(x) of Income Tax Act. [329 G H] Swade Mills Co., Ltd. & Anr. vs Commissioner of Income tax, U.p., ; followed.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of which he was a member. On January 13, 1954, the management and the Union filed a joint petition for dismissal of the respondent company on the ground that the appellant had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and prayed for an order directing the company to record compromise or hearing. The Tribunal held that the agreement was collusive and mala fide and that the Secretary of the Union was not competent to enter upon the agreement. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken up by the Union, of which the workman is a member, as a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, must be decided on the facts of each case. The principle that the party to a dispute should have a fair hearing, is not applicable to an individual dispute as defined in section 2(k) of the Industrial Dispute Act unless it is taken over by a Union of workmen or by any other workman employed In the industry or by a considerable number of workmen. The question whether in fact the Secretary had any authority to enter on any compromise on behalf of the union, was a question of fact which could not be allowed to be raised at this stage. Central Provinces Transport Service Ltd. vs Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan, ; , referred to. In the present case, the appellant did not dispute that the Union had made an application for separate representation and that it had been made in respect of the same matter as the Union. The only question that arose for decision was whether when the union raised any objection to this representation, the Secretary could claim to have a say in the conduct of the proceedings before the Tribunal. It was not unreasonable to think that section 36 of the Act recognises this position by providing that the workman who is a party to the dispute shall be entitled to be represented by an officer of a registered trade union of which him is a members, and while it will be unwise and indeed impossible to try to lay down a general rule in the matter, the ordinary rule should be that such representation by an official of the trade union should continue throughout the proceedings in the absence of excep tional circumstances which may justify the Tribunal to permit other representation of the workman concerned.

The appellants were the tenants in respect of a portion of a house. The respondent No. 1 instituted a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the ground that they had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2 and that he had been assessed to income tax separately and that the property in dispute was not joint family property or even joint property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants constituted a joint Hindu family and were entitled to continue the appeal. On appeal by the respondent No 1, the High Court held that the respondents were competent to continue their appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the provisions of r. 4 of 0. XLI, r. 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not override the provisions Of r. 9 of O. XXII and (2) the High court had no jurisdiction to hear the appeal as the provisions in r. 3 of 0 . XLI were applicable to the case as the nine appellants constituted joint Hindu Family and the surviving appellants could continue their appeals in view of the provisions contained in O. XLI. r. 31 of the code. HELD : (i) The appellate court had not jurisdiction to proceed with the appeal and reversed or vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants under O.XXII, r, 3. [560 F] (ii) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellant when the appeal by kedar Nath had abated as all the appellants had a common right and interest in getting a decree of ejectment against defendant No 2 and such decree could have been on a ground common to all of them. [561 G H] (iii) The provisions of 0 XLI, rr. 33 and 34 of O XXII were not applicable to it. Rule 3 was therefore inapplicable to the stage when an appeal is filed by all the defendants. [562 D E] (iv) The appellants could not be ejected from the premises when he had a right to remain in occupation of the premises on the basis of the decree holding that Kedar Nath, one of the persons having a joint interest in letting out the property could not take advantage of r, 9 of 0 XXII.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in Delhi. The respondent landlord filed a petition for eviction against the appellant on the ground of bona fide requirement under section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The appellant contended that no notice to quit had been given nor any notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could not be justified as there was a statutory presumption in favour of the respondent landlord that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) of the Act. The Rent Controller held that no such notice was necessary because the lease was created prior to the extension of the lease and therefore, the forfeiture was not valid. On appeal, the High Court held that the notice in writing by the landlord was a condition precedent to a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of a lease under section 108(1) of Transfer of Property Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the lease stood determined by forfeiture and (ii) the forfeiture could not have been made in terms of section 111 (g); and (iii) the notice terminating tenancy was valid as it did not comply with the requirements of the terms and conditions of the Deed of demise. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The requirement of a notice in the lease deed for a specified period even though it expressed itself as for a term less than one year and under section III(a) has expired by lapse of time. [918C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had all along staked his case on the application of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience. The High Court was right in its view that the provisions of the P.T. Act were not applicable to the lease in question and therefore a forfeiture giving rise to a determination of the lessee under section 11(g). [919D] 1:3. The requirement as to written notice provided in the section is not based on any principle of equity. It is not so in express terms it cannot be said that a notice as contemplated by section 111 has been given in writing. [936E] 1 :4. In the present case, there was no specific statutory provision which required the notice to be given in the notice. The notice did not indicate any statutory requirement of law. It was merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the Section by the legislature and was not based upon any well established principles of equity and natural justice. [981F] 1 5. The provisions of section III (g) are but a statutory recognition of the Rules of justice. equity and Good conscience have to be read as applicable to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to 1947 or even subsequent to the coming into force of the Transfer of Wages Act, 1952. [980G H] 1 6. The requirements of a statute which are buta part or other, are intended to be fulfilled in order to determine the lease. It cannot be gainsaid that a statutory authority has a right to present its case before it will have to make out his right and their determination can only be claimed by the lessor. [979A B] 1 7. The rule of justice equity and sound conscience is not such a rigid commodity as it stands today. It must be remembered that in the instant cases, the requirement of notice was not merely statutory but a procedural one. [978B C] 1 8. The proviso to section 111 of the has no application to leases granted prior to 1939 or even earlier prior to 1946 or even thereafter. The very object of the rule is to find out whether the lessee has under gone through the entire tenancy with the result that he has not assented to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine it by giving notice in that behalf. This Court would be reluctant to suppose that every provision in the Act which is but a Statutory recognition of a principle of justice would be rendered nugatory or ineffectual. [977E F] 1 919 2. The statutory recognition must be based on principles of justice and equity.

The appellant was a Superintendent in the State of Assam. He was dismissed from service with immediate effect on charges under section 5(1) (a), 5(2) and 6(3). The Governor passed an order dismissing him from service. On appeal, the High Court held that the order was not justified as the Governor had acted mala fide in passing the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Governor when acting under sub clause (c) of article 311 of the Constitution was satisfied that in the interest of security of the State it was not expedient to give him an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above. HELD : The order of dismissal from service was passed in violation of article 310(2). [488 B] (i) The words used in the Article are "shall not apply" and, therefore, the consultation with the Public Service Commission is mandatory and that this Article does not confer any right on a public servant so that the absence of consultation or any irregularity in consultation does not afford him a cause of action in a court of law. [488 C] (ii) The satisfaction recorded by the Governor under sub cl. (c), therefore, that the appellant had to arrive at was that it was "not expedient to do so" and the Governor 's satisfaction was recorded on the language which was used earlier in the unamended Article 311(2), as it stood before amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963. [489 D] Khem Chand vs The Union of India & Ors., ; , followed. (iii) The consultation with Public Service Commis sioner is not mandatory and the consultation must be consulted before an order is passed by the Government. [490 E] (iv) The opinion recorded by a Governor under article 311(3)(c) was binding on the President, as he had been satisfied that it could not be expedient to provide him with the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity of showing cause against his action proposed as stated in the amended Article 311. [497 G] (v) The Governor ' s satisfaction is recorded by him in the language used earlier and in the light of the interpretation placed on that unamended article by this Court. [492 A B] Khemchand vs State of U.P., ; referred to.

The petitioners and the Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, were alleged to have formed serious infraction and/or infringement of their fundamental rights under articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution in the matter of enjoying their religious faith and performance of religious ceremonies. The petitioners and Shia Community of Mohalla Darbar, Varanasi had filed a representative suit for declaration that the said Shia Muslim community was not entitled to perform their religious ceremonies and functions on the plots and structures thereon as also an appropriate writ, direction or order in the nature of mandamus commanding respondents 1 to 4 not to prohibit or restrain the Shias from performing their religious duties and practices. The Court passed a preliminary decree for declaration of rights in favour of Shia sect and for restraining the ShiAS community from performing its religious ceremonies, practices, observances and functions. In appeal by the Shira Community against the said decree, the High Court held that the petitioners were not entitled under O.XXI, r.8 C.P.C., to institute the suit in question on the assumption that they had made any ground for challenging title either to the plots or to the structures thereon or even the Shiasi community of the structure on those plots and the rights exercisable by the Sunni community over the plots were not justiciable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned order passed by a District Magistrate under O .XXI. r. 8 C. P.C. was a judicial order and it must be pointed out that all the decisions including those of this Court in Haji Mohammed Ismail vs Munshi Barkat Ali & Ors., ; , relied upon, were not applicable to the facts of the case as the petitioners had also claimed that the plots of land and structures on these plots had been registered as Shia Waqfs for purposes of performing their religion, practices and observances. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the order passed under OXXI r. 54 C.p.C was a Judicial Order or quasi judicial order, the function thereunder being essential to the proper adjudication of the legal rights of the Shiab community. [1134D] 2.1 The jurisdiction conferred on the Sunni Central Waqfs Board by section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not limited to the powers of an authority in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger to public tranquility under section 144. It is a judicial power and it has been conferred on "a District Magistrate, a Chief Presidency Magistrate, or any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the State Government" and it was in those circumstances that the High Courts had decided them for the first time in the writ petition. [1105E F] 2:2 The jurisdiction of a Magistrate under section 145 is not wider than that of a Civil Court. It can be exercised only in exceptional cases where there are existing or established rights, and the individuals should not be harassed twice over with the same kind of litigation and in our view neither of these aspects is present here so as to bar the present petition by res judicata or principle analogous to res judicata. [111D E] 2 :3 The High Courts have been given a clear and sharp distinction between cases where the entitlement of the Sunni Muslim community to perform its religious rites, practices etc., on the plot and structures in question has been established and is the subject matter of a judicial pronouncement and decree of Civil Court of competent jurisdiction as also by reason of these properties having been registered under the U.P., U. P., and on the basis of which the members of the Muslim community sought to prove their existing rights, practices or functions, and such claims cannot be regarded as between the same parties who are before this Court; the Shiam community of village Dosiph is a religious minority, who are desirous of freely practising their religious belief and performing their rites, practice, observings and functions without let or hindrance by members belonging to the majority sect of the community namely Sunni Muslims, and as such a positive approach is called for on the part of the local authorities in this regard.

The assessee, a limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim of set off on the ground that when in the assessment years 1957 58, the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computation of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had held that there was no genuine loss. On appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that the loss could not be said to have been determined for the purpose of assessment year 1958 66. The High Court found that the Income Tax officer had wrongly disallowed the assessee 's claim. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the claim for set off was admissible in view of the provisions of Section 80 of the 1961 Act, and that the Tribunal erred in law in holding that the provisions in section 24(3) regarding intimation of losses as notional when he really meant that it was an estimate. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The benefit conferred under Section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding the claim to set off as admissible in the view taken by the Tribunal. [1162E] 2.1 In the instant case, the Income tax Officer did compute the amount by specifying it in his assessment order. When the assessee had made the claim and he took note of it, his failure to comply strictly with the requirement of sub section (3) of Section 24 should not be permitted to be taken advantage of by the revenue nor should it be used to the prejudice of the assessee. [1106G H] 2:2 The benefit under Section24 of 1922 act continued to he given effect only in relation to assessment years prior to the coming into force of the Income Act, 1961 a return could not possibly have been filed under Section 139 because in the year 1962, the assessee was really meant the estimate. It agreed with the conclusion of the Tribunal and found against the Revenue. [1064A B] 2(a) The benefit granted under section 24 of the 1922 Act continues to be available to the assessee for a period of four years immediately succeeding the assessment for which the loss is first computed under the Act or as the case may be. The loss cannot be wholly set off in accordance with the provisions Of that sub section, the portion not so set off shall be carried forward to the following year and so on. [1016B C] (b) The assessee had not made any genuine loss while disposing of the appeal for the said assessment year. Therefore, it was not possible to hold that the benefit conferred by Section 24 could be allowed in the instant cases. [1002C D] 2.(a) In the present case, there is no evidence of any loss as such. The assessee 'reliefs were not determined for assessment years subsequent to the said coming into operation in which the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner had given a clear finding that the losses were notional when the claim was really intended that it should be an estimate and the Income 'tax Officer did not apply his mind to the relevant provisions thereof and he had held the capital loss as notional. [1001F G] (c) The High court reached the correct conclusion and there is nothing in section 80(1)(b) of the Act which would justify the claim on a bare analysis of these provisions, and without reference to anything more, this appeal can be disposed of. [1000B C].

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Research & Development dated 24.12.1985. On his retirement he was re instated as Senior Scientific officer on 30.4.86. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal by way of a writ petition challenging the order of premature retirement which was dismissed by the Central Administrative Tribunal holding that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years, and that he was not entitled to any amount so paid to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members of the DRDS was increased, it could not be held that the respondent who belonged to another unit, viz. DAQAS, was entitled to the said benefit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid, and there is no substance in the present appeal. [316B] 2. The question involved in the instant case is not whether the Government has such power. The fact that the superannuationage of the Members of theDRDS was enhanced, it can not be said that the Respondent who belonged tO the said unit, namely DAQas, was enti tled to the benefit. There is no dispute that the Govern ment had power to vary the service conditions of the member of the service from time to time. The service rules which applied to all the three units were also common, viz., Defence Science Services Rules. [417C D] 3. The High Court has rightly held that there was a right of the Government to prescribe separate conditions of serv ice for the Members belonging to different units and merely on the basis of the superannuation of the Member of the RTA, the service rules would have to run parallel and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to us by the Tribunal. [517D E] 4. The contention that the State Government had power under Rule 12 of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972 to vary its service conditions is not tenable because the question is whether the respondent was also entitled to such benefit.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election petition filed by him was dismissed on the ground that he had committed corrupt practice under section 123(2) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. The first respondent challenged the election of the appellant before the High Court on various grounds. The High Court held that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the trial judge was satisfied that the appellant had been personally responsible for the distribution of the first pamphlet and as such found him guilty of corrupt practice. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the High court was not justified in quashing the order of the trial court under article 226 of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The election petitioner had been rightly convicted by the High 'Court. [975 D] (ii) The first question was whether the appellant proved guilty of a corrupt practice and if so, what punishment should be imposed on him. It is not necessary to decide that question in this case because the trial Judge had jurisdiction to call these two persons as witnesses under the provisions of the Act. [936 G H] (iii) The High ' Court was not called upon to go into this question. There was no evidence on which the judge could have come to the conclusion he did, The first point therefore fails. [981 C D] In the present case, the appellant knew exactly what points he had to meet and evidence was adduced about the publication and distribution of pamphlet by the respondent. It was not for the High Courts to take a different view in exercising jurisdiction under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitu tion. [980 G H; 981 A B] (iv) The allegations of corrupt practices were of a serious nature and if the appellant was found guilty of the commission thereof, the period of five years ' disqualification would certainly not be inappropriate. [979 F G] (v) The allegation that he was responsible for its distribution was not proved by any reliable evidence. The appellant could have had a real cause for grievance if he had asked for an opportunity to rebut the evidence of these two witnesses and had been denied the same but this had not been done. [978 C D]. R. V. P.S. vs Moulanappa, ; , referred to. (vi) The appellant knew how many points he bad to meet.

The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute. In exercise of its powers under section 3 of the Act, the Governor of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification dated March 31, 1956, imposing a tax of six pies in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute to be taxed at such rate not exceeding one anna per rupee as may be specified by the Government. The petitioner challenged the validity of this notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 286(2) of the Constitution, and that the validation Act was beyond the competence of the legislature. Held, that the Validation Act was intra vires the State legislature as it had not been passed by a competent legislature within the meaning of Entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The impugned notification was therefore ultra vires. The Province of Madras vs Boddu Paidanna and Sons (Madras) Ltd., ; , followed. Held further, that there is no substance in the contention that the validating Act is not ultra vires, because it is a law which has been passed after the enactment of the impugned Act. The State Legislature derives its authority to enact a law with respect to tax on sales of goods under entry 54 in the Union List and the competence to enact such a law is plenary and unrestricted subject only to any limitation imposed by the Constitution; that the power conferred on the legislature to impose a tax thereon is plenary, subject onlyto any limitation which the Constitution might impose, and in the exercise of that power it will be competent for the legislature under Entry 54 to enact the law with retrospective operation. The fact that the impugned notification did not purport to make any change in the situation and that it purported to have been issued by a subsequent notification did no affect the competence or the validity Of the Validation act. The question whether the validation was valid or not was one of fact. The expression "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of the Amending Act" in section 3 must be read as qualifying the word "notifications". The State legislature could not have intended to make a law retrospectively. The power conferred by the impugned section on the Government of Uttar pradesh under article 19(1)(f) was a legislative power and such a power could not be exercised with retrospective effect. The Union of India vs Madan Gopal, ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted for the offence of theft and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the sentence imposed on him was not a "habitual" and had no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, barbaricisation, criminal companionship, versatile vices through bio environmental pollution, dehumanised cell drill under 'zoological ' conditions and emergence, at the time of release, of an embittered enemy of society and its values with an indelible stigma as convict stamped on him a potentially good person 'successfully" processed into a hardened delinquent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The sentence imposed by the Sessions Court and confirmed by the High Court is not excessive. [591F] 2.2 In the instant case, the offence committed by the appellant was beyond doubt and he had no sinful antecedents except that of this furillance. He has a young wife and a farm to look after. Given correctional courses through meditational therapy and other measures, his erotic aberration may wither away. A man like the appellant has a reasonable prospect of shaping into a balanced person, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or of reformatory self expression. [592G H] 2:3. The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, queer or orders, the young appellant turns a new book of normal life. [593H; 592A B] Sunil Batra 's case and later that, the incriminating company of lifers and others for long may be counter productive, and in this perspective, it cannot judicial cognizance. The present case is not one of sentencing sentences. [594C D] Sunil Neeti sapiens cannot be deprivates on a lesser offence given propatious social felonisement thanks to the penal illiteracy of the prison system. [595D E] Sunil, Batra ' s case and another vs State of Haryana, ; , referred to.

The respondent assessee was a limited company dealing in land. It maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the , certain plots of land were requisitioned by the Government for public purpose and the compensation payable to the assessee was enhanced by Rs.5,13,624 on March 31, 1956. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable in respect of the said plots. The respondent challenged before the Arbitrator the award on the ground that the income accrued to him on the date of the award. The arbitrator held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assesses and therefore a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax. The Arbitrator also held that it was a trading receipts of the company and was therefore a trading expenditure of the appellant. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Arbitrator. In further appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, the High Court held that compensation received on the basis of the permanent acquisition of the land was the Stock in trade and therefore, the receipt of compensation was not taxable in the assessment year 1956 57. The High Court also rejected the contention of the respondent that the amount of compensation received was not a receipt by the appellant as its income during the previous year ended March 31 1956 relevant to the assessment years 1956 57 and 1959 58. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the sum of compensation which was received by it related to acquisition of lands which were stock in trading trade of tile assessee and therefore the receipt could not be said to have accrued to it as income during that previous year ending March 31. 1956 relevant for the assessment of tax in which he had included the initial compensation awarded by the Collector and recompute the entire income on the footing that the Income tax Officer had received the initial amount of Rs, 24,97249. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law was explained in the judgment of this Court in Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Deputy Land Acquisition officer & Anr., [1962] 1 SCR 676 and Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat, ; , referred to. 2.1 The High court is right in the view taken by it and, therefore. this appeal must be dismissed. [395C D] 2.2 In the instant case, the award was made by the Arbitrator on July 29, 1955 enhancing the amount by Rs 5,13.624. On receipt of this amount, the entire amount was in dispute in the appeal filed by the State Government. Indeed, the dispute was regarded by the Court as real and substantial, because the assessee had not permitted to withdraw the sum deposited by the state Government on April 25, 1956 without furnishing a security bond for refunding the amount in the event of the appeal being allowed. There is no absolute right to receive the amount at that stage. If the appeal was allowed in its entirety the right to payment of the enhanced compensation would have fallen entirely. [396D E] 2:3 The High Courts were called upon to decide without the right of receiving the enhanced compensa tion under the Land Acquisition Act accrued or arose to the asses see when he sought a reference under section 18 of the Act or when the award is made by it, as the award itself was an award and substantial.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the appellants on the ground that they had been in possession of the shop as tenants. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal was also dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The language of section 12(1) says that where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise, the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit. If the agreement or the compromise for the eviction of a tenant is found, on the facts of a particular case, to be in violation of a specified Rent Restriction Act, the court would refuse to record the compromise as it will not be a lawful agreement. [882 D E] (2) The words "in any other suit" occurring in section 12 (1)(f) are clear and definite especially in the background of the pleadings of the parties and in our opinion, it squarely makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of section 13(11). [883 F G] (3) The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the context of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree for eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances, is entitled to have such a decree under the law. It is too late in the day to contend that the provisions Of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [888 F G; 883 A] (4) The expression "in respect of the first part" in section 2(1)(g) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 means that where a tenant has been found to have been in violation thereof, he is entitled under the general law or a statute.

The assessee was a limited company doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. For the assessment year 1955 56, the Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs. 11,88,000/ out of this loss on the ground that it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the Elphinstone Mills Ltd., and that the company suffered a net loss of Rs 11,63,874/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that under the circumstances the Directors were justified in not declaring any dividend in respect of those years. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss and that it could not be taken into consideration in computing its income for the assessment years 1956 57 and 1957 58. In reference, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The loss any reasonable body of Directors of a company would have done just what the Directors of the company did. [864 C] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. , referred to. (ii) In view of the fact that the Directors had suffered a capital losses of Rs 12 lakhs/ it was not open for the Income Tax Officer to constitute himself as a super director. [874 D] Commissioner Of Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., ; , applied. Commissioner of Incometax, WestBengal vs Gangadhar Behera, , referred. (iii) The High Court erred in holding that the assessee had suffered an unjust loss of a capital sum of Rs 2 lakhs and that there was no occasion to take note of the depreciation in the value of the shares in the matter of declaration of dividends. [884 D E] Commissioner, Income tax & Excess Profits Tax vs Williamsons Ltd., , referred C.I.T. vs Williams on Diamond 's Ltd. , distinguished. (iv) The assessee had not in fact incurred any loss though the value was less than that declared by a company. In view Of the fact, there could be hardly any doubt that the appellant had suffered any loss because of the loss sustained by it.

The Consolidation Officer acting under section 12(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, referred the question of title to the Civil Judge for determination. The Civil Judge overruled the objection and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the award. On appeal by special leave, Held, that section 37 of the Act applies only to arbitrations under the consolidation of Holdings. Section 37 does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15 of the . Further, the effect of section 46 and section 47 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations. The effect of s.46 read with sections 46 and 47 of the , is inter alia to apply sections 15 and 39 of the to the proceedings under the Act. Section 18 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holding of Holdings Rules, 1954 provides for appeals against orders of the civil judge. Section 12(6) of that Act does not provide anything inconsistent with this. In the present case, the High Court was right in holding that the decision of the District Judge modifying the Award was appealable under section 39 of that act. Attar Singh vs The State of U. P., ; , followed. Attara Ram vs Civil Judge, Farrukhbad, A.I.R. 1959 All 65 and Hazari Lal vs Badri Prasad, A,I.L.R, 1959 Punj. 1, approved. Attari Ram vs The Temporary Civil Judge of Sultanpur, A.,I. L. R. , referred to. In view of the fact that section 12 (6) was applicable to arbitrations, the provisions Of section 15 and section 39 were not applicable to arbitration proceedings under section 13(4). The effect is that the decisions of the High Courts modifying the awards were appealable under s.39 of the ; and the appeal must accordingly fail. Attri Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh, A,.I. R., 1959 Pun j. 1. 67, referred to, Per Sarkar, J. Section 13(6), of the United Provinces Tenancy Act, 1939, does not apply to arbitration under section 15, and section 37 is not applicable for a statutory arbitration.

The petitioner, a diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation, was appointed as Executive Engineer by the respondent corporation. Till 1974 he was holding the post for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. In 1974, the corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner challenged the said regulations on the ground that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent Corporation is a mere resolution or an executive instruction could not effect such discrimination. [782C] 1.2 In the absence of rules or regulations, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till 1988 by the impugned resolution. The proposition that in the absence Of the rules and regulations, it can be made only a statutory rule or regulation framed under section 64 of the said Act, cannot be accepted since the creation of selection grade in the same category on the strength of their qualification is permissible. [781E F] 1:3. In the instant case, the respondent Board was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. However, since respondent No. 2 was a Degree holder, his promotion was not in accordance with law and was also sought to be done since 1988 by virtue of the resolution. [780F G] 1 :4.
