The principle that for the purposes of promotion, a valid classification can made among members holding the same post on the date of their qualifications is well known and permissible. The respondent Board, therefore, cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this was what was meant till the year 1988 and was further considered to be a statutory Rule or regulation. [779G H] 1 5. The position that in State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao, ; , a Constitution Bench of this Court has clearly held that such a classification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.

The first petitioner, a practising advocate, filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution for a mandamus to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies in the Bombay High Court. The Union of india, on being satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not making the applications within time, filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the same. The High Court dismissed the petition and held that the ratio laid down by this Court in S.P. Gupta 's case was applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The Chief Justice of India is a matter for immediate attention of all concerned and of Government in particular that the need is recognised and administration of justice is ensured. [448C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Chief Justice has quite often both before the Parliament and outside has stated that it has, as matter of policy, not made any appointments to the superior judiciary without the name being cleared by the Chief Minister through the Governor of the State. This is to be done by a judicial recognition of the standard with a concomitant legal and constitutional obligation for the executive to adopt and apply the standard. [459D] 1:3. The Chief justice of India, the chief Justice of the States and the Chief Justices of the High Courts are both in position. In view of what is stated above, it is clear that the primacy of the Chief justice in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. The primacy of a Chief Justice in the exercise of his functions under the Constitution is an over simplification of a sensitive and subtle constitutional sentence and if allowed foul play, would be subversive of the doctrine of judicial independence. [460E F] 1 :4. The judiciary has been given the status and importance of the executive Government. There are unanimity amongst the members of the Executive in the Council of Ministers of the Union and the States. It is, therefore, necessary to have a look at the matter only if the Chief Secretary of the concerned High Court has recommended and recommended that the case be referred to a Chief Minister for initial appointment. [461E F; 462A] 1 5. The executive power of the Central Government is vested in the President of India under Article 239(1) of the constitution. It would therefore, be open to the Central Govern ment to over ride the opinion given by the constitutional function aries required to be consulted and to arrive at its own decision in regard to the appointment of a Judge in the High Court or the Supreme Court. [463B C] 1 6. The responsibility of the administration of the judiciary is that of the highest executive, which is empowered by the Constitution to appoint Judges of the Supreme Courts. It has been recognised and established that the role of the institution of the chief justice of the country is expected to be respected and exercised in the matter of appointments to a High Court and the High court of the states would be at liberty to take such decision as it may think fit in the matters of appointments, if any, of the Judges. [462C D] 1 7. The independence of the Judiciary is an important component of the independence of judiciary. It cannot be said that the Chief Judge of India has been giving any position of primacy amongst the three persons who have to be consulted under Article 217(1). [463E F]. 8. The appointment of Judges in the Supreme court and the Supreme Civil Service are not justiciable.

The respondent was serving as a Reve nue Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the appellant Bank. He was served with a memo dated August 1, 1978 by the Divisional Office of the Bank calling for his explanation and thereafter, on March 27, 1979, he was served a letter dated January 23, 1979 asking him to furnish details of persons who traveled and the amounts received by him from various sources including the appellant. The respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978 which was not found satisfactory. Thereupon, the respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his dismissal. A Single Judge of the High court allowed the writ petition holding that on retirement of the respondent, he had no right to impose punishment on him and hence the order imposing punishment was clearly incompetent and without jurisdiction. The Division Bench also held that since the appellant had submitted to the jurisdiction of Shri U.B. Menon, the initial defect, if any, stood removed and without juris diction. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Officer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the said enquiry conducted by the said Enquiry Officer. [204C] 1.2 In the facts and circumstances of this case, the course suggested by Shri Shetye could be usefully adopted. The appellant 's attitude was not a mere official but a bank employee for that matter an ex employee. The High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of punishment but it should not have ordered payment of all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned orders were bad in law. [205E] 1:3. In the instant case, there is no merit in this contention. The order of removal got merged in the appellate order, and the appellant was informed about his retirement. It is only after he had retired from service that he proceeded with the enquiry. Therefore, the High Courts were right in holding that the order passed by the disciplinary authority was not valid. [206F] 1st Respondent 's appointment as an Enquiry Officer de facto was valid. The re spondent did not deny any bias and mala fides. He could not be described as a person occupying or being in possession of an office to which certain duties affecting the members of the general public can be said to be attached.

The respondents were owners of a building in the mainkhadabad, Delhi. The appellant Corporation had taken on lease for its construction of a new construction and required urgent and extensive repairs. A dispute arose as to whether the proposal was under acquisition and also affected by road widening. The respondents submitted their applications to the Commissioner for approval of the plan. The Commissioner declined to accord sanction. The appellants ' writ petition challenging the order of the Commissioner refusing permission was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Master Plan prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Development Act 1957 had statutory force and that the Commissioner could not refuse sanction for the erection of a road without complying with the provisions of section 336(2) or section 340 of the Corporation Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Commissioner has to give sanction for erection of any building or work in that zone otherwise than in conformity with the Master plan. [173E] (a) The purpose of the Development Act is to provide for the development of Delhi according to plan and for matters ancillary thereto. Section 3(2)(a) provides for the preparation of a Zonal Development Plan simultaneously with the preparation thereof or as soon as may be thereafter, and section 14 provides for a complete outline of the land in each zone. The purpose is not envisaged either by the Master plans or the provisions thereof. [172F] (b) Section 3 of the Act provides that after the commencement of the . the Authority shall proceed with the preparing of a zonal development plan for each of the zones into which Delhi may be divided, and also refer to the various matters which are to be indicated in the same. The Master Plan and the two maps relied on by the appellant do not give any indication that any part of the property belonging to the respondents will be covered by the proposed road or portion of a roads. [171F] In the instant case, the Master Plans have been prepared under Section 7 of Delhi Development act 1957 and it has also come into force as contemplated by section 11. The provisions of Section 7 are in no way indicated by the various matter mentioned in the Master Planning and the zonal development Plan. [174G H] (c) The respondents ' lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part or definite use of land for roads, that is, in conformity to the Master Development Plan or as early as may hereafter be thereafter. [175A B] (d) The provisions under Section 8(2), which, according to them, are in the nature of a preliminary force, have no application to the facts and circumstances of this case. [176F G] (e) The High Court was perfectly justified in issuing the writ of mandamus. [177D] (f) The appellant will pay the costs of the respondents.

The appellant No. 1 was charged with having committed an offence under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and the appellant No 2 was charged under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for having committed offences under section 165A, 165A and 165B of the Penal Code. The Additional District Magistrate acquitted both the appellants but convicted them under section 5(1) (d) read with section 5 (2) Of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On appeal by the appellant no. 1 the Judicial Commissioner set aside his conviction and sentence on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and that there was no evidence in support of the prosecution case against him. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellants No. 2 and convicted them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant No 1 was asked by the police authorities to make the statements to these two witnesses not with a view to avoid the bar of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code or by way of colourable device but by way Of greater caution particularly having regard to the fact that the appellant NO. 2 was asked to make his statement to those two witnesses who were in their turn required to depose to matters transacted by them in their official capacity unregulated by any statutory rules of procedure or conduct whatever. [1115 D E] (ii) The evidence of these witnesses being so strong and satisfactory it could not be said that they had been suffering from any lapse of memory. The evidence was thus worthy of credit and the statements made to them were inadmissible in evidence. [1216 F G] (iii) The statement made by the appellants to the two witnesses was admissible under section 164 Of the Code. [1317 C D] (iv) The statements made by these two persons to the police were not voluntary and were therefore inadmissible in nature. [1517 E] In the present case, the evidence of the two eye witnesses being highly unsatisfactory it could be safely inferred that they were suffering from serious infirmity. [1617 F G]. (v) The High court was right in holding that the statements were admissible under s. 164 Of Cr. P.C. and the conviction of the appellant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 must be set aside.

The respondent was serving as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the appellant along with the Head Constable, and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge against the appellant was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. He was acquitted by the trial court but the suit was decreed in his favour. In appeal, the High Court set aside the decree of the first appellate court and remitted the case to it for fresh disposal according to law. On remand, the suit filed by the respondent was allowed. The appellant appealed against the decision of the High court which dismissed the same on the ground that the second respondent had failed to prove the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the question involved in the suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Courts in limine. It has been argued on behalf of the appellants that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the grounds that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. [825F G] 1.2 In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the Court is permitted to take a decision in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. The defendant appellants filed a regular second appeal before the High COurt against the decree passed by the first Appellate court which was dismissed at the admission stage by merely saving the order of the trial Court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions, and not the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. After heating the learned counsel for the parties, it is clear that the question raised in this appeal should not be lightly brushed down by the Court. [826F G; 826A B] 2.1 The question involved was whether the suit is barred by limitation and whether the order passed on the basis of the judgment of the Trial Court is void on the view that in case of other members of the Police force a wrong decision is taken, it would not preclude the authority to award a minor punishment provided such a punishment has been awarded to the other police officials tried and con victed along with him. [827B C] 2:2 In this case, since the order was passed by an authority not in this regard, and while no further punishment was awarded to any of the respondent, the respondent 's service stands terminated. The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The respondent entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee entered into a contract with the mills for purchase of coal from various parties after paying full price of the goods covered by the delivery orders and transferred those P.D.Os. to buyers after receiving the price fixed for the sale of those goods. The assessee had no godown for keeping the goods and had not handled them. The goods were in the godown of the mills and only the delivery order addressed to the mills changed hands. The amount realised on sale to M/s. Lachhminarain Kenia Mills was credited to the price of goods covered under the delivery Orders and transferred these P. D.Os to buyers. The appellant claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In further appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was only one sale and the delivery was appropriated to the contract so that there could be no completed sale since no property passed but only an agreement for sale. The High Court held that this case came within the scope of section 24(1) read with Explanation 2 and restored the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Courts have correctly stated in their judgment that the property in the goods passed to the ultimate endorsee of the delivery Order went to feed their previously defective titles and ensured to their benefit. His Lordship further observed that this was a correct statement of law. [184 D] Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, ; , followed. (ii) The question whether on the facts of the case there were two separate transactions of sale so as to bring them to charge under section 3 of the Act was not relevant for the purpose of this explanation. A transaction which is otherwise speculative would not be a speculative transaction within the meaning of Explanation 2 if actual delivery of the commodity or the scrips has taken place; on the other hand, a transaction which was not otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery meaning to that expressing for purposes of income tax only.

The appellant was declared elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that he had not been validly nominated and that he was unable to contest the election. The Election Tribunal decided in his favour by a majority, but it held that without "attestation" they were invalid and so rejected them. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the word "subscribe" used in section 33 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, is not defined in the General Clauses Act and therefore the word 'subscribes ' has to be given its ordinary meaning. The word " substitutes" is not used in various senses to indicate different modes of signing and that it includes the placing of a mark. The general words are used in the general sense of the word, but they are not defined. In the General clauses Act, the word is defined as including all names or marks which may be written by an elector in any one of the four nomination papers. The General Clauses Acts also provide for the attestation of certain signatures and the making of a marking. The words "subscribers" have to be read ejusdem generis with the word ,and they are used only in the sense of making a signature and as the Act tells us quite clearly how the different types of " signatures" are to be made, it is clear that the words "sign" and "subscribed" are not used. The use of the words 'sign ' and 'subscribe ' in the case of proposers and seconders who are not able to write their names does not make them technical and unsubs tantial. The provisions of the Act are as necessary and substantial as attestation in the cases of a will or a mortgage and is on the same footing as the originals and it is only when the instrument is necessary that the Registrar can reject them under section 36(4). The General clauses Acts also do not contain any provision for permitting the use of a signature. The requirements of section 33 are mandatory and require the Returning Officer to refuse any nomination when there has been " any failure to comply with any of the provisions of section 32. The Returning Officer rightly rejected these nomination papers because there was a failure to compliance with section 33, unless he could and should have had resort to section 36 (4).

The appellants were employees of the respondent company. During the pendency of the dispute relating to the re instatement of three of the union leaders who had been dismissed by the Company, the company put up a notice stating that the strike embarked upon by the workmen was illegal and those participating in the strike were liable to disciplinary action for misconduct as per company 's certified standing orders Nos. 22(b) and 24(a). The appellants submitted their explanations and thereafter filed a complaint before the Industrial Tribunal alleging that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal, and that they had not abandoned their service and that there were interested parties to the dispute. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned their services and therefore, their names had been struck off from the muster rolls of the company. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the act of the management in removing them from its roll was illegal as they had failed to resume duty and that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the Board 's standing orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service, the appellants were entitled to relief. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The action of respondent No. 2 in removing those names from its records was illegal. [616D] 2.1 The period stretches over six years and Shri Sachine Chaudhary brings to our notice that back wages have to be computed if ordered in full, on a much higher scale because of two settlements which had raised the scales of wages substantially. While there is no case specifically put forward that the workmen concerned have been employed elsewhere during this period, still we take a total view that their being no provision in the certified standing order by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the services of the appel lants in the aforesaid circumstances, the impugned action on the part of the Respondent No. 1 clearly amounted to a change in the condition of service of the Appellants during the admitted pendency of industrial dispute before the Labour Court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced. [625E F] 2:2. The period stretch over six year and Shri S.D. Majumdar brings to your notice that the back wages has to be determined if ordered by the Tribunal in full. [716B C] 3.1 In the instant case, the period stretching over six months and Shri Sahoo went on indefinite strike which ended on October 22, 1972 in response to the strike notice given by the union to the Company to press its demand for re instatedment of its three dismissed leaders and had not only by their letters dated September 21, 1972 and September 26, 1972 unequivocally intimated to the company that they did not intend to abandon the service but had also returned the cheques sent to them by the company on account of their leave salary gratuity etc. The appellants ' contention that the letter of the said company dated September 7, 1972 was received by them on September 20, 1972 is not correct. [613E F; 614A] 3:2 It may be recalled that the Company did not refute the averment made by the appellants in their letter dated September 26. 1972 that passed between the parties. The Company 's action was manifestly illegal and invalid. [512C D] 4.1 There is no substance in the contention of the respondents that the failure to perform the duties pertaining to the office must be with actual or imputed intention, on the face of the surrounding circumstances of each case. [641D] Gopal Chandra Misra vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees executed a trust deed in March 1950, in favour of the appellant for securing repayment of certain sums which were due to him from the trustees. The appellant filed an application under 0. 21 r. 89 C.P.C., for setting aside the sale and deposited Rs. 250 as security for payment to the appellant. The trial court passed a decree against the trustees directing them to execute the sale deed and also to pay interest at 6% per annum from the date of the decree till realisation. In appeal, the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r.89 C. P.C. the executing court had no jurisdiction to set aside the said sale. The High Court in revision held that the appellant was not entitled to commence fresh proceedings for setting it aside on the ground that the trustees were guilty of a breach of trust under an English mortgage executed by the trustees or a sale in terms of a consent decree. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the High Court had no power to set at naught a mortgage decree passed by a court of competent jurisdiction and (ii) the executing Court had not acted illegally or with material irregularity in not deciding the question. HELD: (1) The High Courts have held that under 0 21 r 89 C, P.P., the appellant is entitled to start fresh proceedings as he has failed to do so. [459 E] (2) The expression "sale" in section 54(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1913, includes a sale of the property of a Public Trust in execution of a decree. It does not mean that the sale of property is by itself or of a Division Bench of a Court of Record. [460 E] In the present case, the trustees ' agreement of mortgage was binding on the appellant and the High Courts had no authority to refer the matter to the Full Bench for determination of a question of law arising before them. The appeal must accordingly be allowed. (3) The executing court was right in holding that the requirements under 0, 21 r, 89 C were not complied with. [461 G] (4) The appellant 's contention that the mortgagee having agreed to abandon execution proceedings and to wait for six months for receiving payment of the mortgage dues from the trustee, the condition requiring the judgment debtor to deposit in Court for payment of interest was not fulfilled. The first condition was fulfilled by the appellant before the High court. [463 B] (5) The question whether a precedent of a court is binding reference to section 165 of the Evidence Act is irrelevant. It is irrelevant if the decision of a Full Bench of the High, Court falls to be considered indirectly in this case.

The appellant, who was a clerk in the Post Office of the Director Postal Services, was compulsorily retired from service under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of retirement on the ground that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) and as such the appellant was not entitled to retire at any time after he had completed 30 years of qualifying service. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that there is no in Firmity in rule 2(1) of Pension Rules, 1950 which permits compulsory retirement of a Government servant in public interest after he has completed 30 year of qualifying serv ice. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 2 of the pension Rules on the other hand provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government to retire a government servant at anytime after he was in completed 30 yew years of service. [802C] 2. The object of Rule 2 is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 1(2), however, provides no guidelines for compulsory retirement. A bare reading of the memorandum shows that there has been an obvious fallacy in the argument of the appellant that it does not contain anything to Rule 2. (802D) 3. The Memorandum dated November 30, 1962 is in the nature of executive instructions and is identical with Fundamental Rule 56(j). [803E F] 4. The words "weed out unsuit able employees" can only be read qua the power to retire under para 6 and not under Rule 1 (2). There is thus no force in the contention that the Government of India has issued instruc tions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule. 2(3) of pension Rules can only he exercised to weed out unsuitable employees. [800F G] 5. The instructions being supplementary to the Rule, according to him, the order is not ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. [900G H] 6. The Government has issued instructions dated July II, 1955 which laid down that retirement under rule 2 (1) shall be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interests. The instruction being supplementary must be understood in the sense of a sufficient safeguard against the arbitrary exercise of power by the Government. [902C D] 7. Rule 2046 is a statutory rule and is similar to Fundamental Rule, 56(J). Para 620 of the Manual being executive instructions cannot be supplemented by the execu tive instructions but a statutory provision which is inconsistent with it. The Instructions can only supplement and not supplant the rule. [702D E] 8. The rules are consistent with the Rules. [ 801E F].

The assessee firm was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The income tax authorities held that the assessee was entitled to set off in respect of the deficiency in the year 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable accounting period from 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1944. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order but the Tribunal held that there was no profit attributable to the said chargeable accounting periods and therefore the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency of the said two chargeable accounting years. On a reference made by the High Court under section 66(1) of the Act, the High court held that it was not disputed before them that the business carried on in Nepal on or about 23rd November 1942 and that the sales took place in the next year. The High Court also held that since the chargeable assessment period was the same as in 1940 41 and the deficiency was attributable to manufacturing activity alone, there were no sales during the chargeable account years ending 31st December, 1939 and 31st April 1943. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had wrongly taken the view that since chargeable accountingperiod was the previous year ending 31th March, 1943, the profits earned by the assessee in his business at Raichur were subsequently sold to the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The concept of "accounting period" in the background of the case is possible and the true excess profits, if any, as contemplated by the Act be deter mined. [608C] 2. The term "accountant ' has been defined under section 2(2) which was required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 6 of the Income Tax Act. Section 2(6) defines "chargeable accounting period" to mean a period beginning on the 1st day of September, 1939 ending after amendment on 31st day, 1946. So if there is any deficiency of profits in any particular period it must be determined on that basis. [613D E] 3. The expression "accountal period" is not permissible when one part of the transaction, i.e., manufacture, fails in one chargeable accounting Period and falls in another part of a accounting period, then set off of defi cution in profits under section 7 of the Indian Income Tax Acts is permitted but a necessary pre condition was that profit must be made in the accounting period to which the adventure during the relevant chargeable accounting year must be computed on the basis of the accounting periods. This has to be done by the Court and it must not be borne in mind that though it is wholly immaterial whether the manu facture and sale took place during the previous accounting period or in two different years, the division of time into periods for its assessment must be held to be a single business for the purpose of the income tax. [508C D] 4. The principle of apportionment of profits or gain, and those only enter into the computation which are earned or ascertained in the years to which an accounting period relates, is not permitted when one parts of the transactions, i .e., manu factsure, fail in one taxable accounting period and fall in another, but where the profits arose during the accounting year, and as such whether the deficiency must be set off without computation. [511D E; G H] 5.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department, as per notification dated 16th May 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the State Government (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, among others, the names of candidates who had qualified in Civil engineering or Mechanical engineering of the K University or their equivalent as provided by the Special Rules of the Government of Kerala. The applicants were also interviewed in the same manner. The Public Service Commis sioner and the K PSC selected the candidates holding civil and Mechanical Engineering degrees. The respondents, who were qualified in civil engineering, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the judgment of the Division Bench of the High court. The learned Single Judge allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare two separate lists for Civil and Mechanical Engineers. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the K.PSC had advised candidates according to the separate list for Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engi nees and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had obtained civil engineering degree. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Kerala Public Services Commission is not directed to prepare a common list. Common List was referred to in the earlier orders in this Court through certain misapprehensions. The KP SC has stated in its counter affidavit that there were directions to the KPsSC to prepare separate lists. But facing difficulties, in view of the observations of this Court in its order dated 23rd April 1980, the State of Kerala filed a petition before this Court for clarification. This Court by its order dt. 23rd March, 1979 dismissed all the S.L.P. with directions. [747G H; 748A] 1.2 The K P.SC has advised candidates in the Kerala Engineering Service (Mechanical Branch) to prepare three separate rank lists one for Civil Judge and the Mechanical Engineer candidates. The name of Gopa Kumar appears in the latter list. The rank list for Engineering (Civil) contains names of 152 candidates and the other (Mechanical) contains 204 candidates. All the Civil Engineering selected have already been appointed. [750H; 749A B] 1:3. The Kerala Government or the KpSC was not directed, to prepare the common list, but facing difficulties in giving effect to the directions given by the High Courts. The State of Karnataka filed a writ petition before the Division bench of the Public Service Tribunal challenging the order of the learned Single judge and directing the Government and the Public Services Commis tions to prepare one separate rank list on the basis of examination already conducted. The High Court dismissed all these petitions. [751C D] 1 :4. The special leave petitions are dismissed.

The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts. The appellant defendant No. 1 contested the suit on the ground that the correct value of the suit was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had no interest in the firm. In appeal, the High Court held that the valuation of the business was beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff respondent No. 2 is a partner of a partnership firm along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The plaintiff has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under estimates the relief the court is entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation given by the plaintiff and to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. [511B C] 1.2 The High Court while repelling the argument that the suit is governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the court Fees Act, and not by section 8(iv) (f). The plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. In such a case it is not only open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valuation. [512C D] 1:3. There is no doubt that in a suit of accounts, the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is neither possible nor manifestly inadequate for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, AIR 1936 Bombay 166, relied on. 1.4 The plaintiff non applicant before the High court filed a civil revision application before the Calcutta High Court which was dis missed by the High COurt. The defendant No 2 has not challenged the valuation made by the appellant before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1932 Bombay 166 and Ishwarappa vs Dhanji, AIR 1929 Bombay 166. [ 512C D]. 1.5 In the instant case, the plaintiff non applicants before the trial court were not given the exclusive right or choice to place a valuation whatever they on such Relief and where their plaintiff manifestly & deliberately under estimate the relief, the Court is entitled only to examine its correctness of valuation chosen, but he cannot act arbitrary in this matters.

The respondents in these appeals were manufacturers of various products in the State. The respondents in the other two cases were manufacturing and selling industrial units. In the writ petitions filed by them before the High Court, the High Courts held that the exemption sought for was originally granted but subsequently revoked. However, the State Government issued a notification dated 1 9 1983 exempting certain categories of dealers from payment of sales tax. The High Court took the view that these rules and instructions had no relevance to the claim for exemption put forward under the notifica tion of 23 10 1981. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that the High court had refused to grant the benefit of the notification on the ground that the industries run by them were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the industries running in any of the two categories specified in column (1) or in column 2 of the said Notification are entitled to exemption under it only some of those units which do not fall under rule 14 of the defer ment notification would be the position in regard to the exemption provision also. [610C D] 1.2 The High Courts have rightly pointed out that the question of grant of eligibility certificate by the Industries Department is not an empty formality but before granting the certificate, the Industries department has to see whether all the requirements as laid down in the notification are fulfilled and complied with or not. But, it is open to the State Govern ment particularly in view of section 22D of the Act to frame such scheme for the purpose as it may deem fit. [625E F] 1:3. The State intended the exemption to be availed of by certain categories only some other non traditional units operating in certain situations. In view of this interpretation, the 1987 amendment has the effect of rescinding the exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect of the industries mentioned by it. Section 12 is clear that while a notification under it can be prospective or retrospective, only prospective operation can be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier. [510G H] 1 :4. The two notifications are clear and envisage no denial of exemption to traditional indus tries, this question does not survive. [613H; 614A] 1.(a) The High court has rightly pointed that the State intended to exempt the class of dealers who opt for the alternative concession of deferment of payment of tax, a special provision in the shape of section 23 D has been inserted in the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act 1958 with effect from 1st April 1981.

The petitioners were Judicial Officers of Delhi. They were promoted to the service in consultation with the High Court. The seniority list was prepared on the basis that the rule of "quota and rota" had been applied to them by Rule 7(a) of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1954. The petitioners challenged the validity of the seniority list on the ground that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District and Sessions Judges and that the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined according to the respective date of their actual officiating service, that the direct recruits appointed to the Service in consultationwith the High Courts were not senior to direct recruits and that direct recruits who were appointed as Additional district and Sessions judges after the promotees were so appointed cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that seniority has to be determined by the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the date from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Service or in substantive vacancies to which they are appointed in a temporary capacity. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The inter se seniority of members of Delhi Judicial Service promoted to service shall be the same as in the Delhi Judicial Services. [395G] 2.1 Rule 7 of the Rules and the Constitution is not intended to apply when appointments are made under Rules 16 and 17. It is only when they are appointment in a substantive capacity to a post in the service that they become members of the Service. The rule of 'quota ' does not use the negative language as the proviso to Rule 7. [397A B] 2:2 In the instant case, the members of tho Judicial Service, the petitioners had made representations to the High court and the High courts. They have also made representations in this regard. The rules deal with position between direct recruits on one hand and promotees appointed to temporary posts of Additional District & Sessions Judges on an ad hoc basis or for fortuitous reasons or by way of a stop gap arrangement. [398C D] 2 :3 Rule 8(2) which provides that seniority of the members shall be fixed in accordance therewith, does not provide for any quota for direct recruits. The quota rule is intended to ensure that there is no reservation for direct recruit and promotees. It only enables the appointment of direct recruitment to substantive vacancies in the cadre on a temporary basis. But, before adverting to this principle, it would be useful to draw attention to Rule 8 (2) of Delhi Higher judicial Service Rules which provides for a rotation of vacancies between direct recruit to the post in a service and promotees based on the quotas of vacancies reserved for both categories by Rule 4(1). [398D E] 2.(a) The seniority of promotees vis avis promotees shall, therefore, be determined on the date on which their appointments are to be made in accordance. with the dates when the direct recruit may be promoted, he would rank lower in seniority than the latter. If a direct recruit is appointed after a member of the service, his seniority will be determined from amongst the members who are appointed to that post and not by promotees only, the quota rule contained in the proviso would apply to simultaneous appointments of direct recruit. [399E F] (b) The principle of "equally important" rule is that seniority should be fixed on the dates of continuous officiation in the Cadre post i.e.

The appellant was a partner in a trading venture conducted by the respondent. The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills to income tax and taxed it under section 3 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. During the pendency of the suit, the Income tax Appellate Tribunal restored the order of assessment of the assessee in respect of the business carried on by Debi Parshad. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The expression 'any person ' in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person intimately connected in the aforesaid sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. "In the present case, the income earned by the assessee was assessed to tax as income of an association of persons. The Tribunal set aside the order assessing the income in the status of 'a firm of individuals and directed that the Income Tax Officer should assess the members individually. [392 D E] Commissioner of Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , followed. Commissioner of Incometax, U P. vs Lucknow Coal syndi ners, , referred to. The expression "any person" in the set off of section 31(3) proviso 2 at p. 346 : "Theexpression 'any ' person in its widest connotation may take in any person, whether connected or not with the assessee whose income for any year has escaped assessment but this construction cannot be accepted for the said expression is necessarily circum scribed by the scope of the subject matter of the appeal or revision as the case may be. [394 E F] Commissioner off Income tax U. P. v Kanpur Coal systi cates, , followed and applied. The words 'any other person ' occurring in section 34(3), proviso 2, at p., 346 : are only illustrative. It is not necessary to pursue the matter further. [395 G H] Commissioner Of Income tax vs Kanpur coal Syndiancate, , distinguished. Commissioner off income tax, Uttar Pradesh vs Kanpur Sugar synde, ; and Commissioner of income tax U P vs Kanpur Mining Syndicate Ltd., , referred. The High Court was right in holding that the expression ' any person ' must be construed strictly. [396 A] Commissioner, Income tax and Prashar & Anr. vs Vasantsen Dwarkadas & Ors., ; , applied.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share and the respondent claimed to have purchased the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it on the ground that the memorandum of appeal should be treated as an order under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The question about the levy of fees in a suit falling under section7(iv) of Act is governed by section 7 of the Madras Court Fees Act and not by section 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court was right in holding that the Memorandum of appeal must be treated to be the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction dependent upon the value as determinable for computation of court fees and that is natural enough. (ii)The question about adequacy of court fee leviable on the appellant 's memorandum of appeals was properly referred by the High Courts under section 5 of the Indian Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1940, to the trial court. The proper court fees were paid on the memorandum and the memorandum was treated as a whole. (iii)The High Court had no power to direct the appellant to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the Memorandum. The question whether the memorandum should be taxed for purposes of court Fees under section 8(iv), is a matter which has to be decided solely by reference to the Act, and it is open to the Division Bench to consider the correctness of the view taken by the Chamber Judge. (iv)The appeal must fail. (v)The Court was not justified in directing the appellant, to pay additional court fees on the basis of the valuation of Rs. 15,00,000. The appellant should have allowed the appellant the amount of court Fee paid for the suit on the strength of the value of Rs., 15,000 and the Memorandum filed on the Original Side of the High court was therefore entitled to be taxed under section 6(iv). (vi)The order under appeal was not a proper one. The appeal must accordingly be allowed. (vii)The appellant should pay additional Court fees on his plaint on the value for purposes Of jurisdiction, and not on the memo of appeal. [1036 C D] (viii)The court fee has to he paid either under section 10 or section 7 (iv)(a) of that Act.

The respondent No. 1, a publisher of Newspapers, had filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the decision of the NDMC to accord sanction for construction of certain multi storeyed high rise buildings on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road, New Delhi. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC not to enforce the revised plans. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the plan for the multi storeys was over 15 years in height and attracts bye law 16.4.8.1, which inter alia provides that if a building scheme is proposed to be framed better and more reliable fire safety measures are necessary, it would be desirable to provide adequate fire safety measure in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The approval by the Chief Fire Officer was not in substitution of the requirement of compliance with the objections raised by the appellant. [608D] 2.1 The clearance from the Chief fire officer envisaged under Bye law 17.4 is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the council to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire insurance measures in accordance therewith or will not be covered in ineligible. [509E] 2(a) The approval of the Chief Executive Fire Officer, which is expected to involve and follow a technical assessment and evaluation, obliges the NDMC, to give due weight to it but having regard to the scheme and language of the Bye laws, the decision taken upon such re construction is not binding on the NDMC. [064F] (b) The clearance by the chief Fire Officer envisaged by bye law 17(1) is an addition to a wall constructed in an interior open space which has been designated as a wall and has further reliable fire insurance measure. The clearance of the chief fire officer contemplated by Bye laws 17.1 is an addi tional condition and cannot be binding on NDMC which can and is entitled to examine the question independently of such clearance from its Chief Fire Officers. [074G] (c) The Clearance by the Executive Fire Officers envisaged by Bye law 16(4) is in addition to the requirements of bye laws 16.5.8, the NDMC would not be precluded from accepting them. Whether the plans submitted by Respondent 1 distributing 'Refuge Areas high rise building on the walls abutting an inner open space would not necessarily depend upon the extent of the size and size of the wall.

The joint family carried on business of a grocery shop, liquor shops and other premises. The parties were living separately in the same house. In 1946, the parties entered into an agreement with the appellant for the purchase of liquor shops, and the parties agreed to have arbitrators appointed by the Court for examining the accounts from 1942 up to March 31, 1946. On June 29, 1945, the appellant filed a suit for partition against the respondent on the ground that the compromise was made after due deliberation, that the parties omitted to provide in the compromise about the future conduct of the motor business and that they stood in the position of co owners and as contemplated by section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act. The trial court held that though the motor bus service was still a joint family business, it had been carried on by some members of a family whose names were not entered in the partnership list. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree holding that the dispute between the parties was different from the cause of action in the previous suit and that the suit was barred under section 90. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent did not want his brothers to interfere with his exclusive running of the liquor business after March 31 1946, but he wanted to settle the matter by mutual agreement. He had no real grievance in the matter for though the parties knew that the business might go on afterwards; but if they were carried on, they did not particularly care for providing by the compromise decree following upon it. [106 E F] (ii) The cause of actions in the subsequent suit was different than the cause for action in a previous suit. The cause was different and the suit must be barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure. [107 B C] (iii) The plaintiff 's claim is barred by the provisions of Order II Rule 2(1). [108 E F]. (iv) The defendant could not have any real grievance against the plaintiff over the motor transport business in the earlier suit, because, he had no legal right to go on a new contract. [108 G H] (v) The mere fact that the plaintiff did not intend that accounts of the Motor Transport business should be taken up to the date of the final decree does not mean that the cause must have arisen during the pendency of the suit or subsequent suit. [109 C D].

The appellant was working as a "manufacturing process" under the Factories Act, 1948. The salt works were carried on in the open and not in the factory. The appellant 's salt works had been covered by the Factory Act of 1948. Under section 2 of the Act, " manufacturing process " includes any process incidental to any kind of work done or done for purposes of gain. Section 3(1) defines "factory" to mean a factory as defined in section 2 and includes a mine subject to the operation of the , or a railway running shed. The factory was not a factory within the meaning of the Factories (Act, 1948). The appellant contended that the salt works did not come within the definition of " manufacturing processes " as no process for making, altering, packing, cleaning or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal was carried on. Held, that the expression " premises" in section 3(i) of the includes not only buildings and that they are not confined to buildings alone but also include buildings which are used for working purposes of profit making. The word "factory " in section 4 of the is a general word which is applicable to both open land and to buildings and its use in this sense is not restricted to buildings. The expression " factory" in the definition includes not merely buildings and does not include buildings but also includes buildings constructed on buildings. In the present case, the appellant was manufacturing sea water water into salt and was using it for purposes other than those mentioned in section 93 of the . The process of converting sea water into a salt was carried out in the Salt Works and described as "manufactured" by the respondent. The process did not amount to manufacture within the term "factory". The appellant had been rightly convicted of the offence of working the factory without obtaining a licence. The State of Kerala vs V. Patel, ; , referred to. Held further, that it was for the first time in the present appeal that the Salt works were covered by Factory Act and the salt Works did not fall within the purview of the definition. The processes carried out by the appellant were not incidental to its manufacturing process but were only ancillary to the manufacture of salt. The use of the word " factory " in the Factories Acts was not restricted or limited to buildings which were not intended for the purpose of manufacturing process. The mere fact that the appellant had admitted sea water did not make it a factory and therefore the salt work did not bring within the expression 'manufacturing ' as defined by section 2(f) of Act.

The respondent was a Instructor of Tailoring in the Department of Technical Education and was working as Instructor in the Polytechnics. In 1949, he was promoted to the post of Instructor in May, 1949. He joined duty there on December 1, 1949, and continued to work there till November 28, 1949 when he was again posted as Instructor. On June 11, 1956, the respondent was reverted to his parent department. The respondent filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of reversion. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellant 's services were not justified and directed the absorption of the respondent in the department of Technical education from the date of his initial appointment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High court was right in holding that he was not similarly situated as K. N. Chetty. He was a junior to him in the parent Department and was identically situated. [259 D] (2) It is well settled that in the matter of absorption of an employee, the State Government has evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department, of Technical Educational Education from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date on which he was initially sent. [260 D E] (3) The grant of relief prayed for by the respondent would have unsettled and caused wholesale alterations of the seniority list with regard to the entire cadre of Engineers thus affecting persons who were not before the Court and who would have been r condemned unheard. Further, acceptance of the petitioners ' contentions would have no relevance in the case of the respondents. [261 F G] (4) The acceptance of respondent 's contention would have rendered wholesale alterations. It is not the appellant that this principle which was ignored in the earlier case had been overlooked in the present case. [262 D E]. (5) In the special circumstances of this case, the High Court was justified in granting the relief to the respondent. [263 G H] (6) The State Government had evolved a rule "that the if a persons was deputed by the Department to the department, of technical Education from other departments and he stay on in the same other department, for a period in 1955 56 could not by any reckoning be treated as a break in his service. This period having been treated as leave, nor did it amount u 'to reduction in rank.

The appellant, a foreign national and the Indian Council of Social Welfare, was recognised as an international agency under the Foreigner 's (Regulation) Act, 1986. The respondent No. 1, a resident of India, filed an application before the Court of Small Causes, Calcutta for appointment of a foreigner as a guardian of a child in adoption. The appellant contended that he had been selected by a recognised social or child welfare agency and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to him since he was a citizen of India under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the Act did not apply to the case as it was enacted directly without the intervention of any court in India, and that it was not open to the foreign parents to make an application for appointment as guardian of the child with a view to its eventual adoption. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The Act does not apply in India. It is only if no Indian family comes forward to take a child on adoption within a maximum period of two months that the child may be regarded as available for inter country adoption subject only to one exception namely that if the child is handicapped or is in bad state of health needing urgent medical attention, which is not possible for the social or children welfare agency looking after the child to provide, the recognised social and child welfare agencies will have to approach a recognised Social or child Welfare Organisation. [842C D] 2. The recognised social, or child interest agency through which an application of a foreign parent for taking a child is made directly without its intervention would be illegal if it wants such child to be given in inter country Adoption. Every recognised social/ child welfare organisation must maintain a proper and satisfactory home study report on which the court can rely. [829D] 3. The recognition of foreign parents by foreign parents need not wait until social or Child welfare agencies are recognised by the Government as directed in this order but pending recognition of social or family welfare agencies for the purpose of inter country appointment of an Indian child may he made to the Court only through such recognised social Or child welfare Agency. [827E] 4. The provisions of Act do not apply even to a foreigner who wishes to take the child in adopt, and the recognised Social/ Child Welfare agency must prepare a child study report for the child so as to help the foreigner to come to a decision whether it will be for the welfare of the children to be provided in adoption to the foreigner desiring to take her in adoption, or to adopt any other person. [826F] 5. The recognized social or the child welfare authority should, on receiving an application from the foreign parent, make sure that the said social or a child education agency will provide moral and material stability and security and whether it would be in the interest of the minor child to serve the child and would be able to handle trans portal problems likely to arise from such adoption. [825F] 6. The Central Government should, with the assistance of the foreign mother, make an order appointing the foreign guardian of such a person as guardian for the children with a direction that the foreigner who wants to take them in adoption shall be given at least two months ' notice before the adoption is effected and it will have no difficulty to give any opportunity to grow into the full position of its personality. [824F] 7. The child in question, if he wants to go to the own country where the procedure for making the adoption in accordance with law has been adopted, would be a suitable parent for the minor children. If the adoptive parents are known, they will have the child study reports and certificates from the child visiting such children. [823G H] 8. The Indian Council has in most cases recognised the application of the foreigner for taking the child into adoption. In some cases where the application is made by a foreign parents for being appointed guardian of their child with leave to remove the child out of India and take it to his own country for the purposes of adopting it in accordance therewith, the child ordinarily resides for being chosen guardian of that parent in which the foreigner resides. [821A B] 9. The application of an foreigner for take a juvenile in adoption is made indirectly without the assistance or permission of the Government of India or the Government or the foreign country of social welfare agencies.

The appellant company was a factory in Bombay. It had branches in Bombay, Ahmedabad and Bangalore. The gross profits of the company were Rs. 48,65,450. The Company claimed that it had kept proper accounts which had been audited by a reputed firm of auditors and that the balance 6% should be deducted from its gross profits as per the profit and loss account. The Tribunal held that the computation of allocable surplus was not properly made in accordance with the Act and that several items shown in the profit & loss account were depreciation and therefore, the amount of Rs. 21,06,576 was not deductible from the gross profits. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was justified in adding back the sum of Rs, 2,65.706 to the gross profit. [114D] (ii) The claim of the appellant that it has been paid back is not sustainable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. The claim for deduction of certain items was postponed by the Tribunal on the ground that the company had not furnished the requisite particulars. The company had produced figures for depreciation and there was no evidence to show that the amount in question was more than Rs. 20,000. [115E] (iii) The appellant could not raise any objection in law to the payment of such amount. The appellant had produced a figures for depre profits and renewals. The balance of profit was only Rs. 50,000 and not Rs.20,000 as awarded by the Industrial Tribunal. [116G H] Management of Northern Railway Co operative Society Ltd. vs Industrial Tribunal Rajasthan etc. ; , referred to. (iv) The payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the company on the grounds of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 36(1). [116H] Management, of Northern railway Co operative Bank Ltd. V. Industrial Tribunal, Rajasthan etc., ; , followed. (v) The workmen would be entitled to bonus at 14.02% of their total salary or wages and the amount will be Rs. 14.76,706 and not the amount awarded by it.

The appellant was a member of the Tamil Nadu General Service officer in 1954. He was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1957 and then as Joint Commercial Tax Officer in 1957. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member, Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that the order of November 29, 1974 of the Government was to grant absolution to the appellant from the repercussions of the note of the Deputy Commissioner, of Commercial Tax, made in 1969. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Government had no power to extend the absolution beyond the period of one year on the ground of administrative exigencies and that the said order was not passed without any prior entry in the service Book to his detriment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is set aside. [771 B] 2. The Government is entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80% of the total length of it, which said; "He is sincere and hard working. He 'manages his office very well. He exercises adequate control over subordinates. He maintains a cordial relationship with public. Because of his stiff attitude some of the assessees complain about him stating that he is rude in his behaviour. [781 C D] 3. The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. He is entitled, if he iseded out altogether from service, to be appointed to a very responsible and much desired post in that cadre, what could have happened between the promotion and the right hand. [761 D E] 4. The State Government was entitled to taking into consideration all history of his including that portion of it. He had attained the age of superannuation on May 7, 1975, and he was promoted to a Selection post much later as a Joint Commercial tax officer in 1962. On May 7 1975, he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d). His service book shows that he had an excellent record of service. He has earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him during the period from May to September 28, 1960, were not justified in his retention for good work. [751 D F] 5. The fact that the appellant was sincere and well within the promoted post did not entitle him to take the benefit of the entire History of the including that aspect of it as prior to the promotion of the respondent. One wonders whether the failure to note the result of the enquiry in the personal file led to the impugned order, is no doubt odd to retire a Government servant a few months after promoting him to a selection post. [772 E F] 6. The effect of the order was blotted out by the promotion. There was an adverse entry in his confidential file of the appel lant in 1969 which said: "He was sincere, hard working". He had earned several valuable and grim situation that he attained the maximum age of SO years or after he has completed 25 years of qualifying service. One more months later, nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is impossible to sustain the order. [777 D E; 778 A B] 7. The respondent was entitled only to take in consideration the whole history of tile appellant including the 1969 entry. All that he could find was some stray mild ing entries such as the one in 1964 which said that he bad done in his conduct. He did not retire a government servant a large number of years earlier and nothing even tact, it was indeed odd to retiring him after his promotion. [779 D E].

The appellants who were the owners of certain routes in the Kumool District of Andhra Pradesh challenged the validity of the schemes framed under Ch. IV A of the , on the ground that they had been issued without complying with the statutory requirements of section 68 C and rule 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Motor Transport Corporation (General) Rules, 1962. The High Court dismissed their petitions holding that the scheme was not in conformity with the requirements of s. 68 C but it was open to the State Government to issue a notification under section 68 D(1) of the Act prohibiting the transport operators from plying their transport vehicles on routes which were liable to be modified or cancelled under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The appellants contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to issue the impugned schemes and the validity thereof was also challenged by way of a writ petition. The contentions were: (1) That the scheme framed by the Corporation was not a law which could have been made applicable to them under Ch, IV A; (2) That it was not the Corporation that formed the opinion indicated in section 68C but really the Chief Minister who had signed the scheme and approved it; (3) That even assuming that the Chief Secretary directed the order in which districts were to be taken up for nationalisation, still the scheme under Ch., IV A could not be assailed as invalid on the grounds of violation of r. 4 of Chapter IV A. HELD: (i) The scheme was valid and did not contravene section 68F(1). [353 B] (ii) The contention that the Corporation had published the schemes in the Gazette for nationalisation of transport services in the western half of the Kurnool District, was without substance because the scheme itself contemplated by section 68E was a violation of section 69 E. [354 C D] (iii) The words "any scheme published under section68C" occurring in Ch. I have to be read as a flexible one which is capable of and was intended to be used for the purpose of making a provision for the regulation of road transport services, in the context of which it is left to the unfettered discretion and judgment of the Corporation where that is the State Undertaking or again whether or not the policy decision has to be by a formal Government order in writing. [353 E F] (iv) The word "provides" in Ch, I means the authority to whom the application has to he made, but as the authority is directed to issue it, notwithstanding anything in Ch No. 1, such an authority might be that which would be comprehended by section 69F(I). [354 E F; 355 A] (v) The fact that some of the variations between the maxima and minima in the number of vehicles proposed to be operated on each route are such as, adopting the test suggested by the learned Advocate General himself, to really contravene r.4 of Chapter V A of Motor Vehicles Rules, 1957 as to require the same to be struck down is not a ground for interference under article 136 of the Constitution. [355 E F]. (vi) The High Courts have held that the schemes are vitiated by non compliance with the requirement of section 66 C and the rules made thereunder. [356 G] (vii) The power conferred on the Government by section 47(1)(a) is not unguided or uncanalised but is intended to serve as a rigid or hard and fast rule, but must be exercised in a manner which would satisfy the test of reasonableness. [359 B C].

The appellant was a dealer under the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947. The appellant purchased certain goods from its dealers in respect of which sales were made to them by it. After taking some adjournments of the enquiry the Commercial Tax Officer made an order disallowing the assessee 's claim for exemption under two heads namely, (i) under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act, Rs. 1,33,730 6 6 and (ii) under Section 5(1) (iii) thereof Rs. 69,65,979 9 6. The Commercial Tax officer made an assessment disallowing the appellant 's claimed exemption under both heads. The Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order but the revision filed to the Board of Revenue was dismissed. On appeal by the appellant, a Division Bench of the High Court held that the appellant could not claim exemption under the said sub clause (ii). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the clear terms of the clause read with the proviso to section 5 (2) (a)(i) of Act 19 of 1941 clearly showed that the production of the prescribed declaration is not obligatory but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned. HELD: The expression "on demand" in r. 27A(ii) means only the requirement of the assessee for claiming exemption and not merely qualifying proviso, and does not enable him to ignore a statutory condition to claim exemption. Sub rule (3) of Rule 27A provides that the declaration form is to be furnished by the dealer and r.27A says that it shall be furnished on demand that is to say it fixes the time when the form is required. This reconcilees the provisions of r. 28A with those of section 5, (2)(b) of that Act, whereas the construction suggested by the learned counsel for the appellant is that the Production of the requisite declaration is a condition for claiming the exemption, but only as a directory provision to subserve the substantive provision in a reasonable way, it cannot be construed as laying down a condition. [630 D F] The expression 'on demand ' only fixes the point of time when a declaration forms are to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with section 5.

The Bihar State Legislature enacted the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Section 3 of the said Act provided that no person shall be deprived of his life or liberty except in accordance with the procedure established by law. The State Government issued a notification on 26th February, 1979 under section 3 of which the provisions of sections 5 to 7 were deemed to have been complied with. The petitioners challenged the validity of the aforesaid notifications on the ground that they had been repeatedly detained from time to time and as such could not be prevented from being released by the State Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act was valid and that the provisions thereof did not apply to them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) there were several undertrial prisoners who had been in jail for periods longer than six months, and (2) there was no justification for keeping the under trial prisoners in custody beyond a reasonable period of time. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the state. It is an essential ingredient of 'reasonable, fair and just procedure ' guaranteed by Article 21 and it is the constitutional obligation of the State to device such a procedure as would ensure speedy trials to the accused. [541C D] 2. The law does not permit any Government to deprive its citizens of constitutional rights on the plea that the State has no adequate financial resources to incur the necessary expenditure needed for improving the administrative and judicial apparatus with a view to ensuring speedy trial. The power of the Court is, therefore, clearly an essential element of reasonable, fair or just procedure guaranteed by article 21 and is not an essential part of any reasonable, just and just. [530D E] 3. In order to enable the court to discharge this constitutional obligation it is necessary that the Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. The Court should be having records from which these particulars can be easily gathered. [540F G] 4. It would be the constitutional duty of the state to device a procedure which would ensure expeditious trial to the appellant by pleading financial or administrative inabili ty and fairness in expenditure, but as it is not only a mandate of equal justice implicit in Article 14 and right to life and liberty conferred by Article 22, but also the compulsion of the constitutional directive embodied in Article 39A. [542F G; 542B] 5. The Constitution has a constitutional obligation to ensure expeditious trials and adequate judicial apparatus for a person accused of an offence and it must be held implicit in the guarantee of Article 21. [543E F] 6. It will be the duty of this Court as a guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to ensure that defendants are not deprived of their life or freedom from exploitation by private parties. The right to speedy trial is, however, clearly and unequivocally an essential constituent of the Eighth Amendment. [544F G]. 7. It has been the duty cast upon the State of Bihar to device the said a procedure for speedy trial to be followed in the case of cases where bail, in proper exercise of discretion, is refused, the accused persons have not to remain in jail longer than is absolutely necessary.

The appellant gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he was entitled to the protection of the Act. The trial court held that the provisions of section 34 (2 A) should have been taken into consideration by the Revenue Courts in deciding the application of the landlord under section 29(2). On appeal, the High Court allowed the application and set aside the order of eviction passed against the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 34 was not applicable to proceedings where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending Act came into force, the period of notice had expired and therefore the landlord could not claim relief from the court. HELD : (i) The provisions of the amending Act which came into operation before the tenancy stood terminated by the notice will have to be taken into account in determining the right of the respondent in the matter of the termination of the tenancy, for the Amending Acts put certain fetters on the right to terminate the tenancy and did not speak of any notice at all. Therefore when there is a dispute about the meaning of sub section (2A) that doubt should be resolved in favour of the tenant, for whose benefit the Amending act was passed. [573 D E] (ii) The legislature could not have intended that the benefit of this beneficent measure should not be extended to tenants in whose cases the tenancy has not yet terminated but where there is any doubt about the interpretation of sub s.(2 A), that doubt must be resolved and the tenant would be entitled to possession. [574 D] (iii) The notice under section34(1)(a) was merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the landlords to terminate tenancy, and no further proceedings could be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof. [575 E F] Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai, ; , referred to.
