(iv) The High Court was right in holding that the amendment did not affect any vested right of landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the notice.

The petitioners were displaced persons from Pakistan. The property of the petitioners was evacuee property and they had no right to it. They claimed that their interest in the houses, as evacuee property, could not be declared evacuee property unless they were declared to be evacuees. Held, that the petitioners were entitled to claim the properties on the ground that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the house. The order was without jurisdiction so far as it affected the rights of the evacueers and was therefore invalid. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, ; , applied. Efrahim Abhimaker vsustral Co operative Society Ltd., ; , referred to. The petitioners were not entitled to any interest in their houses. They had been rightly declared to have been displaced persons under the Act and they could not claim any right of property on the basis of the order made under section 7 of the Act. E brahim Abubaker vs Mussammatunnissa Begum, ; referred to, Per Sarkar, J. The orders of January 10, 1952, were without jurisdiction as the properties in dispute had been acquired under the , and therefore they could be declared evacueies. EBrahim Abbi vsustrial Co operative Bank Ltd., , applied, and Ebman Ali 's share in the property was not evacuee property. Egrahim Abimanaker vs Quanwani, A.I.R. 1952 Cal. 971, approved. Ezrahim Abiqaker vs Tholnissa Begum ; , distinguished. Eebrahim Abhoy vsustal Co operative Co operative Credit Society Ltd. and Efman Ali vsusthan, ; applied. The acts of the Custodian in so faras they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. Eabrahim Abaq vsustan, A,I. R. , referred. Ellrahim Abebaker vsuvittee, A., I.R., 1952 Cal, 971 and Ezman Ali vustral Cooperative Society Ltd.; , distinguished, Per Hidayatullah, J: The order of January, 10,1952 was without jurisdic tion so far it affected rights of an evacuee which the petitioners had in any way been affected by the order. Ehiboobaker 's interest in a house cannot be declared to he evacuee property until that person had first been given a notice under section 8 of the ,. Ehabrahim Ababoobaker v Tek Chand, A I. R., 1952 Bom.

The assessee company was running a factory in the State of Poona. It had two departments namely, (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool and (2) for weaving cloth and (3) for the spinning of cotton. The assessee company entered into an agreement with the selling agents on October 20, 1955 under which the agents agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to make payment of 2% interest thereon at 6% per annum on the net profits of the business. The commission was paid by the agent and further stipulated that the commission would be payable on the amount in dispute. The agreement also provided for the payment of 6% of the loss incurred by the assessee company from their remuneration. The agents agreed that the agents would pay 6 % interest on all the advances made by them, and that the net proceeds of sales of goods in India would be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agents. The assessees were not liable to pay any tax on the remuneration paid to the agent. The Income Tax officer disallowed the deduction claimed by the assessees on the ground that the agreement did not amount to a joint venture for the distribution of profit, and therefore the amount paid to them could not be treated as a capital receipt under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer but held that the payments were not legally deductible under section I0(2) (xv). On further appeal the Tribunal held that though the agreement was a contract of agency and not a joint bargain, it was not a contract in which a provision peculiar to the present case could be made for the purpose of carrying on those expenses. The High Court also held that there was no reason why the amount should not be allowed as deduction under section 1O(2). In appeal to this Court by special leave: HELD : (i) The agreement clearly provided for an agency and the agents by contributing to the investments and by sharing the profits as also the E. losses have actually contributed to a jointly venture and ultimate division of the profits with the principals and the agreement must be construed as an agreement for division of profits into shares and not as an arrangement for division or division of profit. [200 C] (ii) The question whether an amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business or for earning profits in a particular manner is relevant to determine whether the transaction amounted to a Joint venture or a transaction which was incidental or ancillary to the main purpose of the assessee 's business. [201 D] (iii) The fact that the assessee had agreed to share the profits and the losses would not take the case out of the ambit of section 10 (2)(XV) of Income Tax Act, 1922. [202 E] (iv) The amount in question was deductible under s.10(2), (xv) and was not deductible under that section. [203 G] (v) The assessee ' company was a private limited company and the payment out of profits and conditional on profits being earned cannot accurately be described as a payment made to earn profits by the employee.

The assessee, a private limited company, was assessed for the assessment year 1959 60 (the relevant previous year being the year ended March 31, 1959) on a total income of Rs. 43,407/ . The Income Tax Officer held that the accumulated profits of the company amounted to Rs. 1,050 only and directed the Income Tax officer to reopen the assessment by virtue of section 147(b)(e) of the Income tax Act, 1961. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the assessee was entitled to a reference to the High Court under section 256(1) of Income Tax Act, 1922. The Revenue preferred an appeal before the Tribunal which held that Rs. 18,950/ were not liable to be included in the accumulated profit of the Company. The Tribunal referred the following question to the Full Bench of the High court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of this case, the Tribunal was legally correct in holding that Rs 10,000/ constituted a 'accumulated profits ' within the meaning of section 2(6A)(e), Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939?" The High Court answered the first question in favour of the assessee. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the words "accumulation" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not take in current profits and therefore, the expression 'accusation ' in section 6(2)(e). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in answering the first questions in favour. [950C] 2. The words "acumulated profit" in Section 2 (p) (c) of Indian Income Tax are wide enough to include current profits. [ 951D] 3. The expression "accusated profits" occurring in section 4(6)(e)(e ) cannot take in closed profits. The word "accu larly" is used in the sense of 'actually ' and not in a technical sense. It has long since been recognised as an application in that behalf by a party desiring a reference under section 254 operates entirely in favour by one party, although in the course of making the order the Appellate Tribunal may have negatived some points of law raised by that party. [951F G] 4. The statute expressly contemplates an application to the extent that it covers the second question and, therefore, relates to the question whether accumulated profits can take in Current profits. If the application is rejected by the Appellate Tribu nal, it is open to the non applicant, in the event of the Appellate 'Tribunal agreeing to refer the case to the Calcutta High Court, to ask for a reference of those questions of law also which arise on its submissions negatived in appeal by the appellate Tribunal. [952C D] 5. The question whether the provision of Rs 11,000 for tax and Rs. 6,900 for dividend can be taken into account when computing the accumulated income as on March 31.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the respondents were the Mahant. The appellant claimed that he had been in possession of certain lands for over 200 years under a Lakheraj grant made prior to the permanent settlement, that they had been granted in permanent settlement by the Maharaja of Burdwan, that their income was taken into account in fixing the revenue payable by the estate, that the respondents had been holding under a Jakheraj Grant made prior before the permanent Settlement, and that they were entitled to fair rent. The District Munsif held that the lands were not Mal lands within the Zamindari of Burdwan but were granted as Lakhe Rajgun jhair in 1841, and decreed the suits. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court agreed with the District Judge on both the points. Held, that a presumption of lost grant could be made only when there was no person capable of making a grant; and if there was any legal impediment to the making of it, the inference to be drawn from that word cannot outweigh the effect of the non exclusion of the lands from the Mal or regularly assessed estate. The fact that the defendants had been dispossessed of land for a long time without payment of rent, could not affect their title. The suit properties formed part of a permanently settled estate and if a grant had been made in favour of the predecessors of the defendants, it must have been made by the Maharaj of Burdwan or by the Rajgun Jhair. It was only in 1931 that the appellants were entitled, to assessment of fair and equitable rent on the holdings in their possession. The respondents could not be said to have asserted a hostile title and the suit properties had been settled on them. Palaniappa Chetty vs Sreenath Devasikamony, (1917) L.R. 44 I.A. 147, approved. The High Court was right in holding that the suits were within time under article 131 of the Limitation Act as the final settlement of records was published on 16 6 1931 and the present suits were filed within 12 years thereof for establishing the right of the institution to assessment. It could not therefore be said that the suit lands had been extinguished by adverse possession for long over 200 decades.

The appellant was the owner of certain agricultural land in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State. The Tenancy Act, 1948 came into force on 15th December 1965. Section 63(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the Tenancy Act provided that when upon a reference a decision is recorded by the competent authority under the Tenancy act, the Civil Court shall decide the issue whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist or not. The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th April 1966. The trial court held that the certificate granted by the Mamlatdar certifying that the plaintiff was an agricultural labourer and the bar imposed by section 63(c) of the Act would not operate, and decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court agreed with the trial court holding that in such a situation the civil court had undoubtedly jurisdiction to decide the question whether the appellant is an agricultural labourers or not and, therefore, the civil Court will have jurisdiction to determine the issue. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the jurisdiction of the Civil court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the tenancy Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by a competent authority is totally ousted; (ii) the civil courts will have no jurisdiction to try and decide the suit in accordance with the decision recorded by them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of Civil Court to settle a dispute under section 70(a), is limited to the Civil Courts only. It does not ipso facto oust the jurisdiction, of the civil Courts to decide that issue even though they arise for decision in a suit properly constituted civil suit before a civil court having jurisdiction to entertain it. [596D] 2. The High Court was right in holding that if an issue arises in a properly constituted suit which the Civil Judge is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of the tenancy law, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arose in a civil suit, the jurisdiction will have to be determined by the Revenue Court and not by the High court. [597F] 3. The expression "any issues which are required to he settled, decide, decided, or dealt With by any authority competent under the Act, is totally ousting the jurisdiction conferred upon the Civil courts by the Tenancy Acts. [598B] 4. The civil Court has no jurisdiction in this behalf and the civil suit has no jurisprudential value to decide it. It is an issue which has to be decided by the revenue court and not a pure question of fact or law. [599F] 5. The Civil Court has jurisdiction to settle the dispute between the parties under some specific provision of the Bombay Tenancy Act. [600H] 6. The suit is maintainable in view of the provisions contained in section 70A of Tenancy Act and, consequently, the District Judge was competent to decide or dispose of the contention which stands in the forefront a reference to the Mamlatdar under section 71 read with Sections 85 and85A is enevitable. [698B C] 7. The Bombay High Court has initially to deal with the problem as to whether the suit is an 'agricultural labourer ' or not, but it does not automatically oust the jurisdic tion of the court to decide such a question. [500E] 8. The word 'any issues ' in section 63 of the Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 would only mean that if upon assertion and denial and consequent contest an issue arise in a particular proceeding between the par ties which are at variance and which have to he determined to finally dispose of by the civil or revenue court, the matter is required to proceed with or dealtwith by any competent authority. [525F] 9. The words 'any issue which are require to be adjudicated upon or dealt wit nesses under the Bombay Act ' in Section 70(b) do not ipso jure oust the Jurisdiction of the Court to decide a question arising in a proper proceeding. [25G H] 10.

The assessee, a heavy engineering concern manufacturing boilers, wagons, etc., was carrying on the business of manufacturing steam parts and for that purpose the assessee was purchasing spare parts. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the steel Foundry Division was an industrial undertaking to which section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 applied. The Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee and accepted the claim of the asses see. In reference the High Court held that both the Steel Foundry and the Jute Mill Division were new industrial undertakings and therefore the assessee could not be said to be an industrial unit within section 15 C. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The two new undertakings are independent producing arti cles which may be of aid to the principal business but yet the undertakings are distinct and not reconstruction out of the existing business of the assesses. Use by the assessee of the articles produced in its existing business or the concept of expansion are not decisive tests in construing section 15A. (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the two new undertaking were formed by reconstruction of the old business of a new industrial undertaking which he certainly does, would not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section 15(C). Commissioner of Income tax vs Gangs Sugar Corpora tion Ltd., ; , referred to. (iii) The assessee continued to be the same for the purpose of assessment. manufacture or production of articles and there was no transfer of any assets of the new business to the new undertaking which takes place when there is reconstruction of a business. The fact that the articles are produced in the existing, business or, it may produce some other distinct marketable products, even commodities which may feed the oldbusiness cannot be ignored. (iv) The new industrial Undertakings were independently producing articles which might be of help to the main business but nevertheless the undertakings were distinct and separate from the existing ones. (v) The fact of spare parts necessary as components to completion of the end product are now manufactured in the business itself. The new undertaking must not be substantially the same old existing business. (vi) The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets up another industrial unit and the new undertakings can exist even after the cessation of the principal 's undertaking. Use of articles produced by the articles in its old business or its concept of replacement are not determinative tests in interpreting section 15. (vii) The finding that the new industrial units could function on their own, cannot be held to be a different question in the course of practical application of the section.

The inam lands were granted to the appellants for performance of services connected therewith. The inamdars were granted Inam rights in the land. The Inamdars were not inams burdened with services and were not resumable under section 44 B(2)(a)(i) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926. The lands were resumed by the Inamdars on the ground that they had been in possession of the inamdars for over 80 years. The appellants filed a suit against the alienees for recovery of the arrears of inam due to them. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the inams comprised both melwaram and melwarnam and the lands were not personal inams burdened by the inamdar or tenants in respect of their services. On appeal, the District Judge held that the Inam Abolition Act was applicable to the inam lands and that the inam was a permanent lease and the inam granted to an office holder as remuneration for services rendered by them was null and void. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the inams were personal inams and were Inamdars burdened with service and were therefore not resuscitated; (2) the inam were granted in favour of the hereditary office holders as remuneration, for services to be rendered by the appellants and were within the purview of section 44B(2) (a)(ii). HELD: (1 ) The inams in question were resumables under section 43 B(1) though the alienations were made before 1934. Section 44 B (2)(b)(i), however, does not apply to a personal inam burdened with a condition of service and is therefore not dependent upon sub section (1). [549 D] (2 ) The Inam Commission confirmed the grants in favour. of the respondents. The question whether an alienee from the inam is entitled to the kudiwaram rights in inam lands against the Government and thereby defeat the latter 's right to resume the inam does not arise for decision, and the appellants are entitled to raise at this late stage the novel contention that the lease was from year to year. [549 E] (3) The inams were granted by the Government on the basis of a grant made to the temple. The inams did not come within the scope of section 43B(1). The inamdar was not therefore allowed to raise the question as regards the rights of the kuwaram right in the inam land against the government and thereby defeating the latter. [598 H] (4) The inam lands are resumments granted to office holders, as remuneration or remuneration for service to be performed by them and were outside the purview Of section 44 A(2). [550 E F] (5) The Inam Commissioners ' order was not a personal inams but an executive order. The grant of inam in favour the hereditary holder as a remuneration for his services connected with the math or temple as also on the grounds that the lands had been alienated or otherwise lost to the institution or service to which it once belonged or on the allegation that the terms of the grant were not observed, was not valid. [550 G] (6) The grant was made by the Collector in 1934 and the Inam Commission 's order was therefore binding on the appellants.

The respondent Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. Under section 2(c) of the Act, the Municipality had imposed a tax on houses or buildings and the trustees duly paid such tax were required to take inspection thereof and make extracts therefrom. The appellant Corporation levied house tax on the basis of gross annual letting value at the rate of 7% of such value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The respondent contended that under section 79(1) of Act, 1951, the tax could be assessed on the annual letting values less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 76(6) of a Municipality is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the same basis as the valuation based on capital or annual lettingvalue is obviously inconsistent with section 73 under which the annual tenancy value would be the gross annual rent less 10%. [131 E] (ii) The appellant was entitled to levy the house tax at 7% on the gross yearly letting value. Under sections 75 and 76 when a municipality adopts a previously prepared list for any subsequent year, it can be done subject to the provisions of sections 75, 77 and 78. In order to prevent such a result the legislature has provided by sub section 2 of section 79 that where a Municipality adopts a previous prepared list in an earlier year is adopted it becomes the list for such subsequent year subject to its procedure laid down in section 76( 6) after disposing of the objections if any and it is then only that it becomes conclusive evidence of the valuation and the tax assessed thereon for that particular official years. If it were otherwise, the annual rent or value estimated on a particular building or house would be static for 4 years during which the Corporation can go on adopting the assessment lists prepared in an later year provided however, that it prepares a fresh list oncein every 4 years and can adopt an earlier assessment list such as a new assessment has been completed at the commencement of that particular officer. [132 G H] (iii) The word "if" appearing in sub section (1) is obviously a mistake and must be read as "as if" because the word "on" standing by itself makes no sense at all. 79 therefore has to be construed to mean that though a Municipality need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year and need prepare such list once in every 4 year, subject to a procedure laid prescribed by section 76 (6) after dispose of the objection if any, and it was then only the basis for the assessment.

The assessee company carried on the business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1944. During that period, there was a sale of chemicals and raw materials for manufacture. The assessee company sold these chemicals to various persons who were in charge of the chemicals and also to others who were selling the chemicals at a profit. In a confidential report made by the Income tax Officer, the assessee company stated that the price obtained from the purchasers was much more than the trading profits and that the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after the company had been wound up. The Income tax authorities held that the transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the trade, but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business and that therefore the excess represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profit. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court held that there could be no such sale in the ordinary course of business or that the excess was liable to tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The assessee Company was wound up at least in so far as its match manufacture was concerned. That the business was sold as a going concern and was in fact worked by the appellant company on behalf of the buyer till the entire consideration was paid, makes no difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the assessee Company had kept the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf Of the buyer. One cannot fairly say, therefore, that a sale is something more than a winding up sale, not with a view to trading in chemicals and manufacturing chemicals. [968 D E] (ii) The fact that the clause in the Memorandum of Association gave power to the company to Bell chemicals could not make it any difference because, the agreement was never in existence. Therefore, it was impossible to infer that the chemicals were sold in the normal way of business. [936 G H; 969 A B] (iii) The High Courts had held that it was not an accretion to capital but a profit on the sale of the appellant 's stock in trade and that there was no identifiable price for the chemicals or raw materials except by comparing the two prices offered to be paid by the buyer, that is to say, the price without the chemicals, and raw material and the price with them. From that alone it is impossible to hold that the chemical and raw goods were sold at once or from time to time. [981 C D] (iv) The question whether the transaction of sale of an chemicals and the raw materials was a slump transaction or a sale in course of trade must be determined on the narrow ground whether the company 's case is one covered by section 2(2)(a) of the Act. [980 E F] (v) The mere fact that there is realisation of assets and raw resources for match manufacture did not make any difference, because the appellant Company was only a small scale industry with which it had employed large quantity of raw materials. Therefore the sale was of the entire stock.
